questiontext:
Health officials claim that because the foods and beverages mentioned or consumed on many television programs are extremely low in nutritional value, watching television has a bad influence on the dietary habits of television viewers.

The claim by health officials depends on the presupposition that
gf:
Conclusion 

Watching TV has a bad influence on the dietary habits of television viewers.

Evidence (because)

The foods and beverages mentioned or consumed on many TV programs are extremely low in nutritional value.

Evaluate

This argument is saying that when we watch a show, the people on the show are eating junk food. Therefore, watching this show has a bad influence on our dietary habits.

That seems to assume watching the show will somehow affect my dietary habits. If I see Tony Soprano eat a Big Mac, does that mean that I'm now more likely to eat a Big Mac? (By that logic, watching Tony Soprano kill a dude makes me more likely to kill a dude?)

Goal

Look for an answer saying that "at least some people are more likely to eat food X if they see food X being consumed on a TV show".

answers.text: the eating and drinking habits of people on television programs are designed to mirror the eating and drinking habits of television viewers
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: designed

This argument is only about what effect TV eating has on real world eating.

This answer choice is about what causes TV eating to be the way it is. The argument has nothing to do with the backstory of the eating/drinking habits of TV characters, only its ramifications.

answers.text: seeing some foods and beverages being consumed on, or hearing them mentioned on, television programs increases the likelihood that viewers will consume similar kinds of foods and beverages
answers.fb:
Correct

In order for the author to say that "if people on TV are eating junk food, then TV had a bad influence on the dietary habits of TV viewers", she has to assume that TV viewers are somehow changed by watching characters on TV eat junk food.

She specifically has to assume that viewers become more likely to copy the eating/drinking habits of the TV characters.

If we negate this answer, it's saying that "seeing people on TV eating/drinking X does not increase the likelihood that a viewer will eat/drink X". That would badly weaken the argument, so that means this is a correct answer.

answers.text: the food and beverage industry finances television programs so that the foods and beverages that have recently appeared on the market can be advertised on those programs
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: food / beverage industry

This argument is only about what effect TV eating has on real world eating.

This answer choice is about what causes TV eating to be the way it is. Do characters on TV eat junk food because they're mirroring how everyday people eat (choice A), or do they eat junk food because the food / beverage industry is paying for timely product placement (choice C).

We only care about the ramifications of TV characters' eating junk food, not the causal backstory behind why they do.

answers.text: television viewers are only interested in the people on television programs who have the same eating and drinking habits as they do
answers.fb:
Too Strong:  only / same

The author didn't commit herself to the absurdly extreme claim that as a TV viewer, I will only watch shows with people who eat and drink the same as I do.

answers.text: the eating and drinking habits of people on television programs provide health officials with accurate predictions about the food and beverages that will become popular among television viewers
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: health officials' predictions

The author is only claiming that the eating/drinking habits shown on TV will somewhat corrupt the dietary habits of viewers.

She hasn't claimed that viewers will exactly copy the same eating/drinking they see, just that their dietary habits will be worsened somewhat.

This answer poses a very specific claim that a health official can watch TV, and then accurately predict the future of which food and beverages will become popular.

TV could have a bad influence on our dietary habits even if it doesn't provide health officials with accurate predictions.

questiontext:
In an effort to boost sales during the summer months, which are typically the best for soft-drink sales, Foamy Soda lowered its prices. In spite of this, however, the sales of Foamy Soda dropped during the summer months.

Each of the following, if true, contributes to reconciling the apparent discrepancy indicated above EXCEPT:
gf:
Given That

Soda sales are usually highest during the summer months, and Foamy Soda lowered its prices in an effort to boost sales.

How Can it Be That

Foamy Soda's sales dropped during the summer months.

Evaluate / Goal

We need to find four different ways to explain Foam's lower sales numbers.

An answer might say that "lower prices" somehow caused lower sales (a contrast between normal price and lower price.

An answer might use a contrast between what happens for typical sodas (good sales during summer) vs. what happens for Foamy (they're different from other sodas in some worse way).

An answer might use a contrast between typical summers (high soda sales) and this summer (bad soda sales for some reason).

But basically we need to know why this summer isn't like typical summers, Foamy isn't like other sodas, lower-price Foamy isn't like regular priced Foamy, or some other mechanism that can explain why Foamy had disappointing sales this summer.

We can preface our reading of every answer choice by saying, "Foamy had poor sales during the summer months, because .... [answer choice]."

answers.text: The soft-drink industry as a whole experienced depressed sales during the summer months.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

"Foamy had poor sales during the summer months, because .... the whole soft drink industry was struggling during the summer months.

So Foamy's attempt to boost sales by lowering prices failed because it's just a bad time for the soda industry in general.

answers.text: Foamy Soda’s competitors lowered their prices even more drastically during the summer months.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

"Foamy had poor sales during the summer months, because .... the other sodas lowered their prices even more.

So Foamy's attempt to boost sales by lowering prices failed because it's ended up still being more expensive than the competition's sodas.

answers.text: Because of an increase in the price of sweeteners, the production costs of Foamy Soda rose during the summer months.
answers.fb:
Correct

"Foamy had poor sales during the summer months, because .... production costs went up?"

Rising production costs would only affect profit. It doesn't affect the volume of people buying your product. The only way that escalating production costs would affect sales volume is if the company decided to raise its prices in response to those higher production costs.

But we already know that baked-into this Paradox is the idea that Foamy was actually cheaper than usual.

answers.text: A strike at Foamy Soda’s main plant forced production cutbacks that resulted in many stores not receiving their normal shipments during the summer months.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

"Foamy had poor sales during the summer months, because .... a lot of stores that usually sell Foamy were out of stock, as a result of a strike at Foamy's main plant."

So Foamy's attempt to boost sales by lowering prices failed because they weren't able to get their inventory into all the usual stores, so it was impossible for those stores to sell Foamy at the rates they otherwise would have been.

answers.text: The weather during the summer months was unseasonably cool, decreasing the demand for soft drinks.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

"Foamy had poor sales during the summer months, because .... it was a weirdly cold summer, and there's less demand for soda when it's cool."

But what a summer it was for the hot cider and hot chocolate industries!

This, like (A), is explaining the failure of Foamy's price discount plan on a condition that is affecting the soda industry broadly.

questiontext:
No one wants this job as much as Joshua does, but he is not applying for it. It follows that there will not be any applicants, no matter how high the salary that is being offered.

The flawed reasoning in the argument above most closely parallels that in which one of the following?
gf:
Conclusion (it follows that)

No matter how high a salary is offered, no one will apply for this job.

Evidence

No one wants this job as much as Josh, and he's not applying for it.

Evaluate

Uhh, if the salary is $1 million / year, I might like to apply. Can I hear the job description?

This argument is clearly silly, since even if Josh doesn't want this job, one of us might (especially given the conclusion's range of "no matter how high the salary"). But how do we put this into something abstract and portable. 

The copycat ideas are This job / Josh  / applying.

We could try to translate the argument as written.

P: No one wants X as much as Y.
P: Y isn't doing Z.
C:  so no one will be doing Z.

Or we might say something more generic like:

P: No one wants X as much as Y.
P:  Y isn't pursuing X.
C: so no one will pursue X.

Or an even more gisty version:
P:  the Person You'd Most Expect isn't doing it
C:  so no one's gonna do it

Goal

Let's look for an argument saying that, "since the Person You'd Most Expect isn't doing it, no one's gonna do it". If we have multiple contenders, we'll get even more picky with the form.

answers.text: Beth knows better than anyone else how to spot errors in a computer program, yet even she has not found any in this program so far. So it is clear that the errors must all be in the rest of the program.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

The premise ain't so bad, since it could definitely fit into
"Since the person you'd most expect [to spot an error] hasn't done so ..."

But the matching conclusion we'd need is,
"then NOBODY's gonna be able to spot an error."

This takes a completely diff turn and says,
"Beth will eventually spot the error; it's just later in the program"

answers.text: If anyone can decipher this inscription, it is Professor Alvarez, but she is so involved with her new research that it will be impossible to interest her in this sort of task. Therefore, all we can do now is hope to find someone else.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

The premise works, since it's saying
"Since the person you'd most expect [to decipher this incription] can't do so ..."

But the matching conclusion we'd need is,
"then NOBODY's gonna be able to decipher this insciprtion."

But instead, this says
"We'll have to ask someone else."

answers.text: Although he has the strongest motive of anyone for buying Anna’s plot of land, Manfred is not pursuing the matter. Therefore, regardless of how low a price Anna is prepared to accept, she will be looking for a buyer in vain.
answers.fb:
Correct

The premise is saying
"Since the person you'd most expect [to buy Anna's plot of land] isn't pursuing it,"

And so we'd want the conclusion to say,
"then NOBODY's gonna buy it"

And that is what is says, in pretentious LSAT-speak!

This even preserved the "no matter how tempting you make it financially" part of the original conclusion.

answers.text: The person initially most interested in obtaining the contract was Mr. Moore, but he of all people suddenly withdrew his bid. This means that, no matter how discouraged the other bidders had been, they will now redouble their efforts.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

The premise works, since it's saying
"Since the person you'd most expect [to obtain the contract] isn't pursuing it ..."

But the matching conclusion we'd need is,
"then NOBODY's gonna pursue the contract."

But instead, this says
"Everyone else will pursue it twice as hard."

answers.text: Three times Paul would have liked to take advantage of a special vacation package for himself and his family, but each time he was indispensable at the factory just then. So the more seniority Paul acquires, the greater are the constraints on his personal life.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence / Conclusion Match

This doesn't work on any level.

Paul isn't identified as "the most likely suspect" for something.

And the conclusion isn't a prediction that "no one will do [something]". It's a volume dial expression: the more X, the more Y.

questiontext:
Many people limit the intake of calories and cholesterol in their diet in order to lose weight and reduce the level of cholesterol in their blood. When a person loses weight, the fat cells in that person’s body decrease in size but not in number. As they decrease in size, fat cells spill the cholesterol they contain into the bloodstream. Therefore, a person who goes on a low-calorie, low cholesterol diet _______ .

Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
gf:
Setup Claims

Many people limit calories / cholesterol in their diet, to lose weight reduce blood cholesterol.

causal chain 

  lose  ⇢  fat cells  ⇢  cholesterol spilled
 weight     smaller,        into bloodstream
               but same #

Conclusion (therefore)

When someone goes on a low-cal, low-cholesterol diet ...

Evaluate

Based on this info, what is caused by a low-cal / low-cholesterol diet? It never officially says, but the first claim insinuates that going on such a diet is thought to lead to lower weight and lower blood cholesterol.

If the person loses weight, their fat cells spill cholesterol into the bloodstream.

So one of the goals is undermining the other goal. The two goals of this diet were "losing weight" and "lowering blood cholesterol". But the causal chain tells us that when you lose weight it actually increases the blood in your cholesterol (at least in one way).

Goal

Look for a safely worded answer that rewards our understanding that losing weight results in higher blood cholesterol (in at least one sense, because fat cells are dumping their cholesterol into the bloodstream).

Maybe something like, "A person who goes on a low-cal / low cholesterol diet in order to both lower weight and lower cholesterol may find that achieving the first thing messes up the second thing".

answers.text: might at first have an increased level of cholesterol in his or her blood
answers.fb:
Correct

This rewards our understanding that if a low-cal / low-cholesterol diet succeeds in helping a person lose weight, then the person's fat cells will dump cholesterol into the bloodstream, creating an uptick in the level of cholesterol in the blood.

This answer is very safely worded:
- they might (reflecting that people on these diets will not necessarily lose weight)
- at first (reflecting that the uptick in blood cholesterol caused by the shrinking fat cells is still offset by lower cholesterol in their diet)

answers.text: will not lose weight any faster than will a person whose diet is high in calories
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison
 

We don't know anything about a diet high in calories, but this answer certainly offends our common sense.

This answer is saying that someone on a high calorie diet will lose weight at least as fast as will someone on a low calorie diet.

answers.text: might lose more weight by going on a low calorie, high-cholesterol diet than by going on the low-calorie, low-cholesterol diet
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison

We don't know anything about a low cal / high cholesterol diet.

Our common sense would tell us that it's less healthy than a low cal / low cholesterol diet, because we know that calories and cholesterol are not particularly good for us (in any degree of excess). 

So we have no support for the notion that someone would lose more weight by eating more cholesterol.

answers.text: will not decrease the size of his or her fat cells
answers.fb:
Opposite, if anything

Since we think that people going on a low-cal / low cholesterol diet might lose weight, and since losing weight causes the fat cells to decrease in size, we would assume that many people who go on this diet will decrease the size of their fat cells.

answers.text: will both decrease the level of cholesterol in his or her blood and gain weight
answers.fb:
Double Opposite

We think that going on this diet will lead to lower weight and potentially more cholesterol (because of fat cells spilling it into the bloodstream).

questiontext:
Advances in photocopying technology allow criminals with no printing expertise to counterfeit paper currency. One standard anticounterfeiting technique, microprinting, prints paper currency with tiny designs that cannot be photocopied distinctly. Although counterfeits of microprinted currency can be detected easily by experts, such counterfeits often circulate widely before being detected. An alternative, though more costly, printing technique would print currency with a special ink. Currency printed with the ink would change color depending on how ordinary light strikes it, whereas photocopied counterfeits of such currency would not. Because this technique would allow anyone to detect photocopied counterfeit currency easily, it should be adopted instead of microprinting, despite the expense.

Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the recommendation made by the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (should = opinion)

The color-changing ink should be adopted, rather than microprinting.

Evidence

Even though the color-changing ink is more expensive, it would allow anyone to detect photocopied counterfeit currency easily.

Meanwhile, microprinting would be easily detected by experts but not by normal people (which is why counterfeits of microprinting often circulate widely before being detected, i.e. those counterfeit bills get used in a lots of different financial transactions before someone realizes the bill is a fake).

Evaluate

We're choosing between Option A (microprinting) and Option B (color-changing ink).

They each have a stated advantage and disadvantage.

Microprinting wins when it comes to being less costly, but loses when it comes to the fact that it's hard for non-experts to detect counterfeit bills when microprinting is the giveaway.

Color-changing ink loses when it comes to being more costly, but wins when it comes to the fact that it's easy for anyone (including non-experts) to detect a counterfeit bill. 

Goal

Since we're Weighing Tradeoffs, we would want to strengthen by adding another positive to colored-ink, another negative to microprinting, or to hear that the positive about colored-ink outweighs the negative.

answers.text: When an anticounterfeiting technique depends on the detection of counterfeits by experts, the cost of inspection by experts adds significantly to the cost to society of that technique.
answers.fb:
Correct

This elaborates on the negative of microprinting. Microprinting depends on detection of counterfeits by expert (we know that because counterfeits of this style usually circulate widely before being detected, meaning that regular non-experts don't notice that it's a fake and so the counterfeit bill gets used in lots of different transactions).

If we have to pay those experts a lot of money to detect the fakes, then maybe microprinting isn't less costly overall.

Said another way, this answer is taking the one advantage that microprinting supposedly had (less costly) and watering down that advantage a lot, since the money we have to pay for the experts significantly adds to the societal cost of that method.

answers.text: For any anticounterfeiting technique to be effective, the existence of anticounterfeiting techniques should be widely broadcast, but the method by which counterfeits are detected should be kept secret.
answers.fb:
No Distinction, No Impact

As soon as we see "for any counterfeiting technique to be effective", we should start suspecting this answer won't help us. 

We don't want any general truth about counterfeiting techniques. We need a specific fact that makes us lean more towards colored ink and more away from microprinting.

answers.text: The process of microprinting paper currency involves fewer steps than does the printing of paper currency with the special ink.
answers.fb:
Weakens, if anything

This seems to describe a positive about microprinting (it takes the mint fewer steps to make it).

We want negatives about microprinting or positives about colored ink.

answers.text: Before photocopying technology existed, most counterfeits of paper currency were accomplished by master engravers.
answers.fb:
No Impact: past methods

This historical footnote about counterfeiting in the days before photocopying existed is totally irrelevant to our present concern.

Today, there are photocopiers. So given that, should we go with microprinting or colored ink?

This answer offers us nothing to help inform that decision.

answers.text: Many criminals do not have access to the advanced photocopiers that are needed to produce counterfeits of microprinted paper currency that cashiers will accept as real.
answers.fb:
Weakens, if anything

This seems to describe a positive about microprinting (a lot of criminals don't have access to the advanced photocopiers you would need to make a microprint counterfeit)

We want negatives about microprinting or positives about colored ink.

questiontext:
Advances in photocopying technology allow criminals with no printing expertise to counterfeit paper currency. One standard anticounterfeiting technique, microprinting, prints paper currency with tiny designs that cannot be photocopied distinctly. Although counterfeits of microprinted currency can be detected easily by experts, such counterfeits often circulate widely before being detected. An alternative, though more costly, printing technique would print currency with a special ink. Currency printed with the ink would change color depending on how ordinary light strikes it, whereas photocopied counterfeits of such currency would not. Because this technique would allow anyone to detect photocopied counterfeit currency easily, it should be adopted instead of microprinting, despite the expense.

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

Special ink should be adopted, despite the expense.

Evidence (because)

The cheaper alternative, microprinting, allows for counterfeits that circulate widely before being detected (it's easy for experts to detect that they're fakes, but it sounds like it's not so easy for non-experts, which is why it circulates widely).

Special ink would make it easy for non-experts to recognize fakes.

Goal

We need some way to argue that special ink isn't a good idea. Maybe we could defend microprinting as a better option. Maybe there's a third option we haven't heard. Maybe we can hear something negative about special ink.

answers.text: The longer the interval between the time a counterfeit bill passes into circulation and the time the counterfeit is detected, the more difficult it is for law enforcement officials to apprehend the counterfeiter.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This strengthens, by making it seem like the bad part about microprinting (circulates for a while before being discovered) is really bad.

answers.text: Sophisticated counterfeiters could produce currency printed with the special ink but cannot duplicate microprinted currency exactly.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is a bad thing about the ink plan (it's possible for sophisticated counterfeiters to get around this) and a good thing about the microprinting plan (it's not possible for them to get around this).

answers.text: Further advances in photocopying technology will dramatically increase the level of detail that photocopies can reproduce.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This strengthens, by making it seem like the good part about microprinting (regular photocopiers can't print this level of detail) will soon disappear.

answers.text: The largest quantities of counterfeit currency now entering circulation are produced by ordinary criminals who engage in counterfeiting only briefly.
answers.fb:
No Distinction
No Impact

Since the idea of "only briefly dabbling in counterfeiting" doesn't have any different effect, whether we went with microprinting or ink, this has no impact.

answers.text: It is very difficult to make accurate estimates of what the costs to society would be if large amounts of counterfeit currency circulated widely .
answers.fb:
Unclear Impact

This is just saying, "we don't know how costly it is to society [to continue using the microprinting method]". 

If it's very costly, that would strengthen.
If it's not costly, that would weaken.

So this really has no impact.

questiontext:
In all mammalian species, the period of a young mammal’s life in which it is most frequently playful coincides with the period of most rapid growth of the neural connections in the mammal’s brain that give rise to various complex patterns of movement, posture, and social response. Indeed, the neural connections created by frequent play during this period later become indispensable for the mammal’s survival and well-being as an adult.

The statements above, if true, serve LEAST well as evidence for which one of the following?
gf:
Statements

In Most Supported / Must Be True, we're primarily reading for Conditional, Causal, Quantified, or Pivot wording.

The first sentence gives a correlation:

most playful period         | |   most rapid growth of
of young mammal's life         neural connections

The second sentences gives a Conditional / Causal Difference-Maker type idea.

Without these neural connections created by frequent play, the mammal's survival and well-being as an adult would be threatened.

Goal

We're looking for an answer that goes against part of this causal story or at least fails to be derived from this causal story:

lots of play   ⇢ lots of neural ⇢ ability to survive
when young     connections        and be well

answers.text: Young mammals of species that are preyed on by other animals are likely to engage in forms of sudden mock flight, bolting away from locations where no predators are to be found.
answers.fb:
Consistent

Given the connection between play and survival as an adult, it makes sense that a species that depends on running away from predators as an adult would have forms of play that rehearse that action, even when no predators are actually around.

answers.text: The young of nonmammalian species such as fish, reptiles, and birds do not normally engage in playful behavior that serves the function served by play in the development of young mammals.
answers.fb:
No Support

We aren't told anything about non-mammalian species. This answer doesn't conflict with anything we read (it's not a soft version of Must Be False), it's just not supported by anything we read. 

People who did think it was supported by this paragraph would be committing the flaw of thinking, "the only thing they talked about is the only thing for which this is true".

answers.text: Adult mammals are more likely to engage in interactive play with their young if they engaged in similar forms of play when they themselves were young.
answers.fb:
Consistent

Given the connection between play and survival as an adult, it makes some sense that adults who played as a child and have potentially seen the utility of those skills as an adult would be inclined to play with their children.

Given the connection between play and neural development, it also might make some sense to think of propensity to play as a genetic trait that would have a hereditary continuity from adult to child.

answers.text: Mammals that cannot engage in certain common forms of play when young are likely to show certain deficits that limit their subsequent success as adults.
answers.fb:
Supported

This one is most clearly supported by the paragraph, since we were told in conditional form that without this play, we wouldn't have the neural connections, and without those we wouldn't have survival and well-being.

answers.text: Young mammals of predatory species tend to practice in their play inoffensive versions of motions and actions that are useful in finding and catching prey when these mammals become adults.
answers.fb:
Consistent, Same as (A)

This has the same logical relationship as choice (A). Since play is connected to adult survival and well-being, adults who needs to hunt and kill in order to succeed as an adult would rehears less-harmful versions of those actions in their play.

questiontext:
Physicist: Determinism is the view that every event has a preceding cause sufficient for its occurrence. That is, if determinism is true, then the events that are presently occurring could not have failed to occur given the state of the universe a moment ago. Determinism, however, is false because it is impossible to know the complete state of the universe at any given time since it is impossible to measure accurately both the position and velocity of any given subatomic particle at a particular time.

The physicist's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?
gf:
Conclusion 

Determinism is false.  
rephrase:  some events that are presently occurring didn't have to happen. They could have failed to occur. They were not caused by the preceding state of the universe, a moment ago.

Intermediate Conclusion (because)

It's impossible to know the compete state of the universe at any given moment.

Evidence (since)

It's impossible to measure accurately both the position and velocity of any given subatomic particle at a particular time.

Evaluate

(If you want to sound super cool around your friends, that final premise is known as the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle in quantum mechanics.)

The missing link from the Premise to the Intermediate Conclusion is that "If you can't measure position and velocity of a given particle at a given time, then it's impossible to know the complete state of the universe".

The author is assuming that, in order to know the complete state of the universe, you need to know the position and velocity of all subatomic particles at any particular time.

Maybe that's not the case; maybe it counts as knowing the complete state as long as we can say the probability of each particle having a certain position or velocity. But overall, it's unlikely that they're testing us on that move.

So let's focus on the move from Intermediate Conclusion to Main Conclusion: "if it's impossible to know the complete state of the universe at any given moment, then it's not the case that each present moment is a necessary consequence of the state of the universe a moment ago". 

We can think, "Given that ... it's impossible to know the complete state of the universe at any given moment, How can we argue that ... determinism is right."

Determinism is the idea that every event is caused by previous events. Each new complete state of the universe is a necessary result of the previous complete state of the universe.

What does the premise have to do with the conclusion? Whether or not we know what the complete state of the universe is at any given moment doesn't tell us anything about whether there is a complete state at that moment.

Goal

Look for an answer saying something like, "even if it's impossible for us to completely determine the state of the universe at any given time, that doesn't mean that the complete state of the universe isn't causally determined by the preceding moment."

answers.text: That it is impossible to measure accurately both the position and velocity of any given subatomic particle does not imply that it is impossible to know either the position or velocity of all subatomic particles.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This answer is structured like this:
That X is true does not imply that Y is true

We're always objecting that, "the fact the evidence is true does not imply/prove the conclusion".

Does the evidence match X and the conclusion match Y?

Yes, the evidence was saying "it's impossible measure both the position and velocity of any given subatomic particle".

But, no, the conclusion wasn't saying "it's impossible to know the position or velocity of all subatomic particles". 

The conclusion was saying, "It's not the case that every event has a preceding cause sufficient for its occurrence / events presently occurring could have failed to occur given the state of the universe a moment ago".

answers.text: That the complete state of the universe at any given time is unknowable does not imply that the states at that time of the individual subatomic particles making it up are unknowable.
answers.fb:
Premise / Conclusion Reversed

This answer is also structured like this:
That X is true does not imply that Y is true

So we want to know, does the evidence match X and the conclusion match Y?

Did the evidence say "the complete state of the universe at any given time is unknowable"? 

Yes, the Intermediate Conclusion said that, and it is evidence for the Main Conclusion.

Did the Main Conclusion say "the states of the individual subatomic particles making it up are unknowable". 

No. The premise was saying something like that. 

This answer essentially is saying, "The fact that the intermediate conclusion is true doesn't imply that the premise is true".

That would never be an objection we would make. We only care whether premises imply conclusions, not whether conclusions imply premises.

answers.text: That it is impossible to measure accurately both the position and velocity of any given subatomic particle at a particular time does not imply that its position or velocity cannot be accurately measured separately.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This answer is also structured like this:
That X is true does not imply that Y is true

So we want to know, does the evidence match X and the conclusion match Y?

Did the evidence say "it's impossible to measure both position and velocity at a particular time"?

Yes, that's the premise.

Did the author use that to support a Conclusion that says, "position or velocity cannot be measured separately"?

No. The author used it to support the conclusion that says, "It's impossible to know the complete state of the universe at any given time."

answers.text: That it is impossible to know the complete state of the universe at any given time does not imply that there is no complete state of the universe at that time.
answers.fb:
Correct

This answer is also structured like this:
That X is true does not imply that Y is true

So we want to know, does the evidence match X and the conclusion match Y?

Did the evidence say "it's impossible to know the complete state of the universe at any given time?" 

Yes, that's the Intermediate Conclusion..

Did the author use that to support a Conclusion that says or assumes, "there is no complete state of the universe at a given time".

Sigh. Yes, kind of?  Determinism is based on the idea that the complete state of the universe at moment X determines the complete state of the universe at moment Y.

The author is trying to refute this idea by saying, "How could that be true? After all, it's impossible for us to know the complete state of the universe at moment X"

And this answer is saying, "Sure, it's impossible for us to know the complete state, but there still is a complete state. Our lack of knowing it doesn't prove it doesn't exist. So determinism could still be correct."

This answer is written in a frustrating style that is pretty hard to hear as correct if you haven't already thought through your objection to the argument. If you want to see a similar example, try this one.

answers.text: That the position and velocity of any given subatomic particle cannot be jointly measured with accuracy does not imply that this is the case for the position and velocity of all subatomic particles.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This answer is also structured like this:
That X is true does not imply that Y is true

So we want to know, does the evidence match X and the conclusion match Y?

Did the evidence say "it's impossible to measure both the position and the velocity of a particle at a particular time"?

Yes, that's the premise. 

Did the author think that idea implied that "it's impossible to accurately measure the position and velocity of all particles at a particular time"?

No. The author used it to support the conclusion that says, "It's impossible to know the complete state of the universe at any given time."

But in addition to this answer not matching the reasoning move the author made, the reasoning move this answer describes doesn't sound bad.

If we say, "It's impossible to know whether any particular M&M has rat poison in it", then it's it fair to say, "Thus it's impossible, for all M&M's, to know whether they have rat poison in them"?

It sounds like a self-justifying truth, but either way it's not a reasoning move our author made.

questiontext:
People cannot devote themselves to the study of natural processes unless they have leisure, and people have leisure when resources are plentiful, not when resources are scarce. Although some anthropologists claim that agriculture, the cultivation of crops, actually began under conditions of drought and hunger, the early societies that domesticated plants must first have discovered how the plants they cultivated reproduced themselves and grew to maturity. These complex discoveries were the result of the active study of natural processes.

The argument is structured to lead to the conclusion that
gf:
Conclusion

Agriculture did not begin under conditions of drought and hunger (it began when resources were plentiful)

Evidence

Agriculture required the active study of natural processes in order to make complex discoveries about how various plants reproduced and grew to maturity. Devoting yourself to the study of natural processes requires leisure, and leisure requires plentiful resources.

Evaluate

Around 50% of all Main Conclusion questions involve a conclusion that is a rebuttal to someone else's thinking. Knowing this tendency helps us to find the conclusion here. "Although anthropologists claim X ... " is our signifier that the author is probably trying to rebut their claim.

If we follow that hint, we see that she definitely is doing just that. They have claimed that agriculture began under conditions of drought and hunger, and our author lays out a case that agriculture, based on what it requires, would have to have began during a time of plentiful resources.

Goal

Find an answer that sounds like "agriculture did NOT begin under conditions of drought/hunger, it began when resources were plentiful".

answers.text: whenever a society has plentiful resources, some members of that society devote themselves to the study of natural processes
answers.fb:
Too Strong

The author said that when plentiful resources are present, people have leisure. Were we told that whenever people have leisure, some members of society study natural processes? 

No, it said that leisure was required for people to devote themselves to studying natural processes. This is acting like leisure guarantees people will devote themselves.

That was not said.

answers.text: plants cannot be cultivated by someone lacking theoretical knowledge of the principles of plant generation and growth
answers.fb:
Too Strong: cannot be cultivated
Out of Scope: theoretical knowledge

This is an extreme idea the author wasn't defending. She definitely thinks that early agriculturalists needed to discover how plants work, but it could be practical knowledge, not theoretical.

Either way, this is not close to the Main Conclusion which should be "agricultural developed in a societies with plentiful resources".

answers.text: agriculture first began in societies that at some time in their history had plentiful resources
answers.fb:
Correct

This rebuts the anthropologists position. Agriculture didn't begin under conditions of drought and hunger. It began under conditions of plenty.

How is it supported?
- developing agriculture happened from people having lots of time to study complex relationships in natural processes, which requires leisure, which requires plentiful resources.

answers.text: early agricultural societies knew more about the natural sciences than did early nonagricultural societies
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison

The author isn't building any case about "who knows more about natural sciences": early agricultural societies or early nonagricultural societies.

answers.text: early societies could have discovered by accident how the plants they cultivated reproduced and grew
answers.fb:
Out of Scope:  by accident

This feels like the opposite of what the author is presenting. She's saying that learning how to cultivate plants required deliberate study, not lucky accident.

questiontext:
In the past decade, a decreasing percentage of money spent on treating disease X went to pay for standard methods of treatment, which are known to be effective though they are expensive and painful. An increasing percentage is being spent on nonstandard treatments, which cause little discomfort. Unfortunately, the nonstandard treatments have proved to be ineffective. Obviously, less money is being spent now on effective treatments of disease X than was spent ten years ago.

Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
gf:
Conclusion

Less money is being spent on effective treatments of X now than ten years ago. 

Evidence

Only the standard treatments for X are effective, 
and
a decreasing percentage of money being spent on treatments of X now than ten years ago.

Evaluate

Let's say we run a business and every month we spend $2000 on advertising -- $1000 is newspaper ads and $1000 is Facebook ads.

We currently spend 50% of our advertising budget on newspaper ads.

If we decide to experiment and add another $1000 into the Facebook ads category, then we'd be spending $1000 on newspaper and $2000 on Facebook.

That means we now spend 33.3% of our ad dollars on newspaper ads.

We now spend a decreased percentage of our ad budget on newspaper ads, but do we spend less money on newspaper ads? 

No, we spend the same amount of money.

The author of this argument is confusing those two things. 

The author is making the move from, "If you spend a lower percentage on standard (i.e. effective) treatments now, then you spend less money on standard (i.e. effective) treatments now."

But we just showed that you can spend a lower percentage on something without spending less money on it. 

If we were trying to contradict the author's conclusion, we could say, "we still spend just as much money on effective treatments --- over the last ten years we poured a lot more money into ineffective treatments, so the money we spend on effective treatments is a smaller % of the overall pie, but we haven't reduced the amount of what we spend on effective treatments."

Goal

The only wiggle room to this argument is if the overall amount of money spent on treating disease X has gone up (that's the only way that a lower % of a total could still end up equaling at least as big a number as before).

i.e. 50% of a $2000 ad budget was the same as
33.3% of a $3000 ad budget

So to lock in the author's conclusion, we want to hear that the total is the same, or that it's lower than before.

answers.text: Varieties of disease X requiring expensive special treatment have become less common during the past decade.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

Since this argument just hinges on whether "lower % of total spending  = less spending", this answer isn't telling us something that could prove the conclusion.

It strengthens the idea that we're spending less money, but it definitely doesn't 100% prove it.

answers.text: Nonstandard methods of treating disease X are more expensive now than they were a decade ago.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Conclusion

The conclusion is about how much money we're spending on effective (i.e. standard) treatments, so hearing about how much nonstandard treatments cost has nothing to do with how much we're spending on effective treatments.

answers.text: Of total medical expenditures, the percentage that is due to treatment of disease X increased during the past decade.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: total medical 

We don't care what % of a nation's total health care expenditures is related to X.

We just care whether the actual amount of money being spent to treat disease X has gone up, stayed the same, or gone down.

answers.text: Most of the money spent on treating disease X during the last decade went to pay for nonstandard treatments.
answers.fb:
No Impact

It doesn't really matter to this argument whether standard or nonstandard treatments claim more or less than 50% of the budget. 

This argument is all about the relative movement of spending on effective treatments over time.  Whether it started out above or below 50% of total spending, it could still be less now than it was ten years ago.

So finding out that standard (effective) treatments are less than 50% of total spending sounds kinda strengthen-ish, but it doesn't mathematically prove the conclusion.

answers.text: The total amount of money spent on treating disease X slowly declined during the past decade.
answers.fb:
Correct

This mathematically proves the conclusion.

A lower percentage of money is spent on effective (standard) treatments nowadays. If the total amount of money being spent on treatments nowadays is lower than before, then we're definitely spending less money on effective (standard) treatments.

A smaller percentage of a smaller total definitely comes out to a smaller actual number.

Here's an example of a percentage and a total going down, which is guaranteed to result in a smaller actual number.

                    Total     % on eff   Amt on eff
10 yrs 
ago           $100k         40%        $40k

 now           $90k         30%         $27k

questiontext:
When an ordinary piece of steel is put under pressure, the steel compresses; that is, its volume slightly decreases. Glass, however, is a fluid, so rather than compressing, it flows when put under pressure; its volume remains unchanged. Any portion of a sheet of glass that is under sustained pressure will very slowly flow to areas under less pressure. Therefore, if a single, extremely heavy object is placed in the middle of a horizontal sheet of glass of uniform thickness and if the glass is able to support the weight without cracking, then the sheet of glass will eventually _______.

Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
gf:
Setup

(Unlike steel) when you put glass under pressure, the volume stays the same because glass is a fluid, so it flows to areas under less pressure.

The Blank

If you have a horizontal sheet of glass of uniform thickness and you put a really heavy object in the middle of it, then assuming the glass can support the the weight without cracking, the sheet of glass will eventually ______ .

Evaluate

We need to use the information we were provided about how glass behaves when it's put under pressure, to fill in this blank about what will happen when we put a horizontal sheet of glass under pressure by putting a heavy object in the middle of it.

We were told that when glass is put under pressure, the fluid glass will flow very slowly from areas under sustained pressure to areas under less pressure.

If we put a heavy object in the center of a sheet of glass, then the center will be under sustained pressure, while areas way from the center (like the four corners, for example) will be under less pressure.

So we know that the fluid glass will flow very slowly away from the center of the sheet of glass. 

Goal

The blank is saying that eventually (this is accounting for the very slow flow of glass) ... what will happen?

Eventually, the fluid underneath the heavy object will flow away from the center to areas under less pressure.

answers.text: become larger in size yet still be of uniform thickness
answers.fb:
Contradicted

Becoming larger in size would mean that the volume had increased. But we were told that glass's "volume remains unchanged" when put under pressure.

answers.text: flow toward the point at which the pressure of the object is greatest
answers.fb:
Contradicted

We were told that "any portion of glass under pressure will very slowly flow to areas under less pressure."

So we would expect the glass will flow toward the point at which the pressure is least.

answers.text: compress, although not as much as a piece of steel would
answers.fb:
Contradicted

This answer is saying that the sheet of glass would compress. 

The second sentence says that, "Glass, however, is a fluid, so rather than compressing, it does [something else]."

answers.text: divide into exactly two pieces that are equal in neither size nor shape to the original piece of glass
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: divide
Too Strong: exactly two pieces

We're talking about glass that can support the weight without cracking, so this paragraph doesn't seem to be leading into glass dividing/cracking into two pieces.

answers.text: be thinner in the portion of the glass that is under the pressure of the object than in those portions of the glass that are not under that pressure
answers.fb:
Correct

This answer feels like a bit of a stretch, but it helps us that the first four answers were pretty much contradicted. That would make anything non-contradictory be the most logical completion.

We were looking for the idea that the flow of glass would move away from the center toward the areas under less pressure. Would this cause the glass under the heavy object to be thinner and the other parts thicker?

Sure, since the glass started out at uniform thickness and now we're moving material away from the center to other areas.

Picture one of those floating rafts people lay on in swimming pools, a rectangular shape with uniform thickness. 

If you put that raft on the sidewalk and then sat in the middle, your butt would sink down close to the sidewalk, while the headrest and footrest of the raft would puff up.

That's because our butt pressure is sending the air from the area under sustained pressure to the areas under less pressure. That's the same phenomenon this answer choice is describing, in relation to a sheet of glass.

questiontext:
The male sage grouse has air sacs that, when not inflated, lie hidden beneath the grouse’s neck feathers. During its spring courtship ritual, the male sage grouse inflates these air sacs and displays them to the female sage grouse. Some scientists hypothesize that this courtship ritual serves as a means for female sage grouse to select healthy mates.

Which one of the following, if true, most strongly supports the scientists' hypothesis?
gf:
Curious Fact

Why does the male inflate its air sac and display it to the female, during the courtship ritual?

Hypothesis

It's so the female can select healthy mates.

Evaluate

The most common way to strengthen a hypothesis is to add plausibility to the causal story the author is telling. We'd love to hear that displaying air sacs is a way for a female to select healthy mates. We'd love a "no cause, no effect" answer that suggests that "when a female isn't trying to inspect the health of mates, the males don't inflate their air sacs". 

Goal

Let's find an answer that supports the plausibility that inflated air sacs help a female to determine how healthy a male is, (or an answer that rules out an alternate explanation for why the male inflates its air sacs during the mating ritual, like "it's NOT to make himself look bigger than other males".)

answers.text: Some female sage grouse mate with unhealthy male sage grouse.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

The fact that some females will mate with unhealthy males, if anything, undermines the author's story that females are investigating whether a potential mate is healthy.

answers.text: When diseased male sage grouse were treated with antibiotics, they were not selected by female sage grouse during the courtship ritual.
answers.fb:
Unclear Impact

It's hard to interpret this because it's not clear whether the males' inflated air sac display looked like that of a sick male or that of a male who was healthy again from antibiotics. 

We can't really tell whether the female rejected them when they still look diseased (which would fit the author's hypothesis) or whether she rejected them even once she were back to normal (which would undermine the author's hypothesis).

answers.text: Some healthy male sage grouse do not inflate their air sacs as part of the courtship ritual.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This is incredibly weak (so unlikely to be correct on Str, Wkn, Paradox) and also off topic, since it's talking about males that don't inflate their air sacs.

It could be relevant if we knew these males were uninterested in mating with females. That would sort of be a "no cause, no effect" strengthener (males who have no interest in mating with females DON'T bother to inflate their air sacs for the health inspection). 

But this is saying there's at least one male that does want to mate but doesn't inflate its air sac. That doesn't help us figure out why the males that DO inflate their air sacs are doing so.

answers.text: Male sage grouse are prone to parasitic infections that exhibit symptoms visible on the birds’ air sacs.
answers.fb:
Correct

If male sage grouse are prone to parasitic infections that exhibit symptoms visible on their air sacs, then a visible cue exists that females can use to judge a male's health based on the appearance of the air sacs. This provides a direct link that supports the hypothesis that the air sac display helps females select healthy mates.

answers.text: The sage grouse is commonly afflicted with a strain of malaria that tends to change as the organism that causes it undergoes mutation.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The fact that sage grouse are commonly afflicted with a particular strain of malaria doesn't tell us anything about whether the malaria presents in the air sacs, or whether females would be able to ascertain any health information by looking at inflated air sacs.

questiontext:
Inez: In these poor economic times, people want to be sure they are getting good value for their money. I predict people would be more willing to buy antiques at our fair if we first have the object inspected by professional appraisers who would remove any objects of questionable authenticity.

Anika: I disagree with your prediction. Our customers already are antiques experts. Furthermore, hiring professional appraisers would push up our costs considerably, thus forcing us to raise the prices on all our antiques.

Anika's response proceeds by
gf:
Inez's Conclusion

If we have our antique objects inspected by professional appraisers who could remove any questionably authentic pieces, people would be more willing to buy antiques at our fair.

Inez's Evidence

In these poor economic times, people want to be sure they're getting good value for their money.

Anika's Conclusion

No, the inspection by appraisers wouldn't make people more willing to buy our antiques.

Anika's Evidence

The customers are already themselves experts, and hiring an appraiser would force us to raise our prices to cover those costs.

Evaluate

This is neither here nor there, but Inez ... in poor economic times, why would anyone buy antiques?!  (ok, just had to say it)

Does Anika's response seem like any of our 3 most common moves on Method:
    - making / breaking an Analogy
    - showing the Faulty Implications of an Idea
    - eliminate / suggesting an Alternative

Sure, it seems like the 2nd would apply. Anika is showing how Inez's recommendation would lead to the bad consequence (faulty implication) of needing to raise prices, in order to cover the costs of the appraisers.

Anika's other point is raising an Overlooked Consideration, that the customers are already antique experts so they don't really crave or benefit from an appraiser testifying to an object's authenticity. 

She's point out that part of Inez's pitch wouldn't be a compelling upsell for their customer base.

Goal

Look for any answer that's descriptively true. It'll probably comment on Anika rejecting Inez's plan by saying it's supposed upside isn't really something their customers would value, or by saying that it comes with a compelling downside (they'd have to raise prices).

answers.text: indicating that a particular plan would have an effect contrary to the anticipated effect
answers.fb:
Correct

The anticipated effect of Inez's plan was people to be more willing to buy antiques.

Was Anika saying that Inez's plan would lead to people being less willing to buy antiques?

Sure. She doesn't explicitly say that, but Anika is saying that Inez's plan would force them to raise prices on their antiques.

Is it common sense to think, "if you raise the price on your antiques, people will be less willing to buy it?"

Yes. 

(There might be a voice in your head saying, "Not necessarily! Sometimes people are more attracted to buying something because the price is higher, like a Fendi bag, or like really expensive wine." Sure, but that's not the typical association. Businesses offer sales and discounts and coupons in order to create demand, in order to make people more willing to buy. They don't raise prices to do that, generally.)

answers.text: claiming that a particular plan should not be adopted because, while effective, it would have at least one undesirable consequence
answers.fb:
Contradicted (while effective)

This answer is wicked tempting because "undesirable consequence" is a great match for the Faulty Implications answer we were anticipating.

Anika did claim that the plan has at least one undesirable consequence (raising prices).

But she never said the plan would be effective. Effectiveness is measured by whether the Plan achieves its Goal of "making people more willing to buy antiques at the fair".

Since Anika says "I disagree with your prediction", she is saying "I don't think the plan would be effective in making people more willing to buy antiques at the fair".

So that part of the answer is contradicted by Anika's statements.

answers.text: arguing that an alternative plan could achieve a desired result more easily than the plan originally proposed
answers.fb:
Out of Scope (alternative plan)

Anika doesn't offer any alternative plan. She just points out problems with Inez's plan.

answers.text: questioning the assumption that authorities are available who have special knowledge of the problem under discussion
answers.fb:
Out of Scope (appraisers' availability)

Nothing Anika says ever touches on whether there would be appraisers available to judge the authenticity of these antiques.

She just says the appraisers are unnecessary (since the customers are already experts), not unavailable.

answers.text: offering a counterexample in order to show that a particular general claim is too broadly stated
answers.fb:
Out of Scope (counterexample)

The only general claim Inez makes is that "in poor economic times, people want to be sure they're getting good value for their money".

A counterexample to that would involve a specific case of poor economic times where someone didn't care about getting good value for their money.

Anika doesn't present anything resembling that.

questiontext:
The number of calories in a gram of refined cane sugar is the same as in an equal amount of fructose, the natural sugar found in fruits and vegetables. Therefore, a piece of candy made with a given amount of refined cane sugar is no higher in calories than a piece of fruit that contains an equal amount of fructose.

The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument
gf:
Conclusion (Therefore)

A piece of candy with x amount of refined cane sugar is no higher calorie than a piece of fruit with x amount of fructose.

Evidence

The number of calories in a gram of refined cane sugar is the same as in a gram of fructose.

Evidence

Given that a gram of refined sugar has the same caloric content as a gram of fructose,

How could we argue that  a piece of candy with x grams of refined sugar does have more calories than a piece of fruit with x grams of fructose?

Well when it comes to the head to head battle of refined sugar vs. fructose, we know they're tied in calories.

But could the candy have other ingredients (fat? carbs? protein?) that also adds calories that the fruit doesn't have?

Goal

This is basically a Part vs. Whole flaw, since the argument is thinking that since the "sugar part" of the candy/fruit would have the same calories, the candy/fruit "overall" would have the same calories.

answers.text: fails to consider the possibility that fruit might contain noncaloric nutrients that candy does not contain
answers.fb:
No Impact (noncaloric ingredients)

Since this starts with fails to consider / overlooks possibility, we would read this answer as a potential objection.

Can we weaken the argument by talking about noncaloric nutrients that candy lacks?

No. Our court case is about arguing that candy has more calories than fruit. An answer about noncaloric ingredients will have no impact on the conversation.

answers.text: presupposes that all candy is made with similar amounts of sugar
answers.fb:
Too Strong (all)

Since this starts with presupposes / takes for granted, we would read this answer like we're doing Necessary Assumption.

Did the author need to assume that EVERY single piece of candy in the universe is made with a similar amount of sugar?

Of course not. That would be a crazy claim to make in the real world. The author never committed herself to that crazy claim. Her conclusion is just saying "IF you find a piece of candy and fruit with similar grams of sugar, then they will have the similar calories overall."

answers.text: confuses one kind of sugar with another
answers.fb:
Bad Description

When we see the confuses X with Y format, we're asking ourselves whether the author considered two different things to be the same thing.

Or, we're asking ourselves whether the author made a move from X to Y.

Was the author thinking that refined cane sugar and fructose are the same thing?

No. She knew that they were different, that refined cane sugar is found in candy whereas fructose is found in fruit.

And her premise about a gram of either type of sugar containing the same calories is just a scientific fact, a similarity they have. If we saw that crows and robins both have beaks, that doesn't mean we're confusing one with the other.

answers.text: presupposes what it sets out to establish, that fruit does not differ from sugar-based candy in the number of calories each contains
answers.fb:
Not Circular Reasoning

When an answer says that the premise repeats the conclusion or assumes / presupposes / presumes the truth of the conclusion, that is what is known as Circular Reasoning.

It's super common as a wrong answer and incredibly rare as a correct answer.

To assess whether this is actually happening, you ask yourself,
"Do I have to believe the conclusion in order to accept the premise?"

Can we accept that a gram of refined cane has the same calories as a gram of fructose, without accepting that a piece of candy with x grams of refined sugar has the same calories as a piece of fruit with x grams of fructose?

Definitely. That means the author wasn't presuming her conclusion.

answers.text: overlooks the possibility that sugar might not be the only calorie-containing ingredient in candy or fruit
answers.fb:
Correct

Since this starts with fails to consider / overlooks possibility, we would read this answer as a potential objection.

Can we weaken the argument by saying that there are OTHER calorie-containing ingredients in candy or fruit?

Heck yeah, that was our prediction. What about carbs / fat / protein / etc?

If there are other calorie-containing ingredients besides the sugar content, then we can't just say that a piece of candy and fruit that are tied when it comes to sugar are tied when it comes to calories. We need a full accounting for all the ingredients that contain calories.

questiontext:
In defending the Hyperion School of Journalism from charges that its program is of little or no value to its students, the dean of the school pointed to its recent success in placing students: 65 percent of its graduates went on to internships or jobs in print or broadcast journalism.

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the defense offered by the dean?
gf:
Conclusion

The Hyperion School of Journalism offers a valuable program to its students.

Evidence

65% of its graduates went on to internships or jobs in print or broadcast journalism.

Evaluate

The dean is defending the utility of the Hyperion School's program by pointing to the success of its graduates in securing positions in the field of journalism. 

GIVEN THAT  65% of grads went on to internships or jobs in journalism, 
HOW CAN WE ARGUE this school's program is not valuable to students?

Maybe we could say the program itself may not be the reason for the graduates' success. We could challenge the idea that the program added significant value by introducing an alternate explanation for the placement success. 

Maybe we could point to an alternate way they could have gotten internships or jobs that would have been cheaper / more efficient. 

Maybe the school places you in an internship/job, but they've prepared you so poorly that you quickly get fired from that position and blacklisted in the industry.

Goal

Let's find an answer that allows us to argue that the school is not offering a lot of value to the students, or that offers an alternate explanation for why a majority of grads do end up getting internships/jobs in journalism.

answers.text: More than half of the school’s students came from jobs in journalism to improve their skills.
answers.fb:
Correct

If more than half of the school's students were already employed in journalism and returned to improve their skills, the success in job placements could be attributed to their prior experience and not necessarily the value added by the Hyperion School's program. 

To put it another way, they didn't need this school to get an internship / job in journalism. They had already done that before they came to the school (Effect w/o Cause). So this undermines the idea that the School provided them with the value of "being able to get a job in journalism". 

The dean was assuming a difference:  that before they came to the school, they wouldn't have been able to get these jobs.

answers.text: Some newspaper editors do not regard journalism schools as a necessary part of the training of a journalist.
answers.fb:
Weaker Impact

It somewhat undercuts the dean's evidence to hear that some people who are hiring for journalism positions don't consider going to a journalism school a necessity.

But this is very weak because it's only talking about "some editors" (at least one), and the dean was never saying that you HAVE to go to a school to get a job. 

She was just saying that getting students a job was part of the value the school provided.

answers.text: The number of cities with more than one major newspaper has declined sharply over the last 25 years.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The number of cities with multiple newspapers doesn't impact whether the program directly contributes to its graduates' success in securing jobs or internships, or otherwise offers value to its students.

answers.text: The program offered by the Hyperion School of Journalism is similar in quality and content to those offered by its peer institutions.
answers.fb:
Unclear Impact

In order for this do do anything, we'd have to know whether the peer institution do or don't provide something valuable to their students.

Without knowing that, the fact these schools are all pretty similar doesn't tell us whether or not they're valuable.

answers.text: The proportion of applicants to the Hyperion School of Journalism that are admitted is lower than it was ten years ago.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The change in the proportion of applicants admitted over the years does not directly relate to the program's value or its graduates' placement success. This just sounds like it's harder to get admitted to the Hyperion School these days, but that doesn't directly speak to whether the school provides any value (if anything, it sounds like students perceive that it DOES provide value, if the application process has become more competitive).

questiontext:
First legislator: Medical research is predominantly done on groups of patients that include only men. For example, the effects of coffee drinking on health are evaluated only for men, and studies are lacking on hormone treatments for older women. Government-sponsored medical research should be required to include studies of women.

Second legislator: Considerations of male/female balance such as this are inappropriate with respect to research; they have no place in science.

Which one of the following rejoinders, if true, most directly counters the second legislator's objection?
gf:
First L's Conclusion

Govt-sponsored medical research should have to include studies of women.

Second L's Objection

(No they shouldn't). Considerations of male/female balance are inappropriate in medical research, and they have no place in science.

Evaluate

Since we're trying to logically counter the 2nd person, we want to defend the 1st person's idea while responding to the 2nd person's.

It sounds like the second person is saying that science is sex-blind, but is it? Didn't science figure out that males have Y-chromosomes and females don't? Aren't there scientific differences between the sexes that make it scientifically relevant whether we're testing males vs. females?

Goal

Let's find an answer that allows us to argue that having some research done on women IS appropriate. It does have a place in science. Doing research only on men is worse.

answers.text: Government-sponsored research is supported by all taxpayers, both male and female.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The fact that government-sponsored research is supported by both male and female taxpayers does not directly address whether considerations of male/female balance are appropriate or necessary within scientific research itself.

answers.text: Serving as a subject for medical research can provide a patient access to new treatments but also can subject the patient to risks.
answers.fb:
No Impact

While serving as a subject can bring both benefits and risks, this does not speak to whether male/female balance is essential for quality scientific outcomes. It doesn't counter the idea that gender balance considerations have no place in research.

answers.text: Government-sponsored medical research is often done in military hospitals or prisons that hold only male residents.
answers.fb:
Opposite Impact

This helps someone defend the practice of having predominantly male-only research subjects:  "This govt sponsored research is being done where there are only males around to test, so of course the subjects are often all male".

We want to reject that approach and agitate for the inclusion of females as research subjects.

answers.text: The training of male and female scientists does not differ according to their sex.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The fact that the training of scientists does not differ by sex does not address the question of whether male/female balance in patient subjects is critical for scientific research.

answers.text: Restriction to males of the patient base on which data are collected results in inadequate science.
answers.fb:
Correct

This counters the second legislator's point by arguing that excluding women results in a lack of comprehensive understanding within the research. 

In other words, "of course a male/female balance has a place in science. After all, when you lack that balance, it results in inadequate science."

questiontext:
Using rational argument in advertisements does not persuade people to buy the products being advertised. Therefore, advertisers who replace rational argument with nonrational appeals to emotion in advertisements will persuade people to buy the products being advertised.

Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?
gf:
Evidence

Using rational argument →  doesn't persuade 
  in advertisements               ppl to buy

Conclusion

Using nonrational appeals → will persuade
     to emotion in ads                  ppl to buy

Evaluate

Consider this analogous argument:
People who drive Toyota's do not live on Mars.
So, ppl who don't drive Toyota's do live on Mars.

We're not allowed to just "flip a lightswitch" on claims. It's an illegal Negation (aka Necessary vs. Sufficient).

Our author's argument was basically this:
Rational arguments don't persuade ppl.
Thus, nonrational arguments will persuade ppl. 

Goal

Look for an argument that is like,
Prem - Things of type X don't do thing Y.
Conc - Things not of type X will do thing Y.

answers.text: People who ask others for favors are refused. Therefore, anyone who has not had the experience of being refused has never asked for a favor.
answers.fb:
Valid Logic

This presents a conditional and then concludes a valid contrapositive.

We're looking for a conclusion that sounds like, "Thus if you're not the 1st thing, you're not the 2nd thing".

This one validly concludes, "Thus if you're not the 2nd thing, you're not the 1st thing."

PREMISE
   ask for favors → refused
CONCLUSION
  ~refused → ~ask for favors

answers.text: In the past, people who have tried to solve their problems by discussing them have often failed. Therefore, in the future, people who try to solve their problems by discussing them will often fail.
answers.fb:
Different Flaw:  past = future

This doesn't "flip the lightswitch" in going from premise to conclusion, it just says that "if discussing problems failed to solve them in the past, then doing the same thing will probably fail in the future too".

answers.text: Using a computer has not improved students’ writing skills. Thus, students should not try to improve their writing skills by using a computer.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

If our premise is saying,
    using a computer has not improved skills
then we would want to see a conclusion saying,
   So, not using a computer will improve skills

Instead, the conclusion is just a normative (should) claim, which doesn't match the premise or the original argument.

answers.text: A person who doesn't have positive letters of reference cannot get a good job. Therefore, the better the letters of reference a person has, the better the job that person will get.
answers.fb:
Different Flaw:  Relative vs. Absolute

This premise establishes that positive letters of reference are required to get a good job. The conclusion then takes that yes/no type of language and turns it into Volume Dial type language.

The better the reference, the better the job.

That is a flaw, but it's not the same as the illegal flip of the lightswitch we're looking for. This answer choice would only match the original argument if the original's conclusion had said,

Thus, the more rational an argument an advertisement makes, the less persuaded people will be to buy the product.

Given this premise
   ~no pos letter of ref  → can't get good job
We would have wanted the conclusion to say
    So, if you have a positive letter of reference, you will get a good job.

answers.text: People never learn to program a computer by reading poorly written directions. Therefore, if people read well-written directions, they will learn to program a computer.
answers.fb:
Correct

This presents a conditional premise and then performs an illegal negation on it.

Premise

   read poorly written directions → don't learn programming

Conclusion

    read well written directions → do learn programming

This matches well with the original:

Premise

   use rational argument → does not persuade

Conclusion

    use nonrational appeal → does persuade

questiontext:
A commercial insect trap consists of a small box containing pesticide mixed with glucose, a sweet substance known to attract insect pests. Yet in households where this type of trap has been used regularly for the past several years, recently installed traps are far less effective in eliminating insect pests than were traps of that type installed several years ago. Research scientists have hypothesized that traps in those households decreased in effectiveness because successive generations of the pests developed a resistance to the pesticide in the traps.

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the hypothesis?
gf:
Curious Phenomenon

Recently installed traps are far less effective than in eliminating pests than were traps installed several years ago.

Hypothesis 

The reason traps in certain households decreased in effectiveness is that successive generations of insects developed a resistance to the pesticide in the traps.

Evaluate

Since the author is presenting a Curious Comparison (the more recently installed traps eliminate far fewer pests than the old ones did) and trying to explain it (the newer pests have developed resistance to the poison inside), we would think about this as we always do when an author is Explaining a Curious Fact:

- could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
maybe the newer traps are less effective because the trap manufacturer changed the glucose/poison formula. maybe the newer traps are less effective because the insects have just learned to avoid them by seeing their friends and relatives enter but never exit. 

- how plausible is the Author's Explanation for the curious fact?
if we were to insert some insects into these households who haven't been living with these traps for successive generations (and thus who wouldn't have been able to develop resistance), do they get killed at the higher rate like when we first installed the traps?

Goal

Since this is Weaken, we want an answer to either
- suggest an Alternate Explanation for why these traps don't seem to be as effective any more, or
- undermine the plausibility of the Author's Explanation that successive generations of pests have developed resistance to the pesticide

answers.text: In households where the traps have been used regularly, the proportion of insect pests that have a natural aversion to eating glucose has increased with each successive generation;
answers.fb:
Correct

This supplies an Alternate Explanation for why the traps are less effective. The pests haven't evolved a tolerance for the poison (pesticide) inside the trap. They've just evolved an aversion to the glucose that is supposed to be baiting them to come inside.

So the real reason the traps aren't effective any more is not that the pests are eating the poison but not dying from it; it's that they aren't even going inside the traps and eating the glucose/poison combo.

answers.text: Even when only a few individuals out of an entire generation of insects survive the effects of a pesticide, the offspring of those individuals are usually resistant to that pesticide.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This increases the plausibility of the Author's Explanation by attesting to the fact that offspring of parents who survived a bout with the pesticide have usually developed a resistance to that pesticide.
