Unstated
Out of Scope: shift away

This doesn't match the final sentence, which is about "harm".

This is about whether shifting away from paper would benefit the nation. That wasn't ever said, so it's not going match our explicit conclusion.

answers.text: at this time more harm is being done to the environment nationwide by the use of paper than by the use of plastics
answers.fb:
Correct

This matches the meaning of the final claim, which is the conclusion indicated by the word "therefore"

currently, plastics do less harm to the environment nationwide than paper

"at this time, more harm to the environment nationwide is done by paper than by plastic"

As we guessed, they are trying to disguise this correct answer by re-wording the conclusion with an inversion. We know that 6 > 5 means the same thing as 5 < 6.

So concluding "Plastic does less harm than paper" is equivalent to concluding that "paper does more harm".

questiontext:
The same task triggers different levels of awareness of one’s surroundings, called environmental awareness, in different individuals. Mathematical puzzles, for example, cause most people to increase such an awareness. Some people—those who formulate the answer visually, imagining the numbers in their mind’s eye—will, in an attempt to freeze the picture, experience a decrease in environmental awareness while solving the puzzle. Other people’s environmental awareness may rise during the exercise, because their brains are signaling a rest at the end of every stage of problem solving.

Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

answers.text: There are some people for whom mathematical puzzles do not cause an increase in their level of environmental awareness.
answers.fb:
Correct

The main clause of that long gross second sentence is that "some people...experience a decrease in environmental awareness while solving the puzzle." That proves that there are some people for whom puzzles do not cause an increased level of awareness.

answers.text: People who visually formulate answers differ from other problem solvers in that the former are aware of their surroundings.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison

The difference between those who visually formulate answers and those who don't is that the visual formulators experience a decrease in environmental awareness, whereas others experience an increase. We're never told in absolute terms that one group is aware of their surroundings and another is unaware.

answers.text: People tend to be more aware of their surroundings when solving mathematical problems than when solving nonmathematical problems.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison

Mathematical puzzles are given as an example, but we're never given information that lets us compare mathematical problems vs. non-mathematical problems.

answers.text: Mathematical problem solvers who rely on visual techniques become aware of their surroundings only during periods of rest.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: only

The "only" in this answer should make us suspicious right out of the gate. None of the statements in the stimulus are conditional, so it's highly unlikely that our answer would be that strong. This is also a bit of a word salad: the information we get about visual techniques in claim 2 isn't related to the concept of rest in claim 3.

answers.text: Mathematical problem solving requires frequent periods of rest in the form of increased awareness of the problem solver’s surroundings.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: requires

Like D, this answer is conditional. That means it's highly unlikely to be correct if the stimulus is not conditional. This stimulus tells us what mathematical problem solving causes, but it doesn't ever tell us what it requires.

questiontext:
Limited research indicates that therapeutic intervention before the onset of mental disorders can mitigate factors identified as major contributors to them. But a much more comprehensive research program is needed to verify these results and allow for the design of specific health care measures. Thus, in order to explore a potential means of cost-effectively helping people prone to mental disorders, we should increase funding for intervention research.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (thus)

To explore cost-effective ways to help people prone to mental disorders, we should increase funding for intervention research.

Evidence

Limited research shows therapeutic intervention before the onset of mental disorders can mitigate major contributing factors.

A comprehensive research program is needed to verify and design specific health measures.

Evaluate

This argument fits the Plan / Goal pattern.

GOAL:  save money helping people prone to mental disorders
PLAN:  increase funding for intervention research

We want to know the plan is feasible, that people will cooperate with it, that it won't backfire in some way that undermines the goal, or that it targets the main source of our current issue/problem.

To assess whether increasing funding achieves the goal, consider the differences between the recommendation-world and the current-world. What are the potential advantages and disadvantages?

The argument relies on the premise that therapeutic intervention can mitigate the contributing factors of mental disorders. Thus, if more funding leads to more effective interventions that are relatively inexpensive compared to treatment, then the recommendation would seem beneficial.

Goal

Let's find an answer that helps us argue that increasing funding for intervention research can lead to more cost-effective help for those prone to mental disorders.

answers.text: Most minor mental disorders are more expensive to treat than other minor health problems.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Comparison

While mental disorders might be more expensive to treat than other minor health problems, this argument is only about mental disorders.

We're just trying to assess whether increasing the budget for intervention research would lead to cost savings in dealing with mental disorders.

answers.text: Prevention research can be coordinated by drawing together geneticists, neurologists, and behavioral scientists.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This option discusses how the Plan might be carried out, but it doesn't give us any insight into whether the Plan would achieve its Goal of saving money. 

If anything, it makes it sound like this prevention research might be pretty expensive, since we'd be paying a lot of experts in different fields.

answers.text: Reducing known risk factors for mental disorders is relatively inexpensive compared to the long-term treatment required.
answers.fb:
Correct

If reducing known risk factors for mental disorders is relatively inexpensive compared to the long-term treatment required, it strengthens the notion that intervention research could be a cost-effective approach. This suggests that increased funding could lead to significant savings and benefits through prevention rather than costly treatment later.

In terms of Plan / Goal patterns, it's reassuring us that this Plan is targeting a key source of the problem. A big source of spending on mental disorders is long term treatment, so if we can avoid that then we're avoiding a lot of expenses.

answers.text: Current funding for intervention research is now higher than it has ever been before.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This option talks about current funding levels but doesn't address whether increasing funding now would lead to more cost-effective interventions.

If anything, it feels like pushback to someone suggesting we increase funding to say, "Psssh, really? It's already at the highest level we've ever had it!"

answers.text: Once a mental disorder disappears, there is a fair chance that it will recur, given that complete cures are rare.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This option discusses the recurrence of mental disorders, but it does not relate to whether increased funding for intervention research could deliver a cost savings.

questiontext:
Unlike newspapers in the old days, today’s newspapers and televised news programs are full of stories about murders and assaults in our city. One can only conclude from this change that violent crime is now out of control, and, to be safe from personal attack, one should not leave one’s home except for absolute necessities.

Which one of the following, if true, would cast the most serious doubt on the conclusion?
gf:
Conclusion (conclude)

Violent crime is now out of control, and, to be safe from personal attack, one should not leave one's home except for absolute necessities.

Evidence

Unlike newspapers in the old days, today's newspapers and televised news programs are full of stories about murders and assaults in our city.

Evaluate

This argument presents a Curious Difference (an asymmetric comparison) in the evidence. Does the author then assume some causal interpretationof that evidence? Yes!

CURIOUS FACT:  How come today's papers and TV news are so much more full of murder/assault stories?

EXPLANATION: Because there's so much more murder and assault these days!

The argument observes that there's an increase in media coverage of violent crime and concludes that violent crime itself is out of control and the city's safety has drastically changed.

The argument assumes that because there's more media coverage of violent crime stories today compared to the past, the actual incidence of violent crime must have increased proportionally.

To weaken this conclusion, we want to consider alternative explanations for the increase in media coverage that do not involve an actual increase in violent crime.

Goal

Let's find an answer that suggests an alternate reason for the observed change in media content, rather than an actual increase in the amount or rate of violent crimes, or an answer that undermines the plausibility of the author's belief that violent crime has gotten much worse in recent times.

answers.text: Newspapers and televised news programs have more comprehensive coverage of violent crime than newspapers did in the old days.
answers.fb:
Correct

This provides an alternate explanation for why violent crime stories are more frequent in today's media. It's not necessarily that violent crime is more rampant, but that media coverage has expanded, making it seem more prevalent.

In other words, the paper is full of murder stories not because there are more murders but because a given murder nowadays is given more comprehensive coverage and so it takes up more space in the paper than a murder report would have back in the day. 

More pages per crime, not more crimes occurring.  

This could also mean they cover more types of violent crime than they used to. So it would be "more types of crime reported on, not a greater number of crimes occurring".

answers.text: National data show that violent crime is out of control everywhere, not just in the author’s city.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

If anything, this could potentially be used to argue that violent crime is indeed out of control, aligning with the conclusion rather than opposing it.

answers.text: Police records show that people experience more violent crimes in their own neighborhoods than they do outside their neighborhoods.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Comparison

The argument doesn't care where crimes occur. The conclusion is saying that crime is out of control everywhere in the city.

We're trying to assess whether current crime is worse than past crime.

This answer is about whether nearby current crime is worse than distant current vrime.

answers.text: Murder comprised a larger proportion of violent crimes in the old days than it does today.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Comparison

The argument doesn't care what proportion of all violent crimes are murder. It's making a claim about whether the entire category of violent crime has greatly increased recently. The argument hasn't made any claims or assumptions about how big the different pieces of the violent crime pie are.

answers.text: News magazines play a more important role today in informing the public about crime than they did in the old days.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This might seem like an alternate explanation for why violent crime is reported on these days.

However, this is about news magazines, whereas the curious fact was about newspapers and TV news shows. This answer doesn't offer any explanation for why newspapers and news TV shows are so much more full of violent crime stories than they used to be. 

We would have to assume that "if magazines play a more important role, then so do papers and tv shows, and if papers/TV play a more important role then they will start reporting more on crime, even if it's the same amount of crime as before".

The correct answer directly gives us "they start reporting more on crime, even if it's the same amount of crime as before", without requiring as many assumptions.

questiontext:
The importance of the ozone layer to terrestrial animals is that it entirely filters out some wavelengths of light but lets others through. Holes in the ozone layer and the dangers associated with these holes are well documented. However, one danger that has not been given sufficient attention is that these holes could lead to severe eye damage for animals of many species.

Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above, if they are true?

answers.text: All wavelengths of sunlight that can cause eye damage are filtered out by the ozone layer, where it is intact.
answers.fb: Too Strong: all

answers.text: Few species of animals live on a part of the earth’s surface that is not threatened by holes in the ozone layer.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: few

This says that most species live in areas that are threatened by holes in the ozone layer. The statements never tell us anything that is true of most species.

answers.text: Some species of animals have eyes that will not suffer any damage when exposed to unfiltered sunlight.
answers.fb:
Too Strong / Out of Scope: won't suffer any

We only heard about animals who are vulnerable to severe eye damage. We have no information about animals who aren't.

answers.text: A single wavelength of sunlight can cause severe damage to the eyes of most species of animals.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: single / most

We didn't receive any fact that is true for most species.

answers.text: Some wavelengths of sunlight that cause eye damage are more likely to reach the earth’s surface where there are holes in the ozone layer than where there are not.

questiontext:
Politician: The bill that makes using car phones while driving illegal should be adopted. My support of this bill is motivated by a concern for public safety. Using a car phone seriously distracts the driver, which in turn poses a threat to safe driving. People would be deterred from using their car phones while driving if it were illegal to do so.

The argument's main conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
gf:
Conclusion

The bill to say "using car phone while driving is illegal" should be adopted.
(i.e. it should be illegal to use your car phone while driving)

Evidence

Using a car phone distracts the driver, which poses a threat to safe driving. 

Meanwhile, if it were illegal to use your car phone while driving, people would be deterred from doing it.

Evaluate

On Sufficient Assumption, if there are any New Terms in the conclusion, they need to be in the correct answer. The big one in this conclusion is should be adopted.

We need to a construct a rule that sounds like 

if .....                                        then ....
the stuff we described in        should adopt
the evidence about this bill     the bill

So what do we know about this bill? 

It would make using your car phone while driving illegal. That would deter people from using their car phone while driving. Using your car phone seriously distracts the driver, which poses a threat to safe driving.

Chunking that all together, this bill would "deter people from doing something that poses a threat to safe driving".

That seems to be the most common sense understanding of the author's rationale for why we should adopt the bill.

Goal

So we just need to hear something like

"Any bill that would deter people from doing something that poses a threat to safe driving ... should be adopted".

answers.text: The more attention one pays to driving, the safer a driver one is.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

Since this doesn't contain the language "should be adopted" it won't allow us to logically derive the wording, "Therefore, should be adopted".

answers.text: The only way to reduce the threat to public safety posed by car phones is through legislation.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

Since this doesn't contain the language "should be adopted" it won't allow us to logically derive the wording, "Therefore, should be adopted".

It definitely feels closer than (A), because if legislation is our only way, then we should adopt some legislation, right?

Yes, but this is Sufficient Assumption. We're not being asked to fill in the blanks with common sense. We would need to spell out even that idea I just uttered, that "if legislation is our only way, then we should take that way".

An additional problem is that this answer would only strengthen the idea that "we should adopt some legislation". It still doesn't give us a mechanism to argue for this bill.

answers.text: Some distractions interfere with one’s ability to safely operate an automobile.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

Weak wording like "some" will be wrong on Sufficient Assumption 99% of the time, since we need an answer to powerfully prove the conclusion in airtight fashion.

Since this doesn't contain the language "should be adopted" it won't allow us to logically derive the wording, "Therefore, should be adopted".

answers.text: Any proposed law that would reduce a threat to public safety should be adopted.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is actually the only eligible answer choice we're offered, since it's the only one to provide us with the wording we need in the conclusion:  should be adopted.

Does this rule apply to the bill being considered?

Would this bill that criminalizes using your phone while driving reduce a threat to public safety?

Sure, if using your phone while driving is illegal, it will deter people from doing so, and doing so seriously distracts the driver, which poses a threat to safe driving.

Since this answer choice applies to the proposed bill we're talking about, it allows us to logically conclude that this proposed bill should be adopted.

answers.text: Car phone use by passengers does not distract the driver of the car.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

Since this doesn't contain the language "should be adopted" it won't allow us to logically derive the wording, "Therefore, should be adopted".

questiontext:
When soil is plowed in the spring, pigweed seeds that have been buried in the soil all winter are churned up to the surface and redeposited just under the surface. The brief exposure of the seeds to sunlight stimulates receptors, which have become highly sensitive to sunlight during the months the seeds were buried in the soil, and the stimulated receptors trigger germination. Without the prolonged darkness, followed by exposure to sunlight, the seeds do not germinate.

The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following statements about a field that will be plowed in the spring and in which pigweed seeds have been buried in the soil all winter?
gf:
Statements

There's a Causal Chain type story presented:

1. buried in the soil all winter
2. churned up to surface when soil is plowed in the spring
3. gets brief exposure to sunlight
4. receptors get stimulated 
5. receptors trigger germination

The final idea is a Conditional that says 

if not 1 → then 3 doesn't trigger 4

Technically, it's "if there isn't prolonged darkness", then 3 doesn't trigger 4.
Being buried all winter is one way to get prolonged darkness, but there are presumably other ways (f.e. watching French films, I'd imagine)

For the last sentence, I would primarily remember it as a Causal Difference-Maker:
the long exposure to darkness is what makes the receptors sensitive enough to get triggered by brief sunlight

It's kinda like, "If you don't spend enough time in the dark, your eyes won't adjust to see faint things".

Goal

The question stem is about pigweed seeds in the exact situation we just had described to us, so it seems like it's just asking us what we can best prove from the paragraph.

We'd expect them, when plowed, to receive brief sunlight, and if they do, and they've truly been exposed to prolonged darkness over the winter, then we expect them to germinate. Otherwise, we'd expect them not to germinate.

answers.text: Fewer pigweed plants will grow in the field if it is plowed only at night than if it is plowed during the day.
answers.fb:
Correct

This answer plays off the Causal Difference-Maker said in the final sentence:

if the seeds don't have that special recipe of Prolonged Darkness followed by Sunlight Exposure, they don't germinate.

So plowing during the day would expose those seeds to sunlight, sparking their germination.

Plowing during the night would churn up all those seeds, but they wouldn't get any exposure to sunlight, so their receptors wouldn't trigger germination. 

Since a plant needs to germinate in order to grow (they're counting on us to have this common knowledge), you'd get more plants if you plow during the day than if you plow at night.

answers.text: Fewer pigweed plants will grow in the field if it is plowed at all than if it is plowed only at night.
answers.fb:
Opposite

The syntax of this one is not agreeing with me. I just don't understand how that's grammatically or logically acceptable. 

It sounds like it's comparing a situation in which we plow "at least once, day or night" to a situation in which we plow "at night, if ever". 

We know from our thinking through (A) that if this field is plowed at night, the seeds won't be exposed to sunlight, so the receptors won't trigger germination, and no pigweed will grow.

So since we know that none of them will grow if plowed only at night, then it's impossible for any situation to have fewer pigweed plants than zero.

answers.text: Fewer pigweed plants will grow in the field if it is plowed just before sunrise than if it is plowed just after sunset.
answers.fb:
Unknown Comparison

Which has more sunlight:
the pinkish aurora before sunrise,
or the pinkish hues around dusk?

Naturally, we don't know and they're probably pretty similar, since they're opposite functions of each other.

So we can't say that just before sunrise is dimmer than just after sunset, and the only way to justify fewer/greater pigweed plants is to establish less/more exposure to direct sunlight.

answers.text: The pigweed seeds that are churned up to the surface of the soil during the plowing will not geminate unless they are redeposited under the surface of the soil.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: unless

We only have one rule provided that allows us to say "therefore, won't germinate", and that's the idea that "they weren't in prolonged darkness followed by exposure to sunlight".

We were told that the seeds are redeposited beneath the surface, not that they need to be redeposited.

answers.text: All of the pigweed seeds that are already on the surface of the soil before the field is plowed will germinate.
answers.fb:
Contradicted

The seeds that are already on the surface haven't had the required prolonged darkness that the seeds that were buried all winter had.

Without the "long darkness + sunlight exposure" cocktail, the seeds don't germinate.

questiontext:
A university study reported that between 1975 and 1983 the length of the average workweek in a certain country increased significantly. A governmental study, on the other hand, shows a significant decline in the length of the average workweek for the same period. Examination of the studies shows, however, that they used different methods of investigation; thus there is no need to look further for an explanation of the difference in the studies’ results.

The argument's reasoning is flawed because the argument fails to
gf:
Conclusion (Thus)

There is no need to look for a further explanation (beyond using different methods) to explain why the university study and the governmental study had two different estimations of the how the average workweek has changed.

Evidence

The university study thinks the average workweek has gotten longer. The governmental study think it's gotten shorter. The two studies used different methods of investigation.

Evaluate

How could we accept the evidence but argue that there is still some need to look further for an explanation of the difference?

There's a curious fact:     
how come the college study says up and the govt. study says down?

There's a potential explanation:    
the college study and the govt study used different methods.

The assumption is that different methods could lead to different measurements. Maybe we both measured the temperature of a lake, and I measured near the top and you measured near the bottom and that's why we got different measurements. 

But maybe the reason we got different measurements is that we used the same method (measure near the top) but your instrument works fine and my thermometer was busted. 

The author is overly confident in assuming that the difference between the college study's results and the govt study's results is that they employed different methods. Maybe something else was the reason.

Goal

Look for an answer complaining that the author is saying, "As soon as we have one possible explanation, we need look no further. We've cracked the case!" Meanwhile, the author is failing to rule out other possible explanations and failing to convince us that different methods led to the different results

answers.text: distinguish between a study produced for the purposes of the operation of government and a study produced as part of university research
answers.fb:
Doesn't Fail To Distinguish

The author isn't blurring the lines between these two studies or failing to distinguish between them. She is clear that they are distinct, given that she's arguing they had different methods and thus different results.

answers.text: distinguish between a method of investigation and the purpose of an investigation
answers.fb:
Out Of Scope: Purpose

The author talks about different methods of investigation, but we never talk about the purpose of either investigation (we'd implicitly assume that the average length of a workweek has changed).

The distinction between method and purpose doesn't have anything to do with our objection. This author thinks that two studies with the same purpose (has the length of the average workweek changed?) used different methods and measured different results.

And we're saying, "Yo, that could be the reason the results are different, but you're being way too hasty to say there's no need to look further."

answers.text: recognize that only one of the studies has been properly conducted
answers.fb:
Unclear Objection

When we're doing Flaw and see answers start with Fails to Consider / Overlooks the Possibility, we want to ask ourselves whether the idea that follows would be an objection.

Could we say, "Hey, author --- the reason the results were different isn't because they used different methods of investigation; it's because only one of them was properly conducted"?

Hmm, it's not great. First of all, it's not clear that this would actually be an Alternate Explanation. If one study used scientifically suspect methods and the other study used good methods, then the author's explanation (the different methods caused the different results) and this answer choice's explanation (the fact that only one of them was properly conducted caused the different results) could both be in agreement.

Also, when we object that the author has failed to consider an Alternate Explanation, we're only allowed to object that this alternate explanation may be the cause. We can't say the alternate explanation is the cause.

for example, this answer is always wrong
(A) mistakes cause for effect

this answer could be correct
(A) author fails to consider the purported cause may be the effect

answers.text: recognize that two different methods of investigation can yield identical results
answers.fb:
Correct

Does it hurt the author to say, 'Yo -- different methods can achieve identical results"?

Yes!

The author is arguing, "These two studies have different results. Why? Well, it turns out they have different methods. Thus, there's no need to look for any other explanation."

The author is acting there like
different methods guarantees different results

And so this answer is punching back at that assumption and saying, "No they don't".

answers.text: recognize that varying economic conditions result in the average workweek changing in length
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Objection

This doesn't pose an Alternate Explanation for why the two studies have opposite results., nor does it hurt the plausibility that "different methods of investigation caused the results to be different".

So it has no power to weaken this argument.

questiontext:
People should avoid taking the antacid calcium carbonate in doses larger than half a gram, for despite its capacity to neutralize stomach acids, calcium carbonate can increase the calcium level in the blood and thus impair kidney function. Moreover, just half a gram of it can stimulate the production of gastrin, a stomach hormone that triggers acid secretion.

Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
gf:
Information

causal (capacity to neutralize, can increase/stimulate)

CC >> neutralize stomach acids
CC >> increase calcium >> impair kidneys
CC >> more gastrin >> more acid secretion

recommendation

Don't take more than 1/2 gram of CC.

Evaluate

We know that the #1 focus of Most Supported questions is cause/effect relationships.

We had a couple causal chains here as well as that initial causal claim about neutralizing stomach acids.

In addition to the obvious overlap where all four claims are about calcium carbonate, we also have two other overlaps:

- multiple claims mention "half a gram" of CC
- multiple claims mention "stomach acids"

If we combine the idea that 1/2 a gram stimulates gastrin and acid secretion with the claim that we shouldn't take more than 1/2 a gram, we could probably derive some takeaway like, "Once you're above 1/2 a gram, the benefits of calcium carbonate are outweighed by the harm of stimulating gastrin / stomach acids."

If we combine the idea that CC can neutralize stomach acids with the claim that 1/2 a gram of it can stimulate stomach acid secretion, we'd get some weird idea like "depending on the dose of CC, it might lessen or increase stomach acids?"

Goal

Look for the most provable claim. It will likely reward us for noticing the cause/effect relationships given.

answers.text: Cessation of gastrin production is a more effective method of controlling excess stomach acid than is direct neutralization of stomach acid.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison

This is getting at the two causal claims involving stomach acids. We heard that CC can neutralize stomach acids, but in large doses can also trigger them.

Since the paragraph is suggesting that we don't take CC, does that imply that it's better to avoid stimulating gastrin (and thus stomach acids) than it is to try to neutralize the existing stomach acid?

No, not necessarily. Perhaps a low dose of CC is the best (like 1/4 a gram), maybe that neutralizes what's there without stimulating the secretion of more.

Furthermore, the recommendation to avoid CC could be based largely on the fact that it can impair kidney function, rather than on its capacity to stimulate gastrin.

answers.text: People who avoid taking more than half a gram of calcium carbonate are less likely than average to suffer from impaired kidney function.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison

The passage doesn't talk about at what dosage calcium carbonate starts to trigger impaired kidney function. So we wouldn't really be able to relate kidney damage to the 1/2 gram dosage. 

We also know nothing about the average risk of impaired kidney function. It might be that 99% of people don't take any calcium carbonate, so the average risk of impaired kidney function is quite low. Thus, avoiding 1/2 a gram of CC might just make you have normal risk of impaired kidneys, not better than average odds.

A better version of this answer would sound like, "All other things being equal, a person who avoids taking more than 1/2 a gram of CC is less likely to suffer impaired kidney function than if they were to take more than 1/2 a gram of CC".

answers.text: Doses of calcium carbonate smaller than half a gram can reduce stomach acid more effectively than much larger doses do.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison

This sounds pretty reasonable, because we might be thinking there's a sweet spot (like 1/4 gram of CC) where you get to neutralize stomach acids but you avoid stimulating acid secretion.

But we don't know at what dosage the neutralizing effects kick in. They might not really kick in until 3/4 gram or more. We just know that CC has the capacity to neutralize stomach acids, but we don't know what dose is required for it to start having that effect.

We also don't know how to compare the acid-neutralizing effects to the acid-stimulating effects. It's not clear whether any dose of CC creates a net reduction or net increase in stomach acids.

answers.text: Half a gram of calcium carbonate can causally contribute to both the secretion and the neutralization of stomach acids.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is our most provable claim. Technically, we don't know whether 1/2 a gram of CC neutralizes your stomach acids.

We know that CC has the capacity to neutralize stomach acids, but we don't know if you need to hit a certain dose to experience that effect.

So this answer isn't bulletproof, but correct answers on Most Supported don't need to be. It's our most provable.

We know that CC has the capacity to neutralize stomach acids and that 1/2 a gram of it can stimulate the secretion of stomach acids, so we have a lot of support for this. And the claim is worded very weakly.

answers.text: Impaired kidney function may increase the level of calcium in the blood.
answers.fb:
Reversal

We were told that increased calcium in the blood can lead to impaired kidney function, not this causally-reversed relationship.

questiontext:
Ringtail opossums are an Australian wildlife species that is potentially endangered. A number of ringtail opossums that had been orphaned and subsequently raised in captivity were monitored after being returned to the wild. Seventy-five percent of those opossums were killed by foxes, a species not native to Australia. Conservationists concluded that the native ringtail opossum population was endangered not by a scarcity of food, as had been previously thought, but by non-native predator species against which the opossum had not developed natural defenses.

Which one of the following, if true, most strongly supports the conservationists' argument?
gf:
Conclusion (concluded)

The native ringtail opossum population is endangered not by a scarcity of food, as had been previously thought, but by non-native predator species against which the opossum had not developed natural defenses.

Evidence

A number of ringtail opossums that were orphaned and subsequently raised in captivity were monitored after being returned to the wild.

Seventy-five percent of those opossums were killed by foxes, a species not native to Australia.

Evaluate

This conclusion has two claims, one of them causal and the other anti-causal. We can reverse engineer from the conclusion what causal mystery they are trying to solve.

Curious Fact: Why is the ringtail opossum population endangered?

Author's Explanation: It's due to non-native predator species, such as foxes, rather than a scarcity of food.

To strengthen this argument, we can either rule out an alternate explanation (such as food scarcity) or increase the plausibility that non-native predators are indeed a significant threat.

Goal

Let's find an answer that either undermines the food scarcity theory or strengthens the idea that non-native predators, like foxes, are a significant threat to the ringtail opossum.

answers.text: There are fewer non-native predator species that prey on the ringtail opossum than there are native species that prey on the ringtail opossum.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

The number of non-native vs. native predator species doesn't affect whether non-native predators are the main threat over food scarcity. The argument is concerned with impact, not quantity.

But even if we equated number with impact, this is diminishing the importance of non-native predators, which works against the author's hypothesis that non-native predators are the reason for the opossum's endangered status.

answers.text: Foxes, which were introduced into Australia over 200 years ago, adapted to the Australian climate less successfully than did some other foreign species.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Comparison

Foxes' success in adapting compared to other non-native species doesn't address whether predation by non-native species like foxes is the primary danger to the ringtail opossum.

answers.text: The ringtail opossums that were raised in captivity were fed a diet similar to that which ringtail opossums typically eat in the wild.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The diet of captured opossums being similar to that of wild ones does not address the argument about the primary cause of their endangerment, which is focused on predation.

It might feel like this is ruling out an alternate explanation -- "the captive opossums who were released into the wild didn't die because they had been raised on an atypical diet while in captivity"

But we already know why those released opossums died (they were eaten by foxes). And the conclusion isn't specifically about the opossums in captivity; it's about the endangered status of that species overall.

answers.text: Few of the species that compete with the ringtail opossum for food sources are native to Australia.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This can be re-worded as "most species competing with the opossum for food are non-native". 

That sort of sounds like, "non-native species are a problem for the opossum" but the hypothesis is specifically about non-native predators, animals who eat opossums, not animals who eat the same food as opossums.

answers.text: Ringtail opossums that grow to adulthood in the wild defend themselves against foxes no more successfully than do ringtail opossums raised in captivity.
answers.fb:
Correct

This provides support for the claim that non-native predators, like foxes, pose a significant threat. If opossums raised in the wild fare no better against foxes than those raised in captivity, it suggests the issue isn't about a lack of natural defenses developed in the wild but rather the overwhelming threat from non-native species.

Someone might have objected to this argument by saying, "the fact that foxes killed most of the released opossums doesn't show that foxes are a big threat to the species -- it just shows that foxes are a big threat to sheltered opossums who didn't know how to act in the wild."

This answer shuts down that line of objection by saying, "No, the wild opossums are equally bad at defending themselves from fox attacks."

questiontext:
Some critics argue that an opera’s stage directions are never reflected in its music. Many comic scenes in Mozart’s operas, however, open with violin phrases that sound like the squeaking of changing scenery. Clearly Mozart intended the music to echo the sounds occurring while stage directions are carried out. Hence, a change of scenery—the most basic and frequent stage direction—can be reflected in the music, which means that other operatic stage directions can be as well.

In the argument, the statement that many comic scenes in Mozart's operas open with violin phrases that sound like the squeaking of changing scenery is offered in support of the claim that
gf:
Conclusion (implied)

An opera's stage directions are sometimes reflected in its music.

Intermediate Conclusion (Hence)

A change of scenery, which is a basic stage direction, can be reflected in the music, so other operatic stage directions can also be reflected.

Evidence

In some of Mozart's funny operas, there are squeaky violin noises that Mozart clearly meant to echo the sounds that are made while scenery is changing (set pieces are often on rolling wooden frames, so they might squeak ... big backdrops are lowered or raised from the rafters via rope and pully).

Evaluate / Goal

They're asking us about the Mozart premise, and asking what claim it was offered in support of. We could say that it was directly supporting the intermediate conclusion that "a change of scenery can be reflected in the music", or that it was ultimately supporting the author's rebuttal to the position in the first sentence; our author is saying "an opera's stage directions are sometimes reflected in its music".

answers.text: a change of scenery is the stage direction most frequently reflected in an opera’s music
answers.fb:
Too Strong: most frequently

The author never claimed that change of scenery is the most frequent way in with an opera's music reflects a stage direction.

She's only claiming it's a way, "which means that other directions can be reflected as well".

She hasn't ever singled out any one type of stage direction as the type that most frequently gets reflected by the music.

answers.text: an opera’s stage directions are never reflected in its music
answers.fb:
Opposite

This is the critics' position, which the author is refuting.

answers.text: an opera’s music can have an effect on the opera’s stage directions
answers.fb:
Effect vs. Reflected

The author wasn't ever saying that the opera's music has an effect on the stage directions, just that the music reflects the stage directions.

We might say that how we drive reflects how we saw our parents drive, but that wouldn't mean that how we drive has/had an effect on how our parents drive.

answers.text: a variety of stage directions can be reflected in an opera’s music
answers.fb:
Correct

The author's main conclusion is rebutting the original position, so she is trying to argue that "an opera's stage directions are sometimes reflected in the music". In her final sentence, she makes two claims.

Because of the example of Mozart using violin phrases to reflect the changing of scenery, we get to the idea that a change of scenery can be reflected in the music, which gets us to the idea that "other operatic stage directions can be as well". 

It's important that this answer says "can", not "are". The author hasn't argued that a variety of stage directions are reflected in an opera's music, but she does explicitly say that other stage directions (in addition to change of scenery) can be reflected.

answers.text: the most frequent relation between an opera’s music and its stage directions is one of musical imitation of the sounds that occur when a direction is carried out
answers.fb:
Too Strong: most frequent

Just like (A), the author never claimed that the Mozart example has any qualities that are true most frequently.

In the Mozart example, the music imitates the sounds of a stage direction being carried out, but she never suggests that this is the most frequent way that an opera's music would reflect its stage directions.

LSAT constantly tries to bait us into thinking that the only thing mentioned is therefore "the only thing to which this applies / the most important thing to which this applies".

questiontext:
More women than men suffer from Alzheimer’s disease—a disease that is most commonly contracted by elderly persons. This discrepancy has often been attributed to women’s longer life span, but this theory may be wrong. A recent study has shown that prescribing estrogen to women after menopause, when estrogen production in the body decreases, may prevent them from developing the disease. Men’s supply of testosterone may help safeguard them against Alzheimer’s disease because much of it is converted by the body to estrogen, and testosterone levels stay relatively stable into old age.

Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?
gf:
Conclusion 

This theory may be wrong.
rephrase:  The reason that women suffer more than men from Alzheimer's might not be because women live longer.

Evidence

A recent study shows that prescribing estrogen to post-menopausal women can prevent them from developing Alzheimer's. Meanwhile, men have a big supply of testosterone, which the body converts into estrogen.

Evaluate

Whenever we do Main Conclusion (and Role) we read the paragraph differently, knowing that 90% of the time the conclusion is the very first sentence, or it's some rebuttal signified with a pivot word (like "but, yet, however"). In either case, 90% of the time the conclusion is earlier than the support, on these two question types.

As we read this first sentence, we ask ourselves whether it's eligible to be a conclusion -- does it sound like an opinion coming from the author? No, it sounds like fact.

But the second sentence contains an attribution (literally). It says "[some people] attribute this to women's longer life span". When we see any attribution in the early going of a Main Conclusion paragraph, then we anticipate that our author will probably be rebutting this position.

Sure enough, the second half of the 2nd sentence has one of those signature pivot words that we're listening for on Main Conclusion (but, yet, however).  

So now we think, "Ah! This looks like the conclusion. The author is rebutting the idea that living longer is why women suffer more from Alzheimer's."

Does the author going to go on and try to convince us of that? Yes, because she builds up a case for an Alternate Explanation. This theory that "longer life span" is why women are more afflicted may be wrong, because the real reason that women are more afflicted could be that estrogen is the secret weapon against Alzheimer's and women have less estrogen than men in their old age.

Goal

The conclusion was "this theory may be wrong", but since this claim includes a pronoun (this theory), we need to make sure we insert the specific language that pronoun is referring to:

It may be wrong to think that longer life span is why women suffer more from Alzheimer's (lack of estrogen may be the real reason that women suffer more from Alzheimer's)

answers.text: A decrease in estrogen, rather than longer life span, may explain the higher occurrence of Alzheimer’s disease in women relative to men.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is our best match for "this theory may be wrong". It's a little unusual that this answer would include the alternate explanation (that low estrogen is the real cause), but that was an implied conclusion, supported by the final two sentences.

It should make us happy that "may explain" in the answer nicely captures the strength of "this theory may be wrong".

answers.text: As one gets older, one’s chances of developing Alzheimer’s disease increase.
answers.fb:
Unstated

The quickest way to eliminate this is that it isn't at all a match for "this theory [that longer life span explains why more women get Alzheimer's] may be wrong".

This doesn't mention women at all. 

The correct answer on Main Conclusion will be replicating the meaning of one of the explicit claims. None of the claims in this argument say that "as you get older, your chance of developing Alzheimer's increases".

answers.text: Women who go through menopause earlier in life than do most other women have an increased risk of contracting Alzheimer’s disease.
answers.fb:
Unstated Inference

This isn't at all a match for "this theory [that longer life span explains why more women get Alzheimer's] may be wrong".

This doesn't mention longer life span at all. 

The correct answer on Main Conclusion will be replicating the meaning of one of the explicit claims. None of the claims in this argument talk about early menopause. 

This answer might appeal to people who feel like we could infer this idea from the paragraph, but that's forgetting our job:  find the explicit claim that is the main conclusion.

answers.text: The conversion of testosterone into estrogen may help safeguard men from Alzheimer’s disease.
answers.fb:
Unstated Inference

This isn't at all a match for "this theory [that longer life span explains why more women get Alzheimer's] may be wrong".

This doesn't mention longer life spans or women.

This answer, like (C), feels like an inference we could derive from what was said, but this wasn't said. It's also technically not even that solid an inference. It's not the conversion that helps men, exactly; it's the fact that they have plenty of testosterone to convert in the first place. 

Women run low on estrogen. Men have a high, stable supply of testosterone, which can be converted.

answers.text: Testosterone is necessary for preventing Alzheimer’s disease in older men.
answers.fb:
Unstated

This isn't at all a match for "this theory [that longer life span explains why more women get Alzheimer's] may be wrong".

This doesn't mention longer life spans or women.

This also tries to bait students into picking an answer that goes beyond what was actually said. In this case, it's also an extremely strong claim (necessary?) that we could support even if there were an Inference question.

questiontext:
Parent P: Children will need computer skills to deal with tomorrow’s world. Computers should be introduced in kindergarten, and computer languages should be required in high school.

Parent Q: That would be pointless. Technology advances so rapidly that the computers used by today’s kindergartners and the computer languages taught in today’s high schools would become obsolete by the time these children are adults.

Which one of the following, if true, is the strongest logical counter parent P can make to parent Q's objection?
gf:
P's Conclusion

Computers should be introduced in kindergarten, and computer languages should be required in high school.

P's Evidence

Children will need computer skills to deal with tomorrow's world.

Q's Conclusion

[Introducing computers in kindergarten and teaching computer languages in high school] would be pointless.

Q's Evidence

Tech advances so quickly that the computers / languages that K-12 would be working on would be obsolete by the time these kids became adults. 

Evaluate

Given that ... the computers / languages that kindergarteners and high schoolers would be working on would be obsolete by the time they reached adulthood

How could we argue ... it wouldn't be pointless -- there is still some value to introducing computers in kindergarten and introducing computer languages in high school?

Maybe using a computer mouse improves hand-eye coordination. Maybe even though the computers the kindergarteners are using will be obsolete, they will still be learning transferable computer skills or awareness (like copy / paste / typing / trash, etc.). Maybe some high schoolers will be able to get a part time job coding in the language they're learning (which would not be obsolete at the time they're learning it). 

Goal

We just need some way of saying, "Even though the tech and language would be obsolete, there is still some point in doing this plan to teach computers more in K-12".

answers.text: When technology is advancing rapidly, regular training is necessary to keep one’s skills at a level proficient enough to deal with the society in which one lives.
answers.fb:
Weak Impact

This is somewhat tempting, in that it addresses Q's concern that the computer stuff we would teach will be obsolete by the time the students grow up.

This is like, "Sure, but that's true no matter what. When tech advances rapidly, we all need to re-train to keep our skills proficient to deal with modern society". 

However, it's not the strongest logical counter, because it doesn't establish that there is any value to teaching K-12 students this stuff in the first place. If we thought that Q was saying, "the downside of doing this plan is that they'd need to be retrained", this answer would seem to say, "Well, everyone will need to be retrained, so no biggie".

But Q is arguing we're not getting anything out of teaching kids soon-to-be-obsolete systems and languages. This answer isn't saying anything to the contrary, because it hasn't yet demonstrated that there is any upside to teaching K-12 students computers in the first place.

answers.text: Throughout history people have adapted to change, and there is no reason to believe that today’s children are not equally capable of adapting to technology as it advances.
answers.fb:
Weak Impact

This is just like (A), in that it addresses Q's concern that the computer stuff we would teach will be obsolete by the time the students grow up.

This is like, "Sure, but kids will be able to adapt to tech as it advances."

However, it's not the strongest logical counter, because it doesn't establish that there is any value to teaching K-12 students this stuff in the first place. If we thought that Q was saying, "the downside of doing this plan is that the students are going to need to learn new computers / new languages by the time they're adults", this answer would seem to say, "Well, everyone will need to be retrained, so no biggie".

But Q is arguing there's no upside to the plan. It's pointless. We're not getting anything out of teaching kids soon-to-be-obsolete systems and languages. Even if kids will have no problem adapting to new technology, what was the point of wasting precious K-12 class time teaching them technology they won't have a chance to use in their professional lives?

answers.text: In the process of learning to work with any computer or computer language, children increase their ability to interact with computer technology.
answers.fb:
Correct

This establishes a benefit to teaching K-12 students computers, even if the specific computer or computer language is later obsolete.

It's not pointless to teach them on computers and languages that will be gone by the time they grow up, if they're still getting something portable / generalizable from this teaching.

This answer is saying, "Yes, they get a transferrable benefit - they increase their ability to interact with (any) computer technology".

answers.text: Automotive technology is continually advancing too, but that does not result in one’s having to relearn to drive cars as the new advances are incorporated into new automobiles.
answers.fb:
Weak Impact

This analogy isn't totally crazy, but it's pretty weak. The idea that I don't have to relearn to drive cars as car technology improves relates to the objection that "kindergarteners won't have to relearn how to use a computer just because the specific computer they had in their classroom is obsolete by the time they grow up".

This answer wouldn't speak to the other half of the discussion, though. Learning a computer language would be more like engineering a car, not driving a car. It's very possible that no one needs to relearn to drive, if they want to drive an electric car like a Tesla. But it's also very possible that car engineers definitely would need to learn a lot of new stuff if they went from designing gas-powered cars to electric cars.

Another problem with the analogy is that it doesn't suffice to make cars / computers "fair to compare" that they both have continually advancing technology.

Computers are being said to advance "so rapidly" that today's stuff will be obsolete in 5-10 years. It's not clear from this answer that car stuff will be obsolete in 5-10 years, just that tech is always advancing.

answers.text: Once people have graduated from high school, they have less time to learn about computers and technology than they had during their schooling years.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This sounds like it's making a good case for, "Let's teach computers in K-12, because those students won't have much time to learn them once they graduate". However, this answer does nothing to address Q's objection:

if the computers they'll be using and language they'll be learning are going to be obsolete by the time they're out in the real world, then won't that computer education have been pointless?

questiontext:
Although marathons are 26.2 miles (42.2 kilometers) long and take even world-class marathoners over 2 hours to run, athletes who train by running 90 minutes a day fare better in marathons than do those who train by running 120 minutes or more a day.

Each of the following, if true, contributes to an explanation of the difference in marathon performances described above EXCEPT:
gf:
Background

Marathons take at least 2 hours to run.

Surprising Claim

It's better to train for a marathon by doing 90 min runs each day than by doing runs of 2+ hours.

Evaluate / Goal

Given that ... the race they're training for is 2+ hours

Why is it that  ... optimal training is only 1.5 hrs?

Maybe you burn yourself out if you practice the full-length thing too much (hint-hint:  LSAT students, don't take test after test as your form of practice)

answers.text: The longer period of time that one runs daily, the greater the chances of suffering adverse health effects due to air pollution.
answers.fb:
Explains

Why don't they run longer? Because the longer you run, the more you taint your body with air pollution.

We have to add the common sense premise that "people suffering from fewer adverse health effects are more likely to fare better in a marathon".

answers.text: The longer the period of time that one runs daily, the easier it is to adjust to different race lengths.
answers.fb:
Correct

First of all, this mentions a good thing about running longer. To solve our paradox, we're looking for a negative aspect about running longer (if there's no negative to running 2+ hours, then why aren't they just training for the actual length of a marathon?)

Secondly, it's pretty irrelevant to marathon runners whether they can adjust to different race lengths. Marathons have a standardized length of 26.2 miles.

answers.text: The longer the run, the more frequent is the occurrence of joint injuries that significantly interfere with overall training.
answers.fb:
Explains

Why don't people training for a marathon run longer?  Because, longer runs are harder on the body. They might result in injuries that prevent the runners from continuing with their training.

answers.text: Runners who train over 90 minutes per day grow bored with running and become less motivated.
answers.fb:
Explains

Why don't people training for a marathon run longer?  Because, longer runs are more likely to disenchant people from running.

They might burn out mentally and not run as hard during the actual marathon.

answers.text: Runners who train over 90 minutes per day deplete certain biochemical energy reserves, leaving them less energy for marathons.
answers.fb:
Explains

Why don't people training for a marathon run longer?  Because, longer runs are harder on the body. They deplete the secret stash of energy reserves that people tap into during an actual marathon.

questiontext:
Gene splicing can give rise to new varieties of farm animals that have only a partially understood genetic makeup. In addition to introducing the genes for whichever trait is desired, the technique can introduce genes governing the production of toxins or carcinogens, and these latter undesirable traits might not be easily discoverable.

The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
gf:
Statements

causal (can give rise to)

  Gene    >>  new varieties of farm animals
splicing       whose genetic makeup not
                      totally understood

causal (can introduce)

  Gene     >>  new genes for whichever
 splicing          trait is desired

  Gene     >>  new genes relate to making
 splicing          toxins or carcinogens

It might be hard to discover these new genes related to making toxins or carcinogens.

Evaluate

We get a few causal reactions that can come from gene splicing. It sounds like we need to proceed very carefully with gene splicing. The appeal of it is that we can introduce new genes for whichever trait is desired (for example:  a cow with a bigger than average milk supply).

But we're also introducing genes that govern production of toxins or carcinogens, and we can't easily detect when we've done so.

So we might successfully make a cow that has a super milk supply, but accidentally also cause the cow to have new toxins or carcinogens in its system.

Goal

Let's look for a safely worded answer that reinforces the uncertain outcomes of gene splicing.

answers.text: All toxin production is genetically controlled.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: all

We can infer that at least some toxin production is genetically controlled, because we're told that some genes can affect production of toxins.

But we can't leap to the extreme claim that all toxin production is genetically controlled.

answers.text: Gene splicing to produce new varieties of farm animals should be used cautiously.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is a safely worded answer that captures the mixed bag of causation we were told about gene splicing.

We can use gene splicing to produce new varieties of farm animals, and the new genes may give the farm animal the desired trait we had in mind, but it also might introduce some hard to detect changes that result in more toxins and carcinogens.

answers.text: Gene splicing is not effective as a way of producing new varieties of farm animals.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: not effective

This is a stronger version of (B). We definitely can infer that there is some potential concern with gene splicing (it can introduce hard-to-detect changes to toxin or carcinogen production).

But we only know that it can do that. We don't know if it frequently does that. It's too strong and sweeping to call gene splicing an "ineffective way to produce new varieties of farm animals".

answers.text: Most new varieties of farm animals produced by gene splicing will develop cancer.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: most

This is also a too-strong version of the caution that (B) speaks to. We know that gene splicing can lead to hard-to-detect changes in an organism's production of carcinogens.

But that doesn't mean we can say that more than 50% of gene spliced farm animals will get cancer.

answers.text: Gene splicing will advance to the point where unforeseen consequences are no longer a problem.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: no longer a problem

We have no support for this optimism, that someday gene splicing will not have potentially problematic unforeseen consequences.

questiontext:
Journal: In several psychological studies, subjects were given statements to read that caused them to form new beliefs. Later, the subjects were told that the original statements were false. The studies report, however, that most subjects persevered in their newly acquired beliefs, even after being told that the original statements were false. This strongly suggests that humans continue to hold onto acquired beliefs even in the absence of any credible evidence to support them.

Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the journal's argument?
gf:
Conclusion (This strongly suggests)

Humans hold onto acquired beliefs even in the absence of any credible evidence to support them.

Evidence

In a study, people read statements that caused them to form new beliefs. Later when they were told that the original statements were false, the subjects maintained those new beliefs.

Evaluate 

The author's conclusion is extremely broad, speaking for all of humankind, based only on a sample of people in a study (who may not be representative). So it's possible that a Weaken answer would attack this Sampling move, where the author reasons, "If it was true for these people, it must be true for people in general."

But we can also attack the notion that the conclusion was even true for the people in the study. Were they examples of "humans who continued to hold onto acquired beliefs even in the absence of any credible evidence to support those beliefs"? 

If we want to fight that categorization, we either have to find a way to argue that the people in the study:
1. DIDN'T hold onto acquired beliefs, or
2. DID have credible evidence to support those beliefs (or both) 

We can't argue that first line of objection, because the evidence explicitly says that most of them persisted in their newly acquired beliefs.

Okay, so is it possible that they did have credible evidence to support those beliefs? They probably didn't have credible evidence for those beliefs prior to the study, since we know it was reading the statements in the study that caused the people to form these new beliefs.

But in between the time they're reading these statements and forming beliefs and the time, "Later," when they're told the statements were false, could they have gotten credible evidence to support the belief? 

Sure, I guess so. You could read a statement like, "Barack Obama plans to invest in a passenger spaceship to Mars" and then form the new belief, "Within the next 50 years, people will be able to take a passenger spaceship to Mars".

Later, we tell you that Obama statement we provided you with was false, but when you got home that day, you Googled "passenger spaceship to Mars" and found out that Elon Musk was actually planning to do this. Your newly acquired belief has some credible evidence, in addition to the statement we provided.

Thus, when we rescind the truth of those statements, it doesn't cause you to jettison that new belief you formed about "within 50 years, passenger travel to Mars". You are not an example of someone who is holding onto an acquired belief even though you have no credible evidence to support it.

Goal

Look for an answer impugning the Sampling move, by saying that what happened in this study is not a generalizable "human" trait.

Or look for an answer exploiting the wiggle room with "Later, ...".  Someone might have found credible evidence to support their new belief in the intervening period. Just because the original reason for the belief turns out to be false, that doesn't mean the belief is false (that's the Unproven vs. Proven False distinction).

answers.text: Regardless of the truth of what the subjects were later told, the beliefs based on the original statements were, for the most part, correct.
answers.fb:
Weaker Impact

This helps weaken somewhat, because if the people who persisted in believing the new beliefs are believing mostly true things, it feels like it could help us make the counterargument that these people did have credible reason to believe them.

They weren't just "stuck" believing them, because of the psychological trick of the experiment. 

But this answer doesn't establish that the subjects knew these beliefs were mostly correct or that the subjects had any credible evidence. An answer that establishes the subjects persisted in holding onto the new beliefs because they were aware of credible evidence for them is a stronger counter.

answers.text: It is unrealistic to expect people to keep track of the original basis of their beliefs, and to revise a belief when its original basis is undercut.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: unrealistic

This answer sounds like it's trying to shield these research subjects from the author's critical glare. 

"Jeez, author --- give them a break, alright? Yes, they look stupid because they're still believing the things they came to believe based on your phony statements, but people can't be expected to remember the origin of their beliefs or to "update their beliefs" when the basis of a belief is undercut."

No one is blaming these research subjects for their behavior. The author isn't concluding, "They should have stopped believing those newly acquired beliefs". The author is descriptively (neutrally) concluding, "They continued believing those new beliefs even though (I assume) they had no credible reason to."

answers.text: The statements originally given to the subjects would be highly misleading even if true.
answers.fb:
Strengthens, if anything

This has the effect of making the original statements sound like fishy statements. "Even if true" suggests that there's a good chance they're not true. And even if they technically qualify as true, they're misleading.

If people are stubbornly hanging onto beliefs even when they're told that the "unlikely / misleading" statements on which they based those beliefs are false, that seems to help the author.

We don't have to worry whether it actually strengthens. We know it doesn't weaken, since it doesn't give us a way to argue that these subjects actually did have credible evidence to support the beliefs they were retaining.

answers.text: Most of the subjects had acquired confirmation of their newly acquired beliefs by the time they were told that the original statements were false.
answers.fb:
Correct

This goes with our anticipated objection. By the time people were told that Obama isn't really planning to build passenger ships to Mars, they had found out that Elon Musk genuinely was.

Thus, when the researchers said, "The original statements we told you were false", the subjects were like, "Oh, were those statements false?  Hmm. Cute.  Well, ... the beliefs I ended up with on the basis of your false statements happened to be true (I know this, because I've acquired confirmation of them since then). So, I'm sticking with my new beliefs, no thanks to you mischievous researchers."

answers.text: Most of the subjects were initially skeptical of the statements originally given to them.
answers.fb:
No Impact

If we had no better answers, maybe we could say that initial skepticism might prompt these research subjects to do some independent research on their own, and that that's why they now retain their newly acquired beliefs. They do have credible evidence! 

But naturally this answer isn't as compelling as the correct one, which spells out the idea that the subjects have their own credible evidence.

questiontext:
Novelists cannot become great as long as they remain in academia. Powers of observation and analysis, which schools successfully hone, are useful to the novelist, but an intuitive grasp of the emotions of everyday life can be obtained only by the kind of immersion in everyday life that is precluded by being an academic.

Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
gf:
Conclusion

Novelists cannot become great as long as they remain in academia.

Evidence

Schools hone observation and analysis (useful to novelists). But an intuitive grasp of everyday emotions can only be obtained through immersion in everyday life, which being an academic precludes.

Evaluate

The argument moves from "academics can't get the intuitive grasp of everyday emotions" to "academics can't become great novelists." That step only works if the intuitive grasp of everyday emotions is something required for greatness. If it were merely nice to have, the argument would not establish that academics are barred from greatness.

Goal

The right answer should fill the gap by establishing that an intuitive grasp of everyday emotions is necessary for greatness. Negation test: if it's not necessary, the argument falls apart.

answers.text: Novelists require some impartiality to get an intuitive grasp of the emotions of everyday life.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope

This answer introduces "impartiality" as a requirement for the intuitive grasp. The argument doesn't depend on impartiality at all — the only quality the argument cares about for getting the intuitive grasp is immersion in everyday life. Negation test: even if impartiality plays no role in obtaining the intuitive grasp, the argument's claims are intact (academics still lack the immersion they need). Not necessary.

answers.text: No great novelist lacks powers of observation and analysis.
answers.fb:
Bad Assumption

This says every great novelist has powers of observation and analysis. The argument doesn't need that. The argument is about what academics lack (immersion), not about what they have. Negation test: even if some great novelists lack observation and analysis powers, the argument's point — that academics can't reach greatness because they lack the intuitive grasp — still goes through. Not necessary.

answers.text: Participation in life, interspersed with impartial observation of life, makes novelists great.
answers.fb:
Too Strong

This says participation plus impartial observation makes novelists great — a claim about what is sufficient for greatness. The argument is about what is necessary, not what is sufficient. Negation test: even if participation interspersed with observation does not, by itself, make novelists great, academics could still be barred from greatness because they lack the necessary intuitive grasp. The argument's structure doesn't depend on this. Not necessary.

answers.text: Novelists cannot be great without an intuitive grasp of the emotions of everyday life.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is the bridge the argument needs. The stimulus shows academics can't get the intuitive grasp (because that requires immersion that academia precludes). To leap from that to "academics can't be great," the argument needs greatness to require the intuitive grasp.

Negation test: suppose great novelists do not require an intuitive grasp of everyday emotions. Then the fact that academics lack it doesn't bar them from greatness — and the conclusion collapses. The argument depends on (D).

answers.text: Knowledge of the emotions of everyday life cannot be acquired by merely observing and analyzing life.
answers.fb:
Bad Assumption

The stimulus already commits to the view that the intuitive grasp can only come from immersion in everyday life — i.e., not from observing-and-analyzing alone. So this is a restatement of a stimulus claim, not a needed assumption. The argument's logic uses that claim as a premise; it doesn't depend on a separate, additional claim of the same content. Negation test gets odd here because the stimulus already asserts essentially this; the gap the argument actually needs to fill is whether the intuitive grasp is required for greatness (which is (D)).

questiontext:
Statistician: A financial magazine claimed that its survey of its subscribers showed that North Americans are more concerned about their personal finances than about politics. One question was: “Which do you think about more: politics or the joy of earning money?” This question is clearly biased. Also, the readers of the magazine are a self-selecting sample. Thus, there is reason to be skeptical about the conclusion drawn in the magazine’s survey.

Each of the following, if true, would strengthen the statistician's argument EXCEPT:
gf:
Conclusion (thus)

There is reason to be skeptical about the conclusion drawn in the magazine's survey.

Evidence

The survey question was biased: "Which do you think about more: politics or the joy of earning money?"

The readers of the magazine are a self-selecting sample.

Evaluate

The statistician is making a case that the results of the magazine's survey are not reliable because the survey question is biased, and the sample is self-selecting, making it unrepresentative. The argument is about questioning the validity and accuracy of the magazine’s conclusion that North Americans care more about finances than politics.

Goal

Let's get rid of four answers that strengthen the argument. We might see evidence that supports the idea that the survey results are not credible due to these issues. This could include evidence about the bias or unreliability of such surveys or additional data suggesting the survey's conclusion is incorrect.

answers.text: The credibility of the magazine has been called into question on a number of occasions.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

The credibility of the magazine being questionable helps us to argue that we should be skeptical of this most recent survey they're publishing.

answers.text: The conclusions drawn in most magazine surveys have eventually been disproved.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

If most magazine surveys' conclusions have been disproved, this casts doubt on the reliability of this survey's conclusion too, thereby strengthening skepticism.

answers.text: Other surveys suggest that North Americans are just as concerned about politics as they are about finances.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This answer contradicts the magazine’s claim by suggesting counter-evidence from other surveys, thereby supporting skepticism about the magazine's conclusion.

answers.text: There is reason to be skeptical about the results of surveys that are biased and unrepresentative.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This choice directly supports the missing link between the evidence and the conclusion, because it highlights the general unreliability of biased and unrepresentative surveys, like the magazine's survey.

answers.text: Other surveys suggest that North Americans are concerned not only with politics and finances, but also with social issues.
answers.fb:
Correct

This survey was just asking a head to head question, "are you more concerned with A or B?" 

That doesn't assume that A and B are the only two things the respondent is concerned with. This answer tells us, "people are also concerned about C!"

Okay, so what? That doesn't have anything to do with judging whether the survey results of a poll about "A vs. B" should be trusted or not. 

Since this has no impact, it's the correct answer.

questiontext:
On the basis of the available evidence, Antarctica has generally been thought to have been covered by ice for at least the past 14 million years. Recently, however, three-million-year-old fossils of a kind previously found only in ocean-floor sediments were discovered under the ice sheet covering central Antarctica. About three million years ago, therefore, the Antarctic ice sheet must temporarily have melted. After all, either severe climatic warming or volcanic activity in Antarctica's mountains could have melted the ice sheet, thus raising sea levels and submerging the continent.

Which one of the following is the main conclusion of the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

The Antarctic ice sheet must temporarily have melted about three million years ago — i.e., Antarctica has not been continuously ice-covered for the last 14 million years.

Evidence

Three-million-year-old ocean-floor-sediment fossils were found beneath the central Antarctic ice sheet. Either severe climatic warming or volcanic activity could have melted the ice and submerged the continent (which is what would have allowed those fossils to settle into ocean-floor sediments at that location).

Evaluate

Identify the main conclusion vs. supporting claims. The "either-or" sentence about volcanic activity or climatic warming is offered as support for the melting-ice claim ("after all, ..."). The melting-ice claim is the main conclusion the author is arguing for; the previous-belief framing (14M years of ice) sets up the contrast.

Goal
