Find the answer that captures the claim "the ice melted three million years ago" — i.e., the ice sheet has not been continuously present.

answers.text: Antarctica is no longer generally thought to have been covered by ice for the past 14 million years.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This is about what is "generally thought" — a claim about people's current beliefs. The author's conclusion is about what actually happened to the ice sheet, not about how widespread some belief is. (And in fact, the stimulus opens with "has generally been thought" — there is no evidence the author is making a sociological claim about whether the belief is now generally held.) Off target.

answers.text: It is not the case that ancient fossils of the kind recently found in Antarctica are found only in ocean-floor sediments.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This is a side claim about where these fossils can be found, not the author's main point. The author uses the fossils as evidence to argue something about the ice sheet — that it must have melted. The claim about fossil distribution is a stepping stone, not the destination.

answers.text: The ice sheet covering Antarctica has not been continuously present throughout the past 14 million years.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is exactly the main conclusion. The author argues that the ice sheet must have temporarily melted three million years ago — which is just to say that the ice has not been continuously present for the last 14 million years. The author signals it with "therefore," and the rest of the stimulus (background about prior belief, plus "after all" supporting reasons) all serves this claim.

answers.text: What caused Antarctica to be submerged under the sea was the melting of the ice sheet that had previously covered the continent.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This claim — that ice melting caused the submersion — appears in the stimulus only as part of the supporting "after all" reasoning, not as the main point. The author is concluding that the ice melted, not making a separate point about what specifically caused the continent to submerge. (The submersion is part of the chain explaining how the fossils ended up where they did.)

answers.text: The ice sheet covering Antarctica was melted either as a result of volcanic activity in Antarctica’s mountains or as a result of severe climatic warming.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This identifies why the ice would have melted (volcanic activity or climatic warming) — but that's the author's supporting evidence, not the conclusion. The conclusion is that the ice melted. The "either ... or" sentence is offered after "after all," which is a premise indicator.

questiontext:
On the basis of the available evidence, Antarctica has generally been thought to have been covered by ice for at least the past 14 million years. Recently, however, three-million-year-old fossils of a kind previously found only in ocean-floor sediments were discovered under the ice sheet covering central Antarctica. About three million years ago, therefore, the Antarctic ice sheet must temporarily have melted. After all, either severe climatic warming or volcanic activity in Antarctica's mountains could have melted the ice sheet, thus raising sea levels and submerging the continent.

The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to which one of the following criticisms?
gf:
Conclusion (therefore)

About 3 million years ago, the Antarctic ice sheet must have temporarily melted.

Evidence (after all)

We recently discovered 3 million year old fossils under the ice sheet covering central America (previously we had only found this type of fossils at the bottom of the ocean).

It's plausible that Antartica could have been submerged under water, since severe climate change or volcanic activity could have melted the ice sheet. 

Evaluate

Since the author is looking at a puzzling piece of archaeological evidence and speculating what it means / what it tells us, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. 

Curious Fact ... why are we finding these 3 million year old fossils under the ice sheet covering Antartica? (Previously we had only found these fossils in ocean floor sediments)

Author's Explanation ... At the time of these fossils, the ice sheet must have been melted, which would raise the water level high enough that Antarctica would be underwater, and so the ocean creature these fossils are from would have been swimming "over" Antarctica, it would have died and sunk to the "ocean floor", which would have been the top of Antarctica, and then later as the water refroze and the continent again rose above sea level, those fossils would be trapped under the ice sheet.

Evaluate

Notice how many blanks we had to fill in for the author just to understand her Causal Story! (I'm not even 100% sure I'm interpreting her causal story correctly)

When Flaw intersects with Curious Fact / Explanation arguments, the most common type of correct answer just calls out the fact that the author is overconfidently assuming one possible causal interpretation of the evidence, when others exist.

When we simply say "the flaw is that the author infers a cause from a mere correlation" we're saying, "Sure, maybe this correlation indicates causality, but we can't be as sure as the author is thinking."

Our author's conclusion is way too strong --- the ice sheet must have temporarily melted?

There aren't any other explanations? If we assumed that Antarctica did not melt and was still above sea level, can we think of any other possible way that the fossils could have ended up where we found them?

Sure, maybe a bird snatched this fish out of the ocean and was flying over Antarctica and dropped it. Maybe a hurricane or an underwater volcano lifted this fish into the air and flung it over Antarctica. Maybe within the ice sheet there used to be underwater tunnels that this fish could have gone through. Maybe this fish was really an amphibian that was able to scoot across the ice.

Goal

When we're doing Flaw and read one of these Curious Fact / Explanation arguments, then we're receptive to three different types of answers:
1. Complain that the author is overly confident in arriving at one possible explanation, where others may exist.

2. Suggest that the author may have failed to consider some alternative explanation.

3. Point out something implausible about the author's explanation.

answers.text: That a given position is widely believed to be true is taken to show that the position in question must, in fact, be true.
answers.fb:
Bad Premise Match

Because of this answer's structure
"that X is taken show that Y" 
means that X is supposed to refer to Evidence and Y to the Conclusion.

In this argument, "Chris is a boy. Thus he must like football", we could say that the flaw in this argument was this:
that Chris is a boy is taken to show that he is a football fan

So does this answer choice match up with our argument? Was there a premise that said
a given position is widely believed to be true?

No, there was a background claim that said it's widely believed to be true that "Antarctica was covered by ice for the past 14 million years".

Did the author conclude that this claim must be true? No, the opposite. Her conclusion is actually saying it must be false, that the ice sheet must have temporarily melted 3 million years ago.

answers.text: That either of two things could independently have produced a given effect is taken to show that those two things could not have operated in conjunction to produce that effect.
answers.fb:
Bad Premise/Conclusion Match

This has the same structure as (A), so we're trying to match the first half with the evidence and the second half of the conclusion.

Did the evidence say that "either of two things could have independently produced a given effect"?

Sure, it said that either volcano or climatic warming could have independently produced a melting of the ice sheet.

Does the conclusion then say that, "those two things could not have operated in conjunction to produce that effect?"  No. The conclusion just says "that effect must have occurred" (the ice sheet must have melted)

This answer would hurt an argument that sounded like this:
Bernadette's perfume and Bernadette's dress each would made Tyrone attracted to her. Thus, Tyrone was not attracted to the combo of her perfume and her dress.

answers.text: Establishing that a certain event occurred is confused with having established the cause of that event.
answers.fb:
Bad Description

The author is trying to establish that a certain event occurred (the ice sheet temporarily melted 3 million years ago). The author brings up a couple causal possibilities for how that would have happened, although the primary evidence for it having happened is the fossils discovered under the ice sheet.

This answer is saying, "Just because we know the event occurred doesn't mean we know that caused the event". That objection wouldn't be relevant to the author's argument since she isn't claiming to know what caused it (bring up possible things that could have caused it is not claiming to know what one thing did cause it). 

We might re-write this answer as a more successful one by saying,
establishing that things could have cause an event is confused with establishing that the event actually occurred

But it would still be a poor answer because the author's primary evidence are the fossils, not his ruminating about what what might have caused the ice sheet to melt.

answers.text: A claim that has a very general application is based entirely on evidence from a narrowly restricted range of cases.
answers.fb:
Wrong Flaw

This refers to the famous Sampling Flaw, but we can't match that to this argument. Could we call the conclusion "a claim that has a very general application"?

Not really -- the conclusion is a specific claim that "about 3 million years ago, the ice sheet temporarily melted".

answers.text: An inconsistency that, as presented, has more than one possible resolution is treated as though only one resolution is possible.
answers.fb:
Correct

"X is treated as though Y" indicates that X is our evidence and we treated it as though it shows that our conclusion Y is true.

Did the evidence feature an inconsistency that, as presented, has more than one possible resolution?

Sure, we found fossils under an ice sheet that had previously only been found in ocean-floor sediments. 

The place we found these new fossils is inconsistent with the place where we have previously always found this type of fossils. Does the author treat this as though only one resolution is possible?

Yes, she concludes that the ice sheet must have melted (i.e. this part of Antarctica must have been underwater at the time this animal died). 

Is there more than one possible resolution?  Yes, as discussed before, maybe a bird dropped it, maybe a hurricane flung it, maybe it was amphibian and crawled there, maybe it swam through an ice sheet tunnel, etc.

If we wanted to customize this to our vernacular, this answer is just saying
"A Curious Fact that, as presented, has more than one possible explanation is treated as though only the author's explanation is possible."

questiontext:
Opponent of offshore oil drilling: The projected benefits of drilling new oil wells in certain areas in the outer continental shelf are not worth the risk of environmental disaster. The oil already being extracted from these areas currently provides only 4 percent of our country’s daily oil requirement, and the new wells would only add one-half of 1 percent.

Proponent of offshore oil drilling: Don’t be ridiculous! You might just as well argue that new farms should not be allowed, since no new farm could supply the total food needs of our country for more than a few minutes.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the drilling proponent's reply?
gf:
Opponent's Conclusion

The projected benefits of drilling new oil wells are not worth the risk of environmental disaster.

Evidence

The oil currently extracted from these areas provides only 4 percent of our daily oil requirement, and the new wells would add just one-half of 1 percent.

Proponent's Reply

That's as dumb as saying we shouldn't allow new farms, since no single farm could feed the country even for a day.

Evaluate

We need to respond to the proponent. The proponent counters with an analogy, arguing that just because a new oil well contributes a small amount to overall oil supply, it doesn’t mean it should be dismissed, just as new farms, which don't provide the entire food supply, shouldn't be prohibited.

To weaken the drilling proponent's reply, we should look for a flaw in this analogy or a reason why the analogy doesn't hold.

Goal

Let's find an answer that highlights a dissimilarity between offshore oil drilling and starting new farms, or shows why the proponent's analogy is misleading or flawed.

answers.text: New farms do not involve a risk analogous to that run by new offshore oil drilling.
answers.fb:
Correct

New farms do not involve a risk analogous to that run by new offshore oil drilling. This answer weakens the proponent’s analogy by pointing out a significant difference. While new oil drilling carries significant environmental risks, new farms do not pose a comparable risk. Thus, this key difference undercuts the analogy.

answers.text: Many of the largest oil deposits are located under land that is unsuitable for farming.
answers.fb:
No Impact

No one was ever suggesting that where we drill for oil and where we farm are the same place. The proponent used farming as an analogy, but wasn't suggesting that farming involves overlapping parcels of land.

answers.text: Unlike oil, common agricultural products fulfill nutritional needs rather than fuel requirements.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This is somewhat tempting, because it also seems to disrupt the oil / farm analogy, but the distinction has less to do with arguing that we shouldn't allow new drilling.

Nutritional needs and fuel requirements are both very important things to a functioning society, so even though that's a difference between oil and farms, it doesn't hurt the proponent's analogy. 

He could say, "Since farming and oil drilling both provide very important things to a functioning society, and since no one farm or drilling field will be enough to support society on its own, we should approve new farms and new drilling fields."

answers.text: Legislation governing new oil drilling has been much more thoroughly articulated than has that governing new farms.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This is somewhat tempting, because it also seems to disrupt the oil / farm analogy, but the distinction has nothing to do with arguing that we shouldn't allow new drilling.

We weren't ever saying we shouldn't allow for new drilling because "the legislation isn't thoroughly enough articulated". We were saying we shouldn't allow it because of the potential environmental damage.

answers.text: The country under discussion imports a higher proportion of the farm products it needs than it does of the oil it needs.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Comparison

This also presents a difference relating to oil vs farms, but we don't care about the ratio of domestic to imported oil is higher or lower than the ratio of domestic to imported farm products. 

The proponent was never thinking both products had a similar domestic/imported ratio. 

The proponent is only saying, "since no one farm is enough to supply our needs, we should approve new farms. Similarly, since no one oil field is enough to supply our needs, we should approve new oil fields."

questiontext:
It is inaccurate to say that a diet high in refined sugar cannot cause adult-onset diabetes, since a diet high in refined sugar can make a person overweight, and being overweight can predispose a person to adult-onset diabetes.

The argument is most parallel, in its logical structure, to which one of the following?
gf:
Conclusion

It is inaccurate to say that a diet high in refined sugar cannot cause adult-onset diabetes.

rephrase: a diet high in refined sugar can cause adult onset diabetes.

Evidence (since)

A high-sugar diet can make a person overweight, and being overweight can predispose a person to adult-onset diabetes.

Evaluate

The evidence presents a causal chain:
high sugar >> overweight >> adult diabetes

The author has thus shown a causal path from high sugar to adult diabetes.

Goal

We want two premises that form a causal chain:
Prem:  A can lead to B
Prem:  B can lead to C

and then a Conc that connects them (or that denies that they can't be connected)
Conc:  A can lead to C
or
Conc:  It's wrong to say that A can't lead to C

answers.text: It is inaccurate to say that being in cold air can cause a person to catch a cold, since colds are caused by viruses, and viruses flourish in warm, crowded places.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This conclusion is denying a causal connection. We want our conclusion to be affirming a causal connection.

The evidence gives us something of a causal chain by saying:
warm/crowded >> virus >> cold

So the conclusion should be saying,
"It's wrong to say that warm/crowded places can't cause a cold".

answers.text: It is accurate to say that no airline flies from Halifax to Washington. No airline offers a direct flight, although some airlines have flights from Halifax to Boston and others have flights from Boston to Washington.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion/Evidence Match

This conclusion isn't causal at all, nor is the evidence.

The evidence also doesn't chain together. It just says some are this, some are that.

answers.text: It is correct to say that overfertilization is the primary cause of lawn disease, since fertilizer causes lawn grass to grow rapidly and rapidly growing grass has little resistance to disease.
answers.fb:
Weaker Conclusion/Evidence Match
Bad Validity Match

The conclusion is affirming a causal connection, but much more strongly than in the original argument.

The original argument is just showing that high sugar can lead to adult diabetes, not that high sugar is the primary cause of adult diabetes.

The evidence provides a chain:
fertilizer >> rapid growth >> vulnerable to disease

But the validity of this argument is much lower than the original, because the evidence only shows that fertilizer has some causal connection to disease, not that it's the primary cause.

answers.text: It is incorrect to say that inferior motor oil cannot cause a car to get poorer gasoline mileage, since inferior motor oil can cause engine valve deterioration, and engine valve deterioration can lead to poorer gasoline mileage.
answers.fb:
Correct

The evidence provides a causal chain:
bad oil >> deteriorating valve >>  poorer mileage

So the author has demonstrated that bad oil can lead to poorer mileage. And the conclusion has the same rebuttal feel as the original, saying "it's wrong to say that bad oil can't cause poorer mileage".

answers.text: It is inaccurate to say that Alexander the Great was a student of Plato; Alexander was a student of Aristotle and Aristotle was a student of Plato.
answers.fb:
Weaker Conclusion/Evidence Match
Bad Validity Match

The conclusion is a rebuttal, but it's not exactly rebutting a causal claim.

The evidence does not provide a causal chain.  And it's questionable whether this conclusion is even valid. After all, if your teacher was taught by Alexander the Great, then in an indirect sense you are "a student" of Alexander the Great.

You're not sitting in class with him, but you're still probably learning from him indirectly.

questiontext:
Zoos have served both as educational resources and as entertainment. Unfortunately, removing animals from their natural habitats to stock the earliest zoos reduced certain species’ populations, endangering their survival. Today most zoo animals are obtained from captive breeding programs, and many zoos now maintain breeding stocks for continued propagation of various species. This makes possible efforts to reestablish endangered species in the wild.

Which one of the following statements is most strongly supported by the information above?
gf:
Information

Zoos function both as education and entertainment.

Causal Chain
Removing animals from natural habitats to stock the first zoos reduced the populations of those species, which then endangered the survival of some of those species.

Contrast
Modern zoos get most of their animals not by removing them from natural habitats but by breeding new animals in captivity (i.e. at the zoo).

Causal Difference-Maker
Maintaining breeding stocks for continued propagation of various species makes possible efforts to reestablish endangered species in the wild.

Evaluate / Goal

This is a pretty varied mix of claims with no obvious momentum for combining facts, so I would head to the answers. We're on guard against language that is Too Strong, makes an Unknown Comparison, goes Against the Passage, or just brings up something Out of Scope.

answers.text: Zoos have played an essential role in educating the public about endangered species.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: essential

We actually don't know for sure that zoos have played any role in educating about endangered species. We know zoos have played some educational role. That's it. These statements don't allow us to derive something as strong as the claim that they've played an essential role.

answers.text: Some specimens of endangered species are born and bred in zoos.
answers.fb:
Correct

This spells out the implicit logic in the Causal Difference-Maker language starting the final sentence:
this makes possible

If they're telling us that by breeding animals within the zoo (i.e. having two zoo pandas mate and breed so that the baby pandas can also grow up in the zoo) makes possible efforts to reestablish endangered species in the wild.

If none of the animals being born and bred in zoos were endangered, then how would the zoos' practice of raising baby animals do anything to help reestablish endangered species in the wild?

The implied idea in the last sentence is that at least some of the animals being born/bred in zoos are from endangered species, and once the babies are robust enough, the zoos will send those babies off into the wild, in an attempt to boost the numbers of an endangered species. 

If we were just rapidly guessing on this problem, we would definitely guess this answer because it has the weakest language.

A) essential
B) some
C) No
D) nearly all
E) the main purpose

answers.text: No zoos exploit wild animals or endanger the survival of species.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: Exploit Wild Animals
Opposite

We never talk about whether zoos are exploiting animals (and many of us would certainly say, "yes, they are!"). We're also told early on in the paragraph that the practice of snatching animals from natural habitats actually endangered the survival of some species.

Even though those were the early zoos and "most" zoo animals today are obtained from captive breeding, there's still plenty of room for some zoo animals to be still snatched from the wild, potentially endangering their species.

This answer is just so strongly worded "Not one zoo is exploiting any wild animal or endangering the survival of any species" that it would be incredibly hard to support.

answers.text: Nearly all of the animals in zoos today were born in captivity.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: "Nearly All"
Obtained By Zoos vs. In Zoos

We were told that most zoo animals nowadays are obtained through captive breeding programs. 

Most = more than 50%.  51% qualifies as most. Does 51% qualify as "nearly all"?

If we said 51% of Senators voted for the bill, we can say most Senators voted for the bill, but we can't say nearly all the Senators voted for the bill.

Nearly all doesn't have a precise definition but we're talking at least 80%. 

The other problem with this answer is that it's talking about the animals in zoos today, not the animals obtained by zoos today. Even though we know most zoo animals nowadays are obtained through captive breeding, that doesn't mean most animals in zoos were obtained through captive breeding.

There could be tons of animals who were snatched from the wild a couple decades ago but are still alive in zoos.

answers.text: The main purpose of zoos has shifted from entertainment to education.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: Main Purpose
Out of Scope: Shifted

We can't comment on what the main purpose of zoos is, since we weren't given any language comparing the importance of purposes. We also have no reason to believe the emphasis, whatever it is, has shifted.

questiontext:
People ought to take into account a discipline’s blemished origins when assessing the scientific value of that discipline. Take, for example, chemistry. It must be considered that many of its landmark results were obtained by alchemists—a group whose superstitions and appeals to magic dominated the early development of chemical theory.

The reasoning above is most susceptible to criticism because the author
gf:
Conclusion

People ought to take into account a discipline's blemished origins when assessing the scientific value of that discipline.

Evidence

Chemistry, for example, had some of its landmark results discovered by alchemists, who believed in crazy stuff like superstitions and magic and helped develop early chemical theory.

Evaluate

This is a weird argument Let's think about the Anti-Conclusion client we're representing:
When we're assessing the value of a scientific discipline, such as chemistry, we do NOT need to take into account its blemished origins.

Given that early chemical theory sounds like some superstitious / magical non-scientific rubbish, how can we argue that this is irrelevant (does not need to be taken into account) when it comes to assessing what value the discipline of chemistry has.

I guess we would argue that even though it has an embarrassing, scientifically dubious origin story, it's still a really successful scientific theory, and some of our fanciest inventions are based on the correct predictions of chemical reactions, according to the laws of chemistry.

Goal

Look for an answer saying "chemistry is an unrepresentative sample", or an answer saying that "the bad stuff about chemistry's early days doesn't have impact on how we assess the current value of chemistry".

answers.text: fails to establish that disciplines with unblemished origins are scientifically valuable
answers.fb:
Illegal Opposite

When we see fails to establish X,
we just ask ourselves, "Did the author need to establish X? Was that one of her assumptions?"

The author seems to be assuming that "if a discipline has blemished origins, we might not think of them being as valuable".

This answer is saying the author was assuming "if a discipline has unblemished origins, then it is valuable", which is trying to pull an illegal opposite with one of the author's actual assumptions.

answers.text: fails to consider how chemistry’s current theories and practices differ from those of the alchemists mentioned
answers.fb:
Correct

Can we object to this argument by talking about how chemistry's current theories and practices differ from those of the alchemists?

Yes, potentially. If we say "author, chemistry is currently a scientific discipline that has nothing to do with magic and superstition. It is a highly rigorous and accomplished science. Thus, if we're assessing the scientific value of chemistry, shouldn't we look at what it is, not what it was?"

If we're assessing the value of a novel, should we take into account the blemishes of the first draft of the manuscript?

answers.text: uses an example to contradict the principle under consideration
answers.fb:
Opposite: Contradict
Not a Flaw

The author used an example to support the principle under consideration.

Also, there's nothing inherently flawed or wrong about using an example to contradict a principle under consideration, so it would be weird to imagine a situation where this would be a correct answer (it would have to be like the famous Internal Contradiction flaw, where an author is arguing for Principle X but introduces an example that contradicts Principle X).

answers.text: does not prove that most disciplines that are not scientifically valuable have origins that are in some way suspect
answers.fb:
Too Strong: Most
Reversed Logic

Does not prove = fails to specify = assumes

Did the author assume
not scientifically → probably have 
  valuable               blemished origins

No, she was closer to assuming
has blemished  → probably not
    origins               sci valuable

answers.text: uses the word “discipline” in two different senses
answers.fb:
Wrong Flaw

This refers to the famous Equivocation flaw, in which the author uses the same term or concept in two very different ways.

There are different meanings to discipline:
Discipline - a field of study
Discipline - punishment
Discipline - rigorous adherence to a standard

But the author only used it consistently to mean "a field of study".

questiontext:
Nutritionist: Recently a craze has developed for home juicers, $300 machines that separate the pulp of fruits and vegetables from the juice they contain. Outrageous claims are being made about the benefits of these devices: drinking the juice they produce is said to help one lose weight or acquire a clear complexion, to aid digestion, and even to prevent cancer. But there is no indication that juice separated from the pulp of the fruit or vegetable has any properties that it does not have when unseparated. Save your money. If you want carrot juice, eat a carrot.

Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the nutritionist's argument?
gf:
Conclusion (implied)

Juicers are a waste of money; just eat the whole fruit or vegetable if you want the juice.

Evidence

There is no indication that juice separated from the pulp contains any special properties compared to when it is unseparated.

Evaluate

GIVEN THAT juice separated from the pulp has no additional benefits over whole fruits and vegetables, HOW CAN WE DEFEND juicers?

To weaken this conclusion, we need to show a benefit or advantage of using a juicer that justifies the expense, regardless of the intrinsic properties of the juice.

Goal

Identify an answer choice that presents a reason why owning a juicer might still be beneficial or desirable, even though the juice isn't inherently more beneficial than the solid food from which it comes.

answers.text: Most people find it much easier to consume a given quantity of nutrients in liquid form than to eat solid foods containing the same quantity of the same nutrients.
answers.fb:
Correct

This choice argues that people find it easier to consume nutrients in liquid form. This suggests that juicers make it more likely that people will consume necessary nutrients, thus providing a practical benefit to juicers that could make them worth the investment.

answers.text: Drinking juice from home juicers is less healthy than is eating fruits and vegetables because such juice does not contain the fiber that is eaten if one consumes the entire fruit or vegetable.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This states that juice is less healthy without fiber, aligning with the nutritionist’s argument against separating juice from pulp, as it implies a disadvantage to using juicers.

answers.text: To most people who would be tempted to buy a home juicer, $300 would not be a major expense.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This argues that $300 isn’t a major expense for potential buyers, which doesn't directly address the nutritional value or benefit offered by the juicer but rather the affordability of it.

answers.text: The nutritionist was a member of a panel that extensively evaluated early prototypes of home juicers.
answers.fb:
No Impact / Strengthens

This states that the nutritionist evaluated early prototypes, suggesting prior knowledge and expertise that might bolster the argument, but it doesn't introduce new information about the juicer's benefits or drawbacks.

answers.text: Vitamin pills that supposedly contain nutrients available elsewhere only in fruits and vegetables often contain a form of those compounds that cannot be as easily metabolized as the varieties found in fruits and vegetables.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This discusses the bioavailability of nutrients in vitamin pills, which is not directly relevant to the debate about the usefulness of juicers vs. actual fruits/vegetables, making it off-topic.

questiontext:
It is widely believed that eating chocolate can cause acne. Indeed, many people who are susceptible to acne report that, in their own experience, eating large amounts of chocolate is invariably followed by an outbreak of that skin condition. However, it is likely that common wisdom has mistaken an effect for a cause. Several recent scientific studies indicate that hormonal changes associated with stress can cause acne and there is good evidence that people who are fond of chocolate tend to eat more chocolate when they are under stress.

The argument employs which one of the following argumentative strategies?

answers.text: It cites counterevidence that calls into question the accuracy of the evidence advanced in support of the position being challenged.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

The evidence for the author's rebuttal (the new studies) doesn't attack the opposing evidence (the correlation between chocolate eating and breakouts). It's actually consistent with that opposing evidence because the studies are trying to explain that same correlation.

answers.text: It provides additional evidence that points to an alternative interpretation of the evidence offered in support of the position being challenged.
answers.fb:
Correct

We have additional evidence (new studies) that points out an alternative interpretation (chocolate is an effect, not a cause) of the evidence offered in support of the position being challenged (chocolate eating and acne are correlated).

answers.text: It invokes the superior authority of science over common opinion in order to dismiss out of hand the relevance of evidence based on everyday experience.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match
Bad Conclusion Match

This one is tempting because the author does invoke new scientific studies as evidence and we do see common view language in the opposing conclusion. That said, the evidence doesn't actually say that science is superior to common views, and the conclusion doesn't dismiss out of hand the relevance of the opposing evidence.

answers.text: It demonstrates that the position being challenged is inconsistent with certain well-established facts.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match
Bad Conclusion Match

The evidence doesn't bring up any well-established facts: it brings up some new studies, which is kind of the opposite of well-established. The conclusion doesn't demonstrate that the opposing conclusion is inconsistent with anything. It just raises an alternative conclusion one might draw.

answers.text: It provides counterexamples to show that, contrary to the assumption on which the commonly held position rests, causes do not always precede their effects.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match
Bad Conclusion Match

The evidence doesn't bring up a counterexample or attack an assumption. And the conclusion is definitely not that causes don't always precede their effects. That's counter to common sense! In order for something to be a cause, it has to come before the effect.

questiontext:
It has been claimed that television networks should provide equal time for the presentation of opposing views whenever a television program concerns scientific issues—such as those raised by the claims of environmentalists—about which people disagree. However, although an obligation to provide equal time does arise in the case of any program concerning social issues, it does so because social issues almost always have important political implications and seldom can definitely be settled on the basis of available evidence. If a program concerns scientific issues, that program gives rise to no such equal time obligation.

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

A program concerning scientific issues gives rise to no equal-time obligation.

Evidence

Equal-time obligations arise for programs on social issues because (1) social issues almost always have important political implications, and (2) social issues seldom can be definitely settled on the basis of available evidence.

Evaluate

This is a weird argument, where the author is trying to explain why we DON'T need equal time for science stuff based on why we DO need equal time for social stuff.

If I said, "You don't have to worry about me acting weird around your sister. The other reason I acted weird around your friend was because I have a crush on your friend", that would imply a difference:  it implies that I don't have a crush on your sister. 

We're arguing that these two situations are different because there's some underlying difference that matters. 

So this author is also Assuming a Difference, thinking that the reasons we need equal time for social issues don't apply to science issues.

Goal

Let's look for an answer that helps us argue that we DO need an equal time obligation for science issues.

It'll probably attack the assumed differences, so it might say that science issues ALSO have important political implications or that science issues ALSO can rarely be settled on the basis of available evidence.

answers.text: No scientific issues raised by the claims of environmentalists have important political implications.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

We wanted to hear that scientific issues ALSO have important political implications and thus they should also have an equal time requirement.

This says the opposite, which strengthens the argument. It provides one of the author's assumed differences.

answers.text: There are often more than two opposing views on an issue that cannot be definitely settled on the basis of available evidence.
answers.fb:
Unclear Impact

We don't know if this "often" overlaps with scientific issues. If we were told that scientific issues can rarely be settled on the basis of available evidence that would weaken, but this isn't that specific.

answers.text: Some social issues could be definitely settled on the basis of evidence if the opposing sides would give all the available evidence a fair hearing.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This is incredibly weak, "at least one social issue". It's also off topic, since we need to hear about scientific issues, since this argument is about evaluating whether scientific issues should have an equal time obligation.

answers.text: Many scientific issues have important political implications and cannot be definitely settled on the basis of the available evidence.
answers.fb:
Correct

Nice! This spells out both of the assumed differences and tells the author that he's wrong on both counts.

The author said the equal-time obligation arises from two features: (1) important political implications and (2) inability to be settled by available evidence. The author assumed scientific issues lacked these. 

(D) makes it seem like scientific issues would have just as much reason to have an equal time obligation as social issues do.

answers.text: Some television networks refuse to broadcast programs on issues that have important political implications and that cannot be definitely settled by the available evidence.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This is very weak wording and doesn't deal specifically with scientific issues.

Also, if a network refuses to broadcast an issue, then it's irrelevant whether we have an equal time obligation. Both sides are getting zero time.

The conversation we're having is only about programs that DO cover contentious issues. The ones that don't cover them are irrelevant.

questiontext:
If Slater wins the election, McGuinness will be appointed head of the planning commission. But Yerxes is more qualified to head it since she is an architect who has been on the planning commission for fifteen years. Unless the polls are grossly inaccurate, Slater will win.

Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the information above?
gf:
Information

conditionals (if = suff, unless = if-not)

  Slater  -->  McG app head
   wins            of Planning C

    Polls are         --> Slater
pretty accurate       wins

contrast

Yerxes is more qualified to head the Planning C than McG is, since she's an architect who's been on Planning C for 15 years.

Evaluate

Whenever we see conditionals on Must Be True / Most Supported, we have two immediate questions:

1. Can I chain this conditional up with any other conditionals?
2. Can I apply this conditional (usually via contrapositive) to a fact that was provided?

We had two conditionals (signified by If / Unless), so we should investigate #1. Do they have a common term that would allow them to chain?

Yes, they're both talking about Slater winning. So the chain looks like this:

    Polls are         →  Slater  →  McG app head
pretty accurate       wins         of Planning C

We could look for a "first to last" inference like, "If the polls aren't grossly inaccurate, then McG will be appointed head of Planning Committee".

What about the middle sentence? Is that just filler or is it usable?

We know that "If McG is appointed head, then a more qualified person (Yerxes) didn't get the job".

Goal

Let's look for something rewarding us for chaining the conditionals together and possibly using the middle sentence, like, "If the polls aren't grossly inaccurate, then the person appointed head of the Planning Commission will not be the most qualified candidate".

answers.text: If the polls are grossly inaccurate, someone more qualified than McGuinness will be appointed head of the planning commission.
answers.fb:
Unknown Trigger / Illegal Negation

We have a conditional (from the last sentence) that says,

If the polls are not  →  Slater wins
grossly inaccurate

We don't anything about what happens if the polls are grossly inaccurate.

This answer is trying to get students to think via an illegal negation. 

We know that 
"if polls are not grossly inaccurate, McGuinness will be appointed head", 

and this is baiting us into thinking 
"If the polls are grossly inaccurate, then McGuinness will not be appointed head".

answers.text: McGuinness will be appointed head of the planning commission only if the polls are a good indication of how the election will turn out.
answers.fb:
Unknown Trigger / Illegal Reversal

"Only if" always indicates the necessary idea to the right of the arrow, so this answer is saying:
   McG appointed head → Polls good indication

We have a conditional whose outcome is that McGuinness will be appointed head:

   Slater wins → McG appointed head

But we don't have any conditional where McG being appointed head is the trigger.

This answer is baiting us into an illegal reversal. We know:

  Polls good  →  Slater wins  →  McG appointed
  indication                                      head

And this answer is trying to backwards from the 3rd idea to the 1st idea.

answers.text: Either Slater will win the election or Yerxes will be appointed head of the planning commission.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: false choice 

If Slater wins, then McG (not Yerxes) will be appointed head.

What about it Slater doesn't win? We have no idea. 

They might still appoint McGuinness. They might appoint Bob. They might appoint Yerxes. We can't say.

So there's no way to limit this down to two possible outcomes:
   Slater wins and McG is head
        vs.
   Slater loses and Yerxes is head

answers.text: McGuinness is not an architect and has not been on the planning commission for fifteen years or more.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: and vs. or

This answer would be good (especially on Most Supported) if it said, "McG is not an architect or he hasn't been on the planning commission for at least 15 years". 

If McGuinness were both an architect and a member of the planning commission for at least 15 years, then that would go against the idea that Yerxes is more qualified, since she is an architect who has been a member for 15 years.

So we can infer that McGuinness does not have this equivalent resume.

But McGuinness could still be one or the other. Maybe he's an architect, but he's only been on the planning commission for 2 years. That would still allow Yerxes to be more qualified. 

According to this answer, though, that's impossible. McGuinness cannot be an architect.

answers.text: If the polls are a good indication of how the election will turn out, someone less qualified than Yerxes will be appointed head of the planning commission.
answers.fb:
Correct

We put together this conditional chain:

    Polls are not        →  Slater  →  McG app head
grossly inaccurate       wins         of Planning C

So we know that "if the polls are a good indication, then they are not grossly inaccurate, so Slater will win, and McG will be appointed head of Planning Commission".

And since we were told that McG is less qualified than Yerxes, we can say that "someone less qualified that Yerxes will be appointed head of the Planning Commission".

questiontext:
Peter: Because the leaves of mildly drought-stressed plants are tougher in texture than the leaves of abundantly watered plants, insects prefer to feed on the leaves of abundantly watered plants. Therefore, to minimize crop damage, farmers should water crops only just enough to ensure that there is no substantial threat, from a lack of water, to either the growth or the yield of the crops.

Jennifer: Indeed. In fact, a mildly drought-stressed plant will divert a small amount of its resources from normal growth to the development of pesticidal toxins, but abundantly watered plants will not.

Jennifer's comment is related to Peter's argument in which one of the following ways?

answers.text: It offers information that supports each of the claims that Peter makes in his argument.
answers.fb: Too Strong: each

answers.text: It supports Peter’s argument by supplying a premise without which Peter’s conclusion cannot properly be drawn.
answers.fb: Too Strong: w/o which can't be drawn

answers.text: It supports Peter’s argument by offering an explanation of all of Peter’s premises.
answers.fb: Too Strong: all

answers.text: It supports one of Peter’s premises although it undermines Peter’s conclusion.
answers.fb: Opposite: undermines P's conclusion

answers.text: It supports the conclusion of Peter’s argument by offering independent grounds for that conclusion.

questiontext:
Peter: Because the leaves of mildly drought-stressed plants are tougher in texture than the leaves of abundantly watered plants, insects prefer to feed on the leaves of abundantly watered plants. Therefore, to minimize crop damage, farmers should water crops only just enough to ensure that there is no substantial threat, from a lack of water, to either the growth or the yield of the crops.

Jennifer: Indeed. In fact, a mildly drought-stressed plant will divert a small amount of its resources from normal growth to the development of pesticidal toxins, but abundantly watered plants will not.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens Peter's argument?
gf:
Conclusion (therefore)

To minimize crop damage, farmers should water crops only just enough to ensure that there is no substantial threat, from a lack of water, to either the growth or the yield of the crops.

Evidence

The leaves of mildly drought-stressed plants are tougher in texture than the leaves of abundantly watered plants.

Insects prefer to feed on the leaves of abundantly watered plants.

Evaluate

This argument fits the Recommendation pattern. Peter is suggesting a course of action (water plants minimally) to achieve a goal (minimize crop damage). 

To assess this argument, we should consider whether following the recommendation would indeed lead to the intended outcome, with a net gain when compared to the current scenario of abundant watering. 

The author thinks insects' preference for softer leaves means that mildly drought-stressed plants will experience less insect damage. The argument assumes that the benefit of reduced insect damage outweighs any negative effects of mild drought stress, so a strong point in favor would be evidence that supports minimizing insect damage as a priority.

Goal

Let's find an answer that highlights that the potential benefits of reduced insect feeding, thanks to watering crops less, outweigh the risks associated with slight drought stress.

answers.text: The leaves of some crop plants are much larger, and therefore absorb more water, than the leaves of some other crop plants.
answers.fb:
No Impact

While it notes differences in water absorption among crops, it doesn't address whether mildly drought-stressed plants will benefit crops overall with reduced insect damage.

answers.text: In industrialized nations there are more crops that are abundantly watered than there are crops grown under mild drought stress.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The relative abundance of crops being abundantly watered versus mildly drought-stressed is irrelevant to the argument about reducing insect damage through less watering for specific crops.

answers.text: Insect damage presents a greater threat to crop plants than does mild drought stress.
answers.fb:
Correct

This choice emphasizes that insect damage is a greater threat to crops than mild drought stress. Thus, if slightly reducing water to gain tough leaves indeed minimizes insect feeding, it provides stronger justification for Peter's recommendation since it focuses on addressing the more serious threat.

answers.text: Farmers are not always able to control the amount of water that their crops receive when, for instance, there are rainstorms in the areas where their crops are growing.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This option points out potential variability in watering due to external factors like rain, but it doesn't discuss how this variability would affect the balance of insect versus drought stress damage.

answers.text: Mexican bean beetles are more likely to feed on the leaves of slightly drought-stressed soybeans than oak lace bugs are to feed on the leaves of abundantly watered soybeans.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)
No Impact

Because this compares two different bugs eating two different versions of the soybean (drier vs moister), it's impossible to derive anything from it.

"Bob is more likely to eat dry X than Karen is to eat moist X". Okay, what does that tell me???

But if anything, this makes it sound like the drier leaves are more likely to be eaten, which works against the author's plan.

questiontext:
High school students who feel that they are not succeeding in school often drop out before graduating and go to work. Last year, however, the city’s high school dropout rate was significantly lower than the previous year’s rate. This is encouraging evidence that the program instituted two years ago to improve the morale of high school students has begun to take effect to reduce dropouts.

Which one of the following, if true about the last year, most seriously weakens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (this is evidence that)

The program to improve the morale of high school students has begun to take effect to reduce dropouts.

Evidence

High school students who feel they are not succeeding in school often drop out.

Last year, the city's high school dropout rate was significantly lower than the previous year's rate.

Evaluate

This argument falls into the Explain Curious Fact pattern because it identifies a change in situation (a Curious Fact) and provides a causal explanation.

Curious Fact: Why is the high school dropout rate is lower this year compared to last year?

Author's Explanation: The program to improve student morale has caused the reduction in dropout rates.

The argument assumes that the program is the main or only reason the dropout rate has decreased. To weaken this argument, we can look for alternative explanations for the reduced dropout rate, or we could challenge the plausibility that the morale program was indeed responsible for the change.

Goal

Let's find an answer that suggests an alternative reason for the reduced dropout rate, one that is unconnected to the morale improvement program.

answers.text: There was a recession that caused a high level of unemployment in the city.
answers.fb:
Correct

If there was a recession causing high unemployment in the city, students might have realized that job prospects were limited, leading them to stay in school rather than drop out and seek work. This provides an alternative explanation for the reduced dropout rate and suggests it might not be due to the morale program.

answers.text: The morale of students who dropped out of high school had been low even before they reached high school.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This statement refers to students who have already dropped out, but does not offer insight into why fewer students dropped out last year.

We don't care what the backstory is for why they had low morale. We're only trying to figure out if the new program had any causal influence in improving morale.

answers.text: As in the preceding year, more high school students remained in school than dropped out.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This statement describes a situation that could have been true regardless of the effectiveness of the program. It doesn't provide a reason for the rate change.

answers.text: High schools in the city established placement offices to assist their graduates in obtaining employment.
answers.fb:
Weaker Impact

This may strike some of us as an Alternate Explanation for why fewer students are dropping out. Maybe it's not because a program improved their morale but because they think if they stay in school and graduate, then a placement office will help them find a job.

It's not a great alternate explanation, though, since we don't know if high school students would be aware of these offices that deal with graduates. And since dropouts have historically dropped out in order to get a job, it doesn't seem like a potential high school dropout is that worried about getting help with finding a job. 

This really only works as an incentive to stay in school if we know that the students considering dropping out are aware of the program and are worried about their ability to find a job without such assistance.

answers.text: The antidropout program was primarily aimed at improving students’ morale in those high schools with the highest dropout rates.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

This seems to make the author's explanation seem more plausible, since the program was primarily aimed at morale, for schools with high dropout rates.

questiontext:
The television show Henry was not widely watched until it was scheduled for Tuesday evenings immediately after That’s Life, the most popular show on television. During the year after the move, Henry was consistently one of the ten most-watched shows on television. Since Henry’s recent move to Wednesday evenings, however, it has been watched by far fewer people. We must conclude that Henry was widely watched before the move to Wednesday evenings because it followed That’s Life and not because people especially liked it.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (must conclude)

Henry was widely watched before the move to Wednesday evenings because it followed That's Life and not because people especially liked it.

Evidence

The television show Henry was not widely watched until it was scheduled for Tuesday evenings immediately after That's Life, the most popular show on television.

During the year after the move, Henry was consistently one of the ten most-watched shows on television.

Since Henry's recent move to Wednesday evenings, it has been watched by far fewer people.

Evaluate

This argument follows the Explain Curious Fact pattern. The author is exploring why Henry was widely watched after being moved to a Tuesday slot following That's Life, but not before, and why its viewership declined with the move to Wednesday.

Curious Fact

Why was Henry widely watched originally only when following That's Life, and then less so after moving to Wednesdays?

Author's Explanation

The viewership of Henry was high because it followed the popular show That's Life, not because of its own merits. 

To strengthen the argument, we need to enhance the author's explanation by showing that the association with That's Life was a significant factor in Henry's viewership, or rule out some alternate explanation for why Henry is struggling on Wednesday nights (maybe the show fundamentally changed for the worse, or it's competing against some other really popular show on Wed nights).

Goal

Let's find an answer that increases the plausibility that Henry's high viewership was due to its position immediately after That's Life, or that rules out an alternate explanation for the decline in popularity.

answers.text: Henry has been on the air for three years, but That’s Life has been on the air for only two years.
answers.fb:
No Impact

Knowing how long each show has been on the air doesn't address why Henry's viewership was high when it followed That's Life but low once it moved to Wednesday.

answers.text: The show that replaced Henry on Tuesdays has persistently had a low number of viewers in the Tuesday time slot.
answers.fb:
Weakens

When Henry was on Tuesday, it was a top 10 show. Its replacement has a low number of viewers. 

That suggests that Henry was a top 10 show because people liked the show, not just because of the time slot (otherwise the replacement show should be doing comparably well in that Tuesday night slot).

answers.text: The show that now follows That’s Life on Tuesdays has double the number of viewers it had before being moved.
answers.fb:
Correct

This increases the plausibility that following That's Life significantly increases a show's audience. Some other show saw its ratings double when it was moved to that same timeslot.

This strengthens the author's explanation that Henry was watched because it followed That's Life.

answers.text: After its recent move to Wednesday, Henry was aired at the same time as the second most popular show on television.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This provides an alternate explanation for why Henry is struggling on Wed nights. It's not because it's an inherently unpopular show; it's because it's going again #2.

Henry was a top 10 show on Tuesday nights, but if people are forced to choose between their 2nd favorite and 8th favorite show on Wednesday nights, then they're going to pick their 2nd favorite (even though they do like that 8th favorite quite a bit!)

answers.text: That’s Life was not widely watched during the first year it was aired.
answers.fb:
No Impact

That's Life not being widely watched in its first year doesn't affect the explanation for Henry's viewership. The conclusion is concerned with the time after That's Life became popular, so this early information is irrelevant.

questiontext:
Telephone companies are promoting “voice mail” as an alternative to the answering machine. By recording messages from callers when a subscriber does not have access to his or her telephone, voice mail provides a service similar to that of an answering machine. The companies promoting this service argue that it will soon make answering machines obsolete, since it is much more convenient, more flexible, and less expensive than an answering machine.

Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the argument made by the companies promoting voice mail?

answers.text: Unlike calls made to owners of answering machines, all telephone calls made to voice-mail subscribers are completed, even if the line called is in use at the time of the call.
answers.fb:
Opposite: strengthens

Says something good about voicemail.

answers.text: The surge in sales of answering machines occurred shortly after they were first introduced to the electronics market.
answers.fb:
No Impact

Doesn't deal with an advantage or disadvantage of answering machine vs. voicemail.

answers.text: Once a telephone customer decides to subscribe to voice mail, that customer can cancel the service at any time.
answers.fb:
Opposite, if anything

Says something seemingly positive about voicemail.

answers.text: Answering machines enable the customer to hear who is calling before the customer decides whether to answer the telephone, a service voice mail does not provide.
answers.fb:
Correct

Points out an advantage answering machines have over voicemail.

answers.text: The number of messages a telephone answering machine can record is limited by the length of the magnetic tape on which calls are recorded.
answers.fb:
Opposite, if anything

Points out a potential disadvantage of answering machines.

questiontext:
In response to office workers’ worries about the health risks associated with using video display terminals (VDTs), researchers asked office workers to estimate both the amount of time they had spent using VDTs and how often they had suffered headaches over the previous year. According to the survey, frequent VDT users suffered from headaches more often than other office workers did, leading researchers to conclude that VDTs cause headaches.

Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the researchers' conclusion?
gf:
Conclusion (to conclude that)

VDTs cause headaches.

Evidence

Researchers conducted a survey asking office workers to estimate their VDT usage and frequency of headaches over the past year.

The survey showed frequent VDT users suffered headaches more often than other office workers.

Evaluate

This argument involves correlational reasoning: it observes a correlation between VDT usage and headache frequency and concludes a causal relationship. 

CUROUS FACT: why is VDT usage correlated with headaches?
EXPLANATION: VDT usage causes headaches.

To undermine the argument, we should consider alternative explanations for the observed correlation or demonstrate that the VDT usage doesn't actually cause headaches. 

A common pattern to consider is Reverse Causality, where possibly the headaches caused people to think they spent more time using VDTs, or Third Factor, where some other variable causes both headache frequency and VDT usage estimation.

Goal

Let's find an answer that suggests an alternative explanation for the correlation, such as a factor that could cause both increased VDT usage estimation and headaches or that undermines the plausibility of the idea that using VDT could cause headaches.

answers.text: Few of the office workers surveyed participated in regular health programs during the year in question.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This states that few workers participated in health programs, which has no direct link to the correlation between VDT use and headaches, failing to address the causal connection.

answers.text: In their study the researchers failed to ask the workers to distinguish between severe migraine headaches and mild headaches.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This indicates researchers didn’t distinguish between headache severities. The conclusion concerns any headaches linked to VDTs, making this distinction irrelevant to the causal claim.

answers.text: Previous studies have shown that the glare from VDT screens causes some users to suffer eyestrain.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This claims glare from VDTs causes eyestrain, indirectly supporting the link between VDT use and headaches, aligning with the causal premise under discussion.

answers.text: Office workers who experienced frequent headaches were more likely than other workers to overestimate how much time they spent using VDTs.
answers.fb:
Correct

This suggests that those who experience frequent headaches overestimate their VDT usage, pointing to a third factor—misreporting—as a reason for the correlation. This challenges the causal link by suggesting that headaches are independent of actual VDT use.

answers.text: Office workers who regularly used VDTs experienced the same amount of job-related stress as workers who did not use VDTs.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This claims VDT users experience the same job-related stress as non-users, ruling out job stress as an alternate explanation and lending support to the VDT-headache causal connection.

questiontext:
Announcement for a television program: Are female physicians more sensitive than male physicians to the needs of women patients? To get the answer, we’ll ask physicians of both sexes this question. Tune in tomorrow.

Which one of the following, if true, identifies a flaw in the plan for the program?
gf:
Advertisement

To assess whether female physicians are more sensitive than male physicians to the needs of female patients, we'll ask male and female physicians.

Flaw

The people who are best equipped to judge "how sensitive was the doctor to the patient's needs" are the patients!

Meanwhile, this TV show is saying they're going to ask the doctors themselves to self-evaluate how sensitive they were to the patient's needs.

This would be like saying, "Who is better at making Mac & Cheese the way Sammy likes it, Mom or Dad? To get the answer, we'll ask both parents this question."

Shouldn't we ask Sammy? Isn't he the arbiter of who make the better Mac & Cheese?

Goal

Look for an answer saying that it's silly to be asking the physicians who was more sensitive to the patient's needs, when only the patient knows what their needs are and only the patient can tell us which doctor was more sensitive to their needs.

answers.text: Physicians are in general unwilling to describe the treatment style of other physicians.
answers.fb:
Not Our Main Objection

It is true that in this show, a male physician may be asked to describe the treatment style of other male physicians vs. female physicians (as treatment style pertains to sensitivity to needs).

But whichever physicians have agreed to be on this TV show probably know that they are going to be talking about male vs. female physicians, so even if most physicians are unwilling, the physicians we have slotted for this show are presumably among the population of physicians that are willing to discuss.

answers.text: There still are fewer women than men who are physicians, so a patient might not have the opportunity to choose a woman as a physician.
answers.fb:
Not an Objection

The topic being addressed has nothing to do with whether there are more / fewer physician of either sex. It's only about assessing who's better / worse at being sensitive to female patients' needs.

We're only judging the show's methodology based on whether or not we think they will be capable of giving a good answer to that question. 

This answer seems worried about what people will do with that answer once they've heard it and need to schedule their next doctor's appointment.

answers.text: Those who are best able to provide answers to the question are patients, rather than physicians.
answers.fb:
Correct

Which would we trust more:
1. the data we get from female patients who have to rate their male/female physician in terms of how well the physician addressed their needs?

or

2. the data we get from physicians appraising their own abilities to meet the needs of the patients?

If we're having a contest to see who can bake the best cupcake, do we care more about hearing the ratings of the judges who tried the cupcake (the patients) or more about hearing the self-ratings of the chefs who baked the cupcakes (the physicians)?

The metric in question, "how well were the patient's needs met", is something that the patient should be telling us, not the physician.

answers.text: Since medical research is often performed on men, not all results are fully applicable to women as patients.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Distinction

No part of this TV show is dealing with medical research, so this fact has nothing to do with our objection. We're not worried about whether all research results are fully applicable to women.

We're worried about whether female patients feels like their physician is more sensitive to their needs when it's a male vs. a female physician.

answers.text: Women as patients are now beginning to take a more active role in managing their care and making sure that they understand the medical alternatives.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Distinction

This doesn't sound like any sort of objection to the plan for tomorrow's TV show.

questiontext:
Doctor: The practice of using this therapy to treat the illness cannot be adequately supported by the claim that any therapy for treating the illness is more effective than no therapy at all. What must also be taken into account is that this therapy is expensive and complicated.

Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the doctor's argument?
gf:
Conclusion

The practice of using this therapy to treat the illness cannot be adequately supported by the claim that any therapy for treating the illness is more effective than no therapy at all.

Rephrase: Effectiveness alone is not enough justification for using this therapy.

Evidence

What must also be taken into account is that this therapy is expensive and complicated.

Evaluate

The conclusion appears in the first sentence and is clarified by the following sentence. This argument fits one of the common patterns, where the conclusion is found in the first sentence and then supported by additional claims or considerations. In this case, the consideration of expense and complication acts as support for the main claim—that effectiveness is not sufficient justification.

Goal

Find the best available meaning match for *effectiveness alone is not enough justification for using this therapy.*

answers.text: The therapy is more effective than no treatment at all for the illness.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison

(A) This answer makes a claim about the therapy being more effective than no treatment, which doesn't align with the main point of the argument. The argument is questioning the adequacy of using effectiveness as the sole justification, rather than comparing the therapy's effectiveness to no treatment.

answers.text: The therapy is more effective than other forms of treatment for the illness.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison

This answer introduces a comparison regarding the therapy's effectiveness against other forms of treatment, which was not discussed in the argument. The argument focuses on whether effectiveness alone is a sufficient justification for using the therapy, not on its effectiveness relative to other treatments.

answers.text: The therapy is more expensive and complicated than other forms of treatment for the illness.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison

This choice introduces a comparison with other forms of treatment that was not made in the argument.

answers.text: The therapy should not be used to treat the illness unless it is either effective or inexpensive.
answers.fb:
Too Strong

This choice implies an absolute condition for not using the therapy, which is not stated or implied in the argument.

answers.text: The therapy’s possible effectiveness in treating the illness is not sufficient justification for using it.
answers.fb:
Correct

This choice accurately reflects the doctor's conclusion that effectiveness on its own is not sufficient justification for using the therapy.

questiontext:
After 1950, in response to record growth in worldwide food demand, farmers worldwide sharply increased fertilizer use. As a result, the productivity of farmland more than doubled by 1985. Since 1985, farmers have sought to increase farmland productivity even further. Nevertheless, worldwide fertilizer use has declined by 6 percent between 1985 and the present.

Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?
gf:
Background

After 1950, farmers greatly increased fertilizer use, which led to a doubling of farmland productivity by 1985.

Since 1985, they've been trying to increase productivity even more.

Surprising Claim

And yet, since 1985, they've started using less fertilizer.

Evaluate / Goal

Given that ... fertilizer was so effective at increasing productivity from 1950-1985
Why is it that ... since 1985, the effort to increase productivity has involved using slightly less fertilizer than before?

It seems like the answer will have to say something like, "Fertilizer stopped working to increase productivity" or "Something else was even better / cheaper as a means of increasing productivity".

answers.text: Since 1985 the rate at which the world’s population has increased has exceeded the rate at which new arable land has been created through irrigation and other methods.
answers.fb:
Doesn't Explain

This seems to just underscore why we would be seeking to increase farmland's productivity even further, but it does nothing to resolve the mystery of why we're now using less fertilizer.

answers.text: Several varieties of crop plants that have become popular recently, such as soybeans, are as responsive to fertilizer as are traditional grain crops.
answers.fb:
Deepens Paradox

We're looking for answer to give us a reason why they aren't using fertilizer as much, and this gives us a reason why they would continue to use fertilizer at least as much:

a new popular crop responds just as well as the crops that responded well in the 1950-1985 period.

answers.text: Between 1950 and 1985 farmers were able to increase the yield of many varieties of crop plants.
answers.fb:
Reiterates Background
Doesn't Help Explain

This just talks about the background. We already know that fertilizer was successful. That's why we're confused by the fact that farmers aren't using as much of it anymore. We're looking for an answer to tell us why they aren't using it as much anymore.

answers.text: After fertilizer has been added to soil for several years, adding fertilizer to the soil in subsequent years does not significantly improve crop production.
answers.fb:
Correct

This supplies a reason why they would be using less fertilizer in the post-1985 era. Since they used it for 35 years, according to this answer choice, adding more fertilizer wouldn't actually do much to improve productivity.

In reality, since it only takes "several years" for this phenomenon to kick in, it's possible that by the late 50s they were already seeing less gains from fertilizer, and that as the 60s and 70s went on, they kept seeing fewer and fewer boosts in productivity from adding fertilizer, so by 1985, they had pretty much learned the lesson that adding more fertilizer was not actually doing anything good for productivity anymore.

answers.text: Between 1975 and 1980 fertilizer prices temporarily increased because of labor disputes in several fertilizer-exporting nations, and these disputes disrupted worldwide fertilizer production.
answers.fb:
Wrong Timeframe

A hike in the price of fertilizer certainly could have worked as a reason why farmers are using less fertilizer in the post-1985 era.

However, this answer is saying that the price temporarily went up (and then back down) between 1975-1980. So it's not giving us any reason why there's less fertilizer use in the 1985-present timeframe.

questiontext:
Lydia: Red squirrels are known to make holes in the bark of sugar maple trees and to consume the trees' sap. Since sugar maple sap is essentially water with a small concentration of sugar, the squirrels almost certainly are after either water or sugar. Water is easily available from other sources in places where maple trees grow, so the squirrels would not go to the trouble of chewing holes in trees just to get water. Therefore, they are probably after the sugar.

Galina: It must be something other than sugar, because the concentration of sugar in the maple sap is so low that a squirrel would need to drink an enormous amount of sap to get any significant amount of sugar.

Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the force of Galina's attempted rebuttal of Lydia's argument?
gf:
Conclusion of Lydia's Argument

Squirrels are attracted to sugar in the sap of sugar maple trees.

Rebuttal by Galina

The sugar concentration in the sap is too low for squirrels to be attracted to it for sugar.

Evaluate

Because we're trying to counter someone's objection, we want to defend the idea that squirrels are trying to get sugar from this sap, while addressing the fact that there's so little sugar content that you'd have to drink tons of sap to get much sugar.

Goal

Given that you'd have to drink tons of sap to get much sugar, how can we still maintain that squirrels are interested in the sap for its sugar content.

answers.text: Squirrels are known to like foods that have a high concentration of sugar.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This indicates that squirrels like foods high in sugar, but it acknowledges Galina's point about low sugar concentration and doesn't address how squirrels might still find the sap appealing.

answers.text: Once a hole in a sugar maple trunk has provided one red squirrel with sap, other red squirrels will make additional holes in its trunk.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This comments on squirrels making additional holes, which doesn’t address Galina’s point about sugar concentration nor provide insight into the sugar’s appeal.

answers.text: Trees other than sugar maples, whose sap contains a lower concentration of sugar than does sugar maple sap, are less frequently tapped by red squirrels.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This states that trees with lower sugar concentration are less tapped, implying sugar preference but not addressing the specific challenge about low sugar concentration in sugar maples.

answers.text: Red squirrels leave the sugar maple sap that slowly oozes out of the holes in the tree’s trunk until much of the water in the sap has evaporated.
answers.fb:
Correct

This states squirrels allow sap to evaporate, increasing its sugar concentration. This counters Galina's argument by showing squirrels have a method for increasing sugar levels, suggesting they indeed target sugar.

answers.text: During the season when sap can be obtained from sugar maple trees, the weather often becomes cold enough to prevent sap from oozing out of the trees.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This mentions cold weather limiting sap flow, which doesn’t connect to the argument about sugar concentration or explain why squirrels are attracted to the sap.

questiontext:
Pundit: People complain about how ineffectual their legislative representatives are, but this apparent ineffectuality is simply the manifestation of compromises these representatives must make when they do what they were elected to do: compete for the government’s scarce funds. So, when people express dissatisfaction with their legislative representatives, we can be assured that these representatives are simply doing what they were elected to do.

The pundit's argument is flawed because it takes for granted that
gf:
Conclusion (So)

When people express dissatisfaction with their legislative representatives, we can be assured that these representatives are simply doing what they were elected to do.

Evidence

Representatives were elected to compete for the government's scarce funds, which requires compromises. 

Those compromises give off the impression of ineffectuality, which people express dissatisfaction about. 

Evaluate
