The conclusion is saying that reps are doing what they are elected to do, and it builds that case by defining what they're elected to do (compete for funds), telling us what's required of that (make compromises), and telling us a by-product of that requirement (you look ineffectual to some people). 

One of the most helpful observations we can make while reading this one is its Conditional Conclusion. 

We don't have to symbolize it, but if we did, it would look like this:

  People expressing                                 Reps doing 
 dissatisfaction with  - - - - -  - - - -> what they were 
their legislative reps                               elected to do

Fighting / Refuting / Rebutting / Contradicting a conditional means saying, "it's possible that the left side is true and the right side is false".

So if we want to fight this conclusion, we need to argue that "it's possible that people are expressing dissatisfaction with their legislative reps, but the reps are not doing what they are elected to do".

The evidence only deals with one specific complaint people make. People will complain that their reps are ineffectual, the author ably shows us how apparent ineffectuality is simply the manifestation of them doing something required of their job. 

But what about other complaints? What people complain that "their representatives are making personally-enriching deals with foreign leaders"?

Is that the representatives simply doing what they were elected to do?

What if people complain that their representatives are making racist / sexist remarks? Is that the reps simply doing what they were elected to do?

Goal

The correct answer will either lock us into the subject matter of the evidence, by giving some Linking idea like,

"Whenever people express dissatisfaction with their legislative reps, they are complaining about apparent ineffectuality"

or it will be a Defender answer ruling out one of these other reasons,

"People do not often complain about their legislative reps making personally-enriching deals with foreign leaders".

answers.text: the apparent ineffectuality of legislative representatives is the only source of popular dissatisfaction with those representatives
answers.fb:
Correct

This is harsh sounding, for a Necessary Assumption answer, but it's also conditional, so we want to look at it as a reasoning move and see if it feels like the author made that move.

"The only" is weird indicator, because it's actually a Left side (sufficient) indicator. Famously, "only / only if" are Right side (necessary ) indicators. 

The only is the only time you'd ever put 'only' on the left, if that dumb mnemonic helps. 

So this answer is saying,

If there's a popular source        it's about their 
   of dissatisfaction with      →     apparent 
legislative representatives        ineffectuality

The author's conclusion begins with the trigger on the left. "Whenever people complain about their reps ...", and the evidence only talks about the complaint of ineffectuality.

The evidence establishes 
                        if the complaint is          the reps are 
                      about ineffectuality →  doing what we 
                                                               elected them to 

The conclusion is claiming, 
   if there's                                              the reps are 
a complaint    - - - - - - - - - - →   doing what we 
                                                             elected them to

So the argument is missing the link being offered by this answer choice:
   if there's             the complaint is
a complaint  → about ineffectuality

Alternatively, we could judge this answer by negating it. If we said, "There are other sources of dissatisfaction besides the apparent ineffectuality of reps", would that weaken?

Yes! That would be taking us into our Objection zone of, "What about when we are popularly dissatisfied that our representatives are personally enriching themselves by making deals with foreign leaders? What about when are leaders say violent or offensive things?"

answers.text: governmental resources that are currently scarce cannot become more abundant except by the actions of politicians
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: more abundant
Too Strong: cannot except by

This sounds harsh as well (only the actions of politicians can make currently scarce recourses become more abundant). Did our author commit herself to that limiting idea?

No.

We can do the same move of analyzing the reasoning move:

      If a politician                 a currently scarce
doesn't take action  →       resource will not
                                       become more abundant

Did our author ever make that move?

No. Even if we contrapose and say, "If a scarce resource is going to become more abundant, it requires the action of politicians", it doesn't match a reasoning move.

The author never talked about whether or not a scarce resource would become more abundant.

answers.text: constituents would continue to be dissatisfied with the effectuality of their legislative representatives if constituents were aware of the cause of this apparent ineffectuality
answers.fb:
Predicts Counterfactual

It's super dubious on Must Be True or Must Be Assumed to pick an answer that judges a hypothetical or a counterfactual.

Is our author assuming that constituents will be dissatisfied with the reps' apparent ineffectuality no matter what.

Whether they understand or not that the need to compromise gives off the appearance of ineffectuality, they'll still be dissatisfied?

We have no reason to commit the author to that view. She might think that people are genuinely confused. They are complaining about ineffectuality because they don't understand its true source. If they did understand its true source, they wouldn't complain.

answers.text: legislative compromise inevitably results in popular dissatisfaction with politicians
answers.fb:
Too Strong: inevitably

This looks scary because of the universal. We can look at it conditionally:

  If there is                then there will be
  legislative    →  popular dissatisfaction
compromise             with politicians

Does that represent some reasoning move the author makes?

No, she never acts like there's a 100% certain connection from compromise to dissatisfaction. She clearly thinks that compromise is sometimes leading to dissatisfaction, but we have nothing to support that she's assuming it always does.

answers.text: only elected public servants tend to elicit dissatisfaction among the public
answers.fb:
Too Strong: only
Out of Scope: non-elected public servants

This answer is indirectly commenting on non-elected public servants, saying the author assumes that non-elected public servants never have the tendency to elicit dissatisfaction from the public.

We don't know anything about how the author feels about non-elected public servants.

questiontext:
When several of a dermatologist’s patients complained of a rash on just one side of their faces, the dermatologist suspected that the cause was some kind of external contact. In each case it turned out that the rash occurred on the side of the face to which the telephone was held. The dermatologist concluded that the rash was caused by prolonged contact with telephones.

Each of the following, if true, provides additional support for the dermatologist's diagnosis EXCEPT:
gf:
Conclusion

The one-sided facial rash was caused by prolonged contact with telephones.

Evidence

Several patients had a rash on just one side of their faces, and in each case the rash was on the same side as the patient's telephone use.

Evaluate

When we're dealing with a "diagnosis / hypothesis / explanation", we know we're dealing with Explain Curious Fact.

CURIOUS FACT:
Why do these patients have a rash on one side of their face?

EXPLANATION:
It's caused by prolonged contact with telephones.

Whenever we're dealing with this template, we know we can strengthen by 
1. ruling out an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact
2. making the Author's Explanation more plausible

Goal

We need to get rid of four answers that strengthen. Typically, with EXCEPT questions, three of those four will do it one way and the other one will do it a different way.

So we might get three answers making the phone hypothesis more plausible and one answer ruling out the idea that the rash comes from something else (e.g. the side of their face that lays on their pillow at night). 

The correct answer will either weaken or be irrelevant.

answers.text: Many telephones are now manufactured using a kind of plastic to which some people are mildly allergic.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This boosts the plausibility of the phone hypothesis by talking about the "causal mechanism". How would a phone cause a rash? Phones are made with a plastic some people are allergic to.

answers.text: Contact between other devices and the patients’ faces occurred equally on both sides of their faces.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This rules out alternate explanations. If the rash were caused by some other device these people were using, we'd expect to see the rash on both sides of their face, since the other devices contact both sides of their face equally.

answers.text: Most of the patients had occupations that required them to use their telephones extensively.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This makes the phone hypothesis more plausible by putting the suspect "prolonged phone contact" at the scene of the crime.

In order to believe that prolonged phone contact is the culprit, we need to know that these people have prolonged contact with phones, and this answer establishes that assumption, which strengthens.

answers.text: Telephones are used by most people in the industrialized world.
answers.fb:
Correct

This just has no impact.

It doesn't make it more likely that the phone caused the rash (do most people in the industrialized world have a rash on one side of their face?)

And it doesn't rule out any alternate explanation.

answers.text: The complaints occurred after an increase in the patients’ use of the telephone.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This adds plausibility to the phone hypothesis by adding a time dimension to it.

The rash started showing up right after an increase in phone use. That looks pretty suspicious, pretty incriminating that prolonged phone use had something to do with the rash.

questiontext:
A year ago the government reduced the highway speed limit, and in the year since, there have been significantly fewer highway fatalities than there were in the previous year. Therefore, speed limit reduction can reduce traffic fatalities.

The argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it takes for granted that
gf:
Conclusion

Speed limit reduction can reduce traffic fatalities.

Evidence

Since we lowered the speed limit a year ago, there have been way fewer highway fatalities than in the previous year.

Evaluate

There is a Curious Comparison -- why are this year's traffic fatalities so much lower than last year's?

The author assumes a Causal Explanation for it -- the new speed limit caused the reduction in fatalities. 

What are the two lenses through which we evaluate every Curious Fact / Explanation argument?
- is there some Other Way to explain the curious fact?
- how plausible is the Author's Way?

How else could one explain a reduction in traffic fatalities?
- fewer drivers
- better road conditions
- more policing, which deters aggressive driving
etc.

How would we assess the plausibility of the author's hypothesis?
- in nearby areas where the speed limit didn't change, were the fatalities still as high as last year?
- are people obeying the new speed limit? i.e., has average driving speed actually decreased?

Goal

Since this is Necessary Assumption, we would primarily look to rule out an Alternate Explanation for why fatalities are lower this year, but we'd also consider an answer that states something required for the author's story to be plausible (such as "drivers have started driving differently in response to the new speed limits").

answers.text: highway traffic has not increased over the past year
answers.fb:
Opposite 

When we see a Necessary Assumption answer choice ruling out a possibility with "not", we get very intrigued. We want to negate it and see if it weakens the argument.

Would this negation hurt the argument?
Highway traffic has increased over the past year.

No that would strengthen the argument. If we have fewer fatalities even though there's more highway traffic, it sounds like something has really helped cut down on fatalities in the past year! (hint-hint:  new speed limit)

We could also say that this negation would strengthen the argument because it rules out the possibility that fatalities are lower this year because highway traffic is lower.

This answer would be correct if it said,
"highway traffic has not significantly decreased over the past year"

answers.text: the majority of drivers obeyed the new speed limit
answers.fb:
Too Strong: most / obeyed

In 99% of cases, the word/concept of "most" will be wrong on Necessary Assumption. When you negate that idea, you go from 51% to 49%.

Does it badly weaken this argument if 49%, rather than 51%, of drivers obeyed the new speed limit? 

Of course not. The author's explanation definitely assumes that "a significant number of drivers have changed their driving speed in reaction to the new speed limit", because if almost no one changed their driving in reaction to the new speed limit, then we couldn't say that the new speed limit explains the drop in highway fatalities.

But this answer is formulated way too strongly and specifically.

answers.text: there is a relation between driving speed and the number of automobile accidents
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: number of accidents

Very close, but the author is assuming there's a relationship between speed limit and the rate of highway fatalities. 

If we say there's no relation between speed and number of accidents, we're saying, "People drive like jerks and there's gonna be ~10,000 accidents a year no matter what". 

But that doesn't badly weaken the author's argument. She can still believe that by lowering the speed limit and thus (she assumes) lowering the average driving speed of cars, that same number of accidents could result in significantly fewer fatalities.

answers.text: the new speed limit was more strictly enforced than the old
answers.fb:
Unnecessary Comparison: more strictly

The author does not need the new one to be more strictly enforced than the old one. If the old one was strictly enforced, then the new speed limit could be just as strictly enforced and the argument would be fine.

The author is assuming that the new posted speed limit is the causal difference-maker. She's not assuming that an increase in police presence is the causal difference-maker.

answers.text: the number of traffic fatalities the year before the new speed limit was introduced was not abnormally high
answers.fb:
Correct 

When we see a Necessary Assumption answer choice ruling out a possibility with "not", we get very intrigued. We want to negate it and see if it weakens the argument.

Would this negation hurt the argument?
the number of fatalities the previous year was abnormally high

Yes, that provides the alternate explanation we were suspecting. This is just an alternate explanation that people don't see much:  regression to the mean ... a return to normalcy.

Consider this analogy:
Our flower shop's revenue was down 45% this month compared to last. At the beginning of this month, we changed the sign on our window, so apparently new signage on your storefront can reduce store revenue.

If we objected, "Yo ... this month is March. Last month was February, aka Valentine's Month, aka a month of abnormally high revenue for a flower shop. Obviously March is going to be 45% lower than February. That's because March is a normal month, and the previous month was just an outlier. We don't need to blame this on the new sign. We can just attribute this to a return to our normal baseline revenue."

This answer rules out an alternate explanation for the curious fact.

Fatalities aren't necessarily down this year because we did something new. we would have expected them to be down even if we had done nothing new, since last month was the outlier / the aberration / the funky thing that needs to be explained.

Normalcy doesn't need an explanation. Deviations from normalcy do.

questiontext:
One-year-olds ordinarily prefer the taste of sweet food to that of salty food. Yet if one feeds a one-year-old salty food rather than sweet food, then over a period of about a year he or she will develop a taste for the salty flavor and choose to eat salty food rather than sweet food. Thus, a young child’s taste preferences can be affected by the type of food he or she has been exposed to.

Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (thus)

A young child's taste preferences can be affected by the type of food he or she has been exposed to.

Evidence

One-year-olds usually prefer sweet to salty. But if you feed a one-year-old salty food for a year, by age two they will choose salty over sweet.

Evaluate

The "experiment" described does involve exposing 1-year olds to salty foods and does involve their taste preferences changing a year later.

So there doesn't seem to be a Missing Link in terms of what the evidence vs. conclusion are talking about. The only difference is that the conclusion is Causal (affected by) and the evidence is just Chronological (a year later, something has changed).

Just because the salty food exposure was followed by a change in preference doesn't mean that the salty food exposure caused the change in preference.

This is essentially an Explain Curious Fact argument where the author is wondering why the kid switches from preferring sweet to preferring salty and chalks it up to that year of exposure to salty foods.

For that type of argument, the author has to assume,
there isn't some Alternate Explanation for the evidence
+ the Author's Explanation is plausible

Goal

Look for an answer ruling out an alternate explanation for why the kids prefer salty foods a year later, or look for something required for the author's story (that exposure to salty changed their preference to salty) to be plausible.

answers.text: Two-year-olds do not naturally prefer salty food to sweet food.
answers.fb:
Correct

This has the lovable Defender "not" right by the verb, so we'll negate and see if this answer weakens.

Would it hurt the argument to say, "Hey, author 2 year olds naturally prefer salty to sweet?"

Definitely! That would be an Alternate Explanation for why the 1 year olds, one year later, are preferring salty foods.

It isn't because of the exposure to salty they got over the year of us forcing them to eat salty things; it's just a natural developmental thing. It would have happened even if we hadn't fed them salty things.

Since the negation weakens, this is the correct answer.

answers.text: A child’s taste preferences usually change between age one and age two.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything) / Too Strong (usually)

If this answer were talking about a child's taste preferences changing for natural reasons, then this would weaken. It would provide an Alternate Explanation for why the 1-year olds switched from liking sweets to liking salty, one year later.

It wasn't from our exposure; it was just because that usually happens as a child ages from 1 to 2.

An author wouldn't assume something that weakens their argument.

And if this answer were saying that a child's taste preferences usually change from exposure to certain foods, then it would be Too Strong.

The conclusion is only saying that a young child's taste preferences CAN be affected by food exposure, not that it's USUALLY affected by food exposure.

answers.text: Two-year-olds do not naturally dislike salty food so much that they would not choose it over some other foods.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

Because of the lovable "not", we'll negate and see if it weakens.

Does it hurt the author for us to say, "Hey, author -- 2 year olds naturally dislike salty food so much that, given the choice between salty foods and some other foods, they would not choose the salty food."

Cluttered sentence, but basically it's just saying, when negated, "2 year olds naturally dislike salty food". That strengthens the argument. The author thinks that two year olds are preferring salty food because of the exposure, not because of natural inclinations.

So negating this answer actually fits the author's argument, which means this is definitely not the correct answer.

answers.text: The salty food fed to infants in order to change their taste preferences must taste pleasant.
answers.fb:
Too Strong (must)
Out of Scope (taste pleasant)

If we negate this, it'd be saying,
"Hey, author, the salty food doesn't need to be delicious in order to change the infants' taste preferences. Even if it's nasty tasting salty food, that will still change the infants' taste preferences."

That negation wouldn't weaken. It would actually strengthen, because it's talking about the food exposure changing the preferences.

answers.text: Sweet food is better for infant development than is salty food.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope (better for development)

This is speculating some causal backstory for the opening sentence. Maybe that's why 1 year olds usually prefer sweet food, but maybe not.

It doesn't make any difference which type of food is better for infant development.

The argument is purely about a preference for one type of food changing to a preference for another type, and about what caused that preference to change.

There isn't anything in this argument relating to whether that change in preference is a good/bad thing for the infant's development.

questiontext:
David: Forbidding companies from hiring permanent replacements for striking employees would be profoundly unfair. Such companies would have little leverage in their negotiations with strikers.

Lin: No, the companies would still have sufficient leverage in negotiations if they hired temporary replacements.

Which one of the following statements is most strongly supported by the exchange between David and Lin?
gf:
David's Explicit Claims

1. Forbidding companies from hiring permanent replacements for striking employees would be very unfair.

2. Companies who aren't allowed to hire permanent replacements would have little leverage in negotiating with strikers.

Lin's Responses

1. UNCLEAR - Lin doesn't quite come out and say "it's fair to forbid companies from hiring permanent replacements". We'd have to infer that belief purely from "No", and that's not a super sound basis.  

2. DISAGREES - he says they would still have plenty of leverage. 

Goal

The question stem isn't actually Agree / Disagree, so it's not clear whether that's how we should be thinking or not. There is an explicit disagreement, so on the first pass let's look for an answer about whether or not companies who can't hire permanent replacements would have a decent amount of leverage with striking workers.

But since it's just a Most Supported question, we just want the most provable answer.

answers.text: David does not believe that the freedom to hire temporary replacements gives companies any leverage in their negotiations with strikers.
answers.fb:
Opposite

David absolutely believes that being able to hire temps gives companies leverage. He thinks that forbidding them from being able to hire temps means they are left with almost no leverage.

answers.text: David and Lin believe that companies should be allowed as much leverage in negotiations as the striking employees.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Comparison (as much)

We can tell they both think that companies should have at least a good bit of leverage in negotiations with striking employees. 

But it's getting overly precise to weigh in on whether they both think that companies deserve equal leverage as the striking employees.

answers.text: David and Lin disagree over the amount of leverage companies lose in their negotiations with strikers by not being able to hire permanent replacements.
answers.fb:
Correct

Well, even though this didn't have a Disagree question stem, it played out just like a Disagree question. We can tell that David and Lin disagree about how much leverage is lost by forbidding companies from hiring permanent replacements.

David thinks it takes companies all the way down to "little leverage", whereas Lin doesn't think it takes them down that far. She thinks they still have plenty of leverage.

When it comes to the four answer that mention Lin, this is really the only idea we have any ammunition to weigh in on. The only thing she said is that a company who can't hire replacements still has sufficient leverage.

answers.text: David and Lin disagree over how much leverage should be accorded companies in their negotiations with strikers.
answers.fb:
Half Scope (should)

Although David is using normative language (unfair), Lin is only using descriptive language, so we have no idea how much leverage she thinks a company should have. She only comments on how much they would have.

answers.text: Lin believes it is unfair to forbid companies from hiring permanent replacements for their striking employees.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

This is David's position. We don't officially know Lin's position, but if anything it looks like she's disagreeing with this.

questiontext:
Logician: I have studied and thoroughly mastered the laws of logic. So to argue that I sometimes violate the laws of logic in ordinary conversation would be like arguing that some physicist circumvents the laws of physics in everyday life.

The reasoning in the logician's argument is questionable because this argument
gf:
Conclusion (So)

Arguing that I violate the laws of conversation would be like arguing that some physicist violates the laws of physics.

Evidence

I have studied and thoroughly mastered the laws of logic.

Evaluate

LSAC loves to clown this haughty logician, by having him (it's gotta be a him, right?) boast about his logic skillz in a Flaw question.

We accept that this logician has thoroughly studied the laws of logic.

How can we reject his conclusion and argue, 
saying that you sometimes violate the laws of logic is not like arguing that some physicists violate the laws of physics

When we're evaluating Comparisons and we want to think of objections, most commonly we're just trying to think of some salient difference between the two things being compared.

In this case, is "a logician breaking the laws of logic" like "a physicist breaking the laws of physics"?

No, because it's possible to break the laws of logic. You can be illogical. You have the freedom to do so. (Cable news exists because of that premise.)

Meanwhile, it's not possible to break the laws of physics. They govern our universe always and everywhere.

Goal

Look for an answer complaining about the unfair comparison between being illogical vs. doing something physically impossible.

answers.text: ignores the fact that our conception of physical laws undergoes constant change
answers.fb:
Not an Objection

fails to consider / ignores possibility = the answer choice is offering a supposed Objection.

We wouldn't be objecting to his conclusion by saying, "Oh, author, you're forgetting that our concept of physics (i.e. Newton's, then Einstein's ... ) is always changing".

Does that attack the conclusion and make it seem like "a logician violating the laws of logic is not like a physicist violating the laws of physics"?

Not in any obvious way. The author is just comparing them on the level of, "in both cases, a specialist is breaking the laws of her field".

It doesn't seem to matter to him whether those laws are permanent or undergoing constant change.

answers.text: presents no evidence that physics is as difficult to master as logic
answers.fb:
Not Assumed

"fails to establish / presents no evidence that" are less typical forms of answer choices describing supposed Assumptions.  (the famous forms of Assumption answers are "presumes / takes for granted")

We'd ask ourselves, "Did the author need to assume that physics is as difficult to master as logic?"

No, the two fields don't need to be identical on that level. The author is only needing to assume that "a specialist breaking a law in logic is similar to a specialist breaking a law in physics".

answers.text: fails to rule out the possibility that some physicist could circumvent the laws of physics in everyday life
answers.fb:
Not an Objection

fails to consider / overlooks possibility = the answer choice is offering a supposed Objection.

We wouldn't be objecting to his conclusion by saying, "Oh, author, you're forgetting that it is possible for some physicist to circumvent the laws of physics in everyday life."

I mean, yes, that would hurt his conclusion, but we would sound like the craziest lawyer in the courthouse. You can't violate the laws of physics. They are the physical laws of the universe:  gravity, electromagnetism, nuclear forces, etc.

What we could say is that the author fails to rule out the possibility that some logician could circumvent the laws of logic in everyday life.  That's our objection.

answers.text: treats two kinds of things that differ in important respects as if they do not differ
answers.fb:
Correct

This is complaining about the unfair comparison. Violating logic differs in an important respect from violating physics, in that the former is possible and the latter is impossible.

answers.text: has a conclusion that contradicts what is asserted in its premise
answers.fb:
Wrong Flaw

This refers to the famous Self-Contradiction flaw, which will be a wrong answer choice 99% of the time we see it.

If the conclusion were contradicting what was asserted in the premise, then the second sentence would have said something like,
So, I have barely even looked at the laws of logic.

questiontext:
Some types of organisms originated through endosymbiosis, the engulfing of one organism by another so that a part of the former becomes a functioning part of the latter. An unusual nucleomorph, a structure that contains DNA and resembles a cell nucleus, has been discovered within a plant known as a chlorarachniophyte. Two versions of a particular gene have been found in the DNA of this nucleomorph, and one would expect to find only a single version of this gene if the nucleomorph were not the remains of an engulfed organism’s nucleus.

Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
gf:
Information

Some organisms form from endosymbiosis, when organism X engulfs organism Y, and Y becomes a functioning part of X.

We found a weird nucleomorph within a plant called a chlorarachniophyte.

Two versions of a gene were found in the nucleomorph.

If the nucleomorph were not the remains of an engulfed organism's nucleus, then we would expect to find only a single version of the gene.

Evaluate

Yikes! This is one of the harder Science-laden stimuli we'll see in LR.

We can get started, though, by focusing on what we typically read Inference paragraphs looking for:

1. overlapping information
2. conditional / causal / math-y wording

Nucleomorphs is mentioned a few times, and engulfed organism shows up twice. The final sentence gives us a conditional rule, signified by if.

Inference questions love to provide a conditional and then provide a fact that triggers the contrapositive of the rule, to test us on whether we're shrewd enough to infer the outcome of that contrapositive.

We were told
  N were not remains  →  find only a 
of engulfed org's nuc         single gene

Contrapositive
  find more than →  N is remains of an
   a single gene        engulfed org's nucleus

They told us that they did find "two versions of the gene". 

So according to this rule, that nucleomorph is the the remains of an engulfed organism's nucleus. Where in the paragraph did we hear about "engulfed organism" before?

The first sentence said that endosymbiosis is a process in which one organism engulfs another. So is that what's going on with this nucleomorph?

Goal

While we can't be certain, it seems like we're being guided towards the suspicion that this nucleomorph (which we know from the final two ideas is the remains of an engulfed organism's nucleus) was involved in some endosymbiosis. 

Endosymbiosis involves one organism engulfing another until the latter is part of the former. Since we know that this nucleomorph was part of an organism that was engulfed, and since we know that now it's hanging out inside a plant called a chlorarachniophyte, we could support the idea that the chlora plant engulfed the nucleomorph's former organism.

answers.text: Only organisms of types that originated through endosymbiosis contain nucleomorphs.
answers.fb:
Too Strong

We're barely comfortable supporting the idea that this nucleomorph is the product of endosymbiosis. We can support that idea, but we can't prove it.

So this answer, which is saying that "if an organism contains a nucleomorphs, it must have originated through endosymbiosis" is too strong.

This was an unusual nucleomorph. So, even if this one did originate through endosymbiosis, there's no reason to think that this would be true of all organisms that have nucleomorphs. 

Inference questions love to put an answer in slot (A) that is very close to what we were anticipating.

answers.text: A nucleomorph within the chlorarachniophyte holds all of the genetic material of some other organism.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: all

Nothing in this paragraph says anything as strong as "contains all the genetic material of some other organism". 

Furthermore, we think the nucleomorph was from the "other organism" that got engulfed by the chlorarachniophyte during endosymbiosis. This answer seems to be positing a third organism.

You have the chlora, which ate the nucleomorph, but then the nucleomorph ate some other organism and got all of its genetic material?

answers.text: Nucleomorphs originated when an organism endosymbiotically engulfed a chlorarachniophyte.
answers.fb:
Opposite Relationship

We know that the nucleomorph was part of the organism that got engulfed (presumably by the chlorarachniophyte).

This answer is saying that the chlorarachniophyte got engulfed by the nucleomorph.

answers.text: Two organisms will not undergo endosymbiosis unless at least one of them contains a nucleomorph.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: unless

There's no way from this passage to derive such a severe connection between endosymbiosis and nucleomorphs.

We can support that this unusual nucleomorph had something to do with endosymbiosis (since we know it was part an organism that got engulfed).

But we can't say, as this answer does, that every single case of endosymbiosis involves a nucleomorph.

answers.text: Chlorarachniophytes emerged as the result of two organisms having undergone endosymbiosis.
answers.fb:
Correct

Since we know that the nucleomorph is the remains of an engulfed organism's nucleus and now is within a chlorarachniophyte, it seemed supportable to say that the nucleo was in organism Y, which got engulfed during endosymbiosis by the chlora.

The weird part about this answer, to me, was the idea that there were two separate organisms that combined into the chlora.

But, if we check the wording of endosymbiosis, it is the origination of an organism. One organism engulfs another, and the engulfee is still a functioning part of the engulfer. But that doesn't mean the resulting organism is still called by the name of the engulfing organism. A new organism has originated from this process.

questiontext:
The government-owned gas company has begun selling stoves and other gas appliances to create a larger market for its gas. Merchants who sell such products complain that the competition will hurt their businesses. That may well be; however, the government-owned gas company is within its rights. After all, the owner of a private gas company might well decide to sell such appliances and surely there would be nothing wrong with that.

Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
gf:
Conclusion

The government-owned gas company is within its rights to sell stoves and other gas appliances.

Evidence

A private gas company would be allowed to sell such appliances without anyone seeing anything wrong with it.

Evaluate

The argument leaps from "a private gas company would be allowed to" to "the government-owned gas company is within its rights to." That works only if government-owned companies have the same rights as private ones (in this domain). The argument needs a principle that licenses transferring permissions from private companies to government-owned companies.

Goal

Find an answer that says: government-owned companies have the right to do what private businesses have the right to do.

answers.text: Government-owned companies have the right to do whatever private businesses have the right to do.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is exactly the bridge the argument needs. The author argues from "a private gas company could do this" to "the government-owned gas company can do this." That move requires the principle that government-owned companies have whatever rights private businesses have. Apply (A) to the facts and the conclusion follows directly: private companies have the right to sell appliances → government-owned companies have that same right.

answers.text: A government should always take seriously the complaints of merchants.
answers.fb:
Bad Match

This says the government should take merchant complaints seriously. The argument's conclusion is that the company is within its rights regardless of merchant complaints — i.e., the merchants' protests don't change the legal/ethical analysis. This principle, if anything, points the other way (suggesting complaints should weigh in). It doesn't justify the conclusion.

answers.text: Private businesses have no right to compete with government monopolies.
answers.fb:
Bad Match

This says private businesses have no right to compete with government monopolies. The argument is about whether the government-owned company can compete with private merchants — the opposite direction. (C) doesn't address whether government-owned companies have the right to compete, which is the question at issue.

answers.text: There is nothing wrong with a government-owned company selling products so long as owners of private companies do not complain.
answers.fb:
Bad Match

This principle ties government rights to whether private companies complain. But the argument doesn't say anything about whether private gas companies are complaining — the complaints come from merchants. And the argument concludes that the company is within its rights without making the conclusion contingent on absence of private-company complaints. The principle adds a wrinkle the argument doesn't need.

answers.text: There is nothing wrong with private companies competing against each other.
answers.fb:
Bad Match

This principle is about private companies competing against each other. The argument is about a government-owned company competing with private merchants — different parties, different framing. (E) doesn't bridge the argument's leap from private rights to government rights.

questiontext:
Toxicologist: A survey of oil-refinery workers who work with MBTE, an ingredient currently used in some smog-reducing gasolines, found an alarming incidence of complaints about headaches, fatigue, and shortness of breath. Since gasoline containing MBTE will soon be widely used, we can expect an increased incidence of headaches, fatigue, and shortness of breath.

Each of the following, if true, strengthens the toxicologist's argument EXCEPT:
gf:
Conclusion

We can expect an increased incidence of headaches, fatigue, and shortness of breath.

Evidence (since)

A survey of oil-refinery workers who work with MBTE found an alarming incidence of complaints about headaches, fatigue, and shortness of breath.

Gasoline with MBTE will soon be widely used. 

Evaluate

There is a causal assumption happening as the author goes from evidence to conclusion.

CURIOUS FACT: how come there is a higher incidence of headaches, fatigue, and shortness of breath among these workers who work with MBTE.

EXPLANATION: The MBTE causes those symptoms.

We can strengthen by making it more plausible that MBTE leads to such symptoms or by ruling out an alternate explanation for why those workers have those symptoms. 

Goal

Eliminate the four answers that help us argue that as MBTE become more widely used, these symptoms will become more widespread.

answers.text: Most oil-refinery workers who do not work with MBTE do not have serious health problems involving headaches, fatigue, and shortness of breath.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This suggests that oil-refinery workers not exposed to MBTE do not experience these symptoms, reinforcing the causal link between MBTE and the symptoms.

This is the classic "No Cause, No Effect" plausibility strengthener.

answers.text: Headaches, fatigue, and shortness of breath are among the symptoms of several medical conditions that are potentially serious threats to public health.
answers.fb:
Correct

This states that the symptoms are common to several medical conditions but doesn't address the causal link to MBTE or support the prediction about the general population, making it irrelevant to the argument.

answers.text: Since the time when gasoline containing MBTE was first introduced in a few metropolitan areas, those areas reported an increase in the number of complaints about headaches, fatigue, and shortness of breath.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This makes the author's causal assumption that MBTE causes these symptoms more plausible, by providing data points where "cause is present, effect is present". 

It's a temporal correlation, that we didn't see the symptoms until MBTE was introduced.

answers.text: Regions in which only gasoline containing MBTE is used have a much greater incidence of headaches, fatigue, and shortness of breath than do similar regions in which only MBTE-free gasoline is used.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This provides more correlative data that where MBTE is present, the symptoms are present, and where it is absent, the symptoms are absent, supporting the causal assumption that MBTE leads to these symptoms.

answers.text: The oil-refinery workers surveyed were carefully selected to be representative of the broader population in their medical histories prior to exposure to MBTE, as well as in other relevant respects.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This notes that the surveyed workers were representative of the broader population, supporting the extrapolation that the general population could experience similar symptoms when MBTE use becomes widespread.

questiontext:
A recent study reveals that television advertising does not significantly affect children’s preferences for breakfast cereals. The study compared two groups of children. One group had watched no television, and the other group had watched average amounts of television and its advertising. Both groups strongly preferred the sugary cereals heavily advertised on television.

Which one of the following statements, if true, most weakens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (reveals that)

Television advertising does not significantly affect children's preferences for breakfast cereals.

Evidence

The study compared two groups of children: one that watched no television and another that watched average amounts. Both groups showed a strong preference for heavily advertised sugary cereals.

Evaluate

This is an Anti-Causal argument, because the conclusion is saying that one thing doesn't affect another thing.

GIVEN THAT kids showed a preference for sweet cereals whether they watched TV or not, HOW CAN WE ARGUE THAT tv ads do significantly affect kids' preferences for cereal?

Goal

Identify an answer choice that provides evidence or a causal mechanism indicating that TV advertising does, in fact, influence cereal preferences, contrary to the conclusion.

answers.text: The preferences of children who do not watch television advertising are influenced by the preferences of children who watch the advertising.
answers.fb:
Correct

This states that the preferences of children who don't watch TV advertising are influenced by those who do, suggesting that TV ads either directly or indirectly affect all children's preferences. This establishes a causal link between TV advertising and preferences, counter to the conclusion.

It offers a different explanation for why TV-kids and non-TV kids both prefer sweet cereals. It's not just because they inherently prefer the sweet cereal. It's because ads brainwashed the TV-kids, and then those kids brainwashed the non-TV kids.

answers.text: The preference for sweets is not a universal trait in humans, and can be influenced by environmental factors such as television advertising.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This proposes that preference for sweets, which can be shaped by TV advertising, isn’t a universal trait, introducing a potential role for ads but lacks direct evidence or scope regarding specific cereal preferences in this context.

answers.text: Most of the children in the group that had watched television were already familiar with the advertisements for these cereals.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This mentions familiarity with ads among TV-watching children without directly affecting non-TV watchers' similar preferences, thus not offering alternate reasoning for shared preferences.

answers.text: Both groups rejected cereals low in sugar even when these cereals were heavily advertised on television.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This reveals both groups rejected low-sugar cereals despite advertising, supporting the claim that advertising doesn’t influence preferences for sugary cereals, reinforcing the conclusion.

answers.text: Cereal preferences of adults who watch television are known to be significantly different from the cereal preferences of adults who do not watch television.
answers.fb:
Weakens (Slightly Relevant)

This hints at a pattern where adult TV watchers' preferences differ from non-watchers, implying TV influence. However, it concerns adults and diverts from the specifics of the children's study.

questiontext:
We are taught that pedestrians should cross the street at a corner and that jaywalking, in the sense of crossing other than at a corner, is dangerous and illegal. It also seems true that drivers anticipate people crossing at corners more than drivers anticipate people crossing elsewhere. Thus we might infer that crossing at a corner is safer than jaywalking. Nevertheless, statistics show that more pedestrians die crossing at corners than while jaywalking.

Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the statistical claim cited above?
gf:
GIVEN THAT ...

Crossing at a crosswalk is safer than jaywalking, since drivers are expecting people to cross at a sidewalk.

HOW CAN IT BE THAT

More pedestrians die crossing the crosswalk than jaywalking?

EVALUATE

This is an often used LSAT trope. More people die using the crosswalk because way more people cross there than jaywalking.

It's kinda like saying, "Flying in a plane is safer than jumping out of a place, but more people die flying in a plane". That's because millions of people fly every year, but only thousands jump out of a plane.

Or like saying, "Covid is a much milder illness than Ebola. Yet, more people die of covid than die of Ebola." That's because tens of millions of people get covid and only a few thousand get Ebola.

We measure safety in terms of %, nor raw numbers. Only 1% of people who get covid die from it, whereas 20% of people who get Ebola die from it. But 1% of 10,000,000 is still a bigger raw number than 20% of 1,000.

Similarly, maybe only 1% of people die from using the crosswalk, whereas 15% of people die from jaywalking. But 1% of a much bigger number is still a higher total than 15% of small number.

GOAL

Look for an answer resolving the paradox by saying that way more people use the crosswalk than jaywalk. (note: we usually can't predict the answer to Paradox questions, but in this case, it's just a familiar LSAT pattern that it's hard to resist).

answers.text: Far more pedestrians cross at corners than jaywalk.
answers.fb:
Correct

As we predicted, this resolves the paragraph by saying, "Sure jaywalking is more dangerous. But there's still a higher number of people dying while using the crosswalk because the total number of people using the crosswalk is way higher than the total jaywalking."

In this way, even though someone is less likely to die using a crosswalk, there will still be a higher raw number of casualties relating to a crosswalk.

answers.text: Some people jaywalk only when there is little traffic.
answers.fb:
Very Weak: Some

Some = at least one

There are very few correct answers on Paradox, Strengthen, and Weaken that use the term Some, because it's only telling us about one measly data point. It's hard for one data point to have impact.

This says "there's at least one person who only jaywalks if there's little traffic". Does that explain why more people die at crosswalks? No, especially because it's very possible that there's at least one person who crosses at a crosswalk only when there's little traffic.

answers.text: Drivers are often unfamiliar with the laws concerning jaywalking.
answers.fb:
Reinforces Background

This is reinforcing the background idea that drivers are expecting pedestrians at crosswalks but not expecting them to be jaywalking.

But it has no power to explain why more people die at crosswalks.

answers.text: Traffic laws in most locations state that the pedestrian always has the right of way, whether or not the pedestrian is crossing at a corner.
answers.fb:
No Distinction

Since we're trying to figure out why there are MORE deaths at crosswalks than via jaywalking, we need an answer to provide a distinction between them.

This says something that is true for both, so it's useless.

answers.text: Good drivers anticipate jaywalkers as much as they anticipate pedestrians crossing at corners.
answers.fb:
No Distinction

Since we're trying to figure out why there are MORE deaths at crosswalks than via jaywalking, we need an answer to provide a distinction between them.

This says something that is the same for both, so it's useless.

questiontext:
Among North American school-age children, there is a strong positive correlation between obesity and the amount of television watched. Therefore, with the arrival of interactive television, obesity among North American school-age children will increase.

The argument requires the assumption that
gf:
Conclusion (therefore)

With the arrival of interactive television, obesity among North American school-age children will increase.

Evidence

Among North American school-age children, there is a strong positive correlation between obesity and the amount of television watched.

Evaluate

Whenever we see a correlation presented in the evidence,
   X is correlated with Y
   ppl who are X are more likely to be Y
   ppl who are X tend to be Y
we anticipate that the author will assume that X causes Y (or vice versa).

Here, there was a correlation between obesity and TV watching. Is the author assuming that one causes the other?

Yes, we can tell from her conclusion that she thinks that TV watching causes obesity, because she thinks the arrival of more TV will lead to more obesity.

Correlations are the most famous of all Curious Facts (asymmetric comparisons). We know that when author's state or assume a causal explanation for a curious fact, we're primarily supposed to ask ourselves about Alternate Explanations.

When an author sees that X and Y are correlated and starts acting like X causes Y, we're supposed to automatically think:
   1. Could it be Reverse Cause (Y causes X)?
  2. Could it be a 3rd Factor (Z causes X and Y)?

#1 would be saying "Hey maybe the obesity came first and it led to more TV watching because it made exercising harder". 

#2 would be saying something like, "Hey maybe there's some underlying condition like working class income, that leads to cheaper junk food that makes us obese and leads to more TV watching because the parent(s) is constantly working and can't afford childcare".

However, there's also a New Concept in the Conclusion, this "interactive television", and the author is making a Prediction.

What if "interactive television" is meaningfully different from other television? Maybe kids won't like it, so they won't watch any additional TV as a result. Maybe the interactiveness will actually burn calories so it will combat obesity.

Goal

A correct answer could rule out an alternate explanation for the correlation. 

Or it could rule out a possible objection that interactive TV will be unlike regular TV, in terms of school-age children watching lots of it and becoming obese.

answers.text: a sedentary lifestyle is among the most important causes of childhood obesity
answers.fb:
Too Strong: most important
Doesn't Address New Concept

The author seems to be thinking that a sedentary (still, motionless, settled, couch potato) lifestyle is a cause of childhood obesity, because she seems to think that TV watching is contributing to obesity.

But she doesn't need to think it's among the most important causes. Even if it's on a lower tier of causes of childhood obesity, the argument still makes sense.

This is the classic Necessary Assumption trap answer pattern where they try to get us to think that the only thing mentioned is therefore the only or most important thing.

They only mentioned TV watching as a cause of obesity, and so they try to get people to think the author is assuming that "only TV watching causes obesity" or "TV watching is one of the most important causes of obesity". 

This answer also doesn't address "interactive television", the New Concept in the Conclusion, which makes it unappealing on a first pass.

answers.text: obesity among North American school-age children increased as cable television became widely available
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: cable TV
Doesn't Address New Concept

The author never mentions cable TV, so she is not assuming anything specific about that.

We're just talking TV ---  it's antennae, it's cable, it's satellite dish. It's everything.

This answer also doesn't address "interactive television", the New Concept in the Conclusion, which makes it unappealing on a first pass.

answers.text: genetics makes no significant contribution to obesity
answers.fb:
Too Strong: no significant contribution
Doesn't Address New Concept

If we negate this and say that "genetics does make a significant contribution to obesity", does that hurt the argument?

Not at all. As we discussed with (A), the author thinks that TV watching is a cause of obesity. She's not saying it's the only cause or the only significant cause.

A correct answer could have ruled out an alternate explanation for the correlation using genetics as the 3rd Factor:
(A) Children with stronger genetic predispositions towards obesity do not watch much more TV than other children

answers.text: North American school-age children will increase their television viewing with the arrival of interactive television
answers.fb:
Correct

(D) and (E) are the only answers to tackle the New Concept in the Conclusion.

Was the author thinking that there would be more TV viewing when interactive TV arrives?

Definitely! Why else would the author be saying that "obesity will increase"? 

The author interprets the correlation in the first sentence to mean that as kids watch more TV, they get more obese.

Since the author is predicting more obesity when interactive TV arrives, he must be predicting more TV watching when interactive TV arrives.

If we negated this and said, "Yo, author -- there isn't going to be any increase in TV watching when interactive television arrives", that would badly weaken the argument. What grounds would the author have for positing that there's going to be an increase in obesity among kids?

answers.text: within a decade of its introduction, interactive television will be almost universally available
answers.fb:
Too Strong: almost universal

This makes an incredibly specific and strong prediction (within 10 years, almost every person has interactive TV).

The author doesn't need to be committed to such a strong idea.

If we said, "actually, within 10 years, only 70% of the population will have interactive TV", would that weaken the argument?

No. If 70% of the population has interactive TV, there could be an increase in TV watching among 70% of the population and an increase in obesity among 70% of the population.

The author doesn't need 95% or more of people to have interactive TV within 10 years in order for there to be an increase in TV watching and thus an increase in obesity.

questiontext:
Drama critic: Audiences will enjoy Warner’s latest play, about the disintegration of a family, because of the superb acting. The chemistry between the actors could not be more intense, and Ziegler, who plays the child, captures convincingly the guilt and despair experienced as the family members grow more estranged from each other.

Each of the following, if true, weakens the argument EXCEPT:
gf:
Conclusion

Audiences will enjoy Warner's latest play.

Evidence (because)

The play features superb acting. The chemistry between the actors is intense. Ziegler convincingly captures the emotions of guilt and despair as the family grows estranged.

Evaluate

We need four answer choices that cast doubt on the conclusion that audiences will enjoy the play. 

Maybe audiences are bummed out by guilt and despair, even when it's well acted.

Goal

Get rid of four answers that give us some way to argue "audiences won't enjoy the play" or that somehow undercut the evidence provided.

answers.text: Generally, audiences enjoy romantic comedies but find tragedies upsetting.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This suggests that audiences typically prefer romantic comedies and find tragedies upsetting, which would imply that the disintegration of a family might not be enjoyable for them.

answers.text: The company staging the play has an unbroken history of dull performances.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This mentions the company's unbroken history of dull performances (i.e. every performance has been dull), giving us a way to argue audiences won't like it.

answers.text: Insiders with the company staging the play have condemned Ziegler’s performance as unexciting.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This is negative, and undercuts the evidence claiming superb acting.

answers.text: The plot of the play is similar in some respects to plots of Warner’s other works.
answers.fb:
Correct

This notes plot similarities with Warner's other works. However, it doesn’t necessarily impact audience enjoyment, as plot similarities don’t inherently reduce the potential for enjoyment, especially if audiences have appreciated Warner's previous works.

answers.text: Audiences usually find drama critics’ reviews unreliable.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This undercuts the overall credibility of the speaker (this might be the only LSAT answer that ever references the person who is delivering the argument).

But it casts doubt on the idea that audiences will agree with the critic's positive assessment.

questiontext:
Therapists who treat violent criminals cannot both respect their clients’ right to confidentiality and be sincerely concerned for the welfare of victims of future violent crimes. Reporting a client’s unreported crimes violates the client’s trust, but remaining silent leaves the dangerous client out of prison, free to commit more crimes.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

Therapists who deal with violent criminals can't simultaneously respect their clients' right to confidentiality and be sincerely concerned for the welfare of future victims.

Evidence

Reporting a client's unreported crimes would violate the client's trust that what they say to their therapist is confidential.

And failing to report a client's unreported crimes would leave the client out of prison, free to commit more crimes.

Evaluate

The conclusion is very harshly worded. It's saying that X is impossible, so to prove this dude wrong, we'd only need to come up with one instance in which X is possible.

Can we think of a scenario in which a therapist who treats violent criminals could manage to both respect the client's right to confidentiality while also showing real concern for potential future victims, were that client to remain out of prison.

The premises are framed as an Binary.

The therapist either reports the violent crimes she learns about from her client or she remains silent about them (doesn't report them).

The author thinks that In Either Case, the therapist has failed to do one of the two things that supposedly can never co-exist. We would need to think of way where in one of those two words, the therapist could still manage to do both things.

When a therapist does report the crimes of their client, could they still be respecting confidentiality and also looking out for future victims? They're definitely looking out for future victims, but it's hard to say they're respecting confidentiality. If you tell the cops what you know, you have failed to keep what you know confidential.

When a therapist does not report the crimes of their client, could they still be respecting confidentiality and also looking out for future victims? They're definitely respecting confidentiality. Could they still be looking out for future victims? Maybe. Maybe they don't consider their client dangerous to future victims? Their violent crime was a crime of passion, not a symptom of a dangerous person?

Goal

Let's find an answer that helps us argue that a therapist could simultaneously keep a client's crimes a secret while still showing proper concern for potential future victims, were that client to remain out of prison.

answers.text: Most therapists who treat violent criminals are assigned this task by a judicial body.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The backstory behind why therapists would end up working with a violent criminal is irrelevant to our assessment of whether it's possible to keep the client's confessions a secret while still being duly concerned for the welfare of future victims.

answers.text: Criminals are no more likely to receive therapy in prison than they are out of prison.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Distinction:  in/out of prison

A comparison between how common it is for criminals in prison vs. out of prison to receive therapy is irrelevant to our assessment of whether it's possible to keep the client's confessions a secret while still being duly concerned for the welfare of future victims.

answers.text: Victims of future violent crimes also have a right to confidentiality should they need therapy.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: victims' confidentiality

This discussion is about whether or not it's possible for a therapist to keep a violent criminal's confessions a secret while still being duly concerned for the welfare of future victims

Whether or not future victims are also entitled to confidentiality in therapy has nothing to do with that discussion. This answer also says tells us something that common sense would already tell us (naturally, they would have a right to confidentiality -- why wouldn't a victim of a violent crime have a right to confidentiality in therapy?), so it isn't a new, impactful idea like what we're looking for.

answers.text: The right of victims of violent crimes to compensation is as important as the right of criminals in therapy to confidentiality.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: compensation

This discussion is about whether or not it's possible for a therapist to keep a violent criminal's confessions a secret while still being duly concerned for the welfare of future victims

Whether or not victims of violent crimes are entitled to monetary compensation has nothing to do with that discussion.

answers.text: A therapist who has gained a violent criminal’s trust can persuade that criminal not to commit repeat offenses.
answers.fb:
Correct

This gives us a potential way to argue that it's possible for a therapist to keep a violent criminal's confessions a secret while still being duly concerned for the welfare of future victims

A therapist might keep the client's unreported crimes a secret, thereby maintaining confidentiality.

But the therapist could simultaneously be showing sincere concern for the potential of future victims by persuading their client not to commit any future crimes.

If the client isn't dangerous going forward, then keeping their checkered past a secret isn't endangering people. Thus, it is possible for a therapist to balance respect for confidentiality and concern for potential future victims.

questiontext:
Failure to rotate crops depletes the soil’s nutrients gradually unless other preventive measures are taken. If the soil’s nutrients are completely depleted, additional crops cannot be grown unless fertilizer is applied to the soil. All other things being equal, if vegetables are grown in soil that has had fertilizer applied rather than being grown in non-fertilized soil, they are more vulnerable to pests and, as a consequence, must be treated with larger amounts of pesticides. The more pesticides used on vegetables, the greater the health risks to humans from eating those vegetables.

Suppose there were some vegetables that were grown in soil to which fertilizer had never been applied. On the basis of the passage, which one of the following would have to be true regarding those vegetables?
gf:
Statements

Don't take preventive measures            Soil
                     and                          →   nutrients
         Don't rotate crops                      depleted


Soil nutrients totally depleted          Crops can't
                   and                         →     be grown
        no fertilizer added


Fertilizer   →  more vulnerable  →   must use
  used                 to pests                pesticides

All other things being equal,
more fertilizer, more vulnerable to pests, more likely treated with pesticides, worse for human health.

Question Stem Fact 

This question stem provides one starter fact … the veggies were grown without fertilizer.

Evaluate

Does anything get triggered by the fact they were grown without fertilizer?

The fact that there was no fertilizer means the crops didn't need pesticide. They were presumably less vulnerable to pests / less likely to have been treated with pesticides.

The fact that they were grown at all triggers one of the two contrapositives.

Crops can         soil nutrients not totally depleted
 be grown   →                       or
                                fertilizer was added

And since we know that fertilizer was NOT added, we know which part of that outcome would have to be true.

Goal

Since these crops were grown (and fertilizer was not added), it must be the case that the soil nutrients were not totally depleted.

answers.text: The soil in which the vegetables were grown may have been completely depleted of nutrients because of an earlier failure to rotate crops.
answers.fb:
Contradicted

We know that the nutrients were not totally depleted. If they were, then crops wouldn't be able to grow there (unless fertilizer is added, which we know there was not).

answers.text: It is not possible that the vegetables were grown in soil in which crops had been rotated.
answers.fb:
No Support: impossible crop rotation

There's no justification for thinking that these crops weren't grown in soil in which crops had been rotated. We weren't given any information that would allow us to prove any crops weren't grown in crop-rotated soil.

answers.text: The vegetables were grown in soil that had not been completely depleted of nutrients but not necessarily soil in which crops had been rotated.
answers.fb:
Correct

Since the crops were grown without fertilizer, we know for sure that the nutrients weren't completely depleted. The second part of this answer has no bearing on us picking it.

Saying “not necessarily with X” / “maybe even with X” isn't really committing to any idea. It's saying we haven't definitively proven or refuted the possibility of crop rotation, which is accurate. We have no idea whether these crops were rotated.

answers.text: Whatever the health risks to humans from eating the vegetables, these risks would not be attributable to the use of pesticides on them.
answers.fb:
No Support: pesticide free
Illegal Opposite

We don't know if these vegetables are pesticide free.

We know that if fertilizer is used, then pesticides must be added.
But we don't know that when fertilizer isn't used, then pesticides are not used.

answers.text: The health risks to humans from eating the vegetables were no less than the health risks to humans from eating the same kinds of vegetables treated with pesticides.
answers.fb:
Opposite

This seems to be going against the gist of the passage. We don't know whether our veggies did or didn't have pesticide, but there's definitely a chance they didn't, and so there's definitely a chance that they are less harmful than the same vegetables but with pesticides added.

questiontext:
Criminologist: Increasing the current prison term for robbery will result in no significant effect in discouraging people from committing robbery.

Each of the following, if true, supports the criminologist's claim EXCEPT:
gf:
Claim

Increasing the prison term for robbery won’t discourage people from committing robbery.

Evaluate

There's no argument to grapple with. It's just one solitary claim. 

Goal

Get rid of the four answers that help us argue that increasing the penalties for robbery won't do much, if anything, to discourage people from robbing.

answers.text: Many people who rob are motivated primarily by thrill-seeking and risk-taking.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This indicates that many who commit robbery are motivated by thrill-seeking and risk-taking. A longer sentence increases the risk, so it might increase the thrill of committing robbery, supporting the claim that harsher penalties won't discourage it.

answers.text: An increase in the prison term for embezzlement did not change the rate at which that crime was committed.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This presents an analogous case where increasing prison terms did not discourage embezzlement, therefore lending support to the claim that a similar approach wouldn't deter robbery.

answers.text: Prison terms for robbery have generally decreased in length recently.
answers.fb:
Correct

This suggests that prison terms for robbery have generally decreased in length without addressing the impact of increasing them. It doesn't provide information that supports or undercuts the claim about the deterrent effect of longer sentences for robbery.

And it almost might suggest to us that prison terms are currently too lax to be a deterrent, but raising them might work.

answers.text: Most people committing robbery believe that they will not get caught.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This claims that most people who commit robbery believe they won't be caught, so the length of the prison term is irrelevant to them, supporting the idea that increased penalties won't act as a deterrent.

answers.text: Most people committing robbery have no idea what the average sentence for robbery is.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This suggests that most people committing robbery are unaware of the prison sentence, indicating they wouldn't be deterred by lengthening it, aligning with the claim that increasing terms won't discourage robbery.

questiontext:
Social critic: One of the most important ways in which a society socializes children is by making them feel ashamed of their immoral behavior. But in many people this shame results in deep feelings of guilt and self-loathing that can be a severe hardship. Thus, moral socialization has had a net effect of increasing the total amount of suffering.

The social critic's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
gf:
Conclusion  (thus)

Moral socialization has had a net effect of increasing the total amount of suffering.

Evidence

Moral socialization works by making children feel ashamed of immoral behavior. In many people that shame produces deep guilt and self-loathing, which can be a severe hardship.

Evaluate

If we're going to try to argue that moral socialization has a net effect of reducing total suffering, we're going to have to counteract the author's evidence which speaks to ways in which moral socialization causes suffering.

Maybe, when the parents are shaming their kids for immoral behavior ("Billy! It was wrong for you to hit all those other kids with the hockey stick. You hurt them!"), the shaming makes Billy suffer, but then he stops hitting the other kids at school with a hockey stick.

It would seem in a case like that like even though Billy's suffering went up, everybody else's suffering went down, and so moral socialization had the net effect of reducing suffering.

Goal

Look for an answer getting at this idea that moral suffering might also reduce suffering in ways the author failed to account for. The evidence for "net effect" is incomplete if you only mention ways it increases suffering but never weigh that against ways it decreases suffering.

answers.text: overlooks the possibility that the purported source of a problem could be modified to avoid that problem without being eliminated altogether
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This is trying to say, "Hey, author -- I know you think that moral socialization is the source of suffering, but we can modify moral socialization! We don't have to completely get rid of moral socialization!"

The author will respond, "I never said we should get rid of moral socialization". There was no normative recommendation. I just descriptively said that moral socialization leads to a net increase in suffering.

answers.text: fails to address adequately the possibility that one phenomenon may causally contribute to the occurrence of another, even though the two phenomena do not always occur together
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

If an answer is structured, "fails to consider that X is true, even though Y isn't true", you'd want X to match the evidence and Y to match the conclusion (or an assumption made en route to the conclusion).

We know from the evidence that moral socialization (a phenom) causally contributes to the occurrence of suffering. 

This answer is saying, "Hey author, even though that's true, that doesn't mean that moral socialization and suffering always occur together."

The author would be like, "Sure, I never said they did. In fact I only said in many people the moral socialization results in suffering."

A correct answer would be more like "fails to consider that one phenom may causally contribute to the occurrence of another, even though the first phenom does not increase the overall occurrence of the second phenom."

answers.text: presumes, without providing justification, that a phenomenon that supposedly increases the total amount of suffering in a society should therefore be changed or eliminated, regardless of its beneficial consequences
answers.fb:
Bad Assumption

This answer accuses the argument of assuming,
"If moral socialization increases the total amount of suffering, then moral socialization should be changed or eliminated."

Just like with (A), the author would way, "I never said we should eliminate or change moral suffering. I just descriptively claimed that it increases moral suffering."

The conclusion of the argument is the trigger of this assumption. We should never see the conclusion in that position.

A correct answer would be more like
"presumes, w/o just, that a phenom that sometimes increases the amount of suffering therefore increases the overall amount of suffering."

answers.text: takes for granted that a behavior that sometimes leads to a certain phenomenon cannot also significantly reduce the overall occurrence of that phenomenon
answers.fb:
Correct

This is saying the author assumes that moral socialization (a behavior that sometimes leads to suffering) does not significantly reduce overall suffering.

Is that true? Hell yeah! That's practically the conclusion.  If we negated that assumption, we'd badly weaken the argument. We say, "Sure morally socializing kids via shaming them increases suffering, but moral socialization also significantly reduces overall suffering, so I don't think you can claim that its net effect is increasing suffering."

This answer finally addresses the missing component of the author's argument. If he's gonna argue a "net effect" claim, then we need to know all the ways that moral socialization increases and decreases suffering.

answers.text: presumes, without providing justification, that if many people have a negative psychological reaction to a phenomenon, then no one can have a positive reaction to that phenomenon
answers.fb:
Bad Assumption
Too Strong (no one)

This accuses the author of assuming,
"If many people have a negative psychological reaction to moral socialization, then no one has a positive reaction to moral socialization."

The argument doesn't claim that no one can have a positive reaction to moral socialization. It just claims many people have a negative reaction to the shame version of it.

The author is failing to account for the ways that moral socialization reduces suffering (which sort of feels like ignoring the positives about moral socialization). But it's too strong to say the author assumes that moral suffering never results in a positive reaction. 

Saying that sometimes moral socialization leads to a positive reaction undermines the conclusion ever so slightly, but it's just one data-point of strength, whereas when we negate the assumption in the correct answer, we get a big sweeping objection to the conclusion.

questiontext:
Antonia: The stock market is the best place to invest your money these days; although it is often volatile, it provides the opportunity to make a large profit quickly.

Maria: I agree that the stock market provides the opportunity to make large profits quickly, but one is just as likely to take a huge loss. I think it is better to invest in savings bonds, which provide a constant, reliable income over many years.

Antonia's and Maria's statements provide the most support for holding that they disagree about whether

answers.text: the stock market is often volatile but provides the opportunity to make a large profit quickly
answers.fb:
Both Agree 

Speaker 1 says this in her second and third claims. Speaker 2 affirms this in her first claim.

answers.text: savings bonds can provide a large return on one’s investment
answers.fb:
Nobody Agrees

Neither speaker claims that a bond can provide a large return. Speaker 2 says bonds provide income that is both constant and reliable, but the amount of return relative to the investment isn't implied.

answers.text: the stock market provides the opportunity for an investor to make a constant, reliable income over many years
answers.fb:
Nobody Disagrees

Speaker two definitely agrees, but Speaker 1 doesn't necessarily disagree.
