answers.text: it is safer to invest in savings bonds than to invest in the stock market
answers.fb:
Nobody Disagrees

Speaker two definitely agrees, but Speaker 1 doesn't necessarily disagree.

answers.text: it is preferable to pick an investment offering a reliable income over a riskier opportunity to make a large profit quickly
answers.fb:
Correct

This one might seem at first to be a "half scope" answer (meaning 1 speaker doesn't address one of the major concepts), but it's the best that we've got. True, speaker 1 doesn't explicitly address the concept of "reliable income," but when she says that the volatile stock market is the best way to invest despite its volatility because of its big potential payoff, that lends strong support to the idea that she'd disagree that it' preferable to pick a reliable investment over a riskier one with a bigger potential payoff.

questiontext:
Very little is known about prehistoric hominid cave dwellers. However, a recent study of skeletons of these hominids has revealed an important clue about their daily activities: skeletal fractures present are most like the type and distribution of fractures sustained by rodeo riders. Therefore, it is likely that these cave dwellers engaged in activities similar to rodeo riders—chasing and tackling animals.

Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the argumentation above?
gf:
Conclusion (therefore)

It is likely that these cave dwellers engaged in activities similar to rodeo riders (chasing and tackling animals).

Evidence

The skeletal fractures these cave dwellers had are most like the type and distribution of fractures sustained by rodeo riders.

Evaluate / Goal

Most of the time on Principle-Strengthen, we just want to prephrase an "If Premise, Then Conclusion" linking idea, so we'd be looking for something like,

"If your skeletal fractures are most like those of rodeo riders, then you probably engaged in activities similar to rodeo riders".

answers.text: The primary source of clues about the lives of prehistoric hominids is their skeletal remains.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The evidence in this argument involved skeletal remains. This answer just tells us that skeletal remains are the most common form of evidence about prehistoric hominids.

But this answer does nothing to get us from, "If prehistoric hominids had the same skeletal fractures as rodeo riders do, then prehistoric hominids probably did stuff similar to rodeo riders."

answers.text: The most important aspect of prehistoric life to be studied is how food was obtained.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This answer isn't explicitly about "how food was obtained" at all. We might read between the lines and see some of that, but that concept is largely out of scope.

This answer doesn't help us get from "hominids had skeletal injuries similar to what rodeo riders have; thus, hominids probably engaged in activities similar to rodeo riders".

answers.text: If direct evidence as to the cause of a phenomenon is available, then indirect evidence should not be sought.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This is a principle that allows us to conclude that we "shouldn't go looking for indirect evidence".

We need a principle that helps us conclude that "early hominids were engaged in activities similar to rodeo riders", so this is miles off target.

answers.text: If there is a similarity between two effects, then there is probably a similarity between their causes.
answers.fb:
Correct

This rule would help us conclude that "there is probably a similarity between causes", and our actual conclusion is "it is likely that cave dwellers engaged in similar activities", so we should consider whether we can make this work. 

The premise talked about a similarity of skeletal fractures. The conclusion is talking about a similarity of activities (chasing and tackling animals).

Can we call "chasing and tackling animals" the cause, and "skeletal fractures'" the effect?

Sure. It's not explicitly said, but that's the common sense interpretation of what this author is suggesting. The whole reason the author surmises that early hominids were also chasing and tackling animals is because she's trying to explain the curious fact of why these early hominids had skeletal fractures like rodeo riders do.

Essentially, the author is thinking, "If these hominids have skeletal fractures that match what rodeo riders have, then they both got these fractures from the same activity."

answers.text: The frequency with which a hazardous activity is performed is proportional to the frequency of injuries resulting from that activity.
answers.fb:
Weak Evidence / Conclusion Match

This argument would help us bridge an argument gap like, "Prehistoric hominids chased and tackled animals three times as much as rodeo riders do. Thus, prehistoric hominids probably had 3 times as many injuries from chasing and tackling animals."

The argument didn't really discuss the frequency of injuries; it talked about the "type and distribution" of fractures.

And the evidence didn't say that hominids' head injuries were from chasing and tackling animals. That's the new idea that the conclusion is trying to establish.

This answer is saying, "If we know you do activity X half as much as Bob, then you'll have half as many injuries from X as Bob does". The idea of Proportionality goes in both directions, so this could also support an argument that says, "Since you have as many injuries from X as Bob does, then you must do activity X half as much as Bob".

This argument did not say:
"Hominids have a similar frequency of injuries from chasing and tackling animals as do rodeo riders. Thus, they probably engaged in chasing and tackling animals about as frequently as rodeo riders do". 

The argument said:
"Hominids have a similar type/distribution of skeletal injuries as rodeo riders do. Thus, they probably engage in activities like chasing and tackling animals, as rodeo riders do."

questiontext:
Studies suggest that, for the vast majority of people who have normal blood pressure, any amount of sodium greater than that required by the body is simply excreted and does not significantly raise blood pressure. So only persons who have high blood pressure and whose bodies are incapable of safely processing excess sodium need to restrict their sodium intake.

Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (So)

Only people with high blood pressure or those who can't process extra sodium need to restrict their sodium intake.

Evidence

For people with normal blood pressure, extra sodium doesn't significantly raise blood pressure because it is excreted by the body.

Evaluate

We can apply our usual Weaken template to this.

GIVEN THAT people with normal BP excrete extra sodium before it raises their BP,

HOW CAN WE ARGUE THAT  these people should still restrict their sodium intake?

Maybe there's some other potential negative effect of sodium consumption that doesn't relate to blood pressure.

Goal

Identify an answer that introduces a reason why people with normal blood pressure might also need to be cautious about sodium intake.

answers.text: High blood pressure is more harmful than was previously believed.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This doesn't give us a way to argue that people with NORMAL blood pressure should reduce sodium intake, since it's about high blood pressure.

answers.text: High blood pressure is sometimes exacerbated by intake of more sodium than the body requires.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This choice also focuses on people who have high blood pressure, which doesn't give us a way to argue that people with NORMAL blood pressure need to watch their sodium intake.

answers.text: Excess sodium intake over time often destroys the body’s ability to process excess sodium.
answers.fb:
Correct

This introduces the idea that excess sodium can eventually impair the body's ability to process it, suggesting that even those with normal blood pressure might face future health issues if they don't restrict sodium, thereby challenging the conclusion that they don't need to be cautious.

answers.text: Every human being has a physiological need for at least some sodium.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This asserts that humans need some sodium, which the argument already accepts. It does not challenge the claim about excess intake and its need for restriction.

answers.text: Any sodium not used by the body will increase blood pressure unless it is excreted.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This statement describes conditions under which sodium would raise blood pressure, but since the premise states that excess sodium is usually excreted, it doesn't practically impact the argument for people with normal blood pressure.

questiontext:
Up until about 2 billion years ago, the sun was 30 percent dimmer than it is now. If the sun were that dim now, our oceans would be completely frozen. According to fossil evidence, however, life and liquid water were both present as early as 3.8 billion years ago.

Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
gf:
Given that ...

The sun, throughout Earth's history until about 2 billion years ago, was 30% dimmer

and that ...

Nowadays, a sun that dim would lead to frozen oceans

Why is it that ..

3.8 billion years ago, there was liquid water?

Evaluate / Goal

There must be something else that was also different about the Earth back then that would allow a dimmer Sun to still warm the Earth enough to keep water in its liquid state.

answers.text: Our atmosphere currently holds in significantly less heat than it did 3.8 billion years ago.
answers.fb:
Correct

This offers us "something else that was different about Earth back then that would allow a dimmer Sun to still warm the Earth enough to keep water in its liquid state". 

Apparently back then, the atmosphere held in way more heat than it does nowadays. This gives us a way to explain how the Earth could end up having a pretty similar global temperature then/now, when it comes to keeping water in its liquid form.

You could get your house to 65 degrees (Fahrenheit) by either blasting the heater, while all your doors and windows are open (that's modern Earth ... stronger heat source, worse heat preservation), or you could get your house to 65 degrees by running the heater 30% less strongly, but closing all the doors and windows so that the house better holds in the heat it acquires.

answers.text: The liquid water present 3.8 billion years ago later froze, only to melt again about 2 billion years ago.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This sort of just creates more confusion. It certainly does nothing to explain how we had liquid water 3.8 billion years ago, despite having a 30% dimmer sun (which nowadays would cause the oceans to free). 

We have no idea how it was liquid 3.8 billion years ago or why it later froze. We might be able to guess that the reason it melted about 2 billion years ago is that the sun became as bright as it  currently is at that point. But our job wasn't to explain why frozen water melted 2 billion years ago. Our job is to explain why liquid water existed 3.8 billion years ago.

answers.text: A significant source of heat other than the sun contributed to the melting of ice sheets approximately 2 billion years ago.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

This isn't going to help us explain how there was liquid water 3.8 billion years ago, when it doesn't even reference anything from around that time period. This is only talking about something that transpired around 2 billion years ago.

answers.text: Evidence suggests that certain regions of ocean remained frozen until much more recently than 2 billion years ago.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

This isn't going to help us explain how there was liquid water 3.8 billion years ago, when it doesn't even reference anything from around that time period. This is talking about stuff that happened less than 2 billion years ago.

answers.text: When large portions of the globe are ice-covered, more of the sun’s heat is reflected and not absorbed by the earth than when only the poles are ice-covered.
answers.fb:
Unclear Impact
No Distinction

We need a distinction between Earth from 3.8 billion years ago and Earth nowadays to resolve this paradox. This answer isn't providing any distinction, unless we know that there was some difference between then and now.

In order for this answer to do the work we need it to do (give us a way "to warm the Earth" enough for their to be liquid water), then we would need to know that nowadays, large portions of the globe are ice-covered whereas 3.8 billion years ago, only the poles are ice-covered (so that even though less heat was coming in from a dimmer sun, more of it was absorbed by the earth).

If anything, we suspect the opposite of that is true. But since we have no idea what parts of the globe were ice-covered 3.8 million years ago, we don't have any way to use this idea anyway.

questiontext:
In 1975, a province reduced its personal income tax rate by 2 percent for most taxpayers. In 1976, the personal income tax rate for those taxpayers was again reduced by 2 percent. Despite the decreases in the personal income tax rate, the total amount of money collected from personal income taxes remained constant from 1974 to 1975 and rose substantially in 1976.

Each of the following, if true, could help to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
gf:
Background

They lowered the personal income tax rate by 2% each of the last two years.

Surprising Thing

In the first year of lowered income tax rate, the overall personal income tax collected was the same as before.
In the second year of even-lower income tax rate, the overall personal income tax collected went up a bunch.

Evaluate / Goal

GIVEN THAT ... 
   the personal income tax rate got lowered 2% in each of the last two years,

HOW CAN IT BE THAT ... 
    total money collected from personal income taxes stayed same and then went up a bunch last year?

4 answers will explain how that could be.  1 will be irrelevant or make the paradox more surprising.

answers.text: The years 1975 and 1976 were ones in which the province’s economy was especially prosperous.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

During the two years when taxes were lower, there was more money in the economy in general (more prosperous).

28% of a richer nation's economy could be more than 32% of a less prosperous nation's economy.

(I'm just making up 28% as the new tax rate after a 32% rate was reduced by 2% for two years in a row)

answers.text: The definition of “personal income” used by the province was widened during 1975 to include income received from personal investments.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

If the definition is widened, then there is more money being taxed as personal income ... 28% of a bigger pool of money is more than 32% of a smaller pool.

answers.text: The personal income tax rate for the wealthiest individuals in the province rose during 1975 and 1976.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

The rich people are being taxed more, so even though most people went from 32% to 28%, rich people went from 40% to 50%.

A smaller tax slice of poorer people combined with a juicier tax slice of richer people could end up netting more tax revenue.

answers.text: The province’s total revenue from all taxes increased during both 1975 and 1976.
answers.fb:
Correct

Other types of tax revenue is out of scope. We're only concerned with explaining how lower rates on personal income tax could result in higher total revenue from personal income tax.

This just restates the paradoxical fact (while adding that non-personal income tax is also rising), but we still don't have a cause for why it's rising.

answers.text: A large number of people from other provinces moved to the province during 1975 and 1976.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

More people move in, more people to tax.  28% of a bigger population could bring more tax money than 32% of a smaller population.

questiontext:
Wealth is not a good thing, for good things cause no harm at all, yet wealth is often harmful to people.

Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
gf:
Evidence (for)

Good things cause no harm        X  →  ~Y

Wealth is often harmful.              W is often Y.

Conclusion

Wealth is not a good thing.         W is ~X.

Evaluate

Because this argument has repeating ideas (wealth  / good things / harmful), it's conducive for putting into an algebraic recipe.

But we could also just say to ourselves "A contrapositive argument structure", if we know what that means. 

Goal

We want two premises that feel something like this:
- All X's are Y
- This thing isn't Y

And a conclusion that then validly concludes the opposite of the original trigger:
- This thing isn't X.

answers.text: Alex loves to golf, and no one in the chess club loves to golf. It follows that Alex is not in the chess club.
answers.fb:
Correct

We have a conditional
chess club  →  ~loves to golf           X → ~Y

We have a fact that denies the outcome
Alex loves to golf                      This thing is Y.

We have a conclusion that denies the trigger
Alex is not in chess club           This thing is ~X.

(It doesn't make any difference, if you're trying to match one contrapositive argument to another, whether the trigger or outcome start out as positive or negative ideas. As long as you're establishing the outcome isn't true and concluding that the trigger isn't true, you're still matching the structure)

answers.text: Isabella must be a contented baby. She smiles a great deal and hardly ever cries, like all happy people.
answers.fb:
Invalid  / Reversed Logic

We have a conditional
happy → smiles / rarely cries           X → Y and Z

We have a fact that affirms the outcome
Isabella smiles / rarely cries.           Isabella is Y and Z.

Then we get an illegal conclusion that uses backwards logic to conclude something resembling the trigger.
Isabella is contented.                     Isabella is X

answers.text: Growth in industry is not a good thing for our town. Although the economy might improve, the pollution would be unbearable.
answers.fb:
Bad Premise Match

There's only one premise (the other idea is a counterpoint), and it's not a conditional. This is a non-starter.

answers.text: Sarah’s dog is not a dachshund, for he hunts very well, and most dachshunds hunt poorly.
answers.fb:
Weak Premise Match / Invalid

We don't have a conditional premise, so this one is hopeless. It's making a pseudo-contrapositive argument with a Most statement, but in order for that to end validly, it should say "Sarah's dog is probably not a dachshund".

No conditional, but a Most claim
Most dachshunds hunt poorly.       Most X's are Y

We have a fact that denies the "outcome"
Sarah's dog hunts very well.                D is not Y.

The conclusion denies the trigger, which is too strong, given that we only said MOST dachshund's hunt poorly, not all of them.
Sarah's dog is not a dachshund.          D is not X.

answers.text: There is usually more traffic at this time of day, unless it is a holiday. But since today is not a holiday, it is surprising that there is so little traffic.
answers.fb:
Bad Premise/Conclusion Match

We have a conditional, kind of. Putting "usually" into conditional form is kind of a lie, since there isn't really certainty. It's more like a Most claim.
holiday → usually more traffic      ~X → usually Y

We have a fact that affirms the trigger.
Today is not a holiday.                   Today is ~X.

The conclusion is neither the trigger nor the outcome. It's just a judgment rendered on the fact that we would usually expect more traffic.

questiontext:
The top 50 centimeters of soil on Tiliga Island contain bones from the native birds eaten by the islanders since the first human immigration to the island 3,000 years ago. A comparison of this top layer with the underlying 150 centimeters of soil—accumulated over 80,000 years—reveals that before humans arrived on Tiliga, a much larger and more diverse population of birds lived there. Thus, the arrival of humans dramatically decreased the population and diversity of birds on Tiliga.

Which one of the following statements, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (Thus)

The arrival of humans dramatically decreased the bird population in terms of both number and diversity on the island.

Evidence

Soil studies show that for the last 3,000 years, since humans arrived, the bird population is less numerous and less diverse compared to the previous 80,000 years.

Evaluate

We can apply the Explain Curious Fact template to this, since we have a conclusion making a causal claim about non-causal evidence.

CURIOUS FACT: How come there was a larger and more diverse population of birds on Tinga before humans arrived?

EXPLANATION: When humans arrived, their activity reduced the number and variety of birds.

To weaken, we either introduce an alternate explanation for the decline in birds or undermine the plausibility of the human causation theory.

Goal

Find an answer choice that provides an alternate cause for the decline in the bird population, or that debunks the story that human arrival is responsible.

answers.text: The bird species known to have been eaten by the islanders had few natural predators on Tiliga.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This indicates that bird species eaten by humans had few natural predators, implicitly ruling out an alternate explanation for why the birds dwindled in number and variety.

answers.text: Many of the bird species that disappeared from Tiliga did not disappear from other, similar, uninhabited islands until much later.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This shows that similar birds persisted longer on uninhabited islands, suggesting a correlation between human presence and bird decline, reinforcing the causal link to humans.

It's a No Cause, No Effect strengthener --- the islands that DIDN'T have humans arrive, DIDN'T have bird species disappearing.

answers.text: The arrival of a species of microbe, carried by some birds but deadly to many others, immediately preceded the first human immigration to Tiliga.
answers.fb:
Correct

This introduces a microbe carried by some birds but deadly to others, which appeared just before humans arrived. It offers an alternate explanation for the bird decline unrelated to human activity, thus weakening the argument.

answers.text: Bones from bird species known to have been eaten by the islanders were found in the underlying 150 centimeters of soil.
answers.fb:
Unclear Impact

If anything maybe this strengthens. It seems to be saying that some of the birds we know these islanders eat were on the island before humans arrived (since they show up in the older soil). 

If islanders are currently eating these birds, then those birds haven't gone extinct yet from the arrival of humans (but maybe they're on their way to going extinct).

answers.text: The birds that lived on Tiliga prior to the first human immigration generally did not fly well.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This notes that birds prior to humans didn’t fly well but doesn’t explain their decline or introduce a factor that distinguishes pre-human and post-human periods in the bird population.

If anything, this strengthens by making it more plausible that humans would be able to trap and kill these (non-flying) birds.

questiontext:
Retailers that excel in neither convenience nor variety of merchandise tend not to be very successful. Yet many successful retailers excel in just one of the areas and meet competitors’ standards for the other. Hence, a retailer’s success need not depend on excellence in both areas.

The structure of the reasoning in the argument above is most parallel to that in which one of the following?
gf:
Conclusion (hence)

A retailer's success need not depend on excellence in both convenience and variety.

Evidence

Many successful retailers excel in only one of the two areas, and are average for the other.

Evaluate

We can probably get away with a conversational summary of this argument since it's build on only one premise.

The argument is saying, "You don't need to be great at both, because there are many examples of things that are only great at one of them"

If we want a little more formality, the conclusion needs the form,
"X doesn't depend on being great at both Y and Z"

And the evidence needs the form,
"there are many examples of X where is Y is great and Z is average, or vice versa".

Goal

Let's start by looking at conclusions, because if they don't have that vibe of "X doesn't depend on Y", then they're hopeless.

Technically, the argument doesn't need to mimic the idea of "great at both".

At its essence, it's saying
"X doesn't depend on Y. After all, there are examples of X without Y."

answers.text: Runners who have only average speed and endurance are unlikely to win long-distance races. Some long-distance champions, however, win by being above average in speed or endurance only; therefore, being above average in both speed and endurance is not necessary.
answers.fb:
Correct

The conclusion does look like a good match for
"X doesn't depend at being great at Y and Z".

Being a long distance champion doesn't require being great at speed and endurance.

Now we just need to make sure there is a premise that says there are examples of long distance champions who either weren't great at speed or weren't great at endurance.

Indeed, it tells us that
Some long-distance champions were only great at speed, or were only great at endurance.

Looks pretty good. It has the same logical essence as the original:
"X doesn't require Y. After all, you can find X without Y."

We might notice a couple superficial differences and keep checking out other answers to see if there's a better match.

OTHER MATCHING LAYERS
This also began with a counterpoint that matches the original. That wasn't necessary for the logic of the actual argument, but it does make (A) even more similar.

MISMATCHING LAYERS
- the premise here is about SOME counterexamples, whereas the original premise is about MANY counterexamples.  That's not logically important, since you only need one counterexample to prove that "X doesn't need Y", but it is different.

- the premise establishes that they are not great at both, like the original. But the original also said that they were average when it came to the not-great trait. This one doesn't say that. Again, not logically important, because the logic comes from the fact that they are champions, even though they are not great at both things. It doesn't actually matter if they're terrible at either thing or just average. As long as we know they're not great at both, it serves the same purpose.

answers.text: Bicyclists who have only average speed are unlikely to win short races, but in a long-distance race such bicyclists can win if they have better-built bicycles than average and better endurance than average. Therefore, most bicycle races are not won by bicyclists with above-average speed.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

We don't need to examine this one beyond its conclusion. It is not making a claim of the form "X does not require Y".

Its conclusion says
"Most X's are ~Y"

answers.text: Excellence in a particular swimming stroke is not always necessary in order for a swimmer to win a race that requires each swimmer to use several different strokes in sequence, and many swimmers win these races without being the best at any of the strokes. Therefore, anyone who does excel at all the strokes is almost certain to win.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

We don't need to examine this one beyond its conclusion. It is not making a claim of the form "X does not require Y".

Its conclusion says
"Anything that is X is almost certainly Y"

answers.text: Apples that are neither especially firm nor especially flavorful are unsuitable for baking; yet while flavor is essential for both baking and eating, many flavorful apples that are soft are suitable for eating. Hence, the apples that are best for eating need not be both firm and flavorful.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

This does have a conclusion the form "X does not require both Y and Z". 

best eating apples don't need to be both Firm and Flavorful.

That means we're checking for a premise that shows at least one example of an apple that was best for eating that was either ~Firm, ~Flavorful, or both.

We do see a premise saying
"many flavorful apples that are soft (~Firm) are suitable for eating"

Hmm, close, but "best for eating" is different than "suitable for eating". 

Also, the evidence is only providing examples of Flavorful but Not Firm. It doesn't also point to examples of Firm but not Flavorful.

In the original and in (A), the premise was saying there are examples of each of the two traits appearing without the other one being present. 

If we didn't catch that discrepancy, we could also notice the premise
- Flavor is required for eating
and think, "The original never said that either of the two traits was required."

We could also hate on the initial counterpoint. If it were going to match the original, it would sound more like,
Apples that are neither really firm nor really flavorful tend to not be the best for eating.

This one is instead talking about baking.

answers.text: Most plants that are neither ornamental nor edible are useless and are thus classified as weeds; yet many such plants are useful for purposes other than food or ornamentation, and are thus not classified as weeds. Hence, not all inedible and non-ornamental plants are weeds.
answers.fb:
Weaker Conclusion Match

The conclusion isn't quite of the form "X does not require Y".

Its conclusion says
"Not all X's and Y's are Z's"

If we were being really charitable, we could say that this is just a paraphrase for, "being X or Y doesn't require Z".

But we don't need to be charitable since we have (A), which doesn't require any translation.

This argument does validly prove its conclusion, because it does provide counterexamples where something is X or Y without being Z.

But it's way less similar to the original than (A).
(A) focused on the idea of "you don't need to be great at both. Here are counterexamples where they're only great at one."

That's way closer to the original argument than, "Not all X's and Y's are Z. There are examples of X's and Y's that are not Z."

questiontext:
Science journalist: Brown dwarfs are celestial objects with more mass than planets but less mass than stars. They are identified by their mass and whether or not lithium is present in their atmospheres. Stars at least as massive as the Sun have lithium remaining in their atmospheres because the mixing of elements in their internal nuclear furnaces is incomplete. Stars with less mass than the Sun have no lithium because the element has been fully mixed into their nuclear furnaces and consumed. A brown dwarf does not have a fully functional nuclear furnace and so its lithium cannot be consumed.

Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the science journalist's statements?
gf:
Facts

causality (identified by, because, and so)

  Mass +     >>  indicates whether Brown Dwarf
Atmos Lith

incomplete mixing        stars as big as Sun
   of elements in     >>   still have lithium 
  nuclear furnace        

  complete mixing        stars smaller than Sun
   of elements in     >>    have no lithium 
  nuclear furnace        

BD lacks fully funct  >> BD still has lithium
   nuclear furnace            in its atmosphere

comparison
              MASS
planets < BD's < stars

Evaluate

Well what should we do with this hot mess of celestial facts? There are bunch of causal ideas, but they don't seem to form any causal chain because they're about three different categories of things (stars as big as the Sun, stars smaller than the Sun, and brown dwarfs).

The overlapping concepts are things like whether or not your nuclear furnace is fully mixed, how massive you are, and whether or not you still have lithium.

If we think about the 2nd sentence, saying that we use how massive you are and whether or not you have lithium to figure out whether something is a brown dwarf, we could now spell out what that means, based on the last three facts:

To be a brown dwarf, we'd expect you to still have lithium in you, but be smaller than a star, and bigger than a planet. 

Goal

As always on Most Supported, we just want the most provable/derivable answer. It's hard to guess where this one is headed.

answers.text: Any celestial object without lithium in its atmosphere is a star with less mass than the Sun.
answers.fb:
Reversal / Negation

We heard about three categories of things:

1. stars as massive as the Sun (have lithium)
2. stars less massive than Sun (no lithium)
3. brown dwarfs less massive than stars (have lithium)

We can say, "if you're a stay with less mass than the Sun, then you are a celestial object without lithium in the atmosphere".

But this answer is the reversal of that. We don't know if smaller-stars are THE ONLY celestial objects that have no lithium in their atmosphere.

Maybe planets, moons, comets, or asteroids are also celestial objects without lithium in their atmosphere.

answers.text: Any celestial object with lithium in its atmosphere has a nuclear furnace that has incompletely mixed the object’s elements.
answers.fb:
Reversal / Negation

We heard about three categories of things:

1. stars as massive as the Sun (have lithium)
2. stars less massive than Sun (no lithium)
3. brown dwarfs less massive than stars (have lithium)

It is true that the two things from this list (1 and 3) that have lithium in their atmosphere also have incomplete furnace mixing. 

But we don't know if big-stars and brown dwarfs  are THE ONLY celestial objects that have lithium in their atmosphere.

Maybe planets, moons, comets, or asteroids are also celestial objects with lithium in their atmosphere. They don't even have nuclear furnaces!

answers.text: No celestial object that has no lithium in its atmosphere is a brown dwarf.
answers.fb:
Correct

The double negative is tough, so consider a couple moves:

1. rewrite one of the negatives so that it doesn't sound like a second negative.

e.g. let's rewrite "has no lithium in its atmosphere" as "Lithium-Free".

No celestial object that's Lithium-Free is a brown dwarf.

That's easier to translate.
"If it's Lithium-Free, then it's not a brown dwarf"

2. The other move is to turn into a logic robot and cite your translation rule for "No A's are B".  Robot knows that looks like "If A, then ~B".

We knew that to be a brown dwarf you had to have lithium and be in between the mass of planets and stars.

So it's true to say,
"If something is Lithium-Free, then it's not a brown dwarf".

This answer is really just derived from the final sentence.

answers.text: No celestial object with lithium in its atmosphere has less mass than the Sun.
answers.fb:
Contradicted

We heard about three categories of things:

1. stars as massive as the Sun (have lithium)
2. stars less massive than Sun (no lithium)
3. brown dwarfs less massive than stars (have lithium)

#3 contradicts this answer. Brown dwarfs are celestial objects with lithium in their atmosphere, and they do have less mass than the Sun.

answers.text: No celestial object less massive than a brown dwarf has lithium in its atmosphere.
answers.fb:
Too Strong (nothing smaller)

We heard about three categories of things:

1. stars as massive as the Sun (have lithium)
2. stars less massive than Sun (no lithium)
3. brown dwarfs less massive than stars (have lithium)

We can't assume that 1 and 3 are the only things in the universe with lithium in their atmosphere, just because they're the only things mentioned in the paragraph. 

Maybe planets, moons, comets, or asteroids have lithium in their atmosphere (they're all celestial objects less massive than a brown dwarf).

questiontext:
Native speakers perceive sentences of their own language as sequences of separate words. But this perception is an illusion. This is shown by the fact that travelers who do not know a local language hear an unintelligible, uninterrupted stream of sound, not sentences with distinct words.

Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
gf:
Conclusion 

This perception is an illusion.

rephrase:  Native speakers are wrong to hear sentences of their own language as sequences of separate words (or, "sentences spoken by native speakers are not sequences of separate words")

Evidence (this is shown by the fact)

Travelers who don't know a local language hear an unintelligible, uninterrupted stream of sound, not sentences with distinct words.

Evaluate

This argument boils down to this structure.

People X say Thing A.
But they're wrong.
This is shown by the fact that People Y say Thing A isn't true.

We sometimes nickname this a He Said / She Said argument, meaning that it's one person's word / point of view vs. another's. The author often arbitrarily sides with one view over the other without justifying their pick (or their attempt to justify favoring one side over the other is super sketchy).

When I listen to Spanish speaking radio, I have a very hard time separating the stream of sound into distinct words. Meanwhile, I'm guessing a Spanish-speaking listener does can comfortably hear the distinct words in a sentence. 

So which of us has the "correct" perception? 

We could say that my perception is more accurate, since I have fresh ears and am not biased by familiarity. We could say that their perception is more accurate, because they have the necessary faculty (they know Spanish) to accurately judge whether sentences are comprised of distinct words.

Goal

Look for an answer establishing a Linking idea like, "If people who don't know a language perceive sentences a certain way, then that is the correct way to perceive those sentences."

Or look for an answer stating the author's assumed preference in this He Said / She Said debate:  "It's better to trust the opinion of the travelers who don't speak the language than to trust the opinion of the natives who do."

Or look for an answer ruling out an objection:  "The travelers are not a poor judge of whether sentences have distinct words, given their ignorance of the distinct words in that language".

answers.text: It is impossible to understand sentences if they are in fact uninterrupted streams of sound.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: impossible
Contradicted

This argument only cares about whether sentences are or aren't sequences of separate words vs. uninterrupted streams of sound.

It doesn't care at all about whether it's possible/impossible to understand an uninterrupted stream of sound.

It would be a very extreme idea for the author to have committed to the idea that it's impossible to understand an uninterrupted stream of sound (it also seems contradicted by the fact that the author thinks sentences are uninterrupted streams of sound but also believes that native speakers can understand them).

answers.text: Those who do not know a language cannot hear the way speech in that language actually sounds.
answers.fb:
Opposite

The author is trusting the opinion of the people who do not know the language, so this sounds like the opposite of what she's assuming.

This answer would be more of a match if it said either
"Those who know a language cannot hear how it actually sounds"
or
"Those who don't know a language can hear how it actually sounds"

answers.text: People pay less close attention to the way their own language sounds than they do to the way an unfamiliar language sounds.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: pay less close attention
Causal Backstory to Premise

This argument only cares about whether sentences are or aren't sequences of separate words vs. uninterrupted streams of sound.

It doesn't care about how close attention we are paying. It only cares about the final evaluation. 

If we say that people pay just as much close attention to the way their language sounds as they do to the way an unfamiliar language sounds, that wouldn't hurt the argument.

This answer is doing the famous trap of trying to assume a potential causal backstory to one of the facts of the case. "Why do the natives hear sentences differently than travelers do?" One possible causal explanation is that the natives pay less close attention and the travelers pay more. 

But the author doesn't need to think that natives have the "wrong" impression about whether sentences are sequences of distinct words because they aren't paying close enough attention. If it's for some other reason (like they're paying so much attention they're guessing what the rest of the sentence will be and thus perceiving each upcoming word as distinct), the argument still works.

answers.text: Accomplished non-native speakers of a language do not perceive sentences as streams of sound.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: accomplished speakers

The author has only told us about View 1 (native speakers) vs. View 2 (outsiders who don't know the language) and has assumed that View 2 is correct.

She hasn't committed to any opinion on View 3 (outsiders who do know the language exceptionally well).

answers.text: Native speakers’ perceptions of their own language are not more accurate than are the perceptions of persons who do not know that language.
answers.fb:
Correct

This has the lovable ruling-out "not" that so many correct Defender answers have. We slow down and negate it.

Would it hurt the argument to say, "Yo, author -- native speakers' perceptions are more accurate than are the perceptions of these travelers who don't know the language"?

Yes! That badly hurts the argument, in fact, because it takes the He Said / She Said tension and tells us that the author is trusting the wrong point of view.

If the natives perception is more trustworthy, then we should be more inclined to think that sentences are sequences of separate words, and that the perception of travelers who don't speak the language (that sentences are just uninterrupted streams of sound) is an illusion.

questiontext:
Jones fell unconscious on the job and it was suspected that he had swallowed a certain chemical, so he was rushed to the local hospital’s emergency room. In making her diagnosis, the emergency-room physician knew that if Jones had swallowed the chemical, a deficiency in the content of a mineral in his blood would result. She also knew that deficiency in the mineral causes inflammation of the skin. Since Jones’s skin was not inflamed when he was admitted to the emergency room, the physician concluded that Jones had not swallowed the chemical.

Which one of the following, if true, would undermine the physician's conclusion?
gf:
Conclusion

Jones did not swallow the chemical.

Evidence (since)

If Jones had swallowed the chemical, it would result in a deficiency of a mineral, leading to inflammation of the skin. Since Jones's skin was not inflamed when he was admitted to the emergency room, the physician concluded he had not swallowed the chemical.

Evaluate

Given that the chemical would lead to inflammation of the skin and that his skin wasn't inflamed, how could we argue that he did swallow the chemical?

Goal

Identify an answer choice that shows why inflammation might not yet be evident in Jones, even if he did swallow the chemical, thus weakening the conclusion.

answers.text: Jones did not know that the chemical was dangerous.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This does not affect the chain of logic concerning the presence or absence of symptoms and doesn't weaken the conclusion.

answers.text: Jones had suffered inflammation of the skin in the past.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This discusses the past, but doesn't indicate current inflammation or challenge the current absence of symptoms due to the chemical in question.

answers.text: It takes 48 hours for the chemical to bring about deficiency of the mineral in the blood.
answers.fb:
Correct

This suggests the symptoms may not have appeared yet, undermining the conclusion that Jones didn't swallow the chemical simply because inflammation wasn't present upon his arrival at the emergency room.

It gives us a way to argue that he DID swallow the chemical. "Yes that chemical will lead to inflammation and he doesn't have inflammation, but give it some time ... the inflammation doesn't show up for at least 48 hrs, because it's triggered by this slow-forming mineral deficiency."

answers.text: Jones often worked with the chemical.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This doesn't address the presence or absence of symptoms at the time of examination.

answers.text: Deficiency in minerals other than the mineral in question can cause inflammation of the skin.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This is irrelevant to the specific chain of logic linking this chemical to symptoms. It doesn't address the immediate context of Jones's condition.

questiontext:
The process by which nylon is manufactured releases large amounts of the gas nitrous oxide, which is harmful to the environment. Since the processing of cotton fiber does not release environmentally harmful gases, there would be less environmental damage done if cotton fiber rather than nylon were used to make products such as thread and rope.

Which one of the following, if true, would weaken the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

There would be less environmental damage if cotton fiber rather than nylon were used to make products like thread and rope.

Evidence (since)

The process by which nylon is manufactured releases large amounts of nitrous oxide, which is harmful to the environment.

The processing of cotton fiber does not release environmentally harmful gases.

Evaluate

This argument is a straightforward comparison of environmental impacts between nylon and cotton fiber. The author suggests that switching from nylon to cotton fiber would lead to less environmental damage. 

To weaken this argument, we need to introduce a factor that counteracts the environmental benefit claimed, perhaps highlighting that the switch to cotton fiber might have its environmental drawbacks or other consequences that were not considered. 

Goal

Let's find an answer that shows how using cotton fiber instead of nylon does not necessarily reduce overall environmental damage, or that it brings an alternative issue that the argument fails to consider.

answers.text: Even if the quantity of nitrous oxide released into the environment decreased, many environmental problems would remain unsolved.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This is saying that even if we stopped using nylon and thus decreased the emission of nitrous oxide, there would still be environmental problems.

Yes of course. We didn't think this would solve every environmental problem. The author is only saying we'll be better-off, not that we'll be 100% fixed.

This choice might suggest a limitation of the switch, but it does not weaken the argument about the relative benefit of reducing nitrous oxide.

answers.text: Even if only some of the thread and rope that is currently being made from nylon were instead made from cotton fiber, some environmental damage would be avoided.
answers.fb:
Opposite Impact

Choice (B) suggests that switching only some products from nylon to cotton reduces environmental damage, which actually supports the idea that using cotton fiber is less damaging environmentally. This does not weaken the argument; rather, it strengthens it.

answers.text: If cotton fiber replaced nylon in the production of thread and rope, there would be a resulting increase in the amount of nylon used in other manufactured products.
answers.fb:
Correct

This suggests that the intended reduction in nitrous oxide emissions might not occur or would be offset by increased nylon use elsewhere, thus negating the environmental benefit the argument claims. This choice effectively weakens the idea that switching to cotton fiber for thread and rope would lead overall to less environmental damage.

There would be less damage coming from thread and rope production, but a commensurate increase of nylon use in other products, so we'd still get the environmental damage from nylon.

answers.text: If the quantity of nylon manufactured annually decreased substantially, the volume of several pollutants that are released into the environment during its manufacture would be reduced.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This seems to say that if switch to cotton and use less nylon, we'll also get less of several pollutants that often come with producing nylon. 

That sounds better for the environment, so it strengthens.

answers.text: If thread and rope continue to be made from nylon, the production of cotton fiber will not increase as rapidly as it would if all thread and rope were to be made from cotton fiber.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Comparison

Choice (E) deals with the production rate of cotton fiber and its impact, not the environmental consequences of using cotton versus nylon. The change in production speed does not inherently affect the environmental damage aspect and thus it does not weaken the comparison made regarding environmental damage.

questiontext:
An antidote for chicken pox has been developed, but researchers warn that its widespread use could be dangerous, despite the fact that this drug has no serious side effects and is currently very effective at limiting the duration and severity of chicken pox.

Which one of the following, if true, helps most to reconcile the apparent discrepancy indicated above?
gf:
GIVEN THAT ...

This chicken pox antidote has no serious side effects and is very effective at limiting the duration / severity of chicken pox.

WHY IS IT THAT ...

Researchers are warning that widespread use of this antidote could be dangerous.

GOAL

We basically need to look for an answer that gives us some story to tell where lots of people take this antidote and bad stuff happens.

If you have outside knowledge about how chicken pox is mild if you have it when you're young but can be much more severe if you get it as an adult, you might be having some premonition here that the "bad stuff" could relate to that.

answers.text: The drug is extremely expensive and would be difficult to make widely available.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal: expensive vs. dangerous

The fact that it would be difficult to make this widely available doesn't answer the question of why it would be dangerous if it were widely available.

This answer sounds like reasons why we shouldn't plan to make this drug widely available, but it doesn't relate to why it would be dangerous (assuming we had the money / ability to do so).

answers.text: The drug has to be administered several times a day, so patient compliance is likely to be low.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal: nothing about danger

This, like (A), relates to the feasibility of whether we could have widespread use of this antidote. But we're seeking an answer that explains the danger of widespread use.

There's no common sense story that "if patients don't follow the dosing instructions (they tend to not take it as much as they should), then something dangerous will happen".

answers.text: The drug does not prevent the spread of chicken pox from one person to another, even when the drug eventually cures the disease in the first person.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal: nothing dangerous

The status quo is that chicken pox is a highly contagious and also miserable to get through. This answer is basically saying "the new drug would make it less miserable to get through, but it would still be highly contagious."

Wouldn't that be an improvement over the status quo? Where is the danger that researchers are worried about?

answers.text: When misused by taking larger-than-prescribed doses, the drug can be fatal.
answers.fb:
Weaker Impact

This answer definitely relates to danger, but the danger only comes into play if people misuse the drug by taking larger-than-prescribed doses.

Should we be worried about people taking larger-than-prescribed doses? Do people often do that?

There's definitely some risk that people will overdose (especially if they have itchy chicken pox and want quicker relief). But that risk is true of almost any drug. If you overdose on Advil or Tylenol, it can be fatal. 

The correct answer presents a danger that isn't limited to edge cases, or that isn't inherent to any drug.

answers.text: Use of the drug contributes to the development of deadlier forms of chicken pox that are resistant to the drug.
answers.fb:
Correct

This answer allows us to say, "If there is widespread use of this drug, it will lead to deadlier chicken pox that can't be treated with this drug."

That sounds like a broader health concern than (D). This answer deals with potentially creating new strains of a disease that could endanger everyone, whereas (D) only dealt with endangerment for the few people who overdose on the drug. 

This answer is similar to the common sense idea that widespread use of antibiotics is dangerous because it can lead to superbacteria that are resistant to antibiotics.

questiontext:
The tendency toward overspecialization in the study of artifacts is unfortunate. Scholars can enhance their understanding of a certain artistic period by studying art from earlier periods that had a significant influence on it. For instance, because of its influence on Spanish artisans, a proper understanding of Arabic porcelain is indispensable for a proper understanding of Spanish porcelain.

Of the following, which one most closely conforms to the principle that the passage as a whole illustrates?
gf:
Conclusion

It's unfortunate how scholars studying artifacts tend to overspecialize nowadays (it'd be better if they had a broader range of expertise).

Evidence

Their understanding of whatever art period they're studying could be enhanced by studying earlier art that influenced it.

Evaluate

When we're trying to extract an implicit principle, we're sort of doing  the upfront work of Parallel reasoning, except we wouldn't usually be diagramming anything, just trying to think of the general essence without referencing the specific topic.

The passage is saying that focusing too much on one thing can lead to a deficient understanding of it. You could potentially understand that thing better by also focusing on some of its influential precursors.

Goal

I'd probably be looking for something like, 
"You could better understand X if you also developed an appreciation for earlier stuff that influenced X."

answers.text: To understand completely the major trends in research on aging, one must understand the influences these trends exert on society’s view of aging.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match (before vs. after)

We wanted something like,
"to understand X, you need to also understand the earlier stuff that influenced X."

This is saying
"to understand X, you need to understand the repercussions of X, the stuff that X causes."

This is focusing on what comes AFTER the thing we're studying, on how the thing we're studying affects other stuff.

The original was focusing on what came BEFORE the thing we're studying, on how that earlier stuff affects what we're studying.

answers.text: To understand fully the historical events of this century, a historian must have an understanding of similar events in earlier centuries.
answers.fb:
Weaker Evidence Match (similar vs. causal)

We wanted something like,
"to understand X, you need to also understand the earlier stuff that influenced X."

This is saying
"to understand X, you need to also understand the earlier stuff that is similar to X."

That's probably valid advice in and of itself, but not as good a match for the original, which specifically talking about earlier things that SHAPED the thing we're studying, not just earlier things that RESEMBLE the thing we're studying.

answers.text: To appreciate fully the French language, one must understand the other languages that share its linguistic ancestry.
answers.fb:
Weaker Evidence Match (cousins vs. parent)

We wanted something like,
"to understand X, you need to also understand X's backstory."

This is saying
"to understand X, you need to also understand other things that share X's backstory." 

The answer would be a better match if it were saying, "To fully appreciate French, you need to understand its linguistic ancestry", because that would talking about the precursors that influenced French.

This isn't asking us to understand the previous generations (the parents); it's asking us to understand the current relatives (the cousins), the other languages that have a similar backstory to French.

answers.text: To understand properly any academic discipline, one must have at least a superficial acquaintance with the practices of the wider academic community.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match 

We wanted something like,
"to understand X, you need to also understand the earlier stuff that influenced X."

This is saying
"to understand X, you need to also understand other stuff currently going on outside of X."

It doesn't have anything to do with the causal precursors of X.

answers.text: To understand completely Aristotle’s philosophy, one must be well acquainted with the philosophy of his intellectual mentor, Plato.
answers.fb:
Correct

We wanted something like,
"to understand X, you need to also understand the earlier stuff that influenced X."

This is saying
"to understand Aristotle, you need to also understand the earlier stuff (Plato) that influenced Aristotle."

We need to add in the common sense that if someone is your mentor, then they influence you, but that's a very reasonable connection to make.

questiontext:
Computer manufacturers and retailers tell us that the complexity involved in connecting the various components of personal computers is not a widespread obstacle to their use, but this is wrong. Customers who install accessories to their personal computers have to take full responsibility for the setting of jumpers and switches to satisfy mysterious specifications. Many accessories require extra software that can cause other accessories to stop working; adding a modem, for instance, may disable a printer.

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (rebuttal)

But this is wrong.

rephrase: The complexity of connecting components to computers is a widespread obstacle to people using computers.

Evidence

Setting jumpers and switches to specific specifications can be confusing, and installing necessary software for components might disrupt the functioning of other computer systems.

Evaluate

We need to counter the rebuttal conclusion that connecting components is a significant obstacle. So we basically need to defend the original position, that there's no reason that connecting components should thwart most people from having a computer. 

Goal

Identify an answer that demonstrates why connecting components, despite potential complexities, does not markedly hinder typical users from setting up and using computers.

answers.text: Personal computer instruction manuals usually explain the purposes of the jumpers and switches.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This claims that manuals clearly explain the purpose of jumpers and switches, but that doesn't address the complexity of connecting the components.

answers.text: Software for accessories can often be obtained for free.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This points out that accessory software is free, which doesn't address the primary concern about compatibility or functional issues, thus not relevant to the stated obstacle.

answers.text: Installing an accessory will become extremely easy in the foreseeable future.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This mentions future ease of installing accessories, but the argument is about the current state of complexity, so it doesn’t address present obstacles.

answers.text: A personal computer is usually sold as part of a package that includes accessories and free installation.
answers.fb:
Correct

This explains that PCs are often sold as part of a package including accessories with free installation services. This greatly reduces any complexity issue for consumers, suggesting that potential obstacles do not prevent them from using computers.

answers.text: Computer manufacturers rarely take into account ease of installation when they are designing programs or accessories.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This notes that manufacturers rarely consider ease of installation, which supports the idea that the process is potentially complicated and can be an obstacle.

questiontext:
Although we could replace the beautiful—but dilapidated—old bridge across Black River with a concrete skyway, we should instead replace it with a cable bridge even though this would be more expensive than building a concrete skyway. The extra cost is clearly justified by the importance of maintaining the beauty of our river crossing.

Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
gf:
Conclusion (should = opinion)

We should replace the old bridge with a cable bridge, rather than a concrete skyway.

Intermediate Conclusion (clearly)

The extra cost of the cable bridge would be justified.

Evidence 

It's important to maintain the beauty of our river crossing.

Evaluate

This argument boils down to a choice between the cable bridge and the concrete skyway. The author identifies some competing interests at play:

concrete skyway - better option when it comes to cost
cable bridge - better option when it comes to maintaining the beauty of our river crossing.

How could we object to the decision to go with the cable bridge? Maybe it's way less safe than the concrete skyway? Could safety concerns override beauty concerns?

Goal

We're probably going to get a Defender style correct answer, where it's ruling out some objection to the cable bridge, for example:
- the cable bridge is not far more prone than is a concrete skyway to catastrophic collapse

Otherwise let's just pick something that relates to how the author is weighing these tradeoffs between cost and beauty.

answers.text: It is no more costly to maintain a cable bridge than a concrete skyway.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: no more costly

It wouldn't hurt the author's argument if a cable bridge is more expensive to maintain. Yes, that's a bad thing about cable bridges, and bad things about cable bridges will generally weaken his argument.

But, he's already acknowledged that the cable bridge costs more. He thinks that cost is less important than maintaining beauty. So telling him that the cable costs more to maintain will just get a response of, "I know --- but clearly it's worth it, given the important of maintaining beauty."

answers.text: A concrete skyway would not have any practical advantages over a cable bridge.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: no advantages

The author doesn't need the concrete skyway to have zero advantages. It could have some advantages, as long as they're lame ones. 

If we negate this and say that "a concrete skyway would have at least one practical advantage over a cable bridge", does that weaken?

Yes, a little. That cuts against the conclusion that we should build the cable bridge rather than the concrete skyway. But it's not really a compelling objection until we know that the practical advantages we're referring to here outweigh the very compelling concern the author has with maintaining beauty.

If this answer said, "A concrete skyway would not have any practical advantages for which it would be worth sacrificing beauty", then we'd definitely pick it.

But if we judge these five answers by the standard of, "Which answer, if negated, most weakens", then this is not the winning objection.

answers.text: The beauty of the river crossing must be preserved.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: must be

The author has already established that "it's important to maintain the beauty of our river crossing", but this answer is saying something stronger. It's an absolute must.

There's a difference between saying
- it's important to brush your teeth every night
and saying
- you must brush your teeth every night

answers.text: If the new cable bridge is built, most people who see it will think the extra money well spent.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: most people

Would it hurt the author's argument if a new cable bridge were built, and only 49% of people who see it think the extra money is well spent?

Does it need to be at least 51% of people having that reaction?

No, so the author doesn't need for most people who see it to have that reaction. The word "most" is wrong on Necessary Assumption 99% of the time we see it.

Furthermore, it could be that the vast majority of people have no idea that the cable bridge cost "extra money". They not be privy to the city planning conversation about "cable bridge or concrete skyway".

answers.text: Building a cable bridge across Black River would produce a more aesthetically pleasing result than building a concrete skyway.
answers.fb:
Correct

The author is trying to decide on cable vs. concrete. Concrete is cheaper, but it's important to maintain the beauty of the river crossing. So let's go with cable.

That implies that the author thinks that cable is better than concrete, when it comes to maintaining the beauty of the river crossing.

If we negated this and said, "the concrete skyway would be at least as aesthetically pleasing as the cable bridge", then we have no reason not to build the cheaper concrete skyway.

Negating this answer badly hurts the argument.

questiontext:
A typical gasoline-powered lawn mower emits about as much air-polluting material per hour of use as does an automobile. Collectively, such mowers contribute significantly to summer air pollution. Since electric mowers emit no air pollutants, people can help reduce air pollution by choosing electric mowers over gasoline ones whenever feasible.

Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

People can help reduce air pollution by choosing electric mowers over gasoline ones whenever feasible.

Evidence (since)

A typical gasoline-powered lawn mower emits about as much air-polluting material per hour of use as does an automobile.

Collectively, such mowers contribute significantly to summer air pollution.

Electric mowers emit no air pollutants.

Evaluate

This argument is presenting a Plan/Goal pattern.

Goal: Reduce air pollution.

Plan: Use electric mowers instead of gasoline-powered mowers whenever feasible.

To strengthen the Plan/Goal, we want to ensure that switching to electric mowers will indeed result in a significant reduction of air pollution. In addition, the argument primarily highlights that electric mowers emit no pollutants directly. To support the argument, we could emphasize that using electric mowers, including their indirect emissions, would still be less polluting than using gasoline mowers.

Goal

Let's find an answer that allows us to argue more persuasively that choosing electric mowers over gasoline mowers will reduce air pollution. Additionally, consider the overall environmental impact, including the generation of electricity needed for electric mowers.

answers.text: Lawns help to clean the air, replacing pollutants with oxygen.
answers.fb:
No Distinction / No Impact

This has nothing to do with comparing electric mowers to gasoline mowers.

answers.text: Electric lawn mowers are more expensive to purchase and maintain than are gasoline mowers.
answers.fb:
No Impact / Irrelevant Comparison

This argument doesn't care at all about what the cost of either mower is. We're only analyzing which one is better when it comes to reducing air pollution.

answers.text: Producing the power to run an electric mower for an hour causes less air pollution than does running an automobile for an hour.
answers.fb:
Correct

If producing the power to run an electric mower for an hour causes less air pollution than running an automobile, it implies that even the indirect emissions (from electricity production) of electric mowers are lower than those from gasoline mowers. This supports the argument that choosing electric mowers will help reduce air pollution.

answers.text: Most manufacturers of gasoline lawn mowers are trying to redesign their mowers to reduce the emission of air pollutants.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

This sounds like gas mowers are getting better, when it comes to emissions of air pollutants.

answers.text: Lawn mowers are used for fewer hours per year than are automobiles.
answers.fb:
No Impact (Irrelevant Comparison)

The comparison of total hours mowers are used versus automobiles doesn't address the pollution impact of substituting electric mowers for gasoline mowers in terms of per-hour emissions.

questiontext:
People are not happy unless they feel that they are needed by others. Most people in modern society, however, can achieve a feeling of indispensability only within the sphere of family and friendship, because almost everyone knows that his or her job could be done by any one of thousands of others.

The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?
gf:
Statements

conditionals (only = right, unless = "if not")

   people don't feel  → people are not happy
  needed by others

quantifiers (most / almost everyone)
causal (because)

  knowing your job     don't feel needed
   can be done by  ⇢ other than family 
  1000s of people       & friends

Evaluate

This one is kind of a mess to break down technically, because there's causality, conditional logic, and quantifiers. So let's get more conversational with our understanding.

Usually when we see a conditional rule in Inference, they want us to chain it to another conditional or apply it to some specific fact. Both of the first two claims are talking about Indispensability / Feeling Needed. Overlapping concepts point us towards possible inferences.

Since people don't feel happy if they don't feel needed, and since they only ever feel needed within their group of family / friends, it means that they don't feel happy outside their sphere of family and friends.

The 3rd claim provides a causal relationship between whether or not we feel needed and whether or not we think we're easily replaceable. 

Goal

Let's find a safely worded answer making use of our knowledge:

Most people feel replaceable at work, so they don't feel needed, so they don't feel happy. (Within the sphere of family / friends, they may feel needed, so they may feel happy)

answers.text: People who realize that others could fill their occupational roles as ably as they do themselves cannot achieve any happiness in their lives.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: can't achieve any

It's way too strong to say that people who feel replaceable at work can't achieve any happiness in their lives. This paragraph left plenty of room for such people to feel needed within their circle of family and friends, and thus room for them to achieve some happiness.

answers.text: The nature of modern society actually undermines the importance of family life to an individual’s happiness.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: undermines importance

The passage doesn't say anything about modern society having a causal relationship on how important family life is to happiness.

If anything, it sounds like "since most people can't feel needed/happy at their jobs, family and friends are more important than ever when it comes to happiness".

answers.text: Most people in modern society are happy in their private lives even if they are not happy in their jobs.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: most are happy

We know most people aren't happy in their professional lives. We have no way to support that most people are happy in their personal lives. 

In fact, we have no way at all to prove that someone is happy. We only have a rule that allows us to prove that someone is NOT happy.
"If they don't feel needed, they won't feel happy"

That doesn't mean that, "if you do feel needed, you will feel happy" (that's an illegal negation).

And even if we knew that, this answer would also require us knowing that most people feel needed in their private lives (we know it's possible to feel needed in your private life, but we don't know that most people do feel needed).

answers.text: A majority of people in modern society do not appreciate having the jobs that they do have.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: appreciate jobs

Nothing in the passage talks about whether or not people appreciate having their jobs.

Perhaps LSAC was trying to fool people who translated that last claim into their brains as, "most people don't feel appreciated at their jobs".

answers.text: Fewer than a majority of people in modern society can find happiness outside the sphere of private interpersonal relationships.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is saying that most people in modern society can't be happy outside their sphere of family / friends, which we can definitely derive from the paragraph.

The paragraph says that "in modern society, most people only feel needed within the sphere of family and friends". And it says that "in order to be happy you have to feel needed".

So we can combine those to derive that "in modern society, most people can only feel happy within their sphere of family and friends".

Most A's are B is the same as Few A's are ~B.

Thus can derive that, "in modern society, few people can feel happy outside their sphere of family and friends".

questiontext:
Literary historian: William Shakespeare, a humble actor, could have written the love poetry attributed to him. But the dramas attributed to him evince such insight into the minds of powerful rulers that they could only have been written by one who had spent much time among them; Francis Bacon associated with rulers, but Shakespeare did not.

Which one of the following logically follows from the literary historian's claims?
gf:
Statements

Shakespeare could have written the love poetry attributed to him.

Meanwhile, the dramas attributed to him are so insightful about the minds of powerful rules that they could only be written by someone who'd hung out with rulers.

Shakespeare didn't. Bacon did.

Evaluate

Since this is Must Be True, the biggest thing on our radar is conditional logic, which here shows up with the word only (a necessary indicator = put the following idea on the Right).

Wrote these insightful        spent lots of time
 dramas about minds   →        with rulers
           of rulers

Do we have another Conditional to chain this to?  No.

Do we have a fact that triggers this rule or triggers its contrapositive? Yes.

The contrapositive says,
didn't spend time  → couldn't have written these
   around rulers                 insightful dramas

We know that Shakespeare didn't associate with rulers, so we can output the inference that Shakespeare couldn't have written the dramas attributed to him.

They are definitely trying to bait us into concluding that Francis Bacon did write those dramas, but that would be reading backwards. 

Francis Bacon may have written the dramas, since he had the required firsthand exposure to rulers, but so could any number of other people who, like Bacon, associated with rulers.

Goal

Pick anything provable, but it's most likely that they're trying to reward us for applying the fact about Shakespeare to trigger the contrapositive of the rule they provided.

So we should anticipate "Shakespeare didn't write the dramas attributed to him".

answers.text: Bacon wrote the dramas attributed to Shakespeare, but could not have written the love poetry.
answers.fb:
Unsupported: Bacon wrote the dramas

We have no way to prove that Bacon wrote the dramas. We only know he's a possibility, since he meets a necessary requirement of whoever it was that did write the dramas.

We also have zero clue whether Bacon did / didn't write the love poetry attributed to Shakespeare.

There's no accident that this answer is (A). They know when their paragraphs are causing students to think thoughts, and they love to put an illegal answer that sounds like what the students were feeling in spot (A) (on Inference questions).

answers.text: Bacon wrote both the love poetry and the dramas attributed to Shakespeare.
answers.fb:
Unsupported: Bacon wrote the dramas

We have no way to prove that Bacon wrote the dramas. We only know he's a possibility, since he meets a necessary requirement of whoever it was that did write the dramas.

We also have zero clue whether Bacon did / didn't write the love poetry attributed to Shakespeare.

answers.text: Shakespeare wrote neither the love poetry nor the dramas attributed to him.
answers.fb:
Unsupported: didn't write love poetry

We know for a fact that Shakespeare didn't write the dramas (we applied the conditional rule and derived it). But we don't know whether Shakespeare did or didn't write the love poetry. 

The author indicated that Shakespeare could have written it, so it's an open question.

answers.text: One person could not have written both the love poetry and the dramas attributed to Shakespeare.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: couldn't be one person

Why couldn't it be one person? We don't have any information about what needs to be true about the person who wrote the love poetry.

It's certainly possible that someone who wrote the love poetry also hung out with rulers and thus was able to write the dramas as well.

answers.text: Shakespeare may have written the love poetry but did not write the dramas attributed to him.
answers.fb:
Correct

The first half of this just repeats the very first sentence. The second half is the inference we derived by combining the fact that "Shakespeare didn't associate with rulers" with the fact that "the dramas attributed to Shakespeare could only be written by someone who associated with rulers".

questiontext:
Charlene: Environmental cleanup increasingly relies on microorganisms to metabolize pollutants. This has its limitations, though, since microbes become less active when a region’s temperature drops below normal.

Olaf: I don’t think that’s right. Researchers studying oil spills in the Arctic and subtropical regions measured the carbon dioxide output of organisms that digest petroleum pollutants and found that Arctic and subtropical microbes ate oil at nearly the same rate.

Olaf's reply suggests that he misinterprets Charlene's use of the term
gf:
Charlene's Conclusion

Using microorganisms to metabolize pollutants has limitations.

Charlene's Evidence

Microbes are less active when a region's temps are below normal.

Olaf's Rebuttal

No. The activity level of microbes is basically the same whether they live in Arctic or subtropical regions. 

Evaluate

The problem with Olaf's rebuttal is he's acting like Charlene said "microbes don't work as well in cold climates", and thus rebutting that by saying "look --- these microbes work as well in the cold (arctic) as they do in the warm (subtropical)."

But Charlene was just saying that microbes don't work as well when the local temperature is lower than average.

So if the average temperature in the Arctic is 0 degrees Celsius, then arctic microbes won't work as well when the temperature drops to -10 degrees.

If the average temp in the subtropics is 27 degrees Celsius, then subtropical microbes won't work as well when the temperature drops to 17 degrees. 

Goal

Olaf's flaw was thinking in Absolute terms of "low temp" when Charlene was talking about a Relative sense of "low temp".

answers.text: relies
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal
