This doesn't have anything to do with whether we're talking about "temperature is low" vs. "temperature is lower than normal".

answers.text: normal
answers.fb:
Correct

By "normal", Charlene meant "what a normal temperature for this region would be" (relative). Olaf seems to think that Charlene means "normal" like "an average temperature, globally".

We certainly think of the equator as hot and the poles as cold, and so stuff that's more temperate would probably be thought of as "normal" by Olaf.

But Charlene was talking about "whatever is a normal temperature for that reason".

answers.text: cleanup
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

This doesn't have anything to do with whether we're talking about "temperature is low" vs. "temperature is lower than normal".

answers.text: limitations
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

This doesn't have anything to do with whether we're talking about "temperature is low" vs. "temperature is lower than normal".

Olaf is thinking of limitations in the same way, insisting that there shouldn't be limitations since, in his distorted understanding, the activity rate of microbes is the same whether it's a hot climate or a cold climate.

answers.text: active
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

This doesn't have anything to do with whether we're talking about "temperature is low" vs. "temperature is lower than normal".

Olaf is thinking about "active" just as Charlene is -- how quickly a microorganism would be metabolizing pollutants.

questiontext:
Film historians have made two major criticisms of Depression-era filmmakers: first, that they were too uncritical of the economic status quo; and second, that they self-indulgently created films reflecting their own dreams and desires. However, these filmmakers made their movies with an eye to profit, and so they provided what their audiences most wanted in a film: a chance to imagine being wealthy enough not to have a care in the world. Thus, the second criticism cannot be accurate.

The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
gf:
Conclusion (Thus)

The second criticism cannot be accurate.
rephrase:  Depression-era filmmakers did not self-indulgently create films reflecting their own dreams and desires.

Evidence

These filmmakers made their movies with an eye to profit and provided what their audiences most wanted in a film.

Evaluate

We're trying to prove that certain people "didn't self-indulgently create films reflecting their own dreams and desires", but the argument has provided any proving mechanism for such wording. So the correct answer will need to give us a rule that is like:

   if xyz → then didn't self-indulgently create
                   films to reflect own thinking

We're trying to prove this wording in relation to Depression-era filmmakers. The argument provided two facts about them, so the correct answer could use either / both of the facts to get us to that magical conclusion wording.

Goal

Look for,

  made movies with → did not self-indulgently
    an eye to profit         make films reflecting
                                    own dreams / desires

                                      or

 provided audiences        did not self-indulgently
    with what they       →    make films reflecting
     most wanted                own dreams / desires

answers.text: To avoid self-indulgence, filmmakers should take a critical stance toward the existing economic system and should allow audiences to form their own personal aspirations.
answers.fb:
Too Weak

This is a guideline for someone who wants to avoid self-indulgence.

We need a rule that says, "If x is true, then you did not self-indulgently make films". Even if someone satisfied both conditions here, (1. take critical stance toward existing economic system, 2. allows audiences to form their own personal aspirations), that wouldn't prove that you have avoided self-indulgence.

Similarly, if I said "to get into Harvard, students should apply as early as possible and submit at least one letter of recommendation" that wouldn't mean that satisfying those two conditions guarantees that you get into Harvard.

answers.text: It is unjustified to demand of all filmmakers that their films engage in criticism of the economic status quo.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

We need a rule that says, "If x is true, then you did not self-indulgently make films reflecting your own dreams / desires". This answer doesn't have any of that necessary conclusion language.

answers.text: The people who regularly went to movies during the Depression were those likely to have been most satisfied with the economic status quo.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

We need a rule that says, "If x is true, then you did not self-indulgently make films reflecting your own dreams / desires". This answer doesn't have any of that necessary conclusion language.

answers.text: Depression-era filmmakers who did not make films for profit could not take radical critical stances toward then-current economic and political issues.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

We need a rule that says, "If x is true, then you did not self-indulgently make films reflecting your own dreams / desires". This answer doesn't have any of that necessary conclusion language.

answers.text: It cannot be self-indulgent for a filmmaker to give an audience what it most wants.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is the only answer with a proving mechanism for the wording in our conclusion, that the filmmakers "did not self-indulgently create films reflecting their own dreams and desires".

This says

filmmaker gives an audience → cannot be 
    what it most wants               self-indulgent

We were told that the Depression-era filmmakers provided what their audiences most wanted in a film. According to this rule, it cannot have been self-indulgent for the filmmakers to have done this.

So we have proven that the Depression-era filmmakers were not self-indulgently creating films. 

Since this was the only answer that provided the New Concept in the Conclusion (only choice A otherwise had anything about self-indulgence), this was the only answer really worth reading or thinking about.

questiontext:
In contemplating major purchases, businesses often consider only whether there is enough money left from monthly revenues after paying monthly expenses to cover the cost of the purchase. But many expenses do not occur monthly; taking into account only monthly expenses can cause a business to overexpand. So the use of a cash-flow statement is critical for all businesses.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (so)

The use of a cash flow statement is critical for all businesses.

Evidence

Businesses can get into trouble by over-expanding if they only account for monthly expenses, ignoring non-monthly expenses. 

Evaluate

"Cash flow statement" is a New Concept in the Conclusion, so we can ask ourselves, "What is the author assuming about this new concept?"

Since they're telling us that it's critical for businesses to account for non-monthly expenses, they must be assuming that cash flow statements solve the problem of tracking both monthly and non-monthly expenses.

Goal

Identify an answer that effectively demonstrates how cash flow statements are indispensable for tracking non-monthly expenses or proves there are no viable alternatives, reinforcing their critical role.

answers.text: Only a cash-flow statement can accurately document all monthly expenses.
answers.fb:
Weaker Impact

This does make cash-flow statements sound uniquely good at something, but the argument was stressing the need to document non-monthly expenses, and this answer doesn't tell us that a cash flow statement can do that.

answers.text: Any business that has overexpanded can benefit from the use of a cash-flow statement.
answers.fb:
Weaker Impact

This states that cash flow statements benefit some businesses, which does little to enhance the claim that they're critical for all businesses.

answers.text: When a business documents only monthly expenses it also documents only monthly revenue.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This doesn't tell us anything about cash flow statements, so it does nothing to support the idea that they're critical for all businesses.

answers.text: A cash-flow statement is the only way to track both monthly expenses and expenses that are not monthly.
answers.fb:
Correct

This states that cash flow statements are the only way to track both monthly and non-monthly expenses, arguing for their necessity in preventing over-expansion and supporting their critical role for all businesses.

answers.text: When a business takes into account all expenses, not just monthly ones, it can make better decisions.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This doesn't tell us anything about cash flow statements, so it does nothing to support the idea that they're critical for all businesses.

questiontext:
Essayist: Many people are hypocritical in that they often pretend to be more morally upright than they really are. When hypocrisy is exposed, hypocrites are embarrassed by their moral lapse, which motivates them and others to try to become better people. On the other hand, when hypocrisy persists without exposure, the belief that most people are good is fostered, which motivates most people to try to be good.

The essayist's statements, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
gf:
Statements

Many people say they're more morally upright than they are.

Conditionals (When = sufficient indicator)

 Hypocrisy  →  embarrassed  → motivates ppl
  exposed        by moral lapse      to be better

   Hypocrisy  →  Fosters belief  → motivates ppl
 not exposed     most ppl good       to be good

Evaluate

We're given binary triggers: "If hypocrisy is exposed, X happens. If it's not exposed, Y happens." When you have a set of binary triggers, you're guaranteed that one or the other will be triggered.

So if there's any common denominator to the right sides, then we can infer that "In Either Case, Z will happen."

Is there a common denominator to these two right sides? Yes, they both end in people being motivated to become better people / to try to be good.

Goal

Let's look for something like "when people are hypocritical, it leads to ppl being motivated to try to be better (whether or not that hypocrisy is exposed)".

answers.text: The existence of hypocrisy encourages people to believe that no one is morally blameless.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: the existence of

We could possibly say that the exposure of hypocrisy leads people to see that we all will have moral lapses.

But when hypocrisy is not exposed, it fosters the belief that most people are good. We don't have any support for the idea that unexposed hypocrisy leads people to think "everyone has some moral faults". 

Thus, it's too strong to say that the mere existence of hypocrisy encourages people to think that none of us are morally perfect.

answers.text: The existence of hypocrisy encourages people to make efforts to live by moral standards.
answers.fb:
Correct

Whether hypocrisy is exposed or not, it leads to motivation (i.e. encouragement) to be better / to try to be good (i.e. to live by moral standards).

We had binary triggers, so we know that one or the other will always be triggered, and their common denominator was motivating people to be better.

 Hypocrisy  →  embarrassed  → motivates ppl
  exposed        by moral lapse      to be better

   Hypocrisy  →  Fosters belief  → motivates ppl
 not exposed     most ppl good       to be good

answers.text: The existence of hypocrisy in some people encourages others to fall into moral lapses.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: encourages lapses

The only motivation / encouragement we talk about in the passage is encouraging people to be better people / to try to be good.

answers.text: The hiding of hypocrisy is a better way of motivating people to try to be good than is the exposing of it.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: better way

We have no way to rank which of these trigger ideas is the better one. Both of them lead to motivating people to do better. That's all we know.

answers.text: There is no stronger motivator for people to try to be good than the exposing of hypocrisy.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: no stronger motivator

We have no way to rank which of these trigger ideas is the stronger motivator one. Both of them lead to motivating people to do better. That's all we know.

questiontext:
Although fiber-optic telephone cable is more expensive to manufacture than copper telephone cable, a telephone network using fiber-optic cable is less expensive overall than a telephone network using copper cable. This is because copper cable requires frequent amplification of complex electrical signals to carry them for long distances, whereas the pulses of light that are transmitted along fiber-optic cable can travel much farther before amplification is needed.

The above statements, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
gf:
Statements

pivot / math-y (although, >, <)

         MANUFACTURING
   Fiber-optic  >  copper
                         $

OVERALL COST OF NETWORK
   Fiber-optic  <  copper
                         $

causal (this is because)

Fiber optic is cheaper than copper, to run your network on, because cooper requires frequent amplification, whereas fiber optic can go for a while without needing amplification.

Evaluate

We can tell from the mathematical comparison in the first sentence that other aspects of running a fiber-optic network outweigh the extra cost you pay to manufacture the fiber-optic cable, since a fiber-optic network is cheaper overall than a copper network. Then the second sentence tells us, "Let me tell you why a fiber-optic network comes out to be cheaper, despite the higher upfront cost to make the cable."

When we see Causal Connector Language like "X is true. This is because Y is true", there is a very strong likelihood that the correct answer wants to test us on whether we understand this causal connection.

The order of these statements is "Effect. This is because Cause". So we want to restate this relationship in our more intuitive ordering of Cause leads to Effect.

The fact that copper requires frequent amplification leads to copper being a more expensive cable to run a network off of, despite the fact that copper is cheaper to manufacture than is fiber optic cable.

Goal

Let's look for a safely worded answer that potentially reinforces this idea that "needing to frequently amplify the signal makes a copper network cost more than a fiber-optic one, despite the fact that copper cable is cheaper to produce."

answers.text: The material from which fiber-optic cable is manufactured is more expensive than the copper from which copper cable is made.
answers.fb:
Too Speculative

This answer is attempting to explain why fiber-optic is more expensive to manufacture than is copper.

But it might have nothing to do with more expensive materials. Maybe it's a more laborious manufacturing process so it's pricier because it takes longer to make.

We shouldn't be speculating the backstory of the facts we're reading. We want to find an answer that's more or less provably true based on the facts we do possess.

answers.text: The increase in the number of transmissions of complex signals through telephone cables is straining those telephone networks that still use copper cable.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: # of transmissions

We don't have any information about any current increase in the number of transmissions, nor do we get any sense that any network is straining.

answers.text: Fiber-optic cable can carry many more signals simultaneously than copper cable can.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: carry more signals

Nothing in the passage gets into comparing how many signals each type of network can carry at any given time.

answers.text: Signals transmitted through fiber-optic cable travel at the same speed as signals transmitted through copper cable.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: speed of transmission
Too Strong: same

The passage never compared the speed at which signals travel, so we have no way to derive the extreme claim that both signals travel as the same speed.

answers.text: The cost associated with frequent amplification of signals traveling through copper cable exceeds the extra manufacturing cost of fiber-optic cable.
answers.fb:
Correct

We were told that copper is cheaper than fiber-optic to produce, but a network based on copper cable is more expensive overall, because on the copper network you have to frequently amplify the signal.

So that implies that the extra money you have to spend on amplification outweighs the money you saved on the cheaper cable.

questiontext:
Dr. Theresa Pagano, a biologist, has found that the checkerspot butterfly is becoming more prevalent in regions farther north than before and less prevalent in regions farther south. The northward shift of the butterflies is almost perfectly correlated with the northward shift of the warm zones in the global climate, and Dr. Pagano has therefore concluded that the changing climate is responsible for the northward movement of the butterflies.

Each of the following, if true, supports Dr. Pagano's reasoning EXCEPT:
gf:
Conclusion (therefore concluded)

The Checker Spot Butterfly is moving north due to changing climate conditions, specifically the northward shift of warm zones.

Evidence

Checker Spot Butterflies have become more prevalent in northern regions and less so in southern regions.

Evaluate

We have a causal conclusion ("responsible") and an curious comparison in the evidence ("more prevalent").

CURIOUS FACT: how come this butterfly is more prevalent in the north and less in the south?

EXPLANATION: the northern areas have warmed from climate change, and that warmth brought the butterfly there.

Goal

Get rid of the four answers that strengthen. Strengthening answers will either rule out alternate explanations for why the butterfly is found more in the north / less in the south, or they will corroborate the hypothesis that it's because of the climate shift.

answers.text: Checkerspot butterfly colonies observed under laboratory conditions are critically affected by small temperature changes.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This states that in lab conditions, butterfly colonies are critically affected by small temperature changes, heightening the plausibility that climate-induced temperature shifts impact their movement.

answers.text: Climate does not affect checkerspot butterflies themselves directly, but the plants they depend on thrive best in warm climates.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This makes the author's hypothesis more plausible. While climate change doesn't directly affect the butterflies, it influences their food sources, which thrive in warm climates. It indirectly supports the hypothesis by linking climate change to butterfly movement through their dependency on plants.

answers.text: Experimental evidence suggests that the checkerspot butterfly can adapt easily to a wide range of temperatures and geographic conditions.
answers.fb:
Correct

This suggests that the Checker Spot Butterfly can adapt easily to various temperatures and conditions, which does nothing to strengthen, and may even undermine the idea that a warming shift would make enough different to influence the butterfly's habitat.

answers.text: In recent years, abnormally low average temperatures have been correlated with a reduced checkerspot butterfly population.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This provides data showing fewer butterflies in lower temperatures, backing the idea that higher temperatures are favorable, and supporting the causal link between climate change and their movement.

Since the author thinks warmer temps in the north led to more butterflies, this is the classic "no cause / no effect" strengthener, where an absence of warmth goes hand in hand with an absence of butterflies.

answers.text: Several studies have shown that several other species of butterfly closely related to the checkerspot butterfly survive only in warm climates.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This boosts the plausibility of the author's hypothesis, noting that closely related butterfly species only survive in warm climates, offering analogous reasoning to support the idea that checkerspot Butterflies might similarly require warm climates.

questiontext:
Everyone likes repertory theater. Actors like it because playing different roles each night decreases their level of boredom. Stagehands like it because changing sets every night means more overtime and, thus, higher pay. Theater managers like it because, if plays that reflect audience demand are chosen for production, most performances generate large revenues. It is evident, therefore, that more theaters should change to repertory.

The argument above would be strengthened if which one of the following were true?
gf:
Conclusion (evident therefore)

More theaters should switch to repertory theater.

Evidence

Repertory theater generates large revenues if the selected plays reflect audience demand. Additionally, actors, stagehands, and theater managers all like repertory theater for various reasons.

Evaluate

Since this is a Recommendation, the author is assuming that for the theaters that aren't already repertory, the upsides of becoming repertory would outweigh the downsides.

Maybe actors / stagehands / theater managers like it better, but it's way less profitable than other forms of theater. Maybe the audiences don't like it as much. The evidence offered an Untriggered Conditional:  if you choose the right shows, then they usually generate lots of revenue. But do repertory theaters usually choose the right shows? 

Goal

Find an answer that helps argue in favor of repertory theater or undermines one of the objections we considered.

answers.text: In a repertory theater, a large capital outlay is required at the beginning of each season.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This highlights that switching requires a large capital outlay, suggesting a financial risk, which does not support the argument for switching to repertory.

answers.text: In a repertory theater, patrons need to pay overly close attention to the schedule in order to make their theater plans.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This states that patrons need to pay close attention to schedules, suggesting inconvenience, which is a disadvantage, thus not strengthening the recommendation.

answers.text: In a repertory theater, storage space for sets for more than one production must be available.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This indicates a need for ample storage space for sets, highlighting logistical challenges that theaters might face, not supporting the switch to repertory.

answers.text: In a repertory theater, plays can be rescheduled to meet audience demand.
answers.fb:
Correct

This suggests that repertory plays can be rescheduled to meet audience demand. Although weakly worded, this slight flexibility is a benefit that supports the argument for switching to repertory, contrasting with the negative implications of other options.

answers.text: In a repertory theater, some actors who change roles from night to night find it difficult to master all of the roles they play.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This notes that changing roles from night to night is difficult for some actors, suggesting a potential downside to repertory theater that doesn't support the argument.

questiontext:
Researcher: All defects in short-term memory are caused by a malfunction of a part of the brain called the hippocampus. In short-term memory, the mind holds a piece of information for only a few moments, after which it is either stored in long-term memory or forgotten. Learning is the accumulation of new information in long-term memory. Thus, whenever a child exhibits a learning deficit, the hippocampus is malfunctioning.

The reasoning in the researcher's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that this argument
gf:
Conclusion (thus)

If a kid has a learning deficit, the hippocampus is messed up.

Evidence

Learning is the process of acquiring new info in long-term memory.

New information is held in short-term memory for a few secs, and then either moved into long-term or forgotten.

If there's a short-term memory defect, the hippocampus is messed up.

Evaluation

The evidence seems to prove that a messed up hippocampus could lead to a learning deficit, since we know that short-term memory is crucial to learning (by transferring info into long term memory, which is what we mean by 'learning') and we know that when the short-term memory is messed up, it's because of the hippocampus.

But just because the hippocampus could be involved in a causal story leading up to a learning deficit, it's not clear why the author thinks he can say that all learning deficits trace back to problems with the hippocampus.

Goal

This has the fuzzy vibe of Necessary vs. Sufficient, since the author has provided us info to give us a causal chain moving one way:
bad hippo → bad short-term → no long term → can't learn

But he's trying to go the other way:
can't learn → bad hippo

We need to point out this flaw or point out what it ignores: there could be other possible causes of learning deficits besides a bad hippocampus leading to messed up short term memory.

answers.text: draws a general conclusion based on too small a sample of learning deficits
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

Does the author draw a general conclusion?  Yes, "Whenever a child has a learning deficit ...".

Is the author's evidence a limited sampling of learning deficits? No, it's a discussion about short term memory and the hippocampus.

answers.text: presumes, without giving justification, that all learning deficits in children involve short-term memory
answers.fb:
Correct

Conditionally, this answer looks like, 
"If learning deficit → bad short term memory"

Does it feel fair to say the author's argument is making that move? Yes, since the conclusion says, 
"if learning deficit → bad hippocampus", and we know from the author's evidence that, 
"bad short term memory → bad hippocampus".

If we combine the author's assumption with her evidence, we see where she derived her conclusion. 
"learning deficit → bad short → bad hippo"

Pushing back against this assumption is the same as making our objection, "Couldn't there be other sources of a learning deficit besides this one short term memory / hippocampus story you're telling?"

answers.text: presumes, without giving justification, that short-term memory is disabled whenever the hippocampus is disabled
answers.fb:
Backwards Logic

The author said 
"defective short term  →  defective hippo"

and this answer accuses him of thinking,
"defective hippo  →  defective short term"

answers.text: fails to quantify precisely the length of time during which the mind holds a piece of information in short-term memory
answers.fb:
Never a Flaw

This is a reasoning test, not a science or math test. We never need precise times, weights, measurements. We don't even need precise definitions of terms, as long as they given us some definition of terms.

answers.text: takes for granted that learning deficits in adults have a cause unrelated to the cause of learning deficits in children
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: adults vs. kids

The conclusion is just about kids. We don't care in analyzing this argument what's going on with adults.

questiontext:
New evidence suggests that the collapse of Egypt’s old kingdom some 4,000 years ago was caused by environmental catastrophe rather than internal social upheaval. Ocean sediments reveal a period of global cooling at the time, a condition generally associated with extended droughts. There were, no doubt, serious social problems in Egypt at the time, but they resulted from a severe dry spell.

Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

The collapse of Egypt's Old Kingdom was caused by an environmental catastrophe rather than internal social upheaval.

Evidence

Ocean sediments reveal a period of global cooling at the time, a condition generally associated with extended droughts. The author acknowledges that while there were serious social problems in Egypt at the time, they resulted from a severe dry spell.

Evaluate

Since we have a causal conclusion, we can use our Explain Curious Fact template.

CURIOUS FACT: what caused the collapse of Egypt's Old Kingdom?

EXPLANATION: an environmental catastrophe (specifically a long drought) caused the collapse.

Goal

To strengthen the argument, we want to rule out an Alternate Explanation for the collapse (such as social issues) or boost the plausibility of the author's explanation that it was related to environmental reasons such as drought.

answers.text: Historically, most civilizations have succumbed to internal strife rather than external factors.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This states that most civilizations collapse due to internal strife rather than external factors, which undermines the argument's conclusion that environmental factors caused the collapse.

answers.text: The social problems in Egypt’s old kingdom at the time of its collapse were serious enough to have caused the collapse.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This claims that Egypt's social problems were severe enough to cause the collapse, supporting the idea of internal upheaval rather than environmental causes as the main driver.

answers.text: At the time of the collapse of the old kingdom, several isolated but well-established civilizations near Egypt underwent sudden declines.
answers.fb:
Correct

This suggests that nearby isolated civilizations underwent sudden declines at the same time as Egypt's collapse, implying a broader regional issue like environmental catastrophe, rather than localized social problems, reinforcing the author's argument about environmental causes.

answers.text: Egyptian records recovered from the time of the collapse explicitly refer to the deteriorating conditions of the society.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This mentions that Egyptian records explicitly referred to deteriorating societal conditions, adding weight to the idea that social problems were significant during the collapse.

answers.text: Shortly after the collapse of the old kingdom, Egypt was thrust into a civil war that lasted most of the next two centuries.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This tells us that a civil war occurred shortly after the collapse, hinting that social strife was significant, aligning with internal causes rather than the external environmental factors.

questiontext:
Analyst: A recent survey showed that although professors of biology who teach but do not pursue research made up one twentieth of all science professors, they were appointed to fewer than one twentieth of all the scientific administrative positions in universities. We can conclude from this survey that failing to pursue research tends to bias university administrators against appointing these professors to scientific administrative positions.

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the support for the analyst's conclusion?
gf:
Conclusion

University administrators tends to be biased against appointing professors to scientific administrative positions, if those professors have failed to pursue research.

Evidence

In a survey, it was found that bio professors who haven't pursued research are disproportionately underrepresented among all scientific administrative positions in universities.

They're 1/20 of all science professors, but they fill
less than 1/20 of sci admin positions.

Evaluate

Disproportionate representation is one of those asymmetric Comparisons we refer to as a Curious Fact. The author's conclusion offers an Explanation.

Curious Fact ... why are bio professors who don't pursue research underrepresented in scientific admin positions?

Author's Explanation ... it's cuz they haven't pursued research. The people at the university who decide on whom to appoint to this scientific admin positions are biased against professors who haven't pursued research.

Goal

Since this is Weaken, we're expecting a correct answer to 

1. Suggest an Alternate Explanation for why these research-less bio professors are under-appointed to scientific admin positions
      or
2. Undermine the plausibility of the Author's Explanation, making it seem like university higher-ups are not biased against professors who haven't pursued research.

answers.text: In universities there are fewer scientific administrative positions than there are nonscientific administrative positions.
answers.fb:
No Impact: nonscientific admin positions

A possible Alternate Explanation for why these research-less bio professors are under-appointed to scientific admin positions could be that there just aren't a lot of admin positions available for biology professors. 

This answer almost feels like it's giving us this alternate explanation, but it's not saying that the number of admin positions is so low that there just aren't enough available spots for bio professors who haven't pursued research to reach that 1/20 proportion.

Instead, it's just saying there are fewer spots than nonscientific admin positions. We know nothing about how many nonscientific positions there are, so this comparison is meaningless to us.

answers.text: Biologists who do research fill a disproportionately low number of scientific administrative positions in universities.
answers.fb:
Correct

This badly undermines the author's explanation that "failing to pursue research" is the reason for the disproportionately low proportion of those bio professors. After all, the ones who have pursued research are also disproportionately underrepresented. 

If failing to pursue research were really the Causal Difference-Maker, then we'd see a difference between the bio professors who have and who haven't pursued research.

This doesn't point us to any other specific Alternate Explanation, but it strongly suggests there must be some other explanation for the underrepresentation (maybe the bias from the university faculty is really against biology professors, whether or not they've pursued research).

answers.text: Biology professors get more than one twentieth of all the science grant money available.
answers.fb:
No Impact: science grant money
Unclear Impact: Biology professors

We're only analyzing whether there's a bias involved in appointing these professors to scientific admin positions. We're not really going to care whether there's disproportionality when it comes to science grant money. Too separate an issue.

Also, this answer is talking about all biology professors. We know that bio professors who don't do research make up 1/20, but we know what fraction of science professors are biology professors.

If bio professors who don't do research are 1/20, then when we add in all the bio professors who do do research, we know that bio professors collectively make up more than 1/20 of science professors.

How much more? We have no idea, so we can't judge whether this answer is even telling us that the proportion for getting grant money is higher / lower / same.

answers.text: Conducting biological research tends to take significantly more time than does teaching biology.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This answer might help explain why some professors are unable or unwilling to embark on research on top of their teaching schedules.

But it has nothing to do with offering an alternate explanation for why non-researching bio professors are disproportionately underrepresented in scientific admin, or with hurting the story that university bigwigs are biased against appointing non-researching professors.

answers.text: Biologists who hold scientific administrative positions in the university tend to hold those positions for a shorter time than do other science professors.
answers.fb:
Strengthens, probably

This has no chance of having more impact than the correct answer, but if we learned that non-researching bio professors have much longer tenures on the admin board than other professors did, we might say, "Oh, author, if the university bigwigs are so biased against these non-researching bio professors, then how come those professors serve on the admin board longer than others do?"

But this answer goes the other direction. 

It doesn't technically differentiate between non-researching bio professors and researching bio professors, so the answer has Unclear Impact, but since it's going in the wrong direction, it's not tempting.

questiontext:
While 65 percent of the eligible voters who were recently polled favor Perkins over Samuels in the coming election, the results of that poll are dubious because it was not based on a representative sample. Given that Perkins predominantly advocates the interests of the upper-middle class and that the survey was conducted at high-priced shopping malls, it is quite probable that Perkins’s supporters were overrepresented.

Which one of the following statements most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

The results of that poll are dubious

Intermediate Conclusion (because)

The poll was not based on a representative sample.

Intermediate Conclusion

It's quite likely that Perkin's supporters were overrepresented.

Evidence (given that / and)

The poll was conducted at high-priced shopping malls. Perkins advocates for the upper-middle class.

Evaluate

The #1 pattern on Main Conclusion is that the conclusion is some Pivot/Rebuttal claim. The #2 pattern is that the conclusion is in the first sentence. This argument essentially combines those patterns, by putting a rebuttal claim "the results are dubious" in the first sentence. 

When we hear an opinion from the author in the first sentence, we want to guess that it's the conclusion and listen for whether the author seems to be supporting/defending that claim.

Given that X, it is probable that Y is a structure that indicates that X is a premise that supports the conclusion Y. So they are tempting us to pick the last claim of the paragraph, and making it even more tempting because it is *a*, conclusion, just not the main one.

Goal

Find the best available meaning match for "The results of the poll are dubious".

answers.text: The poll was intentionally designed to favor Perkins over Samuels.
answers.fb:
Too Strong / Unrelated to Goal

This answer implies intentional design to favor Perkins, a claim not made in the argument. The conclusion is about the results of the poll, whereas this answer doesn't address the results of the poll. And the argument questions the poll's accuracy due to the sampling methodology, not deliberate bias.

answers.text: Samuels’s supporters believe that they were probably not adequately represented in the poll.
answers.fb:
Opposing Idea / Unrelated to Goal

This answer presumes to speak for Samuels's supporters, which the argument does not do. The argument focuses on questioning the poll's accuracy due to its sampling method, not on what Samuels's supporters might think.

answers.text: The poll’s results probably do not accurately represent the opinions of the voters in the coming election.
answers.fb:
Correct

This accurately captures the main conclusion about the poll's legitimacy. If we're saying that the result of a poll are dubious, we're saying "we can't trust that what the poll says is an accurate reflection of reality".

answers.text: Samuels is quite likely to have a good chance of winning the coming election.
answers.fb:
Inference-Bait / Unrelated to Goal

This tries to go one step farther than the conclusion: "If the author thinks the poll that favors Perkins had dubious results, she must think that Perkins isn't actually favored to win the election, so Samuels must be." We're not being asked to figure out what the author might say "next". We need to just match the actual conclusion: "the poll results are dubious". This answer isn't about poll results, so it can't be a match.

answers.text: Those who designed the poll should have considered more carefully where to conduct the survey.
answers.fb:
Unstated / Inference-Bait

This doesn't look anything like "the poll results are dubious". Since it's not a claim about the poll results, it can't match our conclusion. This is designed to read the author's mind and say something else she'd probably believe. Since she believes the poll was not representative based on where it was conducted, she might presumably say that "the pollsters should have thought more about conducting this in a place that didn't skew towards Perkins". Main Conclusion isn't about invisible ideas. It's about matching the visible conclusion.

questiontext:
Trustee: The recent exhibit at the art museum was extensively covered by the local media, and this coverage seems to have contributed to the record-breaking attendance it drew. If the attendance at the exhibit had been low, the museum would have gone bankrupt and closed permanently, so the museum could not have remained open had it not been for the coverage from the local media.

The reasoning in the trustee's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
gf:
Conclusion (so)

The museum could not have remained open had it not been for the coverage from the local media.

Evidence

The museum could not have remained open if the attendance at the exhibit had been low, and the coverage from the local media contributed to the record-breaking attendance.

Evaluate

To argue against this conclusion, we're trying to think about how we can make the case that "even if there hadn't been local media coverage, the museum could have remained open".

We have a logic rule we have to deal with -- it couldn't have remained open if the attendance at the exhibit had been low. So we'll need to argue that "even without local media coverage, the attendance at the exhibit wouldn't have been low". 

We know that the media coverage contributed to record-breaking attendance, but without media coverage would attendance have still been pretty strong?

Remember, we don't need there to be record-breaking attendance. All we need to make our case is the possibility that attendance would "not have been low".

Formally, the conclusion is trying to argue this: 
Without ---------------------------------> museum 
 media                                                    closes 

The evidence presented is this: 
Without --> less                   low --------> museum 
 media       attendance      attendance       closes 
 

The missing link is whether "having less attendance, without the media coverage, would mean that the exhibit had low attendance".

Goal

The author never established that the local media coverage was necessary to avoid having low attendance. She's assuming that "If X helped this event have record-breaking attendance, then X prevented the event from having low attendance".

answers.text: confuses a necessary condition for the museum’s remaining open with a sufficient condition for the museum’s remaining open
answers.fb:
Not Necessary vs. Sufficient

This is a tempting answer in the sense that this is the #1 Famous Flaw, and there is conditional logic in this argument, but the author didn't perform an illegal reversal or negation (which is what this answer is saying).

Rather, the author equated "less attendance" with "low attendance".

An argument committing this answer choice's flaw would sound like, "In order for the museum to stay open, it can't have low attendance at the exhibit. They didn't have low attendance at the exhibit. Thus, the museum will stay open."

answers.text: takes for granted that no previous exhibit at the museum had received such extensive media coverage
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: previous exhibits

When an answer begins takes for granted / presumes / fails to establish, we can ask ourselves whether the argument needed to assume the idea that follows.

Was this author assuming that this event had more media coverage than any previous exhibit ever?

Of course not. She didn't commit to any extreme idea like that. She said it was extensively covered by local media, not that it was more extensively covered than ever before.

answers.text: takes for granted that most people who read articles about the exhibit also attended the exhibit
answers.fb:
Not Assumed: most

The word "most" is wrong on Necessary Assumption 99% of the time we see it. Did this author need it to be true that at least 51% of people who read an article about the exhibit came to see it?

Would her argument be weakened if it were only 49% of people who read the article and later saw the exhibit?

No her argument wouldn't be impacted, so she doesn't need to assume this idea.

answers.text: fails to address the possibility that the exhibit would have drawn enough visitors to prevent bankruptcy even without media coverage
answers.fb:
Correct

When an answer begins fails to consider / overlooks the possibility, we can ask ourselves whether the argument would be weakened if that idea were true.

Can we hurt this argument by saying, "Hey, author -- even without the media coverage, the exhibit still would have drawn enough visitors to present bankruptcy"?

Sure! That allows us to argue against her conclusion. "You're wrong author, the museum could have remained open, even if there hadn't been coverage from the local media."

This objection speaks to the gap between "less attendance" and "low attendance". It's possible that there was less attendance, but still enough attendance to avoid bankruptcy.

answers.text: presupposes the very conclusion that it is trying to prove
answers.fb:
Not Circular

This answer describes one of the 10 Famous Flaws, Circular Reasoning, in which a premise restates the conclusion or requires the conclusion to be true.

These answers are almost always wrong. No premise in this argument restated or required the idea that "the museum would have closed without coverage from the local media".

questiontext:
Therapist: In a recent study, researchers measured how quickly 60 different psychological problems waned as a large, diverse sample of people underwent weekly behavioral therapy sessions. About 75 percent of the 60 problems consistently cleared up within 50 weeks of therapy. This shows that 50 weekly behavioral therapy sessions are all that most people need.

The therapist's argument is logically most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
gf:
Conclusion (This shows that)

50 weekly behavioral therapy sessions are all that most people need.

Evidence (study)

In a study of 60 different psychological problems, 75% of them consistently cleared up within 50 weeks of behavioral therapy.

Evaluate

Given that ... within this study, most problems cleared up with 50 weeks (75%),

How could we still argue that ... most people would need more than 50 weekly behavioral sessions? 

Actually, we have several options:

- maybe the study is messed up for some reason. We know that it's a "large and diverse sample", though, so it is unlikely that the sample is too unrepresentative. 

- maybe there's a different way to explain the results. We know that within 50 weeks, 75% of problems cleared up, but do we know they cleared up because of the therapy sessions? Maybe these people were also trying other new things during these 50 weeks (more exercise, better diet, meditation) and those are really responsible for the improvement.

- maybe it was the therapy that cleared up the problems, but we can still argue that 50 sessions are not all that most people need. Perhaps 50 sessions is enough to "clear up" the problem, but it will recur soon thereafter if we stop regularly having sessions. Perhaps "most people" suffer from a problem that wasn't tested by the study. 

Goal

There are lots of different options for attacking an argument that has Sampling concerns, Causal reasoning concerns, and a term shift from "50 weeks was all that was needed for most problems" to "50 weeks is all that is needed for most people".

We'll have to judge each answer to see if passes our two part checklist:  
1. Is it descriptively true?  
2. if so, does this sound like a logical complaint?

answers.text: takes for granted that there are no psychological problems that usually take significantly longer to clear up than the 60 psychological problems studied
answers.fb:
Too Strong: no

Since this begins with takes for granted, we can ask ourselves whether the argument needed to assume this claim. 

The author needs to assume that "there are no problems that usually take longer to clear up than the 60 studied and which afflict most people". 

But without that tag, it's too strong. If we negate this assumption and say, "Hey, author -- there is at least one psychological problem that takes longer than any of the problems in the study", it wouldn't weaken the argument.

The author can say, "Cool, yeah, I realize that. I didn't say 50 weeks would be enough for everyone just for most people. I admit, 50 weeks won't be enough for people who have that problem, but that's not most people." Until we say that most people have a sort of problem that takes longer than the 60 studied, it doesn't become much of an objection.

answers.text: fails to address the possibility that any given one of the 60 psychological problems studied might afflict most people
answers.fb:
Correct

Since this starts with fails to consider, we'll ask ourselves if the idea that follows would be an Objection.

Can we hurt the argument by saying that "any one of the 60 studied problems could afflict most people"? Could that give us a way to argue that, "50 weeks would not be enough for most people"?

Yes! 75% is 3/4, so of the 60 problems studied, 45 of them were cleared up.

But what if most people are afflicted with one of the 15 problems that didn't clear up? What if the ones that didn't clear up in 50 weeks are some of the most common ones, like depression and anxiety?

The author was assuming that because most problems cleared up, that would take care of most people. But if the problems that didn't clear up in the 50 weeks are the most common psychological problems, then we have a way to say that "most people would need more than 50 weeks".

answers.text: takes for granted that no one suffers from more than one of the 60 psychological problems studied
answers.fb:
Too Strong: no one

Since this begins with takes for granted, we can ask ourselves whether the argument needed to assume this claim. 

If we negate this assumption and say, "Hey, author — there is at least one person who suffers from more than one of these problems", it wouldn't weaken the argument.

The author can say, "Cool, yeah, I that's fine. I didn't say 50 weeks would be enough for everyone just for most people. I admit, 50 weeks won't be enough for people who have a multitude of problems, but that's not most people." Until we say that most people have more than one problem, it doesn't become much of an objection.

answers.text: fails to address the possibility that some forms of therapy have never been proven to be effective as treatments for psychological problems
answers.fb:
Not an Objection

Since this starts with fails to consider, we'll ask ourselves if the idea that follows would be an Objection.

Can we hurt the argument by saying that "there are some forms of therapy that have never been proven effective for psychological problems?" 

Of course not. They are totally irrelevant to the author's argument, which is specifically about behavioral sessions, which have been plausibly shown to be effective against 75% of the psychological problems in this study.

answers.text: takes for granted that the sample of people studied did not have significantly more psychological problems, on average, than the population as a whole
answers.fb:
Not Necessary

Since this begins with takes for granted, we can ask ourselves whether the argument needed to assume this claim. 

If we negate this assumption and say, "Hey, author -- the people studied did have way more psychological problems, on average, then the general population", would that weaken?

No, not quite. It actually strengthens.

The author could say, "I know, right? The people in this study were way more addled by problems than are most people, and even for them 50 weeks was all that was needed! So you know that 50 weeks would be enough for most people."

The author needs to assume an inverse of this: "the sample of people studied did not have significantly fewer problems, on average, than the overall population". If you negate that assumption, you get an objection. 

We might be thinking, "Yes, but isn't the author just in general assuming that this sample is representative?" No, not necessarily. If the sample is representative that strengthens the argument, but it's not necessary, as the negation test just revealed. If a drug were shown to be effective on the worst headaches, then you would assume that it will help most people with headaches. Proving yourself against tougher competition shows you're ready for ordinary competition.

questiontext:
With decreased production this year in many rice-growing countries, prices of the grain on world markets have increased. Analysts blame this increase on the fact that only a small percentage of world production is sold commercially, with government growers controlling most of the rest, distributing it for local consumption. With so little rice being traded freely, even slight changes in production can significantly affect the amount of rice available on world markets.

Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the analysts' explanation of the price increase?
gf:
Curious Fact

Why is the price of rice on world markets higher?

Author's Explanation

Most of the world's rice production isn't sold on world markets. Most of it is controlled by governments, who distribute it for local consumption. 

Since the open market for rice has a relatively small supply, the decrease in rice production can have a significant affect on rice available to world markets.

Evaluate

We weaken causal explanations in one of two ways: 
     - Point to some other way to explain the curious fact 
                                             or 
         - Undermine the plausibility of the author's way

Goal

        Look for an answer that provides 
      some other way to explain why the 
    price of rice on world markets is higher. 
                                 or 
   Undermine the story that these decreases  
     in production have significantly affected  
the amount of rice available on world markets.

answers.text: Rice-importing countries reduce purchases of rice when the price increases dramatically.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This tells us an Effect of the more-costly rice situation, but we're looking to investigate the Cause of the more-costly rice situation.

answers.text: In times of decreased rice production, governments store more of the rice they control and reduce their local distribution of rice.
answers.fb:
Opposite / Irrelevant

This helps the author to argue that there is a shortage of rice supply, in a sense, since governments are now hoarding their rice and not even distributing it.

More to the point, though, it's kind of irrelevant to the author's hypothesis, since the rice that the government controls is a separate pile from the rice on the world market, and the author's hypothesis is about how much rice is available on the world market. This answer doesn't tell us anything that seems to impact how much rice is available on the world market. It just tells us about how the government does something different with its private rice stash.

answers.text: In times of decreased rice production, governments export some of the rice originally intended for local distribution to countries with free grain markets.
answers.fb:
Correct

This hurts the plausibility of the author's causal storyline. She was saying that there would be a shortage on the world market in times of decreased rice production, but this answer is saying, "Actually, no ... in times of decreased rice production, the governments that have a private stash actually funnel some of their price into the world market (filling in the shortage)."

In order for a shortage of rice on world markets to cause a price increase, there needs to be a shortage of rice! This answer calls that assumption into question.

answers.text: Governments that distribute the rice crop for local consumption purchase the grain commercially in the event of production shortfalls.
answers.fb:
Compatible

The two things that drive prices up are less supply and more demand. This answer is tricky, because it kind of sounds like it's giving an alternate explanation for why the price of rice went up:  more demand. 

When rice production is decreased, governments start buying rice from world markets, so it sounds like there is a new buyer on the scene, and thus that higher demand might raise prices.

The problem with picking this is that it's not really offering an alternate explanation so much as adding onto the existing one. Since we know that the global production of rice goes partly to world market (small %) and the rest to governments that control and distribute rice (large %), it's an open question about what happens when there is less rice production than normal.

Does the world market get its normal amount, and the government portion is reduced. Do the governments get their normal amount and the world market is reduced. Or is it that the world market and the government portion are both reduced in similar proportion? 

It seems like our author's explanation is compatible with the 2nd or 3rd scenario, and this answer seems like it could be the 3rd scenario. Meanwhile, the correct answer brings us closer to the 1st scenario, where we are thinking that the world market actually gets its normal amount.

answers.text: During reduced rice harvests, rice-importing countries import other kinds of crops, although this fails to compensate for decreased rice imports.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: other crops

Whether or not countries import other crops during rice shortages has very little, if anything, to do with why the price of rice went up.

questiontext:
Sharon, a noted collector of fine glass, found a rare glass vase in a secondhand store in a small town she was visiting. The vase was priced at $10, but Sharon knew that it was worth at least $1,000. Saying nothing to the storekeeper about the value of the vase, Sharon bought the vase for $10. Weeks later the storekeeper read a newspaper article about Sharon’s collection, which mentioned the vase and how she had acquired it. When the irate storekeeper later accused Sharon of taking advantage of him, Sharon replied that she had done nothing wrong.

Which one of the following principles, if established, most helps to justify Sharon's position?

answers.text: A seller is not obligated to inform a buyer of anything about the merchandise that the seller offers for sale except for the demanded price.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

We need an answer that helps us conclude the buyer wasn't obligated to inform the seller of the real value of the merchandise. This answer is about the seller not being obligated to inform the buyer of something.

answers.text: It is the responsibility of the seller, not the buyer, to make sure that the amount of money a buyer gives a seller in exchange for merchandise matches the amount that the seller demands for that merchandise.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

This answer shifts responsibility from the buyer to the seller, which lines up with our conclusion that the buyer isn't responsible for telling the seller how much his goods are worth. But this answer does not line up with the facts of the case. The seller charged $10 and the buyer paid $10. The dispute isn't about the amount paid not matching the amount charged. The dispute is about the amount paid not matching the actual value of the merchandise.

answers.text: A buyer’s sole obligation to a seller is to pay in full the price that the seller demands for a piece of merchandise that the buyer acquires from the seller.
answers.fb:
Correct

If the buyer's only obligation is to pay what the seller asks, which Sharon did, that absolves her of any wrongdoing that the seller is accusing her of. This answer is a little tricky because it doesn't use the same language as the judgement in the conclusion: it doesn't talk about right or wrong. But, if we have only one responsibility and we fulfill that responsibility, that implies that we held up our end of the bargain and didn't wrong the other party in the transaction.

answers.text: It is the responsibility of the buyer, not the seller, to ascertain that the quality of a piece of merchandise satisfies the buyer’s standards.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match
Out of Scope: quality

We need a principle that supports the judgment that the buyer did nothing wrong, This answer shifts responsibility from the seller to the buyer, which is the opposite of what we'd expect a right answer to do. It also focuses on ascertaining the quality of the merchandise, which is an out of scope idea.

answers.text: The obligations that follow from any social relationship between two people who are well acquainted override any obligations that follow from an economic relationship between the two.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: well acquainted

This principle is limited to people who are well acquainted. We don't have any evidence that Sharon and the seller are well acquainted, so this principle doesn't apply to them.

questiontext:
Many successful graphic designers began their careers after years of formal training, although a significant number learned their trade more informally on the job. But no designer ever became successful who ignored the wishes of a client.

If all of the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
gf:
Statements

Quantifiers (many / significant #)

Many    successful graph  =   years of formal
                 designers                training

Many    successful graph  =   learned trade
                 designers              informally on job

Quantifier / Conditional (no)

   Successful  →  Did not ignore 
    designer           wishes of a client

Evaluate

Whenever we see a conditional rule on Inference questions, we think,

1. Are there any other conditional rules that might chain together with this one?
Here, there are no other conditional claims. The other two claims are unspecific quantities like 'many' and 'a significant number'. 

2. Can I apply this conditional rule to any of the provided facts? (Might have to contrapose the conditional in order to see its relevance)

In this case, yes!  We could apply our conditional rule to the two facts we were given about "successful designers", because "successful designer" triggers our rule and tells us that they definitely "didn't ignore clients' wishes". 

We know many successful graphic designers began their careers after years of formal training, and did not ignore the wishes of their clients.

And we know that a bunch of successful graphic designers learned on the job, and did not ignore the wishes of their clients.

If we prefer thinking of this in terms of Quantifiers, this problem is basically giving us these ingredients:

 Some Formal Train <-> Successful
Some Learn on Job <-> Successful
                                       Successful --> ~ignore
We can derive
Some Formal Train ---> ~ignore
Some Learn on Job ---> ~ignore

Goal

Find a provable answer, most likely connecting "formal training + don't ignore wishes" or connecting "learned on job + don't ignore wishes".

answers.text: All graphic designers who are unsuccessful have ignored the wishes of a client.
answers.fb:
Illegal Negation

The final sentence provides this conditional:

   successful designer → do not ignore wishes

This answer illegally negates both sides:

   unsuccessful designer → do ignore wishes

answers.text: Not all formally trained graphic designers ignore clients’ wishes.
answers.fb:
Correct

We always translate from negative to positive with "not all".
    Not all A's are B = Some A's are ~B

So this answer is saying
   Some formally trained GD's do not ignore

We can definitely derive this very weak claim. We know there's at least one formally trained graphic designer who doesn't ignore their clients' wishes, because some formally trained graphic designers are successful. And no one ever became successful ignoring their clients' wishes. 

Some  FORMAL  are  successful 
           TRAINED                +
                                if successful, don't ignore
 - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - 
Some  FORMAL       don't ignore  
           TRAINED

answers.text: The more attentive a graphic designer is to a client’s wishes, the more likely the designer is to be successful.
answers.fb:
Relative vs. Absolute

We had a conditional rule that said

  if successful, then don't ignore client's wishes

That is yes/no, on/off logic, which we call Absolute language. This answer choice is switching over into Relative more/less, up/down language. 

We know that "no lawyer ever practiced law who failed the bar exam", which means, "if you're a lawyer, then you didn't fail the bar exam". 

We can't derive from that claim that, "The higher you scored on the bar exam, the more likely you are to be a lawyer".

answers.text: No graphic designers who learn their trade on the job will ignore clients’ wishes.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: no

This makes a conditional connection:

   Learned trade on job  → won't ignore wishes

But "learned trade on job" wasn't part of any conditional claim. It was just "a significant number of people who learned on the job". We don't anything that's true of "every single person who has learned their trade on the job". 

Another way to think about why this answer is wrong is that we could only derive this answer if we knew that "All graphic designers who learn their trade on the job are successful". Since we don't know that, we can't derive this answer.

answers.text: The most successful graphic designers learn their trade on the job.
answers.fb:
Relative vs. Absolute:  most

All three claims only refer to the concept of successful in absolute language. We can talk about whether or not someone is successful.

We don't have any language that lets us talk about someone being more successful than anyone else. So we can't derive anything about who is most successful.

questiontext:
If violations of any of a society’s explicit rules routinely go unpunished, then that society’s people will be left without moral guidance. Because people who lack moral guidance will act in many different ways, chaos results. Thus, a society ought never to allow any of its explicit rules to be broken with impunity.

The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
gf:
Conclusion (Thus)

A society ought never to allow any of its explicit rules to be broken with impunity.

Evidence

 violations of any         people              chaos  
  explicit rule go     →  left without  →  results  
      routinely                moral  
   unpunished              guidance

Evaluate

The author is assuming that society ought to avoid chaos, and we should probably go along with that common sense assumption. It would be an unlikely answer to say, "this is vulnerable to criticism because maybe chaos is awesome! Who says we don't want chaos?"

The contrapositive of that conditional chain would say,

"If you don't want chaos, then don't leave people without moral guidance, and so don't let any of society's explicit rules go routinely unpunished."

Isn't that what the conclusion is saying? Let's look closer.

What we said:  
don't let any explicit rule go routinely unpunished  

What the conclusion says:  
never allow any explicit rule to go unpunished

What's the difference? The contrapositive of the chain the author presented in the evidence is saying we shouldn't let a rule go routinely unpunished. The conclusion is saying we shouldn't ever let a rule go unpunished.

Consider an example -- society has an explicit rule that you're not allowed to run a red light. You're a cop and you pull someone over for running a red light. They tell you that they're having a bathroom emergency and are rushing home / or you see they have a pregnant person in the backseat about to give birth. Should you punish them for running the red light or let them go unpunished?

According to the conclusion, you should never let any rule go unpunished!

But according to the evidence, it's potentially fine to let this rule go unpunished. You can't make a habit out of letting people run red lights with impunity, otherwise they'll all start doing it and chaos will result. But we weren't told of any danger associated with occasionally letting a broken rule go unpunished.

Goal

Let's look for an answer saying that the conclusion is stronger than what's warranted by the evidence. The author would be correct to say "a society ought to avoid letting rules go routinely unpunished", but it's an unwarranted leap to say "a society ought to avoid letting rules ever go unpunished".

answers.text: takes for granted that a society will avoid chaos as long as none of its explicit rules are routinely violated with impunity
answers.fb:
Not Assumed / Illegal Negation

The author presented a conditional chain that told us,

   if explicit rules        then
    are routinely    →  chaos results
    violated with 
       impunity

This answer accuses the author of assuming that 

   if explicit rules         then
 are not routinely  →  chaos will not result
    violated with       
       impunity

That's just an illegal negation of what the author actually said. If I say, "Smoking cigarettes leads to lung cancer. So if you don't want cancer, don't smoke cigarettes", I'm not assuming that "as long as you don't smoke cigarettes, you'll never get cancer".

answers.text: fails to consider that the violated rules might have been made to prevent problems that would not arise even if the rules were removed
answers.fb:
Not an Objection to the Reasoning

Would it hurt the argument to say, "Yo, author --- some rules that get violated are stupid rules that are made to prevent imaginary problems?" 

Almost. We could say, "A society can sometimes allow one of its explicit rules to go unpunished, because some rules are stupid (they were made to prevent imaginary problems)."

However, this is just an objection to the conclusion. It's not an objection to the reasoning. It isn't commenting on how the author's move from her evidence to her conclusion is flawed.

Furthermore, the author would just respond, "It doesn't matter whether a rule is a legit one or a stupid one. If violations of any explicit rule go routinely unpunished, then we lose moral guidance, and chaos results."

answers.text: infers, from the claim that the violation of some particular rules will lead to chaos, that the violation of any rule will lead to chaos
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

When an answer is structured like, "infers, from the claim that X, that Y", then X needs to match the evidence and Y needs to match the conclusion (or the assumption that got the author to the conclusion).

Was the conclusion saying, "Violating any rule will lead to chaos"? No, not even close. The conclusion said, "Society shouldn't let any of its rules be broken with impunity".

That's enough to disqualify this answer, but we could also ask whether the evidence said, "Violating some particular rules will lead to chaos".

The evidence did not say that.

It said "routine nonpunishment of any rule will lead to chaos". It's the lack of punishment that leads to chaos, not the violation of the rule.

answers.text: confuses the routine nonpunishment of violations of a rule with sometimes not punishing violations of the rule
answers.fb:
Correct

This speaks to the gap between the valid conclusion and the one the author actually made.

The valid conclusion was, "(assuming a society wants to avoid chaos), a society ought to never allow any of its explicit rules to routinely be broken with impunity".

The actual conclusion said that rules should never be broken with impunity.

This answer is pointing out that it's potentially fine if rules are sometimes not punished. The problem outlined by the author's evidence related to what happens when rules are routinely unpunished.

When we see answers like confuses X with Y, we want to see that one of those ideas (usually the first one) matches what the evidence was talking about, whereas the other one matches what the conclusion was talking about.

The evidence was talking about whether or not a violation is routinely unpunished. The conclusion is talking about whether or not a violation should ever be unpunished.

answers.text: takes for granted that all of a society’s explicit rules result in equally serious consequences when broken
answers.fb:
Too Strong: all / equally

The argument doesn't discuss any consequences of breaking a rule. It only discusses consequences of routinely letting rule-breakers go unpunished. 

Even if the argument had discussed the consequences of breaking a rule, it would be highly unlikely that any author would commit themselves to the extreme position that "every single rule results in identically serious consequences when broken! whether you break a rule about jaywalking or a rule about murder, the consequences are equally serious!"

questiontext:
Perception cannot be a relationship between a conscious being and a material object that causes that being to have beliefs about that object. For there are many imperceptible material objects about which we have beliefs.

Which one of the following is most closely parallel in its flawed reasoning to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?
gf:
Conclusion

Perception can't be a relationship between a conscious being and a material object that causes that being to have beliefs about that object.

Evidence

We have beliefs about many imperceptible material objects. 

Evaluate

Wow! This is all-timer in terms of being intractable to read. We can make it to the correct answer with a poor-man's understanding of what going on if we can see some of the structural features and overlapping ideas.

CONC:  Term X can't be defined as something with Y and Z.
EVID:  There are many cases of Y and Z that we wouldn't call Term X.

X = perception
Y = material object
Z = beliefs about that object

In conversational terms, the conclusion is saying that "Perception is a relationship between a physical object and something with sight/smell/taste/touch/hearing. When I smell that grapefruit, I perceive it. When I touch that doorknob, I perceive it."

And the author is shooting down that definition by saying, "You can't see your car, which is parked outside your house right now, but you still have a belief about it!  So this definition of Perception fails."

The flaw is that the author is essentially doing a Necessary vs. Sufficient backwards move. The definition of Perception is saying,
IF you're perceiving, you've got a relationship between material object / belief
and the author is acting like it said
ANY TIME you have a relationship between material object / belief, you have perception

Her putative counterexample is aimed at this 2nd, incorrect, rendering of the definition. She's thinking, "What about your parked car on the street? You have beliefs about that material object, even if you're not perceiving the car right now (i.e. not looking at it)."

Goal

Look for an answer saying "You can't define X as a combo of Y and Z, because sometimes Y and Z occur but it's not X"

answers.text: Art cannot be an artifact created by someone with the express purpose of causing an aesthetic reaction in its audience. For we often have aesthetic reactions to artifacts that are not art.
answers.fb:
Correct
