Wrong Conclusion

This principle would morally oblige the seller not to deliberately mislead any prospective buyers, but the argument includes unintentionally misleading any prospective buyers

answers.text: If a home's sellers have indicated in some way that a large appliance is included with the home's purchase, then they are morally obliged not to remove that appliance after showing the home.
answers.fb:
Wrong Evidence

This principle is about what happens when the seller indicates that a large appliance is included but does not cover instances when the seller has not indicated what happens with the large appliances.

questiontext:
Politician: Those economists who claim that consumer price increases have averaged less than 3 percent over the last year are mistaken. They clearly have not shopped anywhere recently. Gasoline is up 10 percent over the last year; my auto insurance, 12 percent; newspapers, 15 percent; propane, 13 percent; bread, 50 percent.

The reasoning in the politician's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
gf:
Conclusion

Consumer price increases have not averaged less than 3% over the past year.

Evidence

Gas is up 10%. Auto insurance, 12%. Papers, 15%. Propane, 13%. Bread, 50%.

Evaluation

Well the author has definitely convinced us that some commodities have gone up by more than 3% over the past year, but the claim he's fighting is about whether consumer prices on average have gone up 3% or more.

We could potentially call this flaw a Sampling flaw, because the author's sample of goods might be highly unrepresentative in terms of average price increases.

We could also maybe call it Part vs. Whole, since the author is thinking "since these individual commodities have gone up by more than 3%, it must be that commodities overall have gone up by more than 3%".

Goal

Look for something saying, "Those are just a few items you may have cherry-picked to prove your point, author. But we're talking about averages, so maybe those dramatic upticks are offset by a lot of products that barely went up, stayed, the same, or even got cheaper."

answers.text: impugns the character of the economists rather than addressing their arguments
answers.fb:
Not Ad Hominem

The author snips a little bit, "Looks like they haven't shopped in my town", but that doesn't count as impugning their character. And the author definitely does address their argument by citing products that are counterexamples to the "less than 3% increase" claim.

answers.text: fails to show that the economists mentioned are not experts in the area of consumer prices
answers.fb:
Opposite

The author is disagreeing with these economists, so he's not under any burden to establish that they're experts. If he were relying on their testimony, agreeing with them, then we would like to know that they're experts.

answers.text: mistakenly infers that something is not true from the claim that it has not been shown to be so
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

The author does infer that something is not true: "it's not true that prices have gone up less than 3% on average", But the author presents specific examples to show that prices have gone up more than 3%. She doesn't have a premise that sounds like, "but the economists have produced insufficient evidence that prices have gone up less than 3%".

This answer describes the famous flaw Unproven vs. Proven False.

answers.text: uses evidence drawn from a small sample that may well be unrepresentative
answers.fb:
Correct

This is a small sample, since five commodities is not a lot of data points (given that there are probably thousands of commodities).

Note that the answer doesn't say that the sample is likely to be unrepresentative, because the argument didn't provide any crumbs that would incline us to think that way. But it is allowing for the possibility that these are unrepresentative.

answers.text: attempts to persuade by making an emotional appeal
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

Nothing in the evidence is an appeal to emotions. It's just a list of five products that have all gone up more than 3%.

This answer choice refers to the famous flaw Inappropriate Appeals.

questiontext:
Physics professor: Some scientists claim that superheated plasma in which electrical resistance fails is a factor in causing so-called “ball lightning. ” If this were so, then such lightning would emit intense light and, since plasma has gaslike properties, would rise in the air. However, the instances of ball lightning that I observed were of low intensity and floated horizontally before vanishing. Thus, superheated plasma with failed electrical resistance is never a factor in causing ball lightning.

The physics professor's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
gf:
Conclusion

Superheated plasma with failed electrical resistance is never a factor in causing ball lightning.

Evidence

If superheated plasma with failed electrical resistance were a factor in causing ball lightning, then that lightning would emit intense light and would rise in the air.

But the instances of ball lightning I've seen were of low intensity and floated horizontally before vanishing.

Evaluate

This stimulus is written to make our brains turn into applesauce. We need to chunk down "superheated plasma in which electrical resistance fails" into one idea, X.

We need to also recognize the rebuttal structure of the argument. Authors often refute a certain claim by saying, "If it were true, it would imply this 2nd thing. Since the 2nd thing isn't true, the original claim must not be true".

When authors say something like, "If this were true ...", we call it Implications of Logic. The right side of a conditional is the implication of the left side. Authors go on to tell us that the implication is untrue / absurd / unacceptable, in order to rule out the original trigger idea, via Contrapositive Logic, 

The argument looks like this:

Some scientists claim X is a factor in causing Y. 
If X were a factor is causing Y, then A and B would follow.
But when I saw Y, there was ~A and ~B.
Thus, X is never a factor in causing Y.

The contrapositive logic checks out. The real gap between the evidence and the conclusion is that the evidence is about "the instances of ball lightning that I observed", whereas the conclusion is about "never a factor, in any instance". 

We are logically sure that that X was not a factor in the ball lightning that the author observed (because neither of the symptoms of such an occurrence, intense light and rising in the air, were present.

But we can't be logically sure that X is never a factor in causing ball lightning, because we don't know whether the instances of ball lightning the author observed are representative of all cases of ball lightning.

Goal

We need to get from "If X (hot plasma etc.) wasn't a factor in causing the ball lightning that the professor has observed, then X is never a factor in causing it."

answers.text: Superheated plasma in which electrical resistance fails does not cause types of lightning other than ball lightning.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: other than ball lightning

This argument is only about ball lightning.

answers.text: The phenomena observed by the physics professor were each observed by at least one other person.
answers.fb:
Too Weak

This strengthens the argument somewhat, to know that the professor's accounts can be corroborated by other people.

But that doesn't "seal the deal" and guarantee the incredibly strong wording of the conclusion that "X is never a factor in causing ball lightning."

answers.text: Ball lightning can occur as the result of several different factors.
answers.fb:
Weakens

If ball lightning has lots of different origins stories, then there's no reason to think that the instances the physics professor observed show the full range of possibility.

The author is boldly saying X is never a factor, so she's really trusting that what she saw speaks for all cases. This answer makes it sound like different cases of ball lightning could be unfair to compare.

answers.text: Superheating of gaslike substances causes bright light to be emitted.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

This is pulling together language from within the premises so that we see some sort of Linking answer and consider it. 

The argument said that superheating plasma (a gaslike substance), were it to spark some ball lightning, would cause that ball lightning to emit intense light.

We already knew superheating gaslike substances can lead to bright light being emitted, so this answer is only pumping up the strength of what we already knew. But it has nothing to do with helping us know for sure that "if X wasn't a factor in the instances the professor observed, then X is never a factor in ball lightning." 

All this answer would be doing is adding more corroboration for the professor's story that the instances of ball lightning she observed are enough for us to say something would never be true about ball lightning.

answers.text: All types of ball lightning have the same cause.
answers.fb:
Correct

We know that when superheated plasma with failed electrical resistance (X) causes ball lightning, there would be intense light and rising in the air.

The instances the professor observed were not-bright light and not-rising in the air. So we know that X was not a factor in those instances of ball lightning.

This answer allows us to generalize from those instances to all instances, by giving us a powerful idea that every case of ball lightning has the same causal factor.

Thus, if X wasn't a causal factor in the instances the professor observed, then X is never a causal factor.

questiontext:
Violent crime in this town is becoming a serious problem. Compared to last year, local law enforcement agencies have responded to 17 percent more calls involving violent crimes, showing that the average citizen of this town is more likely than ever to become a victim of a violent crime.

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

The average citizen of this town is more likely than ever to become a victim of a violent crime.

Evidence

Local law enforcement agencies have responded to 17 percent more calls involving violent crimes compared to last year.

Evaluate

The author is interpreting a statistical change, so we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset. 

CURIOUS FACT: why have local law enforcement agencies responded to 17% more calls involving violent crime?

EXPLANATION:  there is more violent crime!

We can weaken by suggesting an alternative reason for the increased number of calls or undermining the assumption that more calls equate to increased crime rates.

Goal

Identify an answer choice that provides an alternate explanation for the increased call volume or hurts the plausibility of the idea that violent crime is actually on the rise.

answers.text: The town’s overall crime rate appears to have risen slightly this year compared to the same period last year.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This states that the overall crime rate has risen, which aligns with the idea that violent crime (part of overall crime) has also risen, supporting the author’s conclusion.

answers.text: In general, persons under the age of 65 are less likely to be victims of violent crimes than persons over the age of 65.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This discusses the likelihood of violent crime victimization by age group, which doesn't directly address the overall likelihood of violent crimes occurring or the reasoning behind increased call volume.

answers.text: As a result of the town’s community outreach programs, more people than ever are willing to report violent crimes to the proper authorities.
answers.fb:
Correct

This asserts that more people are willing to report violent crimes due to community outreach programs, providing an alternate explanation for the increase in call volume that does not indicate an actual increase in crime rates or risk per citizen.

LSAT loves to test the idea that "a greater awareness of a problem doesn't necessarily mean there's a higher incidence of the problem".

answers.text: In response to worries about violent crime, the town has recently opened a community center providing supervised activities for teenagers.
answers.fb:
Strengthens (if anything)

This mentions a community center providing activities, potentially aiming to reduce crime. However, it indirectly acknowledges worries about crime, which may inadvertently support the author's concern about increased incidents.

answers.text: Community officials have shown that a relatively small number of repeat offenders commit the majority of violent crimes in the town.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This notes that a small number of repeat offenders commit most violent crimes, which doesn’t directly impact the argument’s conclusion about increased call volume and citizen risk, focusing instead on criminal dynamics.

questiontext:
In a recent study, each member of two groups of people, Group A (composed of persons sixty-five to seventy-five years old) and Group B (composed of college students), was required to make a telephone call to a certain number at a specified time. The time when each call was initiated was recorded electronically. Group A proved far better at remembering to make a telephone call precisely at a specified time than did Group B. There were fourteen lapses in Group B but only one lapse in Group A. Clearly, at least one type of memory does not suffer as a person ages.

Which one of the following, if all of them are true, is LEAST helpful in establishing that the conclusion above is properly drawn?
gf:
Conclusion (clearly)

At least one type of memory does not suffer as a person ages.

Evidence

In a study, participants had to remember to make a telephone call to a certain number at a specified time. The time when the participants called was recorded electronically.

In the group of 65-75 year olds, only one person failed to make the call at the right time. In the group of college students, 14 of them failed to make the call at the right time.

Evaluate

The author is using this experiment in which all but 1 person from the 65-75 year old group remembered to make a phone call at a certain time as a way to support the idea that this "type of memory" is just as strong in these 65-75 year olds as it was when they were younger.

How could we accept that they almost all remembered to make this call but still argue that their memory for phone numbers and appointment times has gotten worse as they've aged?

Maybe when they were 50, they could have just memorized this number and call-time but nowadays, knowing that their memories are on the decline, the 65-75 year olds went to great lengths to write down reminders for themselves.

Goal

Since this is an EXCEPT question, we're looking for four answers that could strengthen, that could be helpful in establishing the conclusion.

They will either strengthen by ruling out a possible objection to the existing argument, or they will strengthen by providing more plausibility to the author's claim that memory for numbers / appointments is a type of memory that does not suffer as we age.

answers.text: There was the same number of people in each group.
answers.fb:
Strengthens - Rules Out Objection

This does almost nothing, but because the correct answer does even less.

Does it matter to the author whether the numbers in the two groups are even or uneven?

Honestly, not really. But what LSAC seemed to be thinking was, "What if there were only 5 people in Group A but 100 people in Group B"?

If 1 out of 5 people in Group A failed to make the phone call, then 20% of the 65-75 year olds failed.

Meanwhile if 14 out of 100 people in Group B failed to make the phone call, then 14% of college students failed.

With these numbers, it would seem like the older group actually is struggling more with this memory task. Only 14% of college students forgot but 20% of seniors forgot.

This answer choice is shutting down the possibility of that kind of objection.

answers.text: The same group of researchers answered the calls made by the callers in both study groups.
answers.fb:
Correct

It makes zero difference to any of this study who answered the call on the other end. The time of the call was recorded electronically, and all we care about was whether the people remembered to make the call.

It doesn't matter who picks up the phone: it could be a recorded message, the same researchers both times, different researchers each time.

Once they've made or not made the call, we stop caring for the purposes of this argument. Since learning about what entity answered the call on the other end is totally irrelevant, this answer has no power to strengthen or weaken.

answers.text: Among the college students there were no persons more than forty years old.
answers.fb:
Strengthens - Rules Out Objection

The author's argument is intended to lean on this comparison between an older group A, who seemingly did better when it comes to remembering to make this call, and a younger group B.

But we're never told that group B is younger, just that they are college students. Well, college students can potentially be any age.

What if Group B had a bunch of college students, 14 of which were in their seventies (they decided in retirement to go get that degree they had never gotten)? In this sort of scenario, we could say that the 14 people in Group B who forgot to make the phone call were all super old college students whose memories had suffered from aging.

This answer removes the possibility of making such an objection.

answers.text: Both groups had unrestricted access to telephones for making the required calls.
answers.fb:
Strengthens - Rules Out Objection

The author's argument is intended to lean on this comparison between an older group A, who seemingly did better when it comes to remembering to make this call, and a younger group B.

The author wants us to interpret this experiment by thinking that Group A did better at this "Call X at time Y" task because the older folks in Group A had at least as easy a time remembering to make the call as did the younger folks in Group B.

But we could potentially object with an alternate explanation for why Group B failed to make the call in 14 cases. "It wasn't because the college students couldn't remember to make the call. They all remembered perfectly. 14 of them failed to make the call simply because they had no access to a telephone.

This answer rules out that sort of objection by affirming that everyone had access to a phone.

answers.text: The members of the two groups received their instructions approximately the same amount of time before they were to make their telephone calls.
answers.fb:
Strengthens - Rules Out Objection

The author's argument is intended to lean on the idea that the people in Group A did "a better job remembering" than did those in Group B.

But what if the people in Group A were told to make this call like an hour in advance, whereas the people in Group B were told to make this call like three days in advance.

It's must easier to remember one hour later that you're supposed to Call X and Time Y, whereas it's much harder to remember that days later.

This answer rules out that sort of objection. It levels the playing field in terms of how much lead-time they had on this instructed call.

(A), (D), and (E) are all equalizing the two groups so that we can compare their "lapse rate" and feel like Group A did a better job remembering.

(A) same size groups
(D) they all have access to a phone
(E) they all had similar warning

questiontext:
Consumer advocate: A recent study concluded that top-loading washing machines are superior overall to front-loaders. But front-loaders have the controls and access in front. This is more convenient for wheelchair users, some of whom find it highly inconvenient to remove laundry from top-loaders. So for some consumers front-loaders are superior.

Which one of the following is an assumption upon which the consumer advocate's argument depends?
gf:
Conclusion (So)

For some consumers, front-loaders are superior (to top-loaders).

Evidence

Front-loaders have the controls and access in front, which is more convenient for wheelchair users, who also find it inconvenient to remove laundry from top-loaders.

Evaluate

The conclusion has a very modest goal: it's only trying to prove that for at least some consumers, front-loaders are superior.

The author is building the case that for some wheelchair users, front-loaders are superior.

Why? Front-loaders have the controls and access in front.
The author assumes a difference, that top-loaders do not have control and access in front.

Also, wheelchair users find it highly inconvenient to remove laundry from top-loaders.
The author assumes a difference, that wheelchair users do not find it highly inconvenient to remove laundry from front-loaders.

Beyond those assumed differences, can we think of any objections to this argument?

Given that ... wheelchair users would have controls and access in front and might find it less inconvenient to remove laundry,

How could we still argue that ... top-loaders are superior, even for these wheelchair users?

We'd have to go into Net Gain / Loss mode and argue that even though front-loaders have these stated advantages over top-loaders, top-loaders have other advantages over front-loaders that make them at least as good an option for wheelchair users.

We are helped by the opening opposing idea, which tells us that top-loading washers are superior overall. Maybe they get clothes cleaner while using less water and are much more affordable. That could be enough for a wheelchair user to still make a top-loader a superior option.

Goal

Look for an answer staying one of the assumed differences (top-loaders don't have controls/access in front ... it's not highly inconvenient for wheelchair users to remove clothes from a front-loader).

Or look for an answer ruling out the idea that other aspects of washing machines (how well they clean / how much they cost / how much water they use) do not make top-loaders the better overall choice, even for wheelchair users.

answers.text: For some consumers the convenience of front-loaders outweighs the advantages of top-loaders in assessing which is superior.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is Weighing Tradeoffs in a way that aligns with the author's argument. 

We are told from the outset that, overall, top-loading machines are superior. But the author thinks for wheelchair users, the convenience of having controls and access in the front (rather than on top) would make a front-loader superior.

So he's assuming that the convenience factor outweighs whatever other factors should be considered in terms of making the front-loader the superior choice.

If we negate this answer (negating "some" means "none"), we get:  
for no users would the convenience of front-loaders outweigh the advantages of top-loaders, in assessing which type is superior.

Does that weaken?

Heck, yeah! That totally derails the case the author was making that for wheelchair users, the convenience of front-loaders would turn them from being the inferior option to the superior one.

answers.text: Washing machines of a given type should be compared only with washing machines of that type.
answers.fb:
Opposite, if anything

This argument is comparing washing machines of different types (front loaders vs. top loaders).

So clearly the author is comfortable comparing washing machines of a given type with washing machines of some other type.

answers.text: Convenience is the only important factor in determining which type of washing machine is superior.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: the only

The author doesn't need to assume that convenience is the only important factor. He definitely is assuming that it is an important factor. And he's assuming that the advantage front-loaders have in terms of convenience for wheelchair users isn't outweighed by other important factors.

If we negate this and say that "there are other important factors to consider beyond just convenience", that does weaken the argument somewhat, because it creates room for doubt. It allows us to think, "ooh, maybe some of the other important factors tip towards top-loaders. So who's to say whether wheelchair users would think that overall front-loaders are superior."

It's very weird for there to be a wrong answer choice that definitely does weaken when you negate it.

But if we go by the standard of, "Which answer, when negated, most weakens?", we'll always find the right answer on Necessary Assumption. (That is not to say we should always use this standard, because negating all the answers is often more difficult than other ways of finding the correct answer. But if we're on the fence between two answers, asking ourselves which negation most weakens is a great tie-break.)

Which weakens more?
negated (A):  for no users would the convenience of front-loaders outweigh the advantages of top-loaders in terms of overall superiority.

negated (C): there are other important factors besides convenience. 

(A)'s negation weakens more because it totally shuts down the possibility of using this evidence to prove superiority. (C)'s negation just creates the possibility that other factors might outweigh this evidence.

answers.text: Retrieving clothes from a top-loader is convenient for people who do not use wheelchairs.
answers.fb:
Illegal Opposite

Necessary Assumption loves to write trap answers like this.

If the paragraph says, "Black lives matter", the trap answer says the argument is assuming "non-black lives don't matter".

Here, the paragraph said, "removing clothes from a top-loader is highly inconvenient for wheelchair users".

So this trap answer is saying "removing clothes from a top-loader is not inconvenient for non-wheelchair users."

We're never allowed to take a sentence and just invert its terms that way. If we say, "people who serve in the military are heroes", that doesn't mean "people who don't serve in the military are not heroes".

It's possible that for non-wheelchair users, removing clothes from a top-loader isn't highly inconvenient, it's just mildly inconvenient. The argument doesn't need to assume that it's actually convenient. The argument isn't even concerned with non-wheelchair users.

answers.text: Retrieving clothes from front-loaders is inconvenient for people who are not wheelchair users.
answers.fb:
Illegal Opposite

Again, the argument doesn't care at all about people who are not wheelchair users.

It's trying to support a conclusion that says, "for at least some people, front-loaders are superior", and we can tell that the 'some people' the author has in mind are wheelchair users.

So the author's whole argument is just trying to convince us that for some wheelchair users, front-loaders are superior.

He doesn't need to assume anything about non-wheelchair users. If we negate this and say that non-wheelchair users also find it convenient to unload clothes from a front-loader, that wouldn't weaken. In fact, it would come closer to agreeing with the author's conclusion.

questiontext:
Nutritionist: Because humans have evolved very little since the development of agriculture, it is clear that humans are still biologically adapted to a diet of wild foods, consisting mainly of raw fruits and vegetables, nuts and seeds, lean meat, and seafood. Straying from this diet has often resulted in chronic illness and other physical problems. Thus, the more our diet consists of wild foods, the healthier we will be.

The claim that humans are still biologically adapted to a diet of wild foods plays which one of the following roles in the nutritionist's argument?
gf:
Conclusion (thus)

The more our diet consists of wild foods, the healthier we will be.

Intermediate Conclusion (it's clear that)

Humans are still biologically adapted to wild foods.

Evidence (because)

Humans have evolved very little since the development of agriculture. 

Straying from this wild food diet has often resulted in chronic illness and other physical problems.

Goal

We're being asked about the 2nd claim, which seems to be an Intermediate Conclusion. It has its own support (the first half the sentence begins with BECAUSE, which is a support indicator).

But this claim seems to provide support for the final claim. Why should we believe that the more our diet is wild foods, the healthier we'll be? Because ... we're still adapted to wild foods.

answers.text: It is a conclusion for which the only support offered is the claim that straying from a diet of wild foods has often resulted in chronic illness and other physical problems.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match
Too Strong (the only support)

Our claim is a conclusion, and you could say that the fact that straying from wild diets leads to health problems is support for the idea that we're still adapted to wild diets.

But the other supporting claim is the first one (we've evolved very little since inventing agriculture), which is prefaced by the Support Indicator "because".

answers.text: It is a premise for which no justification is provided, but which is used to support the argument’s main conclusion.
answers.fb:
Bad Description: premise

There is justification provided, which is why this is an Intermediate Conclusion not just a premise.

Because we've evolved very little, it's clear we're still adapted to wild.

answers.text: It is a phenomenon for which the main conclusion of the nutritionist’s argument is cited as an explanation.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

The conclusion is "The more our diet consists of wild foods, the healthier we will be."

The explanation for why we are still adapted to wild foods is that "we've evolved very little since inventing agriculture".

answers.text: It is an intermediate conclusion for which one claim is offered as support, and which is used in turn to support the argument’s main conclusion.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is what we were looking for. 

The first claim "we've evolved little" is provided as support for our claim, and our claim supports the idea that "the more our diet consists of wild foods,  the healthier we'll be".

answers.text: It is a premise offered in support of the claim that humans have evolved very little since the development of agriculture.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

An Intermediate Conclusion is technically still a premise (it's just called a supported premise), but the conclusion our claim is supporting is "The more our diet consists of wild foods, the healthier we will be".

The claim that "humans have evolved very little" is SUPPORT for our claim, not the other way around, as this answer says.

questiontext:
Editorialist: Some people argue that we have an obligation not to cut down trees. However, there can be no obligation to an entity unless that entity has a corresponding right. So if we have an obligation toward trees, then trees have rights. But trees are not the sort of things that can have rights. Therefore, we have no obligation not to cut down trees.

The editorialist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
gf:
Conclusion (therefore)

We have no obligation not to cut down trees.

Evidence

There can be no obligation to an entity unless that entity has a corresponding right.

(If an entity doesn't have a right, then there's no obligation to that entity)

Trees don't have rights.

Evaluate

This argument is famously hard to read. The author provides a conditional relationship in the 2nd sentence:

Entity has no rights → No obligation to entity

Then the author draws an Intermediate Conclusion with "So" that is just spelling out how conditional logic works. In our case, it's spelling out how the contrapositive of what we just wrote would sound, if it were applied to trees:

Do have obligation to trees → trees have rights

We're not going to spend any mental energy fighting that conclusion, since it is airtight. If I introduce a rule that says "You can't be X unless you're Y", then it's absolutely valid for me to then conclude, "So if Pam is X, then Pam is Y". 

When the author tells us "But trees don't have rights", she is triggering the contrapositive of that Intermediate Conclusion.

So, implicitly, she is allowing us to infer, "Okay, if trees don't have rights, then we have no obligation toward trees."

How is that different from the actual Conclusion?

we have no obligation toward trees  
     vs.  
we have no obligation not to cut down trees

There's a good chance we'd be confused enough by the stimulus that we'd have to go check out answer with only a foggy sense of what's going on.

But if we're lucky, we see that tiny gap looks like this:

"If we don't have an obligation toward trees, then we don't have an obligation not to cut down trees." This gap is acting like the only obligation we needed to worry about was one toward trees. If we we're not obliged toward trees, then we're in the clear --- no obligation at all.

If we were trying to argue the Anti-Conclusion, we'd be thinking, "GIVEN THAT we have no obligation towards trees, HOW COULD WE STILL ARGUE THAT we do have some obligation not to cut down trees?"

What came to my mind was  
1. I'm obliged not to cut down the tree in my neighbor's yard, not because I have an obligation towards that tree, but because I'm obliged to respect my neighbor's property.

2. I'm obliged not to cut down the trees in the Amazon Rain Forest, not because I have an obligation towards those trees, but because I have an obligation not to exacerbate climate change for future generations of humans. 

Goal

Look for an answer addressing the gap of, "If we don't have an obligation toward trees, then we don't have an obligation, period." Or look for an answer ruling out some other way in which we'd be obliged not to cut down trees.

answers.text: If an entity has a right to certain treatment, we have an obligation to treat it that way.
answers.fb:
Reversed Logic
Out of Scope: certain treatment

The wording of "certain treatment" doesn't really match up with anything, so this feels fishy from that. But if we closely inspected it, we'd see that it's reversing the logic of something we were told.

We were told
  if there's an obligation, then it has a right

This answer is saying
  if it has a right, then there's an obligation

answers.text: Any entity that has rights also has obligations.
answers.fb:
Reversed Logic

This has the same problem as (A).

We were told
  if there's an obligation, then it has a right

This answer is saying
  if it has a right, then there's an obligation

It is also getting confused in the sense that the argument was talking about whether we have an obligation to X, based on whether X has rights.

This rule is about whether X itself has obligations, so in addition to reversed logic, it's also just distorting what we were even talking about.

answers.text: Only conscious entities are the sort of things that can have rights.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: conscious entities
Too Strong: only

This is probably tempting if we're trying to play Mind Reader and explain the backstory behind the premise that "trees are not the sort of things that can have rights".

But the author's rationale for that does not have to be that "only conscious entities can have rights". In fact, the author may believe that dead people (not conscious) still have rights. Maybe she thinks they have the right to not have their graves robbed, or to not have their likeness used in commercials without their relatives' permission.

answers.text: Avoiding cutting down trees is not an obligation owed to some entity other than trees.
answers.fb:
Correct

Whenever we're doing Necessary Assumption and we see an answer using the ruling out verbiage of "not / no", we should consider it, since so many correct answers are written that way.

If we negate this, does it weaken?

Avoiding cutting down trees is an obligation owed to some entity other than trees.

Heck yeah, it weakens! In this case, it basically contradicts the conclusion! (it doesn't need to do that to be correct; it just needs to weaken more than any other answer's negation would weaken). This negation starts to sound like our counterarguments from before - we have an obligation not to cut down trees, because of the obligation owed to our nextdoor neighbor, who wants to keep her tree, or because of the obligation owed to future generations of humans, who want a livable climate.

If we're not using the Negation Test to see why this is the correct answer, we would be thinking that this addresses the gap we found:

if we don't have an obligation to trees not to cut them down,
then we have no obligation to not cut them down,
because avoiding cutting down trees isn't an obligation owed to any other sort of entity.

answers.text: One does not always have the right to cut down the trees on one’s own property.
answers.fb:
Weakens

According the author's conclusion, we should be able to cut down any tree we want. We have no obligation not to cut down trees.

So this answer actually seems to be undercutting the author's conclusion, because it is placing limits on our right to cut down trees.

questiontext:
It is difficult to grow cacti in a humid climate. It is difficult to raise orange trees in a cold climate. In most parts of a certain country, it is either easy to grow cacti or easy to raise orange trees.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be false?
gf:
Statements

conditional (it is A to be B:   B → A)  

It's hard to grow cacti in a humid climate.  
  Humid climate → hard to grow cacti  

It's hard to raise orange trees in a cold climate.   
   Cold climate → hard to raise orange tree

In most parts of the country, it's easy to grow cacti or easy to raise orange trees. 

Evaluate

The correct answer on Must Be False almost always does one of two things:  
1. Contradicts a conditional relationship provided  
2. Contradicts an available inference we can make by combining claims.

There are two quasi-conditionals in the first two sentences. So a correct answer could say something like, "Most people who live in humid climates grow cacti very easily", or "in most parts of Arrendale, which has a permanently cold climate thanks to Queen Elsa, it's easy to raise orange trees".

Can we combine claims to infer anything?

We see the Overlapping Concept of "easy/difficult to grow cacti" and "easy/difficult to raise orange trees". This suggests that we can combine these claims.

The contrapositive to our conditionals would be, 

      not difficult   →  not humid  
     to grow cacti

     not difficult to   →  not cold  
  raise orange trees

If they tell us that in most parts of the country it's easy to grow cacti or easy to raise orange trees, then we know that in most parts of the country it's either "not humid", "not cold", or both. 

Goal

Look for an answer that contradicts either of the two conditionals in the first two sentences,

or look for an answer that contradicts the inference we made by applying the final sentence to those two conditionals, to derive:

most parts of country → ~Humid or ~Cold

answers.text: Half of the country is both humid and cold.
answers.fb:
Correct

This contradicts the inference we made by combining the Most claim with the two conditionals.

In order to grow cacti easily, it can't be humid.
In order to raise orange trees, it can't be cold.

If half of the country is both humid and cold, as this answer choice says, then in 50% of the country you can't grow cacti easily and you can't raise orange trees easily. 

That would mean in at most 50% of the country can you grow cacti or orange trees easily.

This would contradict the final sentence, which says in more than 50% you can grow one or the other easily.

answers.text: Most of the country is hot.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: hot
Compatible

Temperatures don't exist in a binary where it's always cold or hot. If most of the country is hot, then most of the country is not cold. 

And if most of the country is not cold, then in most of the country it's hard to raise orange trees.

Does that contradict the last sentence?

No, because the last sentence isn't saying, "in most of the country it's easy to raise orange trees", it's saying "in most of the country it's easy to raise orange trees or cacti".

It may be that in 30% of the country it's easy to grow oranges, and in a non-overlapping 30% of the country it's easy to grow cacti. That would mean that in 60% (i.e. most) of the country, you can grow oranges or cacti easily.

answers.text: Some parts of the country are neither cold nor humid.
answers.fb:
Compatible

In order to contradict a weakly worded answer, we would need to have read something extreme.

To contradict this answer, we would need to know that all parts of the country are cold, humid, or both. Were we told that?

Nope, so nothing we read contradicts this answer.

answers.text: It is not possible to raise cacti in the country.
answers.fb:
Compatible

This seems very tempting, since we heard "in most parts of the country, it's easy to grow cacti", didn't we?

Doesn't "easy" imply "possible?

Yes, it would. But we only heard that "in most parts of the country, its easy to grow cacti or raise orange trees".

I can say, "Most NFL players either played football in college or played in a league on the surface of Mars".

I can say, "Most US Presidents have either served their term on planet Earth or served their term on Mars".

These are stupid, vacuously true statements in the sense that there are 0 NFL players and 0 US Presidents who were on Mars. But it's true that most NFL players can check box 1 (college ball) or box 2 (martian ball), so it's a true statement.

Similarly, it might be that in this country it's impossible to raise / grow cacti anywhere. But in 60% of the country, you can easily raise orange trees.

If so, then it's still true to say, "In most of this country you can easily raise orange trees or cacti".

answers.text: Most parts of the country are humid.
answers.fb:
Compatible

If most of the country is humid, then you can only grow cacti easily in at most 49% of the country.

Does that contradict the final sentence, then?

No, because the final sentence is giving us two options:

In most of the country, you can check one or more of these boxes:
[    ]  easy to grow cacti
[    ]  easy to raise orange trees

Up to 49% of the country can check box 1, so as long as at least 2% of non-overlapping parts can check box 2, then the last sentence can still be true.

questiontext:
Essayist: Common sense, which is always progressing, is nothing but a collection of theories that have been tested over time and found useful. When alternative theories that prove even more useful are developed, they gradually take the place of theories already embodied in common sense. This causes common sense to progress, but, because it absorbs new theories slowly, it always contains some obsolete theories.

If all of the essayist's statements are true, then which one of the following must be true?
gf:
Statements

conditionals (always, nothing but)

  Common → Always progressing
    sense

  Common → collection of time-tested 
    sense          theories found useful

conditional (when)

 Alternate theory         eventually
more useful than  →  supplant theories
  common sense        in common sense

causal (causes, because)

  The process of newer,          common
   more useful theories      ⇢  sense
  eventually supplanting         progresses
theories in common sense

  Common sense absorbs       Common sense
      new theories slowly      ⇢  always has some
                                                     obsolete stuff

Evaluate

We're very attracted to Conditional or Causal indicator wording, when we're doing Must Be True and Most Supported. And that's because often conditional as well as causal statements chain together. If A leads to B, and B leads to C, they can test us on our understanding that A leads to C.

But then other times we get a random mess of stuff, like this problem. Diagramming these statements is probably not going to help us, since they don't really chain together. And since there are a few conditional ideas and a couple causal ones, should we anticipate a conditional chain or a causal chain?

In short, we don't know. However, the final sentence does have a pivot (but / yet / however). Usually, when an Inference paragraph Ends with a Pivot, the correct answer deals with the tension created by that pivot idea.

What does it tell us, if anything, that because common sense absorbs new theories slowly, it always contains some obsolete theories?

"Obsolete" means that something is no longer widely used or believed, or its functionality has been superseded. The iPod and iPhones made listening to music on CD's obsolete.

So if some theories in common sense are obsolete, it's because alternative theories have already proven themselves more useful. I guess common sense is like a big corporation. Even when smaller businesses innovate better ways, the big corporation's pace of change is glacial, so it has some outmoded ways of doing things.

Goal

Let's look for anything provable, possibly dealing with the tension created by the fact that common sense always contains some obsolete ideas.

We know three things about "common sense"
- always progressing
- a collection of theories that have been tested over time and found useful
- always contains some obsolete theories

Maybe the correct answer will speak to an overlap between some of those traits.

answers.text: At least some new theories that have not yet been found to be more useful than any theory currently part of common sense will never be absorbed into the body of common sense.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: never be absorbed

We don't have any sort of rule in this paragraph that gives us a way to prove that something "will not be absorbed". 

We only have a rule that says, 
"If alt. theory proves more useful, will be absorbed (eventually)"

answers.text: Of the useful theories within the body of common sense, the older ones are generally less useful than the newer ones.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: generally

Can we really say most of the older theories in common sense are less useful than most of the newer ones?

Nothing in the paragraph let's us quantify a comparison in usefulness.

The temptation in this answer is that a new theory in common sense occurs because that new theory is more useful than the one it's replacing.

But let's say that there are 100 theories in common sense. There might be like 65 ironclad theories that are super useful. It's unlikely an alternate theory that's even more useful will ever be developed. 

Meanwhile, there are 35 decent theories that are somewhat useful. But over time, we keep finding ways to improve on them. They get swapped out for somewhat more useful alternatives.

But that doesn't mean that the average usefulness of those 35 (the newer ones) will be higher than the usefulness of the 65 older theories, that are so useful, they've never been replaced!

answers.text: The frequency with which new theories are generated prevents their rapid absorption into the body of common sense.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Causal Relationship

The passage told us that superior theories are absorbed into common sense slowly.

This answer seems to be positing some causal backstory to explain why they're absorbed slowly (it's saying "there are just so many new theories that common sense doesn't want to overreact, so it takes it slow"?)

We are just told that common sense absorbs new theories slowly. The passage doesn't explain why it absorbs new theories slowly, so we can't prove this causal claim about why it does so.

answers.text: Each theory within the body of common sense is eventually replaced with a new theory that is more useful.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: each theory

Nothing in the paragraph guarantees that every theory in common sense will eventually be replaced.

The only trigger we know that guarantees that a theory will be replaced is when an alternate theory is found that proves more useful.

Do we know that, for every theory in common sense, there will eventually be an alternate theory that is found to be more useful?

No, we weren't told that, which is why this answer is too strong.

answers.text: At least some theories that have been tested over time and found useful are less useful than some other theories that have not been fully absorbed into the body of common sense.
answers.fb:
Correct

As we suspected, this answer deals with the tension created by the ending Pivot idea.

Since common sense always contains some obsolete theories, that means that there are always some alternate theories out there that are superior to some of the theories in common sense. 

"Superior" means that there are always some theories in the world that are more useful than some theories still embodied in common sense.

We know that all theories embodied in common sense have been tested over time and found useful. So we add up claims to derive this answer:

1. CS always contains some obsolete theories (some theories that are less useful than some alternate theory out there in the world) 
                      +
2. all the theories in CS have been proven useful

∴ Some theories in CS are theories that have proven useful, but are nevertheless less useful than alternate theories that haven't yet been absorbed (since CS absorbs new theories slowly). 

We anticipated that the correct answer might try to forge some overlap between some pairing of the three things we knew about "common sense", and this answer is combining the 2nd and 3rd:

- always progressing
- a collection of theories that have been tested over time and found useful
- always contains some obsolete theories

It's saying that "some of the theories in common sense have been tested over time and found useful but are also obsolete".

questiontext:
Archaeologists excavating a Neanderthal campsite found discarded gazelle teeth there whose coloration indicated that gazelles had been hunted throughout the year. The archaeologists concluded that the Neanderthals had inhabited the campsite year-round and thus were not nomadic. In contrast, the archaeologists cite a neighboring campsite of nomadic Cro-Magnons that contained teeth from gazelles all killed during the same season.

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the archaeologists' reasoning?
gf:
Conclusion (concluded / thus)

The Neanderthals inhabited this campsite year-round and thus were not nomadic. 

Evidence

The gazelle teeth we found at the campsite were hunted throughout the year. 

Meanwhile, at a campsite of Cro-Magnon nomads, we found gazelle teeth that were all killed during the same season.

Evaluate

Since the author is looking at archaeological evidence and interpreting its meaning / significance / backstory, we can se our Explain Curious Fact mindset.

Curious Fact ... Why are we finding a year's worth of gazelle teeth at this Neanderthal campsite?

Author's Explanation ... The Neanderthals lived at the campsite year-round and hunted gazelle all year.

Whenever we use this template, we know we're supposed to ask ourselves:
1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?

If we were trying to defend the Anti-Conclusion, that these Neanderthals didn't live at the campsite year round or were nomads, then how could we explain the year's worth of gazelle teeth?

Maybe they roamed all around, saving gazelle teeth wherever they went (perhaps they used it to make jewelry), and they were at this campsite for a bit and happened to lose their stash?

How could we hurt the plausibility of the story that they camped here year-round and hunted gazelle throughout the year?
 

Maybe we could say this campsite wouldn't have been survivable during certain weather extremes throughout a year. Maybe we could say that you wouldn't be able to hunt gazelle for a full year from this campsite, because the gazelle aren't always close enough to the campsite for Neanderthals to go hunt them and then return to the campsite by bedtime.

Goal

Since this is Weaken, we primarily expect an Alternate Explanation for why there's a year's worth of gazelle teeth at this campsite.

But we'll also consider any answer that hurts the plausibility of the storyline that the Neanderthals stayed at this site year round, hunting gazelle.

answers.text: Neanderthals hunted a wide variety of both migratory and nonmigratory animals.
answers.fb:
Mixed Impact

For a group to hunt a migratory animal would potentially support the idea that the group itself is migratory / nomadic. Its hard to hunt a species that migrates if you just return to the same address every night.

However, you could certainly be sedentary and hunt a migratory animal during the season when it rolls through your hood.

Similarly, hunting a nonmigratory animal makes it sound like you stay put in one area. But you could be a nomad and just happen to hunt the nonmigratory animals that are local to whatever area you're passing through.

Since this answer suggests both that Neanderthals were and weren't nomads, it doesn't really have any clear impact on the conversation.

answers.text: Cro-Magnons and Neanderthals sometimes exchanged tools.
answers.fb:
No Impact / Weak

Words that only connote one data point (like some, sometimes, may, could, can, possible, not always, need not) are almost always wrong on Strengthen / Weaken / Paradox / Sufficient Assumption.

Even if the language were stronger than "at least one time they exchanged tools", this still wouldn't have any impact. Who cares if they exchange tools?

That doesn't give us an alternate explanation for the year's supply of gazelle teeth, nor does it impugn the story that Neanderthals lived at this camp year round, hunting gazelle.

answers.text: Neanderthals saved gazelle teeth for use in religious rituals and later discarded them.
answers.fb:
Correct

Here's the Alternate Explanation we were looking for. This let's us argue that, "Neanderthals were nomads. They weren't living at this campsite year round. The real reason there was a year's supply of gazelle teeth at this site is that the Neanderthals would save teeth as they roamed around hunting, and then they would use them in religious ceremonies, and then discard them."

So this is allowing us to say, "Maybe we found a year's worth of teeth at this campsite because the Neanderthals had one of their famous tooth-laden religious rituals here and then discarded the year's worth of teeth when they shipped out of town toward their next destination."

Pretty crazy, right? There's a lot of story we have to fill-in here to understand how this answer works. It's very important that we understand the Explain Curious Fact template so that we're actively listening for Alternate Explanations, because otherwise it's pretty impossible to understand what value this answer could have for us.

answers.text: Cro-Magnons usually followed the migrations of the animals they hunted.
answers.fb:
No Impact

We're not concerned about what the Cro-Magnons did. We know they were nomads and so the fact that they followed migratory animals sounds totally on-brand.

answers.text: Gazelles inhabited the area around the campsites year-round.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This helps the plausibility of the author's hypothesis. If there weren't gazelles near this campsite year-round, it would make the author's story sound impossible:  how could the Neanderthals be living at this campsite and hunting gazelle year round if there are at least some parts of the year when there are no gazelles around?

questiontext:
Literary critic: Samuel Johnson argued that writers should refrain from attributing attractive qualities to immoral characters, since doing so increases the tendency of readers to emulate these characters. Works of fiction would be unrealistic, however, if writers were to follow Johnson's advice.

The conclusion is properly drawn in the literary critic's argument if which one of the following is assumed?
gf:
Conclusion

If writers were to follow Johnson's advice, works of fiction would be unrealistic.

i.e. 
if writers were to refrain from attributing attractive qualities to immoral characters, then works of fiction would be unrealistic.

Evaluate

There isn't really any premise, so it's using the term "argument" pretty loosely in the question stem. We know the first sentence is SJ's argument, because it says, "Samuel Johnson argued that X, since Y". So X was SJ's conclusion and Y was SJ's support.

The rebuttal pivot (but, yet, however) signals to us that the last sentence is the author. 

We're trying to prove the claim that, "if you were writing fiction and you didn't attribute attractive qualities to immoral characters, your work would be unrealistic."

Goal

So the author must be assuming that, "in reality (realistic), immoral people do have attractive qualities."

Or if we want to predict a conditional version of the answer,

"If a fiction writer isn't attributing attractive qualities to immoral characters, then their work will be unrealistic."

answers.text: One-dimensional characters are less entertaining than well-rounded characters.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal
Out of Scope: one-dimensional, well-rounded, entertaining

This is bringing up new stuff and not giving us the old stuff we're looking for.

We need to prove the author's conclusion, so the correct answer has to help us establish that a realistic work of fiction would give its immoral characters some attractive qualities.

This answer doesn't say anything resembling that "immoral characters / attractive qualities".

answers.text: The attractive qualities of characters are more appealing than their immoral behavior.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal
Out of Scope: appealing

The concept of what is more / less appealing has nothing to do with our goal. We need to prove that the attractive qualities of immoral characters is realistic.

answers.text: In reality, all bad people have some attractive qualities.
answers.fb:
Correct

If in reality, all bad people have some attractive qualities, then any fictional work where the bad (immoral) people didn't have attractive qualities wouldn't match reality. Thus, it would be unrealistic.

This answer would allow us to prove that the last sentence is true.

answers.text: In reality, it is difficult to emulate fictional characters.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal
Out of Scope: difficult / emulate

The concept of how easy / difficult it is to emulate (try to copy) a character from a fictional book is totally out of scope.

We're just trying to establish that "it's unrealistic if immoral characters don't have attractive qualities". This answer doesn't say anything like that.

answers.text: It is rarely evident which qualities of fictional characters are intended to be attractive qualities.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal
Out of Scope: intended to be attractive

The concept of which qualities of a character are / aren't intended to be attractive has nothing to do with our agenda.

We are just trying to prove that a work in which immoral character lack attractive qualities would not seem realistic. and this answer doesn't speak to immoral characters or to realism.

questiontext:
Environmentalist: The United Kingdom recently instituted a law requiring that foods containing genetically altered ingredients be labeled accordingly. Food producers, fearing that consumers would understand the labels as warnings and thus avoid their products, rushed to rid those products of genetically altered ingredients. Other countries contemplating such labeling should therefore refrain, because many crops are genetically altered to be pest resistant; loss of demand for these genetically altered crops would necessitate production alternatives, all of which are dangerous and pesticide intensive.

Which one of the following is an assumption on which the environmentalist's argument depends?
gf:
Conclusion 

Other countries contemplating such labeling should refrain, because it would necessitate production alternatives that are dangerous and pesticide intensive.

Evidence

The UK required labels on foods with genetically altered ingredients. Producers got rid of these ingredients because they feared consumers would see the labels as warnings.

Many genetically altered crops are pest-resistant, so without demand for these crops, alternative production methods would need to be used.

Evaluate

The environmentalist is concerned that labeling will lead to a drop in demand for genetically altered (a.k.a. pest-resistant) crops, pushing producers to switch to more dangerous, pesticide-heavy alternatives. How's the argument moving from "this happened in the UK" to "so you shouldn't do this elsewhere"?

The argument heavily relies on the assumption that what happened in the UK will also happen in other countries. If producers around the world react the same way as those in the UK, then the environmentalist's conclusion seems plausible.

Moreover, it assumes that consumers interpret these labels as warnings, prompting behavior changes—specifically avoiding the products.

Goal

Look for assumptions that either connect the UK experience with potential reactions in other countries or deal with consumer interpretation of labels as warnings.

answers.text: In general, people interpret labels stating that some food ingredients are genetically altered as warnings.
answers.fb:
Alternative Considerations

This is tempting. It addresses whether consumers view the labels as warnings which is an underlying thread. However, while it helps the argument, it's already wrapped into the initial setup explaining why UK producers reacted as they did.

answers.text: Before the United Kingdom instituted a law requiring that foods containing genetically altered ingredients be labeled as such, almost all foods sold there contained genetically altered ingredients.
answers.fb: This choice isn’t necessary. It’s not crucial to the argument whether most foods contained altered ingredients before the law. The effects of the law are more pertinent.

answers.text: The reactions of food producers in other countries to laws requiring labeling of foods containing genetically altered ingredients are likely to be similar to the reactions of food producers in the United Kingdom.
answers.fb:
Correct Explanation

The reactions of food producers in other countries to laws requiring labeling of foods containing genetically altered ingredients are likely to be similar to the reactions of food producers in the United Kingdom.

This is what we'd expect. If negated, it would mean food producers in other countries might not react the same way, making the argument fall apart. The whole point is that the environmentalist is warning against similar labeling elsewhere due to predicted similar effects.

answers.text: Warning labels on food products have proven to be effective in reducing consumption of those products.
answers.fb: This choice broadens the scope to warning labels generally, whereas the argument is specific to reactions to genetically altered labels. Not necessary for the conclusion.

answers.text: Countries that institute new food labeling regulations often experience a change in consumer eating habits.
answers.fb: This choice talks about changes in consumer eating habits but doesn’t connect directly to the issue of producers switching to dangerous alternatives due to loss of demand for genetically altered crops.

questiontext:
Only people who are willing to compromise should undergo mediation to resolve their conflicts. Actual litigation should be pursued only when one is sure that one's position is correct. People whose conflicts are based on ideology are unwilling to compromise.

If the statements above are true, then which one of the following must be true?
gf:
Only people who are willing to compromise should undergo mediation to resolve their conflicts.

M → WC

Actual litigation should be pursued only when one is sure that one's position is correct.

L → SC

People whose conflicts are based on ideology are unwilling to compromise.

I → ~WC

answers.text: People who do not undergo mediation to resolve their conflicts should be sure that their positions are correct.
answers.fb:
Unsupported

Falsely assumes that people who do not undergo mediation should pursue litigation.

answers.text: People whose conflicts are not based on ideology should attempt to resolve their conflicts by means of litigation.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Relationship

No relationship can be established between people whose conflicts are not based on ideology and people who should pursue litigation.

answers.text: People whose conflicts are based on ideology are not always sure that their positions are correct.
answers.fb:
Too Strong / Unsupported Relationship

There is a difference between “should be sure” and “are sure.”

Also, this assumes that those who should not undergo mediation are not always sure that their positions are correct.

answers.text: People who are sure of the correctness of their positions are not people who should undergo mediation to resolve their conflicts.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Relationship

Falsely assumes that people who are sure of the correctness of their position are not willing to compromise.

answers.text: People whose conflicts are based on ideology are not people who should undergo mediation to resolve their conflicts.
answers.fb:
Correct

This follows from the first and third statements.

questiontext:
The profitability of a business is reduced by anything that undermines employee morale. This is why paying senior staff with stock options, which allows them to earn more when the enterprise prospers, is not a wise policy because it increases dramatically the difference in income between senior staff and employees who are paid only a fixed salary.

Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
gf:
Conclusion (not wise / this is why)

Paying senior staff with stock options is not wise.

Evidence (because)

Stock options allow senior staff to earn more when the enterprise prospers. This dramatically increases the difference in income between senior staff and employees who are paid a fixed salary.

Profitability is reduced by anything that undermines employee morale. 

Evaluate

We need to get from "paying senior staff with stock options" to "unwise".

They tell us that paying senior staff with stock options will increase the difference in income between senior staff and employees.

So the author is assuming that it's "unwise to dramatically increase the pay disparity between top brass and regular employees".

But the conclusion indicator "This is why" at the start of the 2nd sentence also tells us that the 1st sentence is an important part of the logic.

It's telling us that when you undermine employee morale, you reduce a business's profitability.  The idea of "reduced profitability" is probably intended as a match for "not a wise policy". 

So the author seems to be thinking that when we dramatically increase the pay disparity between senior staff and fixed salary employees, that will undermine employee morale.

The author's overall reasoning chain looks like this:

 Pay SS        greatly       lower     reduce    not
w/ stock → increase →  emp  → profit → wise
                    pay gap     morale

Goal

Let's look for that missing internal link, that "greatly increasing the pay disparity will undermine employee morale".

answers.text: Large income differences between fixed-salary employees and senior staff tend to undermine employee morale.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is the missing link we predicted.

 Pay SS        greatly       lower     reduce    not
w/ stock → increase →  emp  → profit → wise
                    pay gap     morale

If we negated this answer and said, "hey, author -- large differences in income between senior staff and fixed salary employees doesn't tend to hurt employee morale", that would badly weaken the argument.

The only way the author has of arguing that this is "not a wise policy" is by connecting stock options to lower profits, via the idea that paying with stock options will undermine morale.

answers.text: Reductions in the profitability of a company are usually due to low employee morale.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: usually

We were told that a reduction in employee morale leads to a reduction in profitability.

I could similarly say, "being stung by a bee leads to a child crying". That doesn't mean I'm assuming that "the tears of children are usually due to a bee sting".

This author doesn't care if dips in profit are due to low employee morale 51% of the time (usually) vs. only 49% of the time (not-usually). 

This is essentially selling us a soft version of an illegal reversal. We were told this:
 if it lowers morale, then it lowers profits

And this answer is saying
 if profits are lower, then morale is usually lower

answers.text: Business firms that pay senior staff with stock options are less profitable than other firms.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Comparison

The author is only thinking that paying senior staff with stock options makes a company less profitable than it was before, not that it makes a company less profitable than other companies.

If Goldman Sachs, which makes billions in profits, decides to pay senior staff with stock options, the author thinks they will go from $50 B in profits to $40 B. But that doesn't mean the author assumes that Goldman Sachs is less profitable than firms who don't pay senior staff with stock options.

answers.text: Reducing the difference in income between senior staff and employees paid only a fixed salary invariably increases a company's profitability.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: invariably
Illegal Negation 

The author thinks that

   dramatically increasing            leads to 
  the diff in income between →   lower 
   seniors and fixed salary          profitability

This answer is trying to trap people into picking an illegal negation of that:

    decreasing the diff           leads to 
    in income between    →   higher 
 seniors and fixed salary      profitability

Negating this answer would give us, "There is at least one case in which the difference in income between senior and regular employees was reduced, but it did not increase a company's profitability". That wouldn't hurt the argument at all, so we know this answer can't be correct.

answers.text: Employees whose incomes rise as the profits of their employers rise are more productive than those paid only a fixed salary.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: productive

The concept of productivity is never discussed, so the author doesn't need to assume anything about that concept.

questiontext:
Statistics reveal that more collisions between bicycles and motor vehicles occur on roads having specifically designated bicycle lanes than on roads having no such lanes. Hence, adding such lanes to existing roads is unlikely to enhance the safety of bicyclists.

The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
gf:
Conclusion (Hence)

Adding specially marked bike lanes to existing roads is unlikely to enhance the safety of bicyclists.

Evidence

More collisions between bikes and vehicles occur on roads with specially marked bike lanes than without them.

Evaluate

This is an Anti-Causal conclusion, because the author is saying that specially marked bike lanes won't enhance the safety of people biking.

Since our job here is to object to the author's conclusion, we have to try to argue that "Adding marked bike lanes to existing roads would increase safety for bikers."

The author will retaliate by saying, "Then how come we see more collisions between bikes and cars on roads with special bike lanes than on roads without such markings? These statistics make it seem like having a bike lane is actually increasing the danger for bikers!"

We would have to Make an Excuse for that evidence, as we often do on Anti-Causal arguments.

Given our view ... bike lanes do increase safety
How can we explain why ... more collisions occur on roads with bike lanes?

It's probably because bike lanes are on really busy roads, and most collisions occur on really busy roads. It's also possible that bike lanes usually aren't added to a road unless it's a road where collisions between vehicles and bikes are more likely to occur.

Similarly, you would only install speed bumps on a street if that street had a preexisting problem with people speeding through it. 

A parallel argument to this could say, "Statistics reveal that more healthcare dollars are spend on people who suffer from medical conditions than on those who don't.  Hence, spending money on healthcare is unlikely to reduce one's suffering from medical conditions."

Goal

Look for an answer saying the argument fails to consider that bike lanes are taking a bad situation (an area where bikes keep getting hit by cars) and making them a better situation (bikes get hit less, once the bike lanes are installed, even though the number of collisions in these high traffic areas still outnumbers those in mellower roads where bike lanes aren't needed.

answers.text: overlooks the possibility that injuries sustained by bicyclists in accidents on roads with bicycle lanes are as serious, on average, as those sustained by bicyclists in accidents on roads without such lanes
answers.fb:
Not an Objection

Since this answer begins with fails to consider / overlooks the possibility, we can ask ourselves whether the idea that follows would Weaken.

Can we object by saying, "Hey, author --- adding bike lanes does enhance bike safety. After all, the injuries bikers get on roads with bike lanes are on average of the same severity as those bikers get on roads without bike lanes"?

No, if the injury severity is the same, then that doesn't help us argue that bike lanes enhance safety.

answers.text: fails to address the possibility that there are more bicyclists riding on roads with bicycle lanes than there are riding on roads without such lanes
answers.fb:
Correct

Since this answer begins with fails to consider / overlooks the possibility, we can ask ourselves whether the idea that follows would Weaken.

This idea allows us to object by saying, "Hey, author --- adding bike lanes does enhance bike safety. The reason statistics would show that more collisions occur on roads with bike lanes isn't because bike lanes aren't improving safety conditions, it's because there are more bicyclists riding on roads with bicycle lanes than there are riding on roads without such lanes."

answers.text: takes for granted that any road alteration that enhances the safety of bicyclists also enhances the safety of motorists
answers.fb:
Not Assumed / Too Strong: any

Since this answer begins with takes for granted / presumes, we can ask ourselves whether the idea that follows is a Necessary Assumption.

The author commit himself to the view that "every single road alteration ever that enhances bikers' safety also enhances motorists' safety"?

No. In addition to that being incredibly extreme, the argument never discusses improving motorists' safety at all.

answers.text: concludes that adding bicycle lanes to roads will fail to enhance the safety of bicyclists on the grounds that only some roads that currently have such lanes are safe
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

Since this answer has the structure
concludes that X on the grounds that Y
we'll ask ourselves whether X matches the conclusion and whether Y matches the evidence.

Did the author conclude, "adding bike lanes won't enhance safety of bicyclists"?

Yes. Good there.

Was the author's premise saying that, "only some roads with bike lanes are safe"?

Nope, it was a statistical figure that said "more collisions occur on roads w/ bike lanes than on those w/o."

answers.text: takes statistical evidence that fails to support a conclusion concerning the safety of bicyclists as evidence that proves the opposite conclusion
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match
Not "Unproven vs. Proven False"

Since this answer has the structure
takes X as evidence that Y
we'll ask ourselves whether X matches the evidence and whether Y matches the conclusion.

Did the author's evidence cite "statistical evidence that fails to support a conclusion"?

Huh? No. The author presented statistical evidence and considered it support for his conclusion.

This answer alludes to one of the 10 famous flaws, Unproven vs. Proven False.
