without these 
stricter regulations.

answers.text: In the city with the worst air pollution today, the air quality is better than it was 30 years ago.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Relationship

This assumes that the city with the worst air pollution today was one of the most polluted 30 years ago.

answers.text: No city has worse air pollution today than it did 30 years ago.
answers.fb:
Too Strong

While the statements indicate that this is true of the most polluted cities 30 years ago, it is not necessarily true for all cities.

answers.text: Most of the public outcries against pollution came from people in the cities that had the most polluted air.
answers.fb:
Supports the Inference

This supports the inference from the causal chain, but is not necessarily follow from the statements.

answers.text: The most polluted cities today are not the cities that were the most polluted 30 years ago.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Relationship

While it’s not that the most polluted cities improved their air quality, it could be true that all cities improved their air quality. It also could be the amount of improvement was the same everywhere. In which case the cities that were the most polluted 30 years ago would still be the most polluted today.

answers.text: Public criticism led to an improvement in the air quality of the cities that had the most polluted air 30 years ago.
answers.fb:
Correct

This connects the           PO -causes↣ SR -causes↣ IAQ
causal chain implied 
by the statements.

questiontext:
Researcher: Accurate readings of air pollution are expensive to obtain. Lichens are complex plantlike organisms that absorb airborne pollutants and so may offer a cheaper way to monitor air quality. To investigate this, I harvested lichens at sites plagued by airborne copper pollution, determined the lichens' copper concentration, and compared the results with those acquired using mechanical monitoring devices. The lichens were as accurate as the best equipment available. Thus, lichens can effectively replace expensive pollution- monitoring devices without loss of information.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's argument?
gf:
Conclusion (thus)

Lichens can effectively replace expensive pollution monitoring devices without loss of information.

Evidence

Tests have shown that lichens are just as accurate as the best equipment available in measuring copper pollution.

Evaluate

This is a "Strengthen" question where we need to find an answer that reinforces the conclusion about lichens being a viable replacement for pollution monitoring devices. Since the evidence only directly mentions copper, the conclusion's broad claim might be vulnerable to questions about lichens' effectiveness with other pollutants.

Goal

Identify an answer choice that demonstrates lichens' effectiveness across a range of pollutants, thereby reinforcing the conclusion that they can replace existing devices broadly.

answers.text: Mechanical monitoring devices have not already been installed in areas where air pollution is a serious problem.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This discusses the lack of installed devices in areas with severe pollution, which doesn't relate to lichens' effectiveness as pollution monitors or strengthen their utility as replacements.

answers.text: Copper particles are a component of air pollution in several locales.
answers.fb:
Weak Strength

This indicates that copper is a component of pollution in several places, suggesting limited applicability. It doesn't bolster the broad conclusion that lichens can replace devices everywhere.

answers.text: Experiments have shown that lichens thrive in areas where air pollution is minimal.
answers.fb:
Weakens

This claims lichens thrive where pollution is minimal, implying they may not function well in polluted areas, undermining the argument that they can monitor high-pollution environments effectively.

answers.text: Lichens can easily be grown in laboratories.
answers.fb:
Weak Strength

This suggests lichens can be easily grown, hinting at accessibility. However, it doesn't address their effectiveness or capacity for comprehensive pollution monitoring compared to existing devices.

answers.text: Lichens absorb all other significant air pollutants in a manner similar to their absorption of copper.
answers.fb:
Correct

This choice directly strengthens the argument by asserting that lichens are as effective with all other significant air pollutants as they are with copper. It addresses the main objection to the conclusion by showing that lichens' effectiveness isn't limited to copper, but extends to other pollutants, supporting their use as a comprehensive monitoring solution.

questiontext:
Dried parsley should never be used in cooking, for it is far less tasty and healthful than fresh parsley is.

Which one of the following principles, if valid, most clearly helps to justify the argument above?
gf:
Conclusion

Dried parsley should never be used in cooking.

Evidence (for)

It is far less tasty and healthful than fresh parsley is.

Evaluate

Our default mode of prephrasing on Strengthen-Principle is to just write a "IF premise, THEN, conclusion" rule.

We're trying to prove "should never be used in cooking" about dried parsley and what we know about dried parsley is that it's less tasty and less healthful than fresh parsley. 

Goal

So let's look for an answer like any of these:
      if it's less tasty    →  then should never be
   than fresh parsley        used in cooking 

  if it's less healthful  →  then should never be
   than fresh parsley           used in cooking

   if it's less tasty and 
    and less healthful   → then should never be 
   than fresh parsley            used in cooking

answers.text: Fresh ingredients should be used in cooking whenever possible.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This rule helps us prove that we should use something in cooking, but we're looking for a rule that allows us to prove that we should never use something in cooking.

    If fresh ingredients  → then they should
       are possible                  be used

This rule does nothing to prove that we should never use dried parsley. After all, if no fresh ingredients are available, this rule is perfectly fine with us using dried parsley.

answers.text: Only the tastiest ingredients should ever be used in cooking.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is a rule that would allow us to prove we should not use something in cooking. Like so many correct answers on Sufficient Assumption and Strengthen + Principle, it's written in contrapositive form of how we need it. The word "only" or "only if" always signifies a necessary condition (right side of the arrow).

How it's written:
 Should ever be used → Tastiest ingredients

Contrapositive:
  Not tastiest ingredient → Should never be used

Do we know whether or not dried parsley is the "tastiest ingredient"?

Yes! We know it's not the #1 tastiest ingredient, because it's less tasty than fresh parsley. So even within its own division (the Parsley division), it's not #1 tastiest.

This rule applies to dried parsley and outputs the idea that "dried parsley should never be used in cooking", so it actually proves the conclusion true.

answers.text: Ingredients that should never be used in cooking are generally neither tasty nor healthful.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This is putting the conclusion on the Left side of the arrow, but we always have to have the right side of the arrow match the conclusion.

This rule says:

Ingredient should never → probably not tasty
  be used in cooking            and not healthful

That's a total dealbreaker. But even if the conclusion were on the right, if we reversed this rule, we couldn't trigger the other idea.

The evidence never said that dried parsley was "not tasty" or "not healthful". It said it was "less tasty" and "less healthful". That distinction between Absolute and Relative language is crucial throughout LSAT.

answers.text: Parsley that is not both tasty and healthful should never be used in cooking.
answers.fb:
Weak Evidence Match
Relative vs.  Absolute

This is a super tempting answer, because it has our conclusion on the right side of the arrow and the trigger attempts to use both of the facts we were told about dried parsley.

  Not Tasty          Should never
      and         →    be used in 
Not Healthful         cooking

But do we know that dried parsley is "not tasty" and "not healthful"? No. We only know that it's far less tasty and less healthful than fresh parsley is.

Frozen broccoli is far less healthful than fresh broccoli, but would we call frozen broccoli "not healthful"? Peanuts are far less tasty than ice cream, but would we call peanuts "not tasty"?

LSAT constantly measures us on our ability to distinguish between Relative expressions "less healthful / less tasty" and Absolute expressions "not healthful / not tasty".

answers.text: In cooking, dried ingredients are inferior to fresh ingredients.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

This rule allows us to prove that dried parsley is inferior to fresh parsley, but does that mean we should "never use it in cooking"?

It supports that idea somewhat, but the correct answer full-on proves that we should never use dried parsley in cooking, so there's no way that we can say that this answer is the one that most justifies the argument.

questiontext:
The size of northern fur seals provides a reliable indication of their population levels—the smaller the average body size of seals in a population, the larger the population. Archaeologists studied seal fossils covering an 800-year period when the seals were hunted for food by Native peoples in North America and found that the average body size of the seals did not vary significantly.

The statements above, if true, provide the most support for which one of the following?
gf:
Statements

Volume Dial  (the more x, the more y)
The size of northern fur seals is a good indicator of their population levels:

The smaller the size, the larger the population.

Over an 800 year period, the average body size did not vary significantly.

Evaluate

By applying our Volume Dial relationship to this provided fact, we should be able to derive the idea that

Over this 800 year period, the average population size of seals did not vary significantly.

Goal

Since there are only two claims, and the overlapping concept is "body size", we're being sent a strong message that we're supposed to apply this rule to this fact.

So let's look for an answer saying or reinforcing the idea that "in this 800 year period where northern fur seals were hunted for food by Native peoples in North America, average population size of northern fur seals stayed pretty constant".

answers.text: During the 800-year period studied, seal hunting practices did not vary substantially between different groups of Native peoples in North America.
answers.fb:
Speculates Causal Backstory

What we know is that population size of these seals didn't change much, while they were being hunted by Native peoples for 800 years.

Is that because "the Native people didn't change their hunting practices that much"?

Could be. But certainly doesn't have to be. It might be that the Native people changed their hunting practices a lot, but they always kept an eye on population size of these fur seals and aimed to keep it stable.

answers.text: The body size of northern fur seals is not strongly correlated with the overall health of the seals.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: overall health

Since the paragraph never mentions the "overall health" of the seals, we have no idea whether body size is or isn't correlated with overall health.

answers.text: Before the 800-year period studied, the average body size of northern fur seals fluctuated dramatically.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: before this period
Too Strong: dramatically

Since we only received information about this 800 year period, we can't say anything about whether body size or population size fluctuated at all, let alone dramatically in the period prior to this 800 years.

answers.text: Native peoples in North America made an effort to limit their hunting of northern fur seals in order to prevent depletion of seal populations.
answers.fb:
Speculates Causal Backstory

What we know is that population size of these seals didn't change much, while they were being hunted by Native peoples for 800 years.

Is that because "the Native people made an effort to stabilize population size of the fur seals"?

Could be. But certainly doesn't have to be. It might be also be that as the Native peoples increased their hunting of seals, one of the seals' other predators started to vanish from the ecosystem, so the net effect was a similar population size of seals.

answers.text: Hunting by Native peoples in North America did not significantly reduce the northern fur seal population over the 800-year period studied.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is the most neutral (albeit, disguised) restatement of the fact we inferred:  "population size didn't change much over those 800 years".

It isn't speculating a reason why. It's just factually saying, "Hunting by Native peoples didn't make a huge reduction in the seal population".

We could similarly infer, "Asteroid impacts didn't make a huge reduction in the seal population"

How could we infer that? We know that there wasn't a huge reduction in the seal population!

questiontext:
After an oil spill, rehabilitation centers were set up to save sea otters by removing oil from them. The effort was not worthwhile, however, since 357 affected live otters and 900 that had died were counted, but only 222 affected otters, or 18 percent of those counted, were successfully rehabilitated and survived. Further, the percentage of all those affected that were successfully rehabilitated was much lower still, because only a fifth of the otters that died immediately were ever found.

Which one of the following, as potential challenges, most seriously calls into question evidence offered in support of the conclusion above?
gf:
Conclusion

The effort to set up rehab centers in order to save sea otters from the oil spill wasn't worthwhile.

Evidence

900 of the otters the rehab center counted were already dead. 222 of the 357 that were alive were saved. But only 1/5 of the otters that died were ever found.

Evaluation

This question stem specifically asks us to undermine the evidence, as opposed to the typical wording: undermine the argument/reasoning.

What could be wrong with the evidence? It seems like we could say, "saving 222 of 357 is still worthwhile!". Maybe without saving those 222, this sea otter population would have no chance to recover, but saving this many of them at least lets these otters one day rebuild their numbers.

The last claim is also perplexing: they only found 1/5 of the otters that died. How do they know that the dead ones they've found are 1/5 of the dead ones? Where'd they get that total from?

Goal

Look for something making the evidence seem less trustworthy or less likely to lead us to conclude that these efforts weren't worthwhile.

answers.text: Do sea otters of species other than those represented among the otters counted exist in areas that were not affected by the oil spill?
answers.fb:
No Impact

Let's say that at the rehab center, we were counting Species X sea otters. This is asking, "Are there other types of sea otters, of Species Y and Z, that live somewhere far away from the oil spill?"

Who cares? What would they have to do with analyzing the sea otters who were harmed / killed / rehabilitated from the oil spill?

answers.text: How is it possible to estimate, of the sea otters that died, how many were not found?
answers.fb:
Correct

This challenges the evidence in the final sentence. If you were rummaging through your dead Grandma's estate and found ten letters written during WWII, would you be able to say, "This is only 1/5 of the letters she wrote"?
 

Of course not. Not unless you had prior knowledge of how many total letters she wrote during WWII. If you don't know the total, then you can't put a percentage to the number of letters you've found.

Similarly, how would scientists know the total number of otters that died? Did they know the initial size of the local otter population? Did they test all the otters they could and then assume that the ones they didn't see were all dead?

answers.text: Did the process of capturing sea otters unavoidably involve trapping and releasing some otters that were not affected by the spill?
answers.fb:
Not Related To Evience

This might help one argue that the rehab effort was not worthwhile (i.e. "Not only did we not save a ton of otters, but we also trapped and released a bunch of otters that weren't affected"), but it has nothing to do with the question task of challenging the evidence.

answers.text: Were other species of wildlife besides sea otters negatively affected by the oil spill?
answers.fb:
Not Related To Evidence

These rehab centers were "set up to save sea otters", so whether or not other marine life was affected by the oil spill is immaterial to assessing these rehab centers. 

If there were other species negatively affected, how would that challenge either of the evidentiary claims presented about sea otters?

answers.text: What was the eventual cost, per otter rehabilitated, of the rehabilitation operation?
answers.fb:
Not Related To Evidence

In terms of assessing the Conclusion, of whether these efforts for "worthwhile", we could probably consider cost a relevant factor. How many otters did we save and what cost? 

However, the cost per otter wouldn't represent a challenge to either of the pieces of evidence offered.

questiontext:
Plumb-Ace advertises that its plumbers are more qualified than plumbers at any other major plumbing firm in the region because Plumb-Ace plumbers must complete a very difficult certification process. Plumb-Ace plumbers may or may not be more qualified, but clearly the certification process is not very difficult, because nearly everyone who takes the written portion of the certification exam passes it very easily.

The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that it
gf:
Conclusion (clearly)

The certification process at Plumb-Ace is not very difficult.

Evidence (because)

Nearly everyone who takes the written portion of the certification exam passes it very easily.

Evaluate

Given that ... nearly everyone who takes the written portion passes it,
How could we still argue that ... the certification process is very difficult?

For me, this took me back to being 16 again. The written portion of the driver's license test wasn't scary. Almost everyone I knew passed that with little prep. But the driving portion of the driver's license test was famous for flunking people. You had to master 3-point turns, parallel parking, checking blind spots, hands at 10 & 2, etc.

Similarly, maybe it's easy to pass the written portion of this plumbing certification but it's really hard to pass other portions of the test (like where you have to rebuild a toilet from scratch).

This argument seems to resemble one of our top 10 famous flaws, Part vs. Whole. The argument is thinking that because PART of the process is not very difficult (almost everyone passes it very easily) it must be that the WHOLE process is not very difficult.

Goal

Let's look for an answer choice pointing out that other aspects of the test might be really hard to pass.

Or look for an answer describing this flawed move from Part to Whole.

answers.text: treats something that is necessary to make a certification process very difficult as if it were sufficient by itself to make the process very difficult
answers.fb:
Not Necessary vs. Sufficient

This describes the #1 famous flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient, in which an author presents a conditional logic rule as one of his premises, but then applies that rule illegally in some reversed or negated fashion.

There's no conditional logic premise here, so no chance this is correct.

The only premise is "nearly everyone who takes the written portion passes it easily."

answers.text: takes for granted that plumbers are not qualified unless they complete some certification process
answers.fb:
Too Strong: unless
Not Assumed

When a flaw answer starts with takes for granted / presumes / fails to establish, we can ask ourselves whether the author needed to assume the idea that follows.

Did this author logically commit himself to believing this:

  If you haven't completed   →  then you are not
some certification process             qualified

Definitely not. This doesn't reflect any reasoning move the author made. He made only one move:

If the written portion of    →   then the overall
    some certification                process is not
 process is not difficult                  difficult

answers.text: overlooks the possibility that plumbers at other firms in the region complete certification processes that are even easier than that completed by Plumb-Ace's plumbers
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Objection
Relative vs. Absolute

When a flaw answer starts with fails to consider / overlooks the possibility, we can ask ourselves whether the idea that follows sounds like a weakening objection.

Can we hurt the argument by saying, "Hey, author -- the certification at other plumbing agencies is even easier than at Plumb-Ace"?

No. Establishing that other tests are even easier doesn't establish that this test is difficult. It only establishes that this test is more difficult. 

LSAT frequently tests this distinction between Relative and Absolute language.

If I say, "This 2nd grade math test is hard. After all, the 1st grade math test is even easier", you would correctly say, "This 2nd grade math test is not hard. It's harder than a 1st grade test, but it's not hard."

answers.text: infers that a claim is false on the grounds that an inadequate argument has been given for that claim
answers.fb:
Not Unproven vs. Proven False
Bad Evidence Match

This describes the famous flaw, Unproven vs. Proven False, in which an author concludes that someone's claim is wrong, merely because they unsuccessfully tried to prove it was true.

Here, the author does infer that the claim "this certification process is very difficult" is false. Does his evidence describe the argument that Plumb-Ace makes in favor of claiming that it's very difficult?

No. His evidence doesn't reference Plumb-Ace's argument for this claim at all. His evidence merely points to the very high passing rate for the written portion.

answers.text: presumes that since one part of a whole lacks a certain characteristic, the whole must lack that characteristic as well
answers.fb:
Correct

This describes the famous Part vs. Whole flaw.

Because this answer presents a two-part move (since X, Y), we want to ask ourselves whether we can match this to the argument.

Did the author's evidence say that,
one part of a whole lacks a certain characteristic?

Yes. The written portion is a part of the whole certification process, and the author is showing that the this part lacks the characteristic of being "very difficult" (after all, almost everyone passes it very easily).

Does the author's conclusion act like
the whole must lack that characteristic as well?

Yes. The conclusion is that the certification process overall clearly lacks the characteristic of being "very difficult".

questiontext:
While biodiversity is indispensable to the survival of life on Earth, biodiversity does not require the survival of every currently existing species. For there to be life on Earth, various ecological niches must be filled; many niches, however, can be filled by more than one species.

Which one of the following statements most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the argument?
gf:
Conclusion 

Biodiversity does not require the survival of every currently existing species.

Evidence

While life does require various niches to be filled, many niches can be filled by more than one species.

Evaluate

Whenever we do Main Conclusion (or Role) we remind ourselves that the  85-90% of the time the conclusion will be earlier than the evidence.

It's usually the First Sentence or some Pivot / Rebuttal idea in the middle. 

Does this first sentence sound like an opinion from the author? Not really. There's no opinion indicator in there. It sounds more like a science-y nature fact.

But does the paragraph go on to support that first claim? Yes!

All the claims in this argument sound like science-y nature facts, so we can't differentiate the Conclusion by sorting out which claim is the opinion vs. which is the fact.

So we have to use our other tool ("Which claim is being supported by at least one other claim") and if possible to use our test savvy and lean in to the expectation that the conclusion usually is earlier than the evidence.

Goal

We want to find the answer choice that gives us the best meaning match for "biodiversity does not require the survival of every currently existing species". 

We might rephrase that as something like, "Some currently existing species could go extinct without threatening biodiversity".

answers.text: Biodiversity does not require that all existing species continue to exist.
answers.fb:
Correct

This matches the 2nd claim in the first sentence, our conclusion.

It is the only claim in this paragraph that receives support from another claim.

Why should we believe that biodiversity doesn't require all existing species continue to exist?

Because, many ecological niches can be filled by more than one species.

answers.text: There are various ecological niches that must be filled if there is to be life on Earth.
answers.fb:
Premise

This matches the 3rd claim of the paragraph (there are 4 total). The main conclusion was the 2nd claim.

We know this isn't a conclusion because no support is provided. The author gives us no reason why we should believe that various niches must be filled in order for there to be life on Earth.

answers.text: The survival of life on Earth depends upon biodiversity.
answers.fb:
Background Fact

This matches the 1st claim of the paragraph (there are 4 total). The main conclusion was the 2nd claim.

We know this isn't a conclusion because no support is provided. The author gives us no reason to think that the survival of life depends upon biodiversity.

We can rest assured that a conclusion would never be prefaced with concession/qualification wording like "although / despite / while".

answers.text: There are many ecological niches that can be filled by more than one species.
answers.fb:
Premise

This matches the 4th claim of the paragraph (there are 4 total). The main conclusion was the 2nd claim.

We know this isn't a conclusion because no support is provided. The author gives us no reason why we should believe that many niches can be filled by more than one species.

answers.text: The species most indispensable for biodiversity fill more than one ecological niche.
answers.fb:
Unstated

Nothing like this was said in the paragraph, so it can't be our Main Conclusion.

The paragraph never talks about which species are most indispensable.

questiontext:
Scientist: Rattlesnakes prey on young California ground squirrels. Protective adult squirrels harass a threatening rattlesnake by puffing up their tails and wagging them. New results show that the squirrel's tail also heats up when harassing a rattlesnake. Since rattlesnakes have an infrared sensing organ that detects body heat, the heating up of the squirrel's tail probably plays a role in repelling rattlesnakes.

Which one of the following, if true, most helps to support the scientist's hypothesis?
gf:
Conclusion (hypothesis)

When squirrels puff up their tails, the tail heats up, which the snakes can detect through infrared sensing, which causes them to back off.

Evidence

Snakes can be repelled by the way adult squirrels puff up their tails and wag them.

Evaluate

As soon as we see the word "hypothesis" in our question stem, we know this will conform to the Explain Curious Fact framework. 

CURIOUS FACT: why does the puffed squirrel tail repel the rattlesnake?
EXPLANATION: the snake senses the heat from the tail and doesn't like it

Goal

We can strengthen by ruling out an alternate explanation or by boosting the plausibility of the author's explanation. The latter is much more likely on Strengthen questions. In particular, they love to boost plausibility with "no cause, no effect" answers. Here that would sound something like, "when the tail isn't hot / when they can't sense the heat, the snakes aren't repelled".

answers.text: Rattlesnakes do not have the ability to increase the temperature of their tails.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Quality

We're trying to assess whether rattlesnakes are repelled by a squirrel tail's heat, not whether rattlesnakes are capable of heating their own tail.

answers.text: Squirrels puff up their tails and wag them when they attempt to attract the attention of other squirrels.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This discusses another instance in which squirrels puff their tails, which is irrelevant to the instance we're analyzing. 

We're trying to figure out why snakes are repelled by the puffed tail, and this answer has nothing to do with that.

answers.text: Rattlesnakes react much more defensively when confronted with a squirrel whose tail is heated up than when confronted with one whose tail is not.
answers.fb:
Correct

This choice effectively uses a "no cause, no effect" scenario: rattlesnakes react more defensively to a hot tail than a non-hot tail. It supports the hypothesis by illustrating that the heat is a crucial factor in repelling rattlesnakes, thus strengthening the argument.

answers.text: The rattlesnake is not the only predator of the California ground squirrel that causes it to engage in harassing behavior as a defensive mechanism.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This choice mentions that squirrels shake their tails at other predators, which doesn't do anything to strengthen the hypothesis about rattlesnakes being repelled by the heat.

answers.text: Mammals such as the California ground squirrel have no organ for sensing infrared energy.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The hypothesis involves the snakes having an infrared sense, so that they can register the heat of the squirrel's tail and be bugged out. But we don't care whether squirrels have an infrared sense.

questiontext:
Talbert: Chess is beneficial for school-age children. It is enjoyable, encourages foresight and logical thinking, and discourages carelessness, inattention, and impulsiveness. In short, it promotes mental maturity.

Sklar: My objection to teaching chess to children is that it diverts mental activity from something with societal value, such as science, into something that has no societal value.

Talbert's and Sklar's statements provide the strongest support for holding that they disagree with each other over whether

answers.text: chess promotes mental maturity
answers.fb:
Unsupported Disagree Position

Although it's clear that Person 1 believes this, we can't well support that Person 2 believes that "chess does not promote mental maturity".

Our only support would be "chess has no societal value", which isn't nothing, but it's easier with the correct answer to support the Agree and Disagree positions.

answers.text: many activities promote mental maturity just as well as chess does
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: other activities
Unsupported Comparison: just as well

We wouldn't be able to extract this idea from either paragraph. No one is comparing how well chess promotes mental maturity to how well other activities do.

answers.text: chess is socially valuable and science is not
answers.fb:
Unsupported Agree Position

We know that Person 2 thinks that science is valuable. But we couldn't derive from Person 1 that science is not valuable.

answers.text: children should be taught to play chess
answers.fb:
Correct

Person 1 seems to believe this (it's beneficial and has all these positives), while Person 2 seems to think children should not be taught to play chess (it has no societal value and diverts attention from things that do).

answers.text: children who neither play chess nor study science are mentally immature
answers.fb:
Out of Scope

We never talk about kids who don't play chess and don't study science.

questiontext:
Popular science publications that explain new developments in science face a dilemma. In order to reach a wide audience, these publications must rely heavily on metaphorical writing, which usually fails to convey the science accurately. If the writing is more rigorous, they get the science right but fail to reach a wide audience. These publications should therefore give up trying to explain new developments in science to a wide audience.

Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in the argument?

answers.text: Science publications should balance the use of metaphors with more rigorous writing.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

We need an answer that says we should go towards the rigorous, accurate direction and away from the metaphorical, inaccurate direction.

So "balancing them" feels almost like the opposite of what we want.

answers.text: The more recent a scientific development is, the harder it is to explain it accurately to a wide audience.
answers.fb:
No Distinction

We need an answer that says we should go towards the rigorous, accurate direction and away from the metaphorical, inaccurate direction.

This doesn't offer us any distinction between those two options. It just says "newer = harder". 

We know. That was basically a background premise. But how should we deal with these harder / newer developments? The rigorous/accurate way or the metaphorical/popular way?

answers.text: In reporting scientific developments, it is better to fail to reach a wide audience than to be inaccurate.
answers.fb:
Correct

We need an answer that says we should go towards the rigorous, accurate direction and away from the metaphorical, inaccurate direction.

This tips the scales in that direction. The author was Weighing Tradeoffs and her conclusion indicates that she would rather avoid being inaccurate than seek a wide audience.

answers.text: In reporting scientific developments, it is better to reach a wide audience than to be accurate.
answers.fb:
Opposite

We need an answer that says we should go towards the rigorous, accurate direction and away from the metaphorical, inaccurate direction.

This is saying we should go towards the metaphorical direction that reaches a wide audience.

The company president says that significant procedural changes were made before either she or Yeung was told about them. But, according to Grimes, the contract requires that either the company president or any lawyer in the company’s legal department be told about proposed procedural changes before they are made. Thus, unless what Grimes or the company president said is incorrect, the contract was violated.

The argument's conclusion can be properly inferred if which one of the following is assumed?

Conclusion

Assuming what Grimes and the president said is true, the contract was violated.

Evidence

(Assuming the truth of their statements) 
The contract states that a big change can't be made unless the president or a member of the legal department is told. 

Neither the president nor Yeung was told about the big changes.

Evaluate

Okay, so we have a clearly defined goal -- the contract was violated. 
To reach that verdict, we just have to establish that neither the president nor  anyone on the legal team was told about the change in advance.

We already know that president wasn't told in advance.

So we just need to establish that no one on the legal team was told. We know that Yeung was not told, but who cares? We don't know if Yeung is on the legal team, and even if he is, we'd still need to ask the rest of the legal team if any of them were told about the big change.

answers.fb:
Strengthens, Doesn't Prove

Our job is to establish that no one in the legal department was told about this big procedural change.

answers.text: Neither Grimes nor Yeung was told about the procedural changes until after they were made.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

All we care about is whether or not anyone in the legal department was notified of these big changes. If it's not talking about that (as this is not), then it's useless to our goal of proving the contract was violated.

answers.text: No lawyer in the company’s legal department was told about the procedural changes until after they were made.

Correct

answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

All we care about is whether or not anyone in the legal department was notified of these big changes. If it's not talking about that (as this is not), then it's useless to our goal of proving the contract was violated.

While studying a large colony of macaque monkeys, scientists interacting with baby monkeys under a week old found that the babies would imitate some, but not all, of the scientists' actions. The babies readily smacked their lips and stuck out their tongues when the scientists did, but stared impassively when the scientists opened and closed their mouths or made hand gestures. Of these four kinds of actions, only lip smacking and sticking out the tongue are used by adult macaques when interacting with babies.

The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

answers.text: Baby macaques under a week old are natural mimics of whatever they see.
answers.fb:
Contradicted (if anything)

The babies did NOT imitate two of the behaviors they saw from the scientists.

answers.fb:
Too Speculative: can't control muscles

While this could explain why they didn't imitate the hand gestures, so could many other hypotheses. 

We have no support for this specific hypothesis, so it's too speculative.

answers.text: Adult macaques use lip smacking and sticking out the tongue to entertain infant macaques.
answers.fb:
Unsupported Causality: to entertain

This is speculating the causal backstory on why adults smack their lips and stick out their tongues.

Maybe it's to entertain. Maybe it serves a different function. We have no way to support one theory over another.

The fact that the babies only imitated stuff their true parents did suggests more that babies could tell the difference.

answers.fb:
Correct

While "only" feels strong, this is still the best available answer. It matches the available data.

Acme's bank loan must be immediately repaid in full if Acme's earnings fall below $1 million per year. If Acme has to repay the entire loan immediately, it will have to declare bankruptcy. Acme had seemed safe from bankruptcy, having reported annual earnings of well over $1 million in each year it has had the bank loan. The argument requires the assumption that
gf:

ACME will have to declare bankruptcy.

Evidence

ACME has overstated its earnings for last year.

And if its loan must be immediately repaid, then it will have to declare bankruptcy.

Evaluate

The argument is trying to prove that ACME will have to declare bankruptcy, and it provided two conditional premises that end with that idea:

 earnings fall         loan must       have to
below $1 mill  →  be immed  →  declare
  this year               repaid           bankrupty

All the author has to do is tell us that ACME's earnings fell below $1 million last year.

Did she ever say that?

No. She only said that they admitted to overstating their earnings from last year.

Goal

Let's look for the missing Trigger Fact:
their earnings fell below $1 million

It's also possible they would present it as a Missing Link:
if overstated last year's earnings, then earnings were below $1 million

answers.text: Acme's earnings for last year, when accurately stated, are below $1 million

This is the fact that triggers bankruptcy, so the author needs to assume it's true in order to assume they'll have to declare bankruptcy.

If we negated this and said, "Their earnings last year were at least $1 million", then there'd be no reason to think they need to declare bankruptcy.

But the author doesn't need their earnings to be below $1 million this year.

questiontext:
Economist: Unemployment will soon decrease. If total government spending significantly increases next year, the economy will be stimulated in the short term and unemployment will decrease. If, on the other hand, total government spending significantly decreases next year, businesses will retain more of their earnings in the short term and employ more workers, thereby decreasing unemployment.

The conclusion drawn by the economist is properly inferred if which one of the following is assumed?
gf:
Conclusion

Unemployment will soon decrease.

Evidence

If total govt spending significantly goes up, unemployment will decrease.

If total govt spending significantly decreases, unemployment will decrease.

Evaluate

We ascertain that the first claim is the conclusion by seeing that the other two claims are clearly meant to work together. Conjunctions/connections like "and / but / on the other hand" show us that two claims are interacting together to move the argument forward.

Each of the conditional premises involves TWO consequences, one of which is decreasing unemployment. I didn't bother writing out the other half of each outcome, because all we care about is proving that there will be decreasing unemployment.

At first, this argument seems pretty reasonable. It seems like an Either Way You Slice It style of argument:  "Whether spending increases significantly or decreases significantly, we end up with decreasing unemployment. So either way you slice it, we're gonna have decreasing unemployment."

But we know that an argument on Sufficient Assumption can't already be airtight. There has to be some gap, so that the correct answer can make it airtight. 

How would unemployment fail to decrease?

Well, I guess spending doesn't necessarily have to go significantly up or significantly down. It could more or less stay the same.

The author is presenting a False Choice (a false binary / a false dichotomy), acting like spending will either go up a bunch or down a bunch.

But she's failing to consider the middle ground, where spending basically stays the same.

Goal

We just need to rule out the possibility that govt spending will stay basically the same. We need to know that it'll definitely go up or down significantly.

answers.text: Either total government spending will significantly decrease next year or else total government spending will significantly increase next year.
answers.fb:
Correct

Well, that was quick! We're done here. This is what we wanted.

This guarantees that one or the other of the two conditional premises will get triggered, and each of those conditional premises guaranteed that unemployment will decrease.

So this answer gives us the Either Way You Slice It certainty that one way or the other, unemployment will decrease.

answers.text: Government officials are currently implementing policies that are intended to reduce unemployment.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal: nothing about spending

Since this doesn't tell us whether spending will go up or down, it doesn't do the job we need it to do.

answers.text: If there is a significantly increased demand for workers, then there will be a significant decrease in unemployment.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal: nothing about spending

Since this doesn't tell us whether spending will gone up or down, it doesn't do the job we need it to do.

answers.text: A significant increase in total government spending will slow the economy in the long run.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal: nothing about spending

Since this doesn't tell us whether spending will go up or down, it doesn't do the job we need it to do.

answers.text: If the economy is not stimulated and businesses do not retain more of their earnings, then unemployment will not decrease.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal: nothing about spending

Since this doesn't tell us whether spending will go up or down, it doesn't do the job we need it to do.

questiontext:
Archaeologist: Neanderthals, a human-like species living 60,000 years ago, probably preserved meat found in many Neanderthal fireplaces. Burnt lichen and grass have been found in many Neanderthal fireplaces. A fire of lichen and grass produces a lot of smoke but does not produce nearly as much heat or light as a wood fire.

Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the archaeologist's argument?
gf:
Conclusion (probably)

Neanderthals probably preserved meat found in many Neanderthal fireplaces.

Evidence

Burnt lichen and grass have been found in N. fireplaces, and a fire of lichen/grass produces a lot of smoke but doesn't produce nearly as much heat/light as a wood fire.

Evaluate

There is a missing link assumption somewhere, since "preserved meat" appears only in the Conclusion. What is "preserved meat" attached to in the Evidence?

Apparently, we're assuming that fires that produce a lot of smoke but not a lot of heat/light are good for preserving meat.

However, since we're interpreting the significance of archaeological evidence, we could also use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. 

Curious Fact 
What are all these burnt lichen/grass fires all about? They produce a lot of smoke, but they don't produce as much heat or light as a wood fire.

Author's Explanation 
The lichen/grass smoky fires were created to smoke meat, for preservation. 

We're supposed to react to this template by considering 2 different things: 
- could there be an Alternative Explanation for this Curious Fact? 
- how plausible is the Author's Explanation?

So why else might the Neanderthals have been burning smoky lichen/grass fires? Maybe they didn't have any wood, so this was the best they could get. Maybe it kept away some predators. Maybe it was for some other cooking purpose. 

How plausible is the Author's Explanation? His story assumes that there was meat around, that Neanderthals were aware that if you smoked meat it would preserve for longer, that they had any need/use for preserved meat, etc.

Goal

Since this is Weaken, we want an answer to  
suggest an Alternate Explanation for why they were making lichen/grass smoky fires, 
or to 
hurt the plausibility of the story that they were making these smoky fires in order to preserve meat.

answers.text: In close proximity to the fireplaces with lichen and grass are other fireplaces that, evidence suggests, burned material that produced more heat than smoke.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This rules out the idea that they were using lichen/grass fires for their regular cooking, because they were desperate and had to settle for a crappy fire.

According to this answer, they definitely had access to something like wood fires, so using the smoky grass fire was a choice, not a necessity.

That rules out an alternate explanation, so it strengthens.

answers.text: In the region containing the Neanderthal fireplaces in which lichen and grass were burnt, no plants that could be burned more effectively to produce heat or light were available 60,000 years ago.
answers.fb:
Correct

This suggests an Alternate Explanation: they were setting lichen/grass fires for all their fire needs, because they were desperate and had to settle for a crappy fire.

They didn't have any better options for fire than lichen/grass. So we shouldn't interpret their smoky fires in the sense of, "Hmmm, they must have really wanted smoke for some reasons. I know — they were preserving meats!" 

Instead, we should interpret their smoky fires as, "In this area where they lived, that type of fire was the best you could do." They weren't seeking the smoky quality because it would work well for a niche meat-preserving technique. They were stuck with the smoky quality because it was their only source of fire.

Could they still have preserved meats with those smoky fires? Sure. But the reason this answer weakens is because it suffices to explain the smoky fires. We don't need to invent the 'preserved meat' hypothesis in order to explain smoky fires, if smoky fires were the only type of fire possible for these guys.

answers.text: Some of the fireplaces containing burnt lichen are in regions in which lichen is not believed to have been plentiful and so would have had to have been brought in from some distance.
answers.fb:
Too Weak
Strengthens, if Anything

Words that mean "at least one data point", such as some / sometimes / can / may / might / could / not all, are almost always wrong on Strengthen, Weaken, and Paradox. They don't have much impact.

In this case, the data point would be a Strengthening one, anyway. If the Neanderthals are going out of there way to procure this lichen for the sake of getting a smoky grass fire going, then they have some specific plans with this lichen, some specific needs. This boosts the plausibility that they were engaged in some very intentional cooking technique like smoking meat to preserve it.

answers.text: There is clear evidence that at least some groups of Neanderthals living more recently than 60,000 years ago developed methods of preserving meat other than smoking it.
answers.fb:
Strengthens, if Anything

We don't care much about what was happening with Neanderthals later in time. But if the later Neanderthals preserved meat, then that adds some plausibility to the notion that the earlier Neanderthals (of 60,000 years ago) preserved meat.

The fact that the later Neanderthals did so by some way other than smoking the meat doesn't really undermine that. The author's conclusion is that the Neanderthals probably preserved meat. That conclusion doesn't care by what means they preserved it. The author is definitely assuming that these N's from 60,000 years ago with the lichen/grass fires did so by smoking it, but she's not assuming all N's did it that way.

answers.text: The ability to preserve meat through smoking would have made the Neanderthal humans less vulnerable to poor periods of hunting.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This adds some plausibility to the Author's Explanation. It offers a reason why the Neanderthals would have had a vested interest in developing the technique of smoking meat to preserve it.

questiontext:
Jenkins maintains that the movie Firepower was not intended to provoke antisocial behavior, arguing that, on the contrary, it is in the interest of Firepower's director to prevent such behavior. Yet Jenkins's conclusion must be rejected, because the movie has clearly produced antisocial behavior among many of those who have seen it.

The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that it
gf:
Conclusion

Jenkin's conclusion must be rejected.

rephrase: The movie 'Firepower' was intended to provoke antisocial behavior

Evidence (because)

The movie has clearly produced antisocial behavior among many of those who have seen it.

Evaluate

Our author is rebutting Jenkins' conclusion. Jenkins concluded that Firepower wasn't intended to provoke antisocial behavior, based on the premise that it would be in the director's interest to prevent such behavior.

So our author is arguing that, "since the movie has provoked antisocial behavior among many who've seen it, then we can conclude the movie was intended to provoke antisocial behavior".

This is kind of a crazy argument. Just because something happened doesn't mean people intended it to happen. If Gary breaks his wrist while snowboarding, would we conclude "he intended to break his wrist while snowboarding"?

Of course not. This is a semi-famous flaw (Top 15, but not Top 10) we call Intent vs. Result.

Goal

Look for an answer saying the author is assuming that a result was intended to occur, or failing to consider that things we do sometimes have ramifications that we never intended.

answers.text: rejects an argument on the grounds that it was offered by a person who was biased
answers.fb:
Not Ad Hominem
Bad Evidence Match

This refers to the famous Ad Hominem flaw, in which someone dismisses a point of view because the source of the view has a biased interest (or because the source has some conflicting past behavior).

This author does reject an argument, in her conclusion.

But the grounds on which she does so (i.e. the evidence) isn't a claim about the bias of Jenkins.

Rather, the evidence is a claim that "many who've seen this movie were caused to act antisocially".

answers.text: concludes from a mere correlation between certain phenomena that those phenomena are causally related
answers.fb:
Not Correlation vs. Causation
Bad Evidence Match

This refers to the famous Causal Overconfidence flaw, in which an author overconfidently concludes one possible causal explanation for something, without ruling out other possible explanations. 

Any time a Flaw answer is structured
concludes from X that Y
then we can ask ourselves if X matches the evidence and Y matches the conclusion.

Was the evidence "a mere correlation between phenomena"?

No, the evidence was "the movie has clearly produced antisocial behavior among many who have seen it". That verb 'produced' makes this a causal statement, not a correlation.

We could also say that the conclusion is not a causal claim; it's just saying that "the movie was intended to provoke antisocial behavior". 

That's talking about whether or not a certain motive existed; it's not claiming that Thing 1 caused Thing 2.

answers.text: infers that something is true of a whole solely on the grounds that it is true of a part of the whole
answers.fb:
Not Part vs. Whole
Bad Evidence Match

This refers to the famous Part vs. Whole flaw, in which an author assumes that a trait that applies to a collective group also applies to each member within the group (or vice versa). 

Any time a Flaw answer is structured
infers that Y solely on the grounds that X
then we can ask ourselves if X matches the evidence and Y matches the conclusion.

Was the evidence saying some trait is true of a part of a whole?

Not really, but if we really wanted to stretch we could say that saying "the movie has clearly produced antisocial behavior among many who have seen it" is saying that part of the audience has "antisocial behavior" as a trait.

For this answer to be right, the conclusion would then have to be saying, "Therefore, the audience as a whole for this movie behaves antisocially".

But in reality the conclusion says, "Therefore, this movie was intended to provoke antisocial behavior".

answers.text: overlooks the possibility that people can act in a way that is contrary to their expressed interest
answers.fb:
Not an Objection

Whenever a Flaw answer begins with fails to consider / overlooks the possibility, we can ask ourselves whether the idea that follows would weaken.

Can it hurt the argument to say that, "Hey, author -- sometimes people can act in a way that is contrary to their expressed interest?"

No, that would actually strengthen. Jenkins had concluded that Firepower wasn't intended to provoke antisocial since that would have been contrary to the director's interest for such behavior to result.

This would be an objection to Jenkins' reasoning. We would say, "But Jenkins -- just because X is against the director's interests doesn't show that the director wasn't doing X. Sometimes people act in ways that are contrary to their interest."

If we're objecting to Jenkins, then we're strengthening this author's argument.

answers.text: concludes from the mere fact that an action had a certain effect that the effect was intended by the person who performed the action
answers.fb:
Correct

Any time a Flaw answer is structured
concludes from X that Y
then we can ask ourselves if X matches the evidence and Y matches the conclusion.

Was the evidence saying that "an action had an effect"? 

Yes, the evidence was "the movie has clearly produced antisocial behavior among many who have seen it". So the action of 'making this movie' had the effect of 'producing antisocial behavior'.

Is the conclusion saying "the effect was intended by the person performing the action"? 

Yes, it's saying that the director who made this movie intended to produce that antisocial behavior.

Admittedly, part of this answer is weird, because the conclusion is technically "the movie was intended to provoke antisocial behavior", not "the director intended to provoke antisocial behavior", but this is still our best available choice and speaks to the Intent vs. Result flaw.

questiontext:
The word "loophole" is a loaded, partisan word, one that implies wrongdoing and scandal. When "loophole" creeps into news stories, they start to read like editorials. So news reporters should not use the term "loophole" in their stories unless they provide evidence of wrongdoing.

Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in the argument?
gf:
Conclusion (So)

News reporters shouldn't use the term "loophole" in their stories unless they provide evidence of wrongdoing.

Evidence

"Loophole" is a loaded, partisan word that implies wrongdoing and scandal, so when it creeps into news stories, they start to read like editorials.

Evaluate

On Principle-Justify tasks like this, we usually just predict an "If Premise, Then Conclusion" linking idea.

We're trying to conclude that reporters should avoid using a term (unless they've met some exception). So more than anything, as we judge answers, we can ask ourselves, "Can I use this principle, apply it to the word 'loophole', and strengthen the idea that news reporters shouldn't use "loophole".

Conditionally, we could say,

If ....                                      Then ... 
having the word in your  
news story makes it               should not 
read like an editorial               use that 
            or                         →   word in 
the word is loaded and          your news 
  implies wrongdoing              story 
          (and) 
   you've provided no  
evidence of wrongdoing

Goal

Find an answer that says we shouldn't imply wrongdoing without providing evidence of it, or we shouldn't use words that make news stories read like editorials.

answers.text: Making use of a loophole never constitutes wrongdoing or scandal.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

The language of this principle doesn't involve anything like "shouldn't use this word". We need a principle that applies to news reporters and talks them out of using this word.

answers.text: Editorials should meet the same journalistic standards as news stories.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

We want a principle that applies to news reporters writing news stories and allows us to say "should not" use 'loophole'. 

This is a principle that applies to editorials and allows us to say "what journalistic standards editorials should meet".

answers.text: News stories need to give evidence to back up any suggestions of misconduct.
answers.fb:
Correct

We want a principle that applies to news reporters writing news stories and allows us to say "should not" use 'loophole'. 

This is a principle that is defining what news stories "need to give in order to do Y", so it relates to the language of the conclusion.

In other words, we could use this principle to say to a news reporter, "Hey, you shouldn't do that --- you need to do X if you're going to do that". And since we're trying to tell reporters that they shouldn't use the term 'loophole', let's ask ourselves if that word qualifies for this rule.

Is 'loophole' a suggestion of misconduct?

Yes, we were told "it implies wrongdoing and scandal", both of which are synonyms for misconduct. 

So this answer says, "News stories need to give evidence to back up the term 'loophole'."

Is that helping get us closer to saying the conclusion, "If a news reporter hasn't provided evidence of wrongdoing, then they shouldn't use the term 'loophole'?"

Sure! Correct answers on Principle-Strengthen don't need to use all the ideas presented in the Evidence, so the fact that this doesn't use the buzzphrase "reads like an editorial" is not a problem with the answer.

We just test whether the answer has any strengthening utility to it. And this answer sounds like a principle that reinforces the author's argument that, "Since 'loophole' implies wrongdoing, (and since news stories need to give evidence to back up suggestions of wrongdoing), news reporters shouldn't use 'loophole' unless they're providing evidence to back it up."

answers.text: Editorial writers should be free to use loaded partisan words.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

We want a principle that applies to news reporters writing news stories and allows us to say should not use 'loophole'.

This is a principle that applies to editorial writing and allows us to say "they should be free to use the term 'loophole'."

answers.text: News reporters should not report on wrongdoing and scandal that is not a matter of public interest.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: public interest

This answer has the most alluring beginning, because "news reporters should not" is how our Conclusion starts.

But this is a principle about what subjects to report on, not about what word choice to use or what allegations need to be supported by evidence.

This rule is saying,

 if a certain scandal         then a news
or act of wrongdoing →  reporter should
  isn't a matter of             not report on it.
  public interest

We're trying to use a rule in connection with the term 'loophole'. Does using the term 'loophole' mean that you're talking about "a scandal/wrongdoing that isn't a matter of public interest"? 

No, it was never defined in that weird way, so this rule can't be applied to that term.

questiontext:
Expert: Some people claim that, since food production has thus far increased faster than population has, there is no need to be concerned about widespread food shortages. These people fail to recognize that the planet's resources allow for food to be produced at only a few times the current amount, beyond which no increase in production will be possible. Thus, widespread food shortages are inevitable.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the expert's reasoning?
gf:
Conclusion (thus)

Widespread food shortages are inevitable.

Evidence

The planet’s resources will only allow for production to increase up to a certain limit, beyond which it cannot grow.

Evaluate

This is a "Strengthen" question where the task is to support the argument that widespread food shortages will occur. To strengthen the conclusion, we need to ensure that the demand (population) will eventually exceed the supply (food production), potentially by highlighting ongoing or future increases in population.

Goal

Identify an answer choice that suggests the population will continue to increase beyond the planet's food production capacity, making shortages more likely.

answers.text: The world's resources, though limited, are renewable.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

This discusses renewable resources, which does not support the notion of inevitable food shortages. In fact, it suggests that food production could persist, not diminishing the perceived supply issues.

answers.text: Food resources from the world's oceans will eventually be fully utilized.
answers.fb:
Weaker Impact

This states that food from the ocean will be fully utilized, which definitely helps one to argue that food shortages will happen.

But the central doubt in the argument is that the Earth can produce a few times what it currently does, and we don't know whether Earth's population will reach that level of demand.

It's possible that we would exhaust the food in the ocean but still have enough food from land.

answers.text: The world's population has recently remained fairly stable because of falling birth rates.
answers.fb:
Weakens

Indicating that the population has recently remained stable undermines the argument for future shortages, as a stable population implies the current food supply may suffice, countering the prediction of shortages.

answers.text: Periodic regional food shortages have occurred at least briefly throughout history.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This recounts historical periodic regional food shortages. It does not directly impact the argument about future widespread shortages, since isolated past events may not point to global future trends, and since a regional shortage is not nearly as dire as a widespread shortage.

answers.text: Population will continue to grow at least briefly when food production has reached its maximum level.
answers.fb:
Correct

This explicitly states that the population will continue to grow even after food production reaches its maximum level. It directly strengthens the argument by foreseeing a future mismatch where demand from population growth will surpass food supply, leading to shortages.

questiontext:
In the earliest video games, the player typically controlled the movements of a simple icon on the screen. But in newer video games, players often control the movements of detailed human figures—a feature possible because of the greater technical sophistication of these games. It is hard for players to identify with these figures, since the players can see that the figures represent other people. Thus, in this respect the technical sophistication of the newer video games often makes them less compelling to players.

The conclusion of the argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
gf:
Premise

But in newer video games,   
players often control the   
movements of detailed   
human figures.

The players can see that   
the figures represent other   
people.

Intermediate Conclusion

It is hard for players to                 HI  
identify with these figures.

Main Conclusion

Thus, in this respect the                 LC  
technical sophistication of   
the newer video games   
often makes them less   
compelling to players.

Evaluate

The argument assumes that          HI → LC  
when games make it harder   
for players to identify with   
the figure who they control,   
they find the game less   
compelling.

answers.text: There are no newer, more technically sophisticated video games in which the player controls the movements of a simple icon on the screen.
answers.fb:
Supports a Premise

This supports the premise that players often control the movements of detailed human figures.

answers.text: Most early video games in which the player controlled a simple icon on the screen were in other respects less compelling to players than newer video games.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope

The respect that matters in the argument is the difficulty of identifying with the figures, while this answer is about other respects.

answers.text: The technical sophistication necessary for creating detailed human figures in video games cannot in itself make those video games fully compelling even to players who identify with those figures.
answers.fb:
Too Weak

To not be fully compelling is not the same as being less compelling than earlier video games with figures that were easier to identify with.

answers.text: When players cannot easily identify with the figure or icon whose movements they control in a video game, they usually find that game less compelling than it otherwise would be.
answers.fb:
Correct

This bridges the gap            HI → LC 
between players finding  
it harder to identify with  
the figure who they  
control and the game  
being less compelling.

answers.text: If some aspect of a video game's technical sophistication makes it less compelling to players, then that video game contains a human figure with whom it is difficult for players to identify.
answers.fb:
Reversal

This reverses the assumption      LC → HI 
of the argument.

questiontext:
There are many agricultural regions in North America where the growing season is long enough to allow pumpkin production well into autumn with no risk of frost. Nonetheless, pumpkin production in North America is concentrated in regions with long, cold winters, where the growing season is delayed and pumpkin crops are exposed to risk of damage or destruction by early autumn frosts.

Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?
gf:
Given that ...

There are many regions in North America where the growing season is long enough that you could grow pumpkins without risking frost damage.

Why is it that ...

Most pumpkin production in North America takes place in regions that do have a risk of frost damage?

Evaluate / Goal

If we're counterintuitively growing pumpkins in areas that risk frost damage (when other areas with longer growing seasons don't carry that risk), then there must be something really good about those areas with long, cold winters or something really bad about those areas with longer growing seasons.

Look for an answer helping us to justify why it's worth putting up with the frost risk in the regions where we do most of our pumpkin production (better land? easier distribution? etc.)

answers.text: Pumpkins are usually grown to reach maturity in autumn.
answers.fb:
No Distinction

This isn't giving us any sort of fact that makes the regions where we grow most of our pumpkins sound better than the region where we don't grow most of our pumpkins.

answers.text: Pumpkins depend on bees for pollination, and bees are active only in warm weather.
answers.fb:
Deepens Paradox, if anything

This potentially doesn't have any effect. After all, both the regions where we grow pumpkins and the regions where we don't both presumably have warm summer weather when the bees can pollinate the pumpkin crops.

But to the extent that it's saying, "It's better to grow pumpkins where you have warm weather", it would only deepen the paradox, since it seems like the region where we grow most of our pumpkins is colder than the regions where we don't.

answers.text: More pumpkins are sold to consumers in regions of North America with long growing seasons than to those in regions with short growing seasons.
answers.fb:
Deepens Paradox

If more pumpkins were sold to consumers in the short growing season region (long, cold winters), that could work as an answer.

We could say, "even though there's a risk of frost damage in these regions, we grow most of our pumpkins here because most pumpkin buyers live in these regions (it's easier to distribute the pumpkins, the shorter the distance from farm to consumer)."

But this goes the opposite direction. We mysteriously grow most pumpkins in regions that have frost damage risk, even though most pumpkins are sold to people in the regions that don't have frost damage risk.

answers.text: Prolonged cold temperatures kill soil-borne fungus and other sources of disease that would kill or seriously damage pumpkins.
answers.fb:
Correct

Here we got what we wanted ... something good about the regions where we grow pumpkins, to justify our otherwise weird decision to grow them in regions that have higher risk of frost damage.

This is saying, "the higher risk of frost damage is worth it, because the advantage we get out of growing pumpkins in these regions with long, cold winters is that the cold winter kills off potential crop diseases."

If we grew more pumpkins in the warmer regions with longer growing seasons, we'd have no risk of frost damage, but we might have a much higher risk of diseases killing or seriously damaging the pumpkins.

answers.text: Most of the pumpkin seed used by growers in North America is produced in areas where the growing season is long, and plants used for seed production are protected in greenhouses.
answers.fb:
Deepens Paradox, if Anything

Given that seed production takes place in a greenhouse, it doesn't really matter what sort of climate it's done in.

But this answer overall makes it feel more like the longer growing season regions (where we don't grow pumpkins) is where seed production happens. So that makes it more confusing that we don't grow pumpkins in those regions (we make the seeds there, and there's no risk of frost damage).

questiontext:
Council chair: The traditional code of parliamentary procedure contains a large number of obscure, unnecessary rules, which cause us to quibble interminably over procedural details and so to appear unworthy of public confidence. Admittedly, the code is entrenched and widely accepted. But success in our endeavors depends on the public's having confidence in our effectiveness. Therefore, it is imperative that we adopt the alternate code, which has been in successful use elsewhere for several years.

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the chair's conclusion?
gf:
Conclusion

It's imperative that we adopt the alternate code.

Evidence

The alternate code has been successfully used elsewhere for several years.

Even though the current code is entrenched and widely accepted, the current code contains tons of obscure rules, which cause us to forever debate tiny details. Meanwhile the public thinks we suck, and we can't be successful if the public lacks confidence in us.

Evaluate

A lot of arguments that assume a difference have this form:  "X is kind of bad for reason Y. Thus, we should use Z instead of X."

This type of argument assumes that Z is different, in terms of reason Y.

Similarly, in this argument, our author is definitely assuming that this alternate code does not contain a comparable amount of obscure technicalities that will lead to ineffective quibbling over details. But maybe the alternate code is just as riddled with parliamentary complexities.

If we want to think beyond just that one possible objection, we can frame this with our Objection Mindset:

Given that ... this (widely accepted) code leads to endless arguing over tiny details, eroding the public's precious trust in the effectiveness of the council,

How could we say that ... we don't need to adopt the alternate code (there's some other option).

Well first of all, we could ask, "Are there only these two codes to choose from? Why I do I have to go from this traditional one to the alternate one?"

We could ask, "Is it feasible to make the switch? Could we just fix the current code we have and get rid of the excess technicalities we hate? Could we just live with no code at all?"

Since the author's conclusion goes out on a limb of, "It's imperative that we switch to the alternate code", we will be creating some weakening doubt with any storyline that makes it seem like we could keep the existing one or that we could choose a path other than adopting the alternate one.

Goal

Look for something saying "the alternate code is just as bad when it comes to procedural details we'd fight over" or just as bad when it comes to "losing public confidence", or an answer suggesting an alternate viable path that shows we don't need to adopt the alternate code.

answers.text: The council's use of the problematic rules in the traditional code is intermittent.
answers.fb:
Too Weak

This feels like it's trying to weaken by saying, "Sure, sure, the traditional code sucks, but at least we only need to use the problematic rules intermittently."

That does somewhat degrade the importance of solving this problem, of switching codes, but it's not much of an objection.

"Because this problematic thing is only intermittently problematic, let's not do anything about it." Given that the existing code is entrenched, there is some weakening effect to say that "if it's not that big a problem, do we really need to uproot the old code and switch to an alternate one?"

But given that even the intermittent problematic nature is enough to cause enough quibbling that the council appears "unworthy of public confidence", it still seems like a problem worth solving.

answers.text: Those who have adopted the alternate code sometimes attempt to use it to obscure their opponents' understanding of procedures.
answers.fb:
Too Weak

Answers that only reflect "at least one" data point (some, sometimes, can, may, might, not all, not always) are almost always wrong on Strengthen, Weaken, and Paradox, since they have such little impact.

Does it hurt this argument to say, "There has been at least one instance in which someone used the alternate code to obscure their opponent's understanding of procedure"? 

No. There's been at least one person who died in an elevator, but that doesn't mean it's a compelling reason to not ride in an elevator.

answers.text: Revision of the traditional code is underway that will eliminate the problematic rules.
answers.fb:
Correct

This gives us a way to argue the Anti-Conclusion.

Nuh-uh, author. We don't need to adopt the alternate code. We have another viable option --- let's just wait to complete the already-begun process of fixing the existing code.

That way we'll get rid of the problematic stuff you're worried about without uprooting an entrenched, widely accepted code.

answers.text: It is not always reasonable to adopt a different code in order to maintain the public's confidence.
answers.fb:
Too Weak

Answers that only reflect "at least one" data point (some, sometimes, can, may, might, not all, not always) are almost always wrong on Strengthen, Weaken, and Paradox, since they have such little impact.

Does it hurt this argument to say, "There has been at least one instance in which it was not reasonable to adopt a different code in order to maintain public confidence?"

Sure. It hurts the argument a tiny, tiny smidge. But it doesn't have nearly the force that the correct answer does.

answers.text: The alternate code contains few provisions that have thus far been criticized as obscure or unnecessary.
answers.fb:
Strengthens

This actually affirms the difference that the argument was assuming. Since our author wants to get rid of the traditional code because of its obscure / unnecessary rules, he must be assuming that his proposed replacement doesn't suffer from that same problem.

This answer helps to affirm that assumption, so it strengthens.

questiontext:
Businesses frequently use customer surveys in an attempt to improve sales and increase profits. However, a recent study of the effectiveness of these surveys found that among a group of businesses that sold similar products, profits declined in most of the businesses that used surveys during the course of the study but not in most of the businesses that did not use any surveys during the course of the study.

Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the profits of businesses that did not use customer surveys did not decline while the profits of those that used surveys did decline?
gf:
Given that ...

Business frequently use customer surveys in an attempt to improve sales and increase profits.

How can it be that ...

In this study, most of the businesses using the surveys had declining profits whereas most of the businesses that didn't use surveys did not have declining profits.

Evaluate

The paradox is that most of the businesses using this tool that's supposed to help a business improve profits have declining profits. 

It's not some widespread economic downturn, because businesses not using this tool do not have declining profits.

Technically, if we're attuned to Relative vs. Absolute language, there isn't really a paradox here. The customer survey is supposed to improve profits. Are the businesses who are using the survey seeing improved profits?

Maybe! We don't know. We know they have declining profits, but maybe that was already the case before they started using the customer surveys.
