answers.text: The researchers also found that some unprotected areas outside of the park have substantially higher numbers of certain reptile species than comparable areas inside the park.
answers.fb:
Restates Paradox

This reinforces the idea that animals are mysteriously doing better outside this park than inside it, but it doesn't help us to explain why that is.

answers.text: Researchers tagged a large number of birds inside the park; three months later some of these birds were recaptured outside the park.
answers.fb:
Weaker Impact

We might say that this answer allows us to say, "there are more birds outside the park than inside because some of the birds are moving from inside the park to outside the park", but that still doesn't give us any reason WHY those birds are moving, the way the correct answer does.

answers.text: Both inside the park and just outside of it, there are riverside areas containing willows and other waterside growth that the bird species thrive on.
answers.fb:
No Distinction

Since this presents something true for both outside/inside, it's useless for our purposes of explaining a difference between them.

answers.text: The park was designed to protect endangered bird species, but some of the bird species that are present in higher numbers in the unprotected areas are also endangered.
answers.fb:
No Distinction

Since this presents something true for both outside/inside (both endangered species), it's useless for our purposes of explaining a difference between them.

questiontext:
When researchers discovered that cuttlefish have the ability to make themselves suddenly appear larger, they presumed that this behavior, called a “startle display,” was used to scare off predators. A long-term study, however, reveals that cuttlefish never use startle displays to scare off predators but instead only use such displays to scare off small fish that do not prey on cuttlefish.

Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why cuttlefish use startle displays?

answers.text: Cuttlefish feed primarily on small fish and mollusks.
answers.fb:
Opposite

If cuttlefish feed on small fish, why do they use the "startle display" to scare small fish away?

answers.text: Groups of small fish are likely to attract a cuttlefish’s predators.
answers.fb:
Correct

This indicates that the "startle display" might indirectly protect cuttlefish from predators. The cuttlefish could be scaring the small fish away so that they don't attract predators to wherever the cuttlefish is doing cuttlefish stuff.

answers.text: Small fish are more easily scared off by a startle display than are a cuttlefish’s predators.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The fact that small fish are scared off more easily doesn't explain why cuttlefish scare them off and don't try to scare off predators. Do they scare small fish just because it's easy, and fun? That sounds like something a 13-year-old human would do, but we aren't given any reason to believe that cuttlefish act like middle school bullies.

answers.text: Cuttlefish have acute senses and are able to change colors.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope

Acute senses and the ability to change colors are cool abilities, but they don't explain why the cuttlefish only use the "startle display" to scare off small fish. We need to make a lot of assumptions in order for this to explain the way that cuttlefish use the startle display.

answers.text: Unlike insects that use startle displays, cuttlefish are usually able to move faster than their predators.
answers.fb:
Half Scope

This could explain why cuttlefish don't use the startle display with predators, but it doesn't explain the other half of the paradox. Why do they scare off the smaller fish?

questiontext:
If the winner of a promotional contest is selected by a lottery, the lottery must be fair, giving all entrants an equal chance of winning. Since 90 percent of the winners selected by the lottery in a recent promotional contest submitted their entry forms within the first 2 days of the 30-day registration period, it is clear that this lottery did not meet the fairness requirement.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

The lottery did not meet the fairness requirement.

Evidence

The fairness requirement is that all entrants have an equal chance of winning.

90% of the winners selected by this lottery submitted their entry forms within the first 2 days of the 30 day registration.

Evaluate

Let's say there were 100 winners to this contest. If every day was equally likely to have contest winners, then there would be 3.3 winners per day for the 30 days the registration period was open.

Our author is picturing this math in her head, and saying if 90% of winners came from the first 2 days, it seems like every day wasn't equally likely to have a contest winner.

Of course the actual fairness rule is that "all entrants (not days) had an equal chance of winning". So why is it that the author thinks some entrants had a bigger / smaller chance? 

She's assuming that there were a comparable number of entrants on each of the 30 days. If that were the case, then the people who submitted sometime between day 3 and day 30 would be like, "hey, how come only 10% of us won, but 90% of the people from day 1 and day 2 won?"

But if most people got their entries in right when the registration period opened, then we would expect a bigger percentage of winners to have come from that time period. 

Pretend we have 1000 entrants over a 10 day period, 100 entries per day.
100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100

If 90 of the 100 winners came from the first two days, that would seem fishy and unfair.

But suppose most of the entries came in the beginning of the 10 day period.
500, 400, 20, 15, 15, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10

Now, wouldn't we expect most of the contest winners to be people who submitted during the first two days?  After all, 90% of the entries came in the first two days, so we'd expect 90% of the randomly drawn winners to come from the first two days.

Goal

Since this argument is vulnerable to one big mathematical objection (what if 90% of the entries were submitted in the first two days?), we should probably expect an answer that rules out that idea.

answers.text: The family members of the organizer of the contest were not permitted to participate in the contest.
answers.fb:
Weakens, if anything

This is very weak and tangential, but if anything it would weaken the idea that this was an unfair lottery.

answers.text: The manner in which the contest winner would be selected was publicized prior to the selection of the winner.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This is so bland and generic that it doesn't change the conversation at all. If anything, the fact that the contest was transparent about how they would select the winner would make it seem more like a fair lottery.

answers.text: The contest entry forms were submitted at a consistent rate throughout the registration period.
answers.fb:
Correct

This rules out the big objection we had -- "what if 90% of the entries came in the first two days?"

answers.text: The rules of the contest were posted conspicuously by those who organized the contest.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This is just like (B). The fact that the contest was transparent about the rules and the winner-selection process doesn't help us evaluate the author's case at all.

The author is just claiming that the lottery didn't meet the fairness requirement -- its winner-selection process might violate the fairness requirement, even if the contest was transparent about the rules and the selection process.

answers.text: The number of people entering the contest far exceeded the expectations of the contest organizers.
answers.fb:
No Impact

Having a higher or lower than expected total number of contestants doesn't matter. We only care about whether 90% or way less than 90% of the entries were received in the first 2 days of the registration period.

questiontext:
Godinez: In the past, land was sometimes measured by the amount of time required to plow it. Thus, two plots of equal physical dimensions were considered unequal if one was more difficult to plow than the other. However, knowing how long an area takes to plow reveals little about how many apartment complexes it can hold. Therefore, it became necessary to adopt new measures of land, such as acreage, when land uses diversified.

Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in Godinez's argument?
gf:
Conclusion

It became necessary to adopt new measures of land (beyond "plow time") when land uses diversified.

Evidence

The initial convention for measuring land was "plow time". But knowing how long it takes to plow a piece of land doesn't tell you how many apartment complexes could be built on that parcel. 

Evaluate

For years and years, LSAC avoided putting the conclusion in the final sentence on Main Conclusion questions (too obvious a place to look for it). But recently it's become more common, mostly as a way of trolling test prep advice.

There are three keywords we might lean on here:  thus, however, therefore.

The first "Thus" is an implication being drawn of the "plow time" method. 
We used standard X. Thus, according to standard X, this thing would be different from that thing.

Although "thus" is usually indicating a conclusion the author is drawing, it can also be used to designate cause/effect relationships, or in this case, rule/implication relationships.

"However" usually means that we are leaving background ideas and entering the Author's argument, but we still have to figure out whether the author's argument will go Support, then Conclusion or go Conclusion, then Support.

The "Therefore" tells us that this argument is going Support, then Conclusion.

We can always test whether we've found the right claim as the conclusion by asking, "Why should I believe that?" and making sure that there's a supporting idea provided.

Why should we believe that as land uses diversified, we needed to adopt new measure of land?

Because, the old measure (plow time) wouldn't tell someone how many acres a given plot of land was, if they wanted to build apartment complexes on it.

Goal

Just pick the answer that is closest in meaning to the final sentence, which was the Conclusion.

answers.text: It is now easier to measure a piece of land in terms of acres than in terms of plowing time.
answers.fb:
Never Stated: easier to measure

We don't want to pick an answer on Main Conclusion that wasn't actually said (unless it's a weird question stem like Main Point or Implied Conclusion).

This doesn't match the last sentence at all, since the last sentence doesn't discuss whether new measures were easier or harder than the old one.

answers.text: For modern purposes, newer methods provide a more accurate measure of land than plowing time does.
answers.fb:
Unstated Inference

The last sentence does not say anything about more accurate, so we can eliminate this.

This type of trap answer tries to appeal to a different part of an LSAT student's brain. This idea sounds true, because it seems like we could infer this, but we're not trying to do anything deep or insightful.

The conclusion is the last sentence and we just want an answer that repeats what was said in the last sentence.

answers.text: Some plots of land that would have been considered unequal by plowing-time measurements are of equal physical dimensions.
answers.fb:
Intermediate Conclusion

This isn't really an intermediate conclusion, in the sense that the author's eventual conclusion isn't using this idea at all.

But this answer is trying to mimic what was said in the second sentence which was a conclusion / implication derived from the logic of the old measurement method. 

We could say this claim is supported/implied by the first sentence, but we can't say this is the main conclusion, since the paragraph goes on to Pivot with "however" and then end with a main conclusion, signaled by "Therefore".

answers.text: Modern measures of land were adopted when people realized that plowing time was an inadequate measure for some land uses.
answers.fb:
Weak Match

This seems pretty close to regurgitating the last sentence. However, the last sentence doesn't mention modern measures. 

And the last sentence says that new measurements were adopted when land uses diversified.

This answer says new measurements were adopted when people realized plow time was inadequate for some land uses.

Those are pretty close, but (D) doesn't convey the same idea the conclusion does, that people were actually beginning to use land in different ways. Instead, we could read (D) as saying, people looked around at the ways they were already using land and decided that "plow time" was inadequate for some of them.

Ultimately, we'd probably be okay picking this answer and living with its slight differences if we didn't have a tighter lock for the last sentence available.

answers.text: The advent of diversified land uses made new measures of land necessary.
answers.fb:
Correct

This matches the meaning of the last sentence.

"The advent" = "the beginning / the start"

When land uses diversified 
    (the advent of diversified land)

it became necessary to adopt new measure of land 
        (new measures of land were necessary)

questiontext:
Last year the Lalolah River was ranked by the Sunvale Water Commission as the most polluted of the fifteen rivers in the Sunvale Water District. Measures taken to clean up the river must be working, though, since this year the Lalolah River is ranked as only the third most polluted river in the district.

The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument
gf:
Conclusion (must be = causal speculation)

Measures taken to clean up the river must be working.

Evidence (since)

This year the Lalolah River is ranked as only the 3rd most polluted river in the district.

Last year it was ranked #1.

Evaluate

This argument has a common structure. The evidence is an Asymmetric Comparison (it used to be ranked 1st most polluted, but now it's ranked 3rd most polluted).

And the author's conclusion states or assumes a causal explanation for that Curious Fact, that asymmetric comparison.

Curious Fact .... Why did the river go from being the most polluted to the 3rd most polluted?

Author's Explanation .... they took some measures to clean up the river, and so now the river is less polluted than before.

The two pressure points for these arguments are always the same:
1. Alternate Explanations for the curious fact
2. the plausibility of the author's explanation

On Flaw, we're primarily concerned with the #1. They want us to see that the author is overconfidently jumping to one possible causal explanation while failing to consider that there could be other explanations.

What could be an alternate explanation for why the Lalolah River went from being the most polluted to the 3rd most polluted? 

Maybe that river didn't get any cleaner, but the two rivers that are now ranked higher than Lalolah got worse. 

It's possible for Elon Musk to go from being the richest person in the world to the 3rd richest without him losing any money. It could be explained by people who previously had less money than him gaining enough money to surpass him.

Goal

Let's look for something like, "The author fails to consider alternate explanations for the change in pollution ranking (such as other rivers getting more polluted than before)."

answers.text: interprets lack of evidence for a claim as support for an opposing claim
answers.fb:
Not Unproven vs. Proven False

This answer refers to one of the 10 Famous Flaws, Unproven vs. Proven False, in which an author treats a failure to prove X true as evidence that X must be false.

This argument has no rebuttal qualities (as Unproven vs. Proven False normally would). The author's evidence never calls out a certain claim that lacks evidence.

answers.text: relies on an ambiguity in the expression “most polluted”
answers.fb:
Not Equivocation

This answer alludes to one of the 10 Famous Flaws, Equivocation, in which an author uses the same term or concept in two very different ways. 

(This answer is almost always wrong.)

The way the author used "most polluted" was clear and consistent: it means "more polluted than any other river in the District".

answers.text: does not disclose the basis for the ranking used
answers.fb:
Never a Flaw

Answers that ask us for specific numbers/measurements or definitions are basically always wrong.

The specific details behind the premises aren't what's being tested when we're being asked about the problem with reasoning. We're supposed to grant the truth of the premises and think about how they still fail to prove the conclusion.

So we'll accept that Lalolah was ranked 1st and is now ranked 3rd. We aren't supposed to object by saying, "Why should I believe those premises? What was the basis for these rankings?"

We're supposed to think, "GIVEN THAT ... it went from being ranked 1st to being ranked 3rd, HOW CAN I FIGHT THE CONCLUSION?"

answers.text: confuses the state of the individual rivers in the water district with that of the water district as a whole
answers.fb:
Not Part vs. Whole

This answer refers to one of the 10 Famous Flaws, Part vs. Whole, in which the author assumes that a trait/property that applies to each part of a whole also applies to the whole itself (or vice versa).

This argument didn't do that. That would have felt like, "Each river in the district is polluted. Thus, the district as a whole is polluted."

answers.text: equates a decrease relative to the other ranked rivers with an absolute decrease
answers.fb:
Correct

For all Flaw answer choices, we can ask ourselves:
1. Did this really happen? Is it descriptively true?
2. Does it matter? Does it point to some problem with the logic?

It's certainly true that the author goes from Evidence about a relative decrease (the Lalolah River went from being more polluted than all other rivers, to being less polluted than two rivers) to a Conclusion that assumes an absolute decrease (she thinks that cleanup measures led to the river having less pollution than it had before).

This answer points to a problem with the logic (very indirectly) by suggesting the Alternate Explanation for the curious fact:

No, author, the river didn't get less polluted, it's just that two other rivers got so much worse that they surpassed Lalolah in the pollution rankings.

If we had read the argument, "Last year Elon Musk was the richest person in the world. This year, he is the 3rd richest. So apparently his decision to buy Twitter has caused him to lose a bunch of money", then this answer choice would apply just the same. 

We would be able to object, "Wait a sec --- maybe he didn't lose any money over the past year and the real reason that he's now 3rd is simply because two people who used to be under him in terms of wealth have gained enough wealth to surpass him. Just because his wealth changed in relative terms (in terms of how he compares to other) doesn't mean that his wealth changed in absolute terms (it doesn't mean that he now has less money).

questiontext:
If an activity significantly reduces chronic lower back pain, doctors should be prepared to discuss the merits of that activity with patients who ask about it. A recent study compared practicing yoga to taking stretching classes with a physical therapist and found that both activities lead to equal reductions in chronic lower back pain. Thus, doctors treating patients with chronic lower back pain should be prepared to discuss the merits of yoga.

Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
gf:
Conclusion

Doctors treating chronic lower back pain patients should be prepared to discuss the merits of yoga.

Evidence

 If activity significantly               doctors should
reduces chronic lower    →    be prepared to talk
          back pain                              about it

Recent study showed that practicing yoga leads to an equal reduction in chronic lower back pain as does taking stretching classes with a physical therapist.

Evaluation

The conclusion is saying "Doctors should do X"
                                     +
There's a rule that says, "Y → doc should do X"

So we know we have to establish Y. In this case, we need to establish that yoga significantly reduces chronic lower back pain, in order to trigger that initial conditional.

Were we told that yoga significantly reduces chronic lower back pain?
No, we were only told that yoga reduces chronic lower back pain as much as stretching classes with a physical therapist does.

Okay .... does stretching classes with a physical therapist significantly reduce chronic lower back pain?

Goal

It seems like we should be on the lookout for an answer that reassures us, "yes, stretching with a physical therapist significantly reduces chronic lower back pain".  Since we know that yoga achieves an equal reduction, then yoga, too, would significantly reduce lower back pain and the author can trigger that conditional that he seems to think he's triggered.

answers.text: There are no activities that lead to more significant reductions in chronic lower back pain than do stretching classes with a physical therapist.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: no activities that lead to more

The author doesn't need to believe that stretching with a physical therapist is the absolute #1 way to reduce chronic lower back pain.

She only needs to assume that stretching with a physical therapist achieves a significant reduction.

answers.text: Taking stretching classes with a physical therapist significantly reduces chronic lower back pain.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is what we thought we were looking for. If we negated this, it would be a big objection to the argument. If stretching with a physical therapist doesn't significantly reduce, then yoga also doesn't significantly reduce. Thus, yoga would trigger that rule that says that doctors should be prepared to talk about it.

answers.text: Few treatment options for those with chronic lower back pain are available.
answers.fb:
Too Strong:  few

Just because we're only mentioning two treatment options (yoga and stretching with a physical therapist) doesn't mean those are the only two options. There might be many, many more options. That wouldn't affect the author's argument in any way.

Doctors should be prepared to talk about any of those many options that achieve a significant reduction in pain.

answers.text: No previous studies have compared practicing yoga to taking stretching classes with a physical therapist.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: no past studies

Who cares whether this is the first study to compare yoga to stretching with a physical therapist or if it's the 379th study to do so?

Neither would affect the logic of the author's argument.

answers.text: Many doctors treating patients with chronic lower back pain discuss with their patients the merits of taking stretching classes with a physical therapist.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope:  should vs. actually do

We want to know whether stretching with a physical therapist causes significant reductions in pain. If it does, then by the conditional rule in the first sentence, the author would be assuming that doctors should be prepared to talk to their patients about taking stretching classes with a physical therapist.

But the author doesn't have to assume anything about whether doctors actually do talk to their patients about stretching classes.

questiontext:
Horses, although descended from a forest-dwelling ancestor, thrive in grasslands. In the last 2 million years, horses have gone through three cycles of population increase followed by a rapid decline in population. The most recent cycle peaked 25,000 years ago during a cold period that preceded a period of warming.

Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the horse population peaked 25,000 years ago and then rapidly declined?

answers.text: The forest-dwelling ancestor of horses was many times smaller than horses.
answers.fb:
No Impact

We would need a lot more information to know how the size of the horses' ancestor would have any impact on this situation.

answers.text: The only true wild horse existing today, Przewalski’s horse, inhabits the cold grasslands of Central Asia.
answers.fb:
Half Scope

This indicates that grasslands can exist in cold areas, and that wild horses live in these cold grasslands. To some degree, it helps explain why the horse population was large during a cold period. But it doesn't explain the other half of the paradox. Why did the horse population decline during the warmer period that followed?

answers.text: Some modern species that are related to horses, such as zebras, inhabit the warm grasslands of Africa.
answers.fb:
Unclear Impact
Opposite (if anything)

It's possible that some fact about zebras could help explain the paradox we're given. But this answer doesn't explain why horse populations peaked during a cold period and then declined during a warming period.

The fact that grasslands exist in warm areas, and animals related to horses live in those grasslands, does the opposite of what we want, if anything. It's evidence that horses might have thrived during the warming period discussed in the stimulus.

answers.text: During cold periods there are extensive grasslands, but these tend to revert to forest when the climate warms.
answers.fb:
Correct

It's normal to expect grass to grow when it's warm, not when it's cold, but this answer states that the opposite is actually true. This indicates that the grasslands where horses thrive were more common during the cold period 25,000 years ago and less common during the warm period that followed. Hence, the horse population declined during the warm period.

It's helpful to note that the stimulus never said how cold it got 25,000 years ago. It's easy to envision an ice age, or at least a very wintery, snowy climate where grass is unlikely to grow, but we're never told it was actually that cold. The LSAT very frequently does this, tricking us into assuming something that wasn't actually stated.

answers.text: Several cycles of a cold period followed by a period of warming have occurred in the last 2 million years.
answers.fb:
No Impact

We already know that horse populations have gone through cycles during the past 2 million years. We know that there appears to be some connection between the most recent cycle and a shift from a cold period to a warmer one. If anything, this answer is just consistent with information that we've already been given. It doesn't help explain why the horse population peaked 25,000 years ago and then rapidly declined.

questiontext:
Editorial: Some primary schools’ early education reading programs encourage children to read by paying them for each book they read outside of class. Such programs should be viewed with suspicion. While paying kids to read might get them to read more, it also might teach them to regard reading as a chore rather than as a source of intrinsic satisfaction.

Which one of the following principles, if valid, most strongly supports the editorial’s reasoning?

answers.text: Early education reading programs should focus more on getting children to read challenging books than on getting them to read a large number of books.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope

Encouraging children to read challenging books does not play any role in this particular argument. We might think that a book being challenging has something to do with children viewing reading as a chore, but the argument never states that. This answer might sound like it somehow supports the conclusion, but it doesn't strengthen the link between the evidence and the conclusion.

answers.text: Children will be more likely to develop into regular readers if they choose the books they read than if they do not.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope

Having children choose the books that they read does not play any role in this particular argument. The evidence discusses children reading more books because they're being paid to do it. What happens when children choose their own books is not relevant. This answer might sound like it somehow supports the conclusion, but it doesn't strengthen the link between the evidence and the conclusion.

answers.text: Parents will usually play a more important role than teachers in instilling in children a love of reading.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Comparison

The argument never discusses exactly how parents or teachers are involved in the early reading programs. A comparison between the role of parents and the role teachers is irrelevant.

answers.text: The goal of early education reading programs should be to instill in children a love of reading.
answers.fb:
This is one of those cases where the LSAT rewards us for reading very literally. The evidence discusses the possibility that kids will regard reading as a chore rather than as a source of intrinsic satisfaction. But the evidence presents this in a very factual way, and never actually states whether this is a good thing or a bad thing. 

We can strengthen the argument by stating that these reading programs should instill a love of reading in children. If they encourage children to view reading as an unsatisfying chore then the programs aren't achieving this goal, which is a reason to view them with suspicion.

answers.text: Improving children’s facility with reading will get them to enjoy reading.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

The evidence states that encouraging kids to read might cause them to view reading as a chore, not as something they intrinsically enjoy. This answer choice indicates that helping kids read will have the opposite result.

We should also note that improving someone's facility with reading means to make reading easier. Making reading easier is not exactly the same as encouraging children to read. It's possible to encourage someone to do something even if the person finds it difficult.

questiontext:
Salmon farmer: Farm-raised salmon is preferable to wild salmon due to its year-round availability, consistent quality, and cheaper price. But the best reason to prefer farmed salmon is ecological: as consumers’ desire for farmed salmon increases, the market for threatened wild salmon drops, which in turn leads to more wild fish being allowed to live and multiply freely, thus increasing their numbers.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the salmon farmer's argument?
gf:
Evidence

As consumers’ desire for farmed salmon increases, the market for threatened wild salmon drops, which in turn leads to more wild fish being allowed to live and multiply freely.

Intermediate Conclusion

Wild salmon numbers will increase.

Main Conclusion

The best reason to prefer farmed salmon is ecological.

 

Evaluate

The evidence is generally about the popularity of farmed salmon leading to an increase in wild salmon numbers. Base on this, the conclusion claims that a preference for farmed salmon provides some ecological benefit.

What if the process of farming salmon somehow causes ecological harm? What if consumers' increased desire for farmed salmon is drastically increasing this harm? If any of this is true, it weakens the argument.

However, there's another potential flaw in the argument. There's potentially a gap between the evidence and the intermediate conclusion. If we have a reason to believe that "more wild fish being allowed to live and multiply freely" might not actually increase wild fish numbers, that weakens the argument.

Goal

Keep an eye open for a correct answer that would weaken the argument in one of these two ways.

answers.text: Farmed salmon are fed with large quantities of small fish caught in areas where wild salmon attempt to feed.
answers.fb:
Correct

This highlights the potential gap between the evidence and the intermediate conclusion. If this answer is true, the process of farming salmon could reduce the amount of food available for wild salmon. Wild salmon might starve even if a declining market allows them to "live and multiply freely." If this happens, it's not guaranteed that the wild salmon numbers will increase.

answers.text: Though some wild salmon may be of lesser quality than farmed salmon, some is far better.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope

This answer doesn't give us much new information, if any. The first sentence already states that the quality of farmed salmon is more consistent than wild salmon. And that first sentence is an opposing idea that the argument pivots away from. Quality doesn't play a direct role in the actual argument. This answer doesn't weaken any link between the evidence and intermediate conclusion, or between the IC and the main conclusion.

answers.text: Most people who eat salmon are not aware of any differences between the taste of wild salmon and that of farmed salmon.
answers.fb:
Opposite (if anything)

The taste of fish is an element of the quality, so we might say that this answer is out of scope for the same reason that choice B is out of scope. Quality doesn't play a direct role in the actual argument. 

However, the conclusion does indicate that quality isn't the best reason to prefer farmed fish over wild fish. If anything, this answer gives us another reason to believe that quality (taste) isn't the best reason. This answer might strengthen the argument, not weaken it.

answers.text: Limits on the number of salmon that can be taken from the wild have led to increases in the price of wild salmon.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope

This answer is similar to choice B. It doesn't really give us any new information. The first sentence already states that farmed salmon is cheaper. And price doesn't play a direct role in the actual argument. This answer doesn't weaken any link between the evidence and intermediate conclusion, or between the IC and the main conclusion.

answers.text: Wild salmon are more likely than farmed salmon to have consumed pollutants that may be harmful to humans.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope

This answer seems to be giving us another reason to prefer farmed salmon. But it doesn't impact the actual argument. It doesn't impact the assumption that more wild salmon being allowed to live and multiply freely will result in their numbers increasing. And it doesn't impact the assumption that an increase in the number of wild salmon due to a preference for farmed salmon creates an ecological benefit.

questiontext:

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

answers.text: Large warm-blooded animals keep their core body temperature slightly higher than the body temperature in their limbs.
answers.fb:
No Impact: slightly
Too Narrow: Large

answers.text: The fossilization process introduces changes to bones such that their original oxygen isotope ratios cannot be predicted.

answers.text: Oxygen was more abundant in Earth's atmosphere during the period in which the dinosaurs lived.

answers.text: Small warm-blooded animals like mice tend to have more uniform body temperatures than do large warm-blooded animals like elephants.

answers.text: Warm-blooded animals are more active and use more oxygen than cold-blooded animals.

questiontext:
A recent study has found that, surprisingly, the risk of serious injuries to workers is higher in industries that are monitored by government safety inspectors than in industries that are not so monitored.

Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the surprising finding described above?

answers.text: Government safety inspectors not only monitor but also train employees of the inspected firms to follow safe practices.
answers.fb: Opposite: deepens the paradox

answers.text: Government safety inspectors do not have the authority to enforce safety regulations.
answers.fb: Cheats the Paradox: explains why regulated industries are still risky but not why they are MORE risky than unregulated industries

answers.text: Only those industries with an inherently high risk of on-the-job injury are monitored by government safety inspectors.
answers.fb: Correct

answers.text: Workers behave especially cautiously when they believe their performance is being monitored by government safety inspectors.
answers.fb: Opposite: deepens the paradox

questiontext:
Mr. Xu: The arctic squirrel gets so cold while hibernating that its blood temperature falls well below the temperature at which water freezes. Although the squirrel's blood is about 70 percent water, the blood never freezes while the squirrel is hibernating. Ms. Yerky's response proceeds by

Politician: Tightening air quality standards that regulate industrial emissions would cause industries to move to locations with less stringent standards concerning these emissions. So current standards, which are already quite stringent, should not be raised, since there is not enough evidence that the decreased pollution that would admittedly result from raising the standards would compensate for the loss of jobs caused by the relocation of key industries.

When and as the ice caps shrink, the concentrations of this heavy oxygen in seawater decrease. During one 30,000-year period, concentrations of this heavy oxygen in sea shellfish increased for about 20,000 years, then decreased for 10,000 years.

The information given most strongly supports which one of the following hypotheses about the period described above?

answers.text: Average global temperatures 10,000 years after the beginning of the period approximately equaled average global temperatures 20,000 years later.

Too Specific: average global temperatures 10,000 years after the beginnning of the period
Unsupported Comparison: approximately equaled

answers.text: Polar ice caps at the beginning of the period were larger than they were at the end of the period.

questiontext:
People would not follow a leader if they felt that there was nothing they could gain by following that leader. Therefore, even those leaders who are incompetent or evil bring some good to their followers.

Which one of the following is most similar in its flawed reasoning to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?
gf:
Conclusion (therefore)

Even incompetent or evil leaders bring some good to their followers.

Evidence

If people felt there was nothing to gain from following a leader, they wouldn't follow them.

Evaluate

By contrapositive, the premise is saying
"If you followed a leader, you felt there was something to gain from following them". 

So we know that people who followed an evil or incompetent leader felt there was something to gain by following them.

But the conclusion is claiming that there was something gained by following them.

So this is a variation of the famous Intent vs. Result flaw (or Belief vs. Fact) People intended to gain something by following a leader, but whether that resulted in gain is another question.

Goal

The essence of that flaw is, "Just because they felt that X would be true doesn't mean that X was actually true". So we can look for arguments vulnerable to a similar objection.

If the answer were going to mirror the structure more, then we'd have an argument like,

Prem:  if ppl didn't believe X, then wouldn't do Y.
Conc:  So when it comes to people who did Y, we know X is true.

answers.text: Because people expound upon only theories they believe are true, any theory that is expounded upon by someone contains at least a grain of truth.
answers.fb:
Correct

This works. We get a conditional saying,
"If you expound on a theory, you believe the theory is true."

And then a conclusion acting like the Belief is Reality.
"thus, the theories they expounded on are partially true".

The premise here doesn't need to be contraposed (a closer match would be "People wouldn't expound on a theory if they didn't believe it was true), but that doesn't matter. Contraposing is just equivalently rephrasing something, so it doesn't impact the logic.

The conclusion is similarly weak to the original one:
"bring some good" / "contains at least a grain of truth"

And the essence is the same:
"Just cuz they thought they'd gain something from following the leader doesn't mean that they DID gain something"

vs.

"Just cuz they thought the theory was true doesn't mean the theory IS true."

answers.text: Because there is some good to be found in even the worst circumstances, the world's most vicious people must have brought about at least some good.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match / Topic Trap

Since the premise here has nothing to do with someone's Belief / Intent, there's no way we'll be able to match it up with our flaw.

This is trying to get us with Topic/Word bait in the conclusion, because it's also talking about "at least some good".

answers.text: To be a worthy leader, one must bring some good to people. Therefore, those who bring about some good make worthy leaders.
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

Since the premise here has nothing to do with someone's Belief / Intent, there's no way we'll be able to match it up with our flaw.

answers.text: Because people can never completely separate what is true from what they wish to be true, no theory is ever completely true.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

To some extent, the premise is discussing what people believe, but the argument isn't treating that belief as fact. To the contrary, it's saying there is a gap between what is and what they believe.

answers.text: Even leaders of scientific revolutions are influenced by the false theories of their predecessors.  Therefore, the influence of earlier false theories never completely disappears.
answers.fb:
Bad Conclusion Match

To some extent, the premise is discussing what people believe (they believe the false theories of their predecessors), but the argument isn't treating that belief as fact. To the contrary, it's saying that those are false theories.

questiontext:
A recent study found that small rats were approximately twice as likely, and large rats only half as likely, to suffer from heart problems than were rats of average size.

Each of the following, if true, contributes to an explanation of the correlation given above between size and heart disease in rats except:
gf:
Compared to Normal Rats, How Come ...

small rats are 2x as likely to have heart problems?
and
large rats are 1/2 as likely to have heart problems?

Goal

Since it's Paradox EXCEPT, there will be four answers that help explain this pattern.

Overall, the bigger the rat, the less likely the heart problem.

You could picture the continuum of risk as:
   SMALL    NORMAL     LARGE
   200%         100%           50%

What is it about smaller rats that's bad for the heart?
What is it about bigger rats that's good for the heart?

answers.text: Small rats are more likely than large rats to suffer from fatal diseases that tend to strike earlier than do heart problems.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is dealing with fatal diseases unrelated to heart problems (they actually strike earlier than heart problems do), so it has no power to tell us why small rats have a higher rate of heart problems.

answers.text: Small rats generally have smaller blood vessels than do large rats, vessels that can more easily be clogged with fatty deposits.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

The smaller the rat, the smaller the blood vessels, and thus the more likely the blood vessels will be clogged with fatty deposits.

It's common sense that clogged arteries are a common form of heart problem, and that having a "clogged vessel" in general is a bad thing.

The heart is the muscle that pumps blood, so we can connect "bad blood vessels" to "more heart problems".

answers.text: The larger a rat is, the more successful it will be at defending itself, and therefore the less stressful its existence will be.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

The larger the rat, the less stressful its existence. 

It's common sense that stress is hard on the heart, that people sometimes have heart attacks when they're undergoing lots of stress.

So it makes sense that less stress leads to less heart problems.

answers.text: In addition to being the leading cause of weak hearts in adult rats, malnutrition at early stages of development causes rats to be undersized.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

There is a common cause of being small and having heart problems: malnutrition.

Rats that suffer from malnutrition will be both smaller and have weaker hearts, and that can explain why the rate of heart problems amount smaller rates is higher (they have weaker hearts!)

answers.text: Although large rats are no more active than rats of average size, they tend to be much more active than small rats, resulting in greater cardiovascular conditioning.
answers.fb:
Helps Explain

Weirdly this brags at the start that it will be unhelpful in distinguishing larger rats from normal size.

But this is saying large rats have better cardiovascular conditioning than small rats, so it makes sense why large rats have a lower rate of heart problems than small rats. 

This doesn't explain why large rats have fewer heart problems than average rats, but because it explained something it did still contribute to an explanation of the correlation between size and heart disease.

questiontext:
Geologist: As a spinning object's radius decreases, its rate of rotation increases; for example, figure skaters can twirl faster by bringing their arms closer to their sides. This law of physics helps to explain why, over the past decade, Earth's rate of rotation increased. For earthquakes have increased in number and severity during the past decade; and since immediately after an earthquake Earth's tectonic plates move toward the center of the earth, their movement causes Earth's radius to decrease.

Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the geologist's explanation of why Earth's rate of rotation increased over the last decade?

answers.text: In the beginning of the twentieth century, geologists observed an increase in number and severity of earthquakes, accompanied by a decrease of Earth's radius.
answers.fb: Opposite (if anything): more correlation strenthens, if anything

answers.text: During the past decade, other geological events have counteracted the movements of the tectonic plates that occur immediately after earthquakes.
answers.fb:
Correct

Disrupts the assumption that the tectonic plate movement causes a net decrease in the Earth's radius by raising the possiblitiy that any decreases are counteracted by other movements.

answers.text: Only skillful figure skaters succeed in twirling faster by bringing their arms closer to their sides.
answers.fb:
No Impact

Limiting the example to a subset of skaters doesn't change the law of physics the example is exemplifying.

answers.text: Since the time of the ancient Egyptians, Earth's rate of rotation has been known to fluctuate.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This might seem at first like an alternative explanation for the current rate of rotation increase. It isn't, however, because the reason for the historic fluctuations aren't specified. We can't, therefore, say the current change in rotation rate is any less likely to be due to the contraction of Earth's radius that it was before we knew that similar rotation fluctuations have happened throughout history.

answers.text: Increased volcanic activity over the last ten years suggests that the overall movement of the tectonic plates has increased.
answers.fb:
No Impact

The overall amount of tectonic movement increasing in the last decade doesn't attack the idea that the movement ultimately leads to a net decrease in the size of the Earth.

questiontext:
When a resource's price reflects its full cost to society, consumers pay directly for externalities—the unintended but harmful consequences to society of using a resource. Further, the price of a resource deters misuse of that resource only if it reflects the resource's externalities. So, since sound management of a resource requires that the price of the resource deter its misuse, it also requires that the price reflect whatever unintended harm to the environment the use of that resource causes.

The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
gf:
Conclusion (So)

Sound management of a resource requires that the price reflect whatever unintended harm to the environment the use of that resource causes.

Evidence (since)

Sound management of a resource requires that the price deters misuse.

Deterring misuse requires that the price reflects the resource's externalities (the unintended but harmful consequences to society of using a resource).

Evaluate

The conclusion is trying to prove that "Sound management requires X", and the evidence has provided us with a conditional chain that says, "Sound management requires Y and Z".

Sound → price deters → reflects externalities
mgmt          misuse       (unintended but harmful
                                      consequences to society)

Most Sufficient Assumption answers are trying to get us from What We Know to What We Wanna Prove.

We know from the evidence that sound management requires reflecting "the unintended but harmful consequences to society of using a resource", and we're trying to prove that sound management requires reflecting "the unintended harm to the environment".

Goal

So we need to know that "in order to reflect the unintended harm to society, you'd have to reflect the unintended harm to the environment."

Since "unintended harm to the environment" is a New Concept in the Conclusion, it needs to be in our correct answer and we can pretty much flatly reject any answer that doesn't have it.

answers.text: Whatever constitutes unintended harm to the environment also constitutes unintended harm to society.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is actually the only answer that uses the New Concept in the Conclusion, so even if we were massively confused on this question, we could guess this correct answer!

We wanted to know that, "In order to reflect the unintended harm to society, you'd need to reflect the unintended harm to the environment".

Conditionally, that could look like
reflecting unintended  → reflecting unintended
  harm to society              harm to environment

Meanwhile, the answer looks like
  unintended harm  → unintended harm
    to environment          to society

So it's natural to worry that this is an Illegal Reversal of what we wanted. But modern Sufficient Assumption questions make you think more about the meaning of things, rather than just giving you perfect term matches.

Our prediction was about "reflecting"; this answer isn't.

This answer is saying that all unintended harm to the environment counts as unintended harm to society.

So if you didn't mention unintended harm to the environment, then you wouldn't be fully mentioning all unintended harm to society.

In order to fully account for (i.e. "reflect") all the unintended harm to society, you'd have to include unintended harm to the environment. 

^ that was our prediction!

questiontext:
If the natural history museum stays within this year's budget, it will be unable to stay within next year's budget, for renovating next year will make the museum's expenditures exceed next year's very tight budget. After all, the museum will have to renovate next year if it does not do so this year, because work from previous renovations is deteriorating rapidly.

The argument's conclusion can be properly inferred if which one of the following is assumed?
gf:
Conclusion

If museum stays within this year's budget, it won't be able to stay within next year's budget.

Premise (for)

Renovating next yr will make expenditures exceed next year's very tight budget.

Intermediate Conclusion (after all)

If they don't renovate this year, they'll have to renovate next year.

Premise (because)

Work from previous renovations is deteriorating rapidly.

Evaluate

We can tell the first claim is the conclusion, because every claim after that is introduced by some Support indicator (for, after all, because --- awww, it's almost the whole FABS gang; Since must feel so left out).

So we're trying to prove/create this logic path:
stay w/in                                             won't stay
 this yr's  --------------------------------->  w/in next yr's
 budget                                                budget

The first thing to ask ourselves is whether the premises already provided some sort of rule that would prove "don't stay within next year's budget".

They did!        
                                       renov             won't stay
                                      next yr ----->  w/in next yr's
                                                             budget

So now we know we're trying to prove that they will renovate next year. Did the premises provide us with a way to prove that they'll renovate next yr?

They did!        
                   don't            renov    
                   renov ---->  next yr 
                   this yr                     

So now we know we're trying to prove that they won't renovate this yr. Did they give us a way to prove that they won't renovate this yr?

Nope. The final claim, that previous renovations are deteriorating rapidly, is useless to us because it doesn't connect to this chain. They're asking us to prove that the museum won't be able to stay within next year's budget, and they've given us a mechanism to do so:

                   don't            renov             don't stay
                   renov ---->  next yr ----->  w/in next yr's
                   this yr                                 budget

The correct answer is definitely making use of this conditional chain, and that 'deteriorating rapidly' premise doesn't interact with this chain at all, so we can ignore that.

Goal

This is the logic path we want to create:

stay w/in                                                  won't stay
 this yr's  ------------------------------------>  w/in next yr's
 budget                                                    budget

This is what we have so far, from the evidence:

                     don't            renov             don't stay
                     renov ---->  next yr ----->  w/in next yr's
                     this yr                                 budget

So the missing piece we need to add in order to build the logic path of the conclusion is:

stay w/in         don't
 this yr's  --->  renov
budget            this yr

We can also get ready for an answer saying the contrapositive version: 

    do          won't stay
 renov --->  within this
 this yr         yr's budget

The idea of "staying within this year's budget" is a New Concept in the Conclusion, so it needs to be in our correct answer. We can quickly ditch any answer that doesn't have it.

answers.text: The museum will stay within this year's budget.
answers.fb:
No Impact

This just speaks the New Concept in the Conclusion, but it doesn't connect it to anything. 

The fact that the museum will say within this year's budget doesn't tell us anything. It doesn't activate any of the conditionals.

These are the ideas from the evidence

- if don't renov this yr, have to renovate next yr
- if renov next yr, won't stay within budget
- previous renovations are deteriorating rapidly

Saying "we're going to stay within this year's budget" doesn't interact with any of those claims. It goes nowhere.

A correct answer on SA will always interact with at least one premise in order to allow us to derive some inference.

answers.text: This year's budget is less than next year's budget.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal

This doesn't mention the New Concept in the Conc of "staying within this year's budget", so it's useless to us. 

None of the premises mentioned that concept, so if the answer we pick ALSO doesn't mention that concept, then it would be impossible to derive a conclusion that involves that concept.

answers.text: The museum will not renovate next year.
answers.fb:
Unrelated to Goal / Opposite

This doesn't mention the New Concept in the Conc of "staying within this year's budget", so it's useless to us. 

Also this fundamentally weakens. 

The way we're going to prove that we're unable to stay within next yr's budget is to say that we're going to renovate next year, and this is preventing us from saying that.

answers.text: The museum will exceed this year's budget if it renovates this year.
answers.fb:
Correct

This is our prediction, but naturally it's in contrapositive form.

This says
"If renovate this year, then exceeds this year's budget"
and thus by contrapositive
"If stays within budget, then won't renovate this year". 

That's what we wanted. This is the conclusion's logic path:
stay w/in                                                  won't stay
 this yr's  ------------------------------------>  w/in next yr's
 budget                                                    budget

This is what we have so far, from the evidence:
                     don't            renov             don't stay
                     renov ---->  next yr ----->  w/in next yr's
                     this yr                                 budget

This answer adds this, which snaps onto the chain from the evidence, in order to prove the conclusion.

stay w/in         don't
 this yr's  --->  renov
budget            this yr

Conversationally, this says "staying within this yr's budget would require not renovating this year". We know that not renovating this year means we'll renovate next year. And we know that renovating next year means that we'll exceed next year's budget.

So we've proven that "staying within this yr's budget" leads to "exceeding next year's budget".

answers.text: The museum will stay within this year's budget if it does not renovate this year.
answers.fb:
Reversal

We wanted
"if stay within this year's budget, won't renovate this year".

This provides an illegal reversal of that:
"If not renovate this year, then stay within this year's budget"

This is what we were trying to create:

stay w/in                                                  won't stay
 this yr's  ------------------------------------>  w/in next yr's
 budget                                                    budget

This is what we have so far, from the evidence:
                     don't            renov             don't stay
                     renov ---->  next yr ----->  w/in next yr's
                     this yr                                 budget

This answer adds this, 

                     don't            renov             don't stay
                     renov ---->  next yr ----->  w/in next yr's
                     this yr           and                  budget
                                      stay within
                                      this yr's budget

It doesn't allow us to create the desired logic path.

questiontext:
Some have argued that using food crops to produce fuel represents an unprecedented attack on the food supply. It seems immoral to divert crops from the food supply while there is a need for food. But we currently divert crops from the human food supply to feed livestock. So the diversion of food to fuel is not actually a radical break with traditional practices.

The argument proceeds by
gf:
Implied Rebuttal Conclusion (so)

It could be okay to use food crops to produce fuel.

Intermediate Conclusion (so)

Diverting food to fuel isn't a radical break with traditional practices.

Evidence

We currently divert food crops to feed livestock.

Evaluate

The big 3 most common moves on Method are Analogies, Faulty Implications, and Alternatives.

This argument seems to involve an Analogy. The author is saying that diverting food crops to produce fuel is analogous to diverting food crops to feed livestock.

It also involves the idea of a Counterexample. The opposing claim is that diverting food crops for fuel would be an unprecedented move, and the author is trying to argue, "No, there's precedent. Something we're currently doing is essentially the same."

Goal

Let's pick any answer that is descriptively true. It will probably comment on the analogy or counterexample.

answers.text: arguing that the bad consequences of a practice are outweighed by the good consequences of that practice
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

Nothing in the evidence mentions the positive consequences of diverting food crops to produce fuel.

answers.text: countering the charge that a practice has a bad consequence by trying to show that the practice does not actually have that consequence
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

There isn't any change that a practice (diverting food crops to produce fuel) has a bad consequence. The charge is simply that it's immoral to use food that way, when there are people who need food to eat.

So naturally, the author never counters a charge that was never made.

answers.text: rebutting a charge that a practice is radical by contending that the practice is analogous with an existing one
answers.fb:
Correct

This captures the counterexample and analogy components we anticipated.

The charge was that this proposal was an "unprecedented attack". That qualifies as saying that the proposal is radical.

And the author undermines that view by saying "it's not a radical break from tradition", since we analogously divert food crops to feed livestock.

answers.text: rejecting the charge that a practice is immoral by trying to undercut the moral foundation of the charge
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence Match

The author's rebuttal is more about countering the idea that this is unprecedented / radical. She doesn't weigh in on whether it's immoral (it might also be immoral to divert food crops to feed livestock).

Nothing in her evidence addresses the morality of the proposal. The evidence only addresses how we currently do something similar.

answers.text: supporting a moral objection to a practice by trying to show that the practice is actually different from practices that might seem similar
answers.fb:
Bad Evidence  / Conclusion Match

The author never supports the idea that this is immoral, and she's trying to show that this new proposal is similar to other practices, not different.

questiontext:
A recent study found that most individuals believe that they sleep less than most other people. However, it is obviously not possible that most people sleep less than most other people. Therefore, _______.

Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
gf:
Facts

pivot tension (however)

Most ppl think they sleep less than most other people.
but
it's impossible for most ppl to sleep less than most people.

Evaluate

When we're doing MBT or Most Supported (like this one) and we see two claims put in tension with each other via a Pivot word, the correct answer almost always addresses that tension.

If we hear, "Most ppl think they are X, but it's impossible for X to be true of most ppl", it seems to force us to believe that some of them must be wrong.

It's impossible for them to all be correct, so some of the people who think they sleep less than most people don't actually sleep less than most people.

Goal

Let's look for the most provable answer. It will probably address the Pivot tension by conveying that "some of the ppl who think they sleep less than most are incorrect".

answers.text: some people believe things that could not possibly be true even in principle
answers.fb:
Too Strong (even in principle)

We know that some people think
"I sleep less than most other people"
and are wrong about that belief.

But can we say that "I sleep less than most other people" can't possibly be true, even in principle?

No. That could definitely be a true claim for some people, so it could in principle be true.

Saying it isn't actually true is different from saying it couldn't even in principle be true.

If I were to believe that "most people sleep less than most other people", then I would be guilty of believing something that cannot even in principle be true. It's a self-contradictory claim.

answers.text: most people are not aware of how much they sleep
answers.fb:
Too Strong (most)

We know that some of these people who think they sleep less than most others are wrong, but we can't prove that most of them are wrong.

Also, for them to be wrong, it doesn't have to be because they're unaware of how much they sleep. They might be unaware of how much most other people sleep.

answers.text: most people underestimate how much they sleep in comparison to others
answers.fb:
Too Strong (most)

We know that some of these people who think they sleep less than most others are wrong, but we can't prove that most of them are wrong.

This otherwise fits the gist of the paragraph. If you're thinking, "Compared to most other people, I get way less sleep" and you're wrong, then you are underestimating how much sleep you get in relation to others.

In case numbers would help, pretend there are 100 people, and most of them (51 of them) get at least 7 hrs of sleep per night.

49 of them get 6 hrs or less of sleep per night. Let's say that all 49 of those people (correctly) believe "I get less sleep than most".

If we grab two people from the 7+ hr group and say that they also believe "I get less sleep than most", then we'd have 51 people believing they get less sleep than most.

So most of our population believes they get less sleep than most.

But only 2 of them are actually wrong. Only 2 of them are underestimating how much sleep they get in comparison to others, not most of them, as this answer choice says.

answers.text: most people think that they do not sleep as much as they should
answers.fb:
Out of Scope (should)

We'd be very skeptical of this answer from the strength of MOST, but then we can definitely get rid of it when we see it's talking about how much sleep they should get.

That concept is not discussed at all in the stimulus.

answers.text: some people incorrectly believe that they sleep less than most other people
answers.fb:
Correct

If we know that most people believe that they are X, but it's impossible for X to be true of most people, then that means that at least some of them have an incorrect belief.

So at least some people incorrectly believe they sleep less than most other people.

questiontext:
If legislators are to enact laws that benefit constituents, they must be sure to consider what the consequences of enacting a proposed law will actually be. Contemporary legislatures fail to enact laws that benefit constituents. Concerned primarily with advancing their own political careers, legislators present legislation in polemical terms; this arouses in their colleagues either repugnance or enthusiasm for the legislation.

Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
gf:
Conclusion

Contemporary legislatures fail to enact beneficial laws.

Evidence

Legislators have to consider the consequences of a potential law, or else that law won’t benefit constituents. Contemporary legislatures present legislation in polemical terms, arousing polemical reactions of strong support or strong rejection.

Evaluation

This argument is murderously tough to parse. First, ‘polemical’ is a vocab word many might not know. It means “divisive, extreme, polarizing” language. 

Mainly, though, it’s hard to know what they want us to consider the Conclusion, since the connection between Evidence and Conclusion is so thin or non-existent. Ultimately, they want us to see the 2nd sentence as the conclusion, but there really aren't strong clues. I thought the 1st sentence, which is prescriptive in nature, was the conclusion, until I saw the correct answer choice. 

If we treat the 2nd sentence as the conclusion, then the argument wants to prove this path:

Contemp  --------------------------------------> laws don't
legislature                                                  benefit

The 1st sentence is a proving mechanism that would allow us to say "laws don't benefit". 
                                                 don't ---> laws don't
                                             consider      benefit
                                             conseq.

So the argument must be assuming that in Contemporary Legislatures, they aren't considering the consequences of proposed laws. We are never told that, but we are told that they are presenting legislation in polemical terms, arousing repugnance or enthusiasm. 

Contemp --> present -> arouse
legislature     polem      hate/love

Goal

So the author must be assuming that, “As legislators present legislation in polemical terms, arousing extreme reactions, they are not considering the consequences of the potential law.” Maybe there could be a conditional that says, “When you feel repugnance or enthusiasm for a potential law, you don’t consider the consequences of enacting it.”

answers.text: Legislation will not benefit constituents unless legislators become less concerned with their own careers.
answers.fb:
Irrelevant Comparison: "less concerned"

This feels somewhat close to describing, “What we’re doing is not the same as what we need to do in order to achieve goal X”. 

The problem is that our author is saying “legislators need to consider consequences”, not “legislators need to become less concerned with their careers”. 

Unless there were some logical link between those two ideas, the author doesn’t have to insist on legislators’ caring less about their careers.

answers.text: Legislatures that enact laws that benefit constituents are successful legislatures.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: Successful legislatures

The author isn’t committed to believing that every legislature that enacts laws is a successful one. 

She never uses the concept of whether legislatures are successful or not, and she could certainly believe that passing beneficial laws is only one component of being a successful legislature (maybe refraining from graft is another).

answers.text: The passage of laws cannot benefit constituents unless constituents generally adhere to those laws.
answers.fb:
Too Strong: cannot unless
Out of Scope: adhere to laws

Did the author ever make this reasoning move:

If constituents       Then passage of
  don't mostly    →  laws can't benefit
adhere to laws       constituents

No. The argument never discusses whether or not constituents adhere to laws. 

Even though it seems very common sense true to think “if people aren’t following a law, then how could it benefit them?”, ‘adhering to the law’ is not part of the author’s evidence or conclusion.

answers.text: Legislators considering a proposed law for which they have repugnance or enthusiasm do not consider the consequences that it will actually have.
answers.fb:
Correct

This supplies that missing link between premises we were looking for.

We know that contemporary legislators present proposed laws in ways that arouse repugnance or enthusiasm, and we know that the author assumes that they aren't considering the consequences of those proposed laws. 

So this answer is connecting those two ideas. 

If we negated this, we would have a huge weakener: “When legislators have repugnance or enthusiasm they DO consider the consequences of the proposed law!”

answers.text: The inability of legislators to consider the actual consequences of enacting a proposed law is due to their strong feelings about that law.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope:  "inability to consider"

This is very tempting, but the author never says that legislators are unable to consider consequences. We can infer that the author thinks that they currently don’t consider them, but that could be due to inability or to unwillingness or to compulsion from outside forces. 

If someone is currently getting music through YouTube and an author is suggesting that they should instead get music through Spotify, he doesn’t have to assume that “getting music through YouTube makes them unable to get music through Spotify”. 

They might not even know Spotify exists. The author is merely assuming that “getting music through YouTube is not the same as getting music through Spotify”.

questiontext:
Sociologist: Suggestions for improved efficiency that derive from employers are unlikely to elicit positive responses from employees, who tend to resent suggestions they did not generate. An employer should therefore engage the employee in a nonthreatening dialogue that emphasizes the positive contributions of the employee to the development of such ideas. Then the ideas employers want to try will be implemented more quickly and effectively.

Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the sociologist's reasoning?
gf:
Conclusion (therefore)

Employers should engage employees in nonthreatening dialogues that emphasize the positive contributions of the employee to the development of ideas that improve efficiency.

Intermediate Conclusion

This more employee-centered approach will help the employers implement their ideas more quickly and effectively.

Evidence

Top-down suggestions (from employer to employee) for improved efficiency are unlikely to elicit positive responses.

Evaluate

This argument is a little hard to organize. We don't necessarily have to call that last idea an Intermediate Conclusion, but it seems like an opinion we could potentially object to or ask about.

In terms of how the plan is supposed to work, the author assumes that
"if a plan is unlikely to elicit positive reactions from employees, it'll take longer for the ideas to be implemented" whereas "if a plan is more likely to elicit positive reactions, it'll take less long for the ideas to be implemented".

But in terms of getting from the last sentence to the Main Conclusion, the author assumes that
"if a plan would result in ideas getting implemented more quickly and effectively, then an employer should do that idea."

Goal

We either want to be more convinced that the plan will achieve the goal, or we want to connect the positive idea of "implemented more quickly and effectively" to the conclusion language of "should do it".

answers.text: Employees are more likely to accept suggestions for improved efficiency when these suggestions are not obviously directed at them.
answers.fb:
Weak Conclusion/Premise Match

This principle seems somewhat relevant but helps us to establish that employees are more likely to accept suggestions. We're trying to justify that "ideas will be implemented more quickly and effectively" or that "employers should do this". The idea of employees' accepting suggestions seems in the same conversation, but not directly using the right language.

Similarly, it feels like the plan being recommended would involve "suggestions less obviously directed at employees", but the language of the premise is "more likely to elicit positive response" or "emphasizes positive contributions of employee".

answers.text: Employees are more likely to carry out ideas for improved efficiency that they believe they have participated in generating.
answers.fb:
Correct

This connects the plan to the supposed result. The plan is supposed to emphasize employees' contributions (which we can assume would make one think, "Hey, I helped!"). The result is supposed to be that the employer's ideas will be implemented more quickly.

The author was Assuming a Difference about this plan:
- a plan in which employees don't feel like they generated suggestions will not get ideas implemented as quickly/effectively as would my alternative plan that does make the employees feel like they generated some of the ideas

answers.text: Employees are more likely to implement ideas for improved efficiency that derive from a dialogue in which they have participated than from a dialogue in which they have not participated.
answers.fb:
Not as Good as (B)

This answer seems fiendishly mean. It has the same structure as (B), but this answer hinges on an idea that isn't a clear difference between the two plans being considered, whereas (B) hinged on an idea that was a clear difference.

There were two plans being compared:
employer gives suggestions
employer engages employees in a dialogue

Since the first plan didn't involve "a dialogue", we can't use this answer choice to compare the suggested plan to the alternative plan. It does, however, somewhat strengthen the idea that there's a connection between participating in a dialogue and being more likely to implement ideas.

But, for (B), it was established that there was a difference between the suggested plan and the alternative plan in terms of whether or not employees would have felt like they had participated in generating the suggestions. So (B) has a more powerful effect in filtering between the two plans.

answers.text: Employees are more likely to generate good ideas for improved efficiency when they do not feel resentment about the process that attempts to formulate such ideas.
answers.fb:
Weak Conclusion Match

This principle would allow one to conclude that "employees are more likely to generate good ideas", but the language we're looking to support is "employers should do it" or "employer's ideas will be implemented more quickly/effectively".

answers.text: Employees are more likely to resent employers who attempt to implement the employers’ rather than the employees’ ideas for improved efficiency.
answers.fb:
Out of Scope: resenting employers

We only talked about employees resenting suggestions that they didn't come up with. This answer does reinforce that idea, but we don't need to be convinced that employees will resent their employers as well.

We need to be convinced that engaging employees in a dialogue will lead to better implementation of the employers' ideas. If anything, this answer seems to undermine that concept by making it seem like if there IS a group dialogue, the employees will be insisting on their ideas being implemented, not the employers' ideas.

questiontext:
The probability of avoiding heart disease is increased if one avoids fat in one's diet. Furthermore, one is less likely to eat fat if one avoids eating dairy foods. Thus the probability of maintaining good health is increased by avoiding dairy foods.

The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?
gf:
Conclusion

If you avoid dairy foods,       avoid  >> prob GH
probability of maintaining     dairy       increased
good health is increased.

Evidence

If you avoid dairy foods,        avoid  >> eat less
you're less likely to eat fat     dairy         fat

If you avoid eating fat,     avoid       prob of
probability of avoiding       fat    >>  avoiding 
heart disease goes up                   HD goes up

Evaluation

The author is arguing this causal chain:

avoid  >>  eat less >>  prob of   >> prob GH
dairy         fat              avoiding      increased
                                 HD goes up

We go from talking about "being less likely to eat fat" to "avoiding fat in one's diet". There's a little different there, so an answer could call out that gap.

But more likely to be addressed in the answer is the last gap, where we go from saying "you've increased the probability of avoiding heart disease" to "you've increased the probability of maintaining good health".

Goal

Look for an answer that addresses the difference between avoiding heart disease and maintaining good health.

answers.text: The argument ignores the possibility that, even though a practice may have potentially negative consequences, its elimination may also have negative consequences.
answers.fb:
Correct

Is there a practice that may have potentially negative consequences here?
